The passage defines SD memory-card command, status, timing, and performance behavior. CMD55 (APP_CMD) causes the next command to be interpreted as an application-specific command; the APP_CMD response bit distinguishes accepted defined ACMDs from undefined commands treated as normal commands, while illegal commands produce an error. Certain ACMD numbers are reserved, and ACMD41 has special status handling.

CMD6 provides a switch function for querying or changing card functions. Its 512-bit status reports supported and selected functions, busy states, and maximum current or power. Function groups cover access or bus speed, command-system extension, driver strength, and power limit. Function 0 is the default; mode 0 checks support, mode 1 sets functions, invalid selections prevent switching, and busy functions cannot be changed. The default power limit is 0.72 W, with higher settings subject to bus and host limits. High-Speed mode provides a 25 MB/s interface. CMD34-37, CMD50, and CMD57 have standard, vendor-specific, or mobile-commerce interpretations depending on the selected command-system function.

CMD8 is issued in Idle state to verify the host supply voltage before ACMD41; an accepting card returns R7 with the voltage range and check pattern. SDSC cards use byte addressing, whereas SDHC and SDXC cards use 512-byte block addressing and fixed 512-byte memory blocks without partial or misaligned access.

The host may vary or stop the bus clock subject to timing limits and required completion clocks, with special polling and clock-frequency rules after ACMD41. CRC7 protects commands, most responses, CID, and CSD; CRC16 protects data blocks and is calculated separately for each line in wide-bus mode. Failed CRC checks and illegal commands cause no response or state change and set the corresponding error bits. Read, write, and erase timeouts vary by operation and card type; UHS-II write-busy indications may last up to one second per data burst.

All commands use 48-bit CRC-protected codewords. Command classes and CCC data identify supported functionality, while state-transition rules determine command legality. Response types include R1/R1b, R2, R3, R6, and R7. Card Status reports command errors and state, SD Status reports card-specific features, and Task Status reports queued operations.

Speed-class methods cover Speed Class 2, 4, 6, and 10; UHS Speed Grade 1 and 3; and Video Speed Class 6, 10, 30, 60, and 90. Allocation units contain recording units. SDSC/SDHC performance includes fragmented-AU move operations, while SDXC requires sequential writes to entirely free allocation units and supports exFAT FAT, bitmap, directory-entry, and continuous-information updates. CMD20 is mandatory for SDXC and optional for SDHC; its Start Recording, Update DIR, and Update CI functions prepare recording and identify metadata writes.

Using CDC WONDER death-certificate data from 1999–2020, researchers compared non-Hispanic Black and White people under age 85, calculating age-adjusted excess mortality and years of potential life lost (YPLL), with White life expectancy as the reference. They also examined trends by sex, age, and cause of death.

The study estimated 658,356 excess deaths among Black females and 1,154,108 among Black males, corresponding to 34.9 million and 47.0 million excess YPLL, respectively. Disparities declined substantially during the early 2000s, then stalled and reversed in 2020. Excess mortality reached 192 deaths per 100,000 Black females and 395 per 100,000 Black males, while excess YPLL rose to levels comparable to or worse than earlier benchmarks. COVID-19 contributed 47 and 80 excess deaths per 100,000 Black females and males, respectively.

Heart disease produced the highest excess mortality rates, and perinatal deaths produced the highest YPLL rates. Mortality disparities were especially large among infants and generally increased from adolescence or early adulthood through older ages. Black-White infant mortality and YPLL rate ratios exceeded 2.3.

The authors concluded that excess deaths and YPLL could serve as national and local measures of health-equity progress, but noted limitations from inaccurate race classification on death certificates and uncertain causes of death. They emphasized the need for renewed strategies addressing social determinants, access to care, structural barriers, and bias.

A simple moving average (SMA) is the continuously updated arithmetic mean of an asset’s closing prices over a specified number of periods. Traders use its direction, price crossovers, and longer-period levels to identify trends and momentum, generate buy or sell signals, and mark potential support or resistance. Shorter SMAs react faster to price changes, while longer SMAs smooth volatility and better represent long-term trends. SMAs can also be applied to volume or economic data and combined with other indicators or strategies.

Backtests described in the passage found that short-period SMA strategies tend to favor mean reversion—buying when prices cross below the average and selling when they cross above—while long-period strategies favor trend following, buying above the average and selling below it. The strongest reported result came from buying when the close crossed above a 200-day SMA and holding for 200 days, averaging 10.93% per trade before dividend reinvestment.

The SMA lags prices because it weights every observation equally, whereas an EMA gives recent prices greater weight and reacts faster. SMA settings can also produce false signals in range-bound or highly volatile markets, lag behind rapid price movements, or misrepresent seasonal and cyclical patterns. The calculation’s starting point can affect its value in volatile conditions, though an SMA can equal zero only if the price closed at zero throughout the entire period.

There is no universally best SMA period or moving average type; the appropriate setting and strategy should be backtested for the asset and market conditions.

The DAWN-plasma study was a prospective, multicenter, randomized, open-label phase II proof-of-concept trial comparing standard supportive care with supportive care plus convalescent plasma in hospitalized adults with COVID-19. Between May 2020 and January 2021, 499 patients were assessed and 489 were randomized 2:1 to plasma plus supportive care (n=326) or supportive care alone (n=163). The primary analysis set included 483 patients—320 in the plasma group and 163 controls—after excluding one patient without confirmed COVID-19 and five who withdrew consent immediately after randomization. Baseline characteristics and concomitant therapies were similar between groups.

The plasma intervention consisted of four units totaling approximately 800–1,000 mL. Two units were administered within 12 hours of randomization and two more 24–36 hours later, for a 48-hour intervention period, with follow-up for 90 days. The median administered volume was 884 mL, and 80.7% of units came from donors with neutralizing-antibody titers of at least 1/320. Six plasma-group patients received no plasma, while 294 (91.9%) received all four units.

The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients alive and free of mechanical ventilation on day 15. This occurred in 83.7% of the plasma group and 84.1% of controls (odds ratio 0.99; p=0.976). No statistically significant between-group differences were found in secondary endpoints, including mortality, clinical status, oxygenation, ventilation, hospitalization, thromboembolism, or quality of life. Per-protocol results were similar. A prespecified subgroup analysis showed an interaction between treatment and age for the primary endpoint (p=0.023).

Adverse-event rates were similar between groups. Treatment-emergent adverse events affected 28.13% of plasma patients and 30.06% of controls; serious adverse events affected approximately 20.6% in each group, and fatal adverse events affected 10.31% and 9.82%, respectively. Fourteen treatment-related adverse events occurred in 12 plasma patients, and seven treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in seven patients. Transfusion-related side effects were reported in 19 of 320 plasma patients, with no TRALI cases. Laboratory and vital-sign trends were also comparable.

Neutralizing-antibody titers increased between baseline and day 6 regardless of treatment assignment. Higher titers at baseline and day 6 correlated with better outcomes, but the intervention did not affect antibody titers or clinical outcomes. Overall, early transfusion of four high-volume, high-titer convalescent-plasma units did not significantly improve clinical status or safety outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and ICH Good Clinical Practice guidelines and required ethics review and informed consent.

This prospective, hospital-based study assessed surgical diagnoses and postoperative outcomes of acute intestinal obstruction among adults treated at Amana, Mwananyamala, and Temeke regional referral hospitals in Dar es Salaam from December 2021 to July 2022. Eligible patients were at least 18 years old, had a clinical or radiological provisional diagnosis of acute intestinal obstruction, and underwent laparotomy. Patients referred after failed surgery elsewhere were excluded, and follow-up continued through postoperative discharge.

Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, medications, operative diagnoses, postoperative interventions, morbidity, mortality, and length of stay. Quantitative variables were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges, while categorical variables were summarized using frequencies and proportions. Multivariable binary logistic regression was the main analytic method.

The study included 228 patients, 75.4% male, with a median age of 34 years and a median hospital stay of four days. Surgical diagnoses included adhesions in 98 patients, hernia in 48, volvulus in 37, and abdominal tumors in 20; some patients had multiple diagnoses. Adhesions were the most frequent diagnosis, while adhesions, abdominal tumors, hernia, and volvulus were significantly associated with intestinal obstruction.

Among postoperative outcomes, 173 patients (76%) were discharged home, 20 (9%) developed superficial surgical-site infections, two had wound dehiscence, one had an anastomotic leak, eight were referred elsewhere, 12 (5.3%) died, and 12 (5.3%) had unknown outcomes. Confounder and interaction tests were nonsignificant.

The authors noted that the predominance of adhesions and relatively low frequency of hernia could reflect changing epidemiology or referral bias because the hospitals were tertiary referral facilities. The 5.3% mortality rate and unknown outcomes in approximately one in twenty patients warrant further investigation, including assessment of socioeconomic factors. The prospective design reduced concern about recall bias, and the absence of an upper age limit allowed inclusion of older adults.

Averaging down means buying additional shares of a stock after its price has fallen, reducing the average purchase price and the subsequent rise needed to reach breakeven. It does not eliminate existing losses or guarantee recovery, and further price declines can increase total losses.

The breakeven price is calculated by dividing the total cost of all purchases by the total number of shares acquired. For example, buying 100 shares at $40 and another 100 at $20 lowers the average price to $30, but the investor remains $10 below the initial purchase price until the stock recovers to at least $30.

Whether averaging down is appropriate depends on the investor’s strategy, conviction, analysis, and risk tolerance. It may suit long-term investors who understand the company and are scaling into a planned position size at lower prices. It is riskier for short-term traders who cannot distinguish a temporary decline from a fundamental problem, because they may continue buying into a falling trend. Averaging down is therefore best treated as part of a well-planned, backtested entry strategy rather than a standalone investment plan. Averaging up can also be used to scale into a position, with lower—but not eliminated—risk if the price reverses.

In a backtest using SPY and RSI signals, equity was divided into two 50% positions, with the entire position sold on a sell signal. Adding to the first position produced nearly the same final capital as the strategy without averaging down, but with a smoother equity curve, improved trading metrics, reduced drawdowns, and more efficient use of capital. The passage states that stocks are particularly suitable for averaging down because they tend to mean-revert, while other markets may be less favorable, making backtesting and a margin of safety important.

Therapeutic antibodies must bind their targets effectively and possess developability properties such as thermostability, low hydrophobicity, and good expression. Although diffusion models can generate antibodies, candidates often require costly, iterative wet-lab refinement. Bayesian optimization is well suited to these low-data settings, but its success depends on selecting suitable surrogate models and acquisition functions. Prior studies have not incorporated structural information, whose relevance remains unclear for intrinsic developability versus binding, especially when antibody–antigen binding poses are unknown. This work examines how to integrate structural information, when it aids optimization, whether antibody-specific models outperform general protein models, and whether structural information is necessary. It also proposes using a protein language model “soft constraint” to incorporate sequence-only prior information. Bayesian optimization uses an uncertainty-aware surrogate and an acquisition function balancing exploration and exploitation, with Gaussian processes serving as a common surrogate for noisy observations.

This medRxiv preprint presents PhenoID, a transformer-based pipeline for extracting abnormal dysmorphology findings from free-text EHR examinations and normalizing them to Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) identifiers. Researchers created a standardized EHR interface, manually annotated 3,826 organ-system observations from 1,655 individuals, including 935 HPO terms, and used Bio-ClinicalBERT models for mention extraction and normalization. The pipeline was evaluated against six existing phenotype normalizers and two BIO annotation strategies for disjoint or overlapping terms.

PhenoID achieved an F1 score of 0.717 for extraction and normalization, outperforming all compared systems, whose highest F1 was 0.633. With gold-standard spans provided, normalization reached 0.820, close to the 0.844 inter-annotator agreement, indicating that span extraction was a major source of error. The extractor correctly ignored 98.4% of negated, normal findings. Error analysis identified ontology deficiencies, descriptive clinical language, misplaced model attention, and overly general or specific predictions as recurring causes of normalization errors. The authors concluded that PhenoID achieved state-of-the-art performance, while noting limitations in semantic understanding and the diversity of authors and documentation practices represented in the dataset.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 is scheduled to launch an HPE “Spaceborne Computer” to the International Space Station. The commercial supercomputer is designed to perform one trillion calculations per second, with software intended to protect it from radiation and other hazards. After activation, engineers will conduct 2.5-hour functionality tests, followed by a year of testing on the station. Successful operation could lead NASA to send more powerful computers and support future Mars missions, where onboard processing would help overcome communication delays or outages. The system could also process high-resolution satellite imagery aboard the station, reducing data transmission needs for applications such as crop-growth and oil-exploration monitoring. Some experts questioned whether it could survive and operate in space.

In a retrospective observational study of 2,097 Project Baseline Health Study participants, a deep-learning chest radiograph model (CXR-Age) was compared with the first-generation Horvath and second-generation DNAm PhenoAge epigenetic clocks. CXR-Age correlated moderately with chronological age (r=0.50), whereas the epigenetic clocks correlated strongly (r=0.95 and 0.93). CXR-Age and DNAm PhenoAge age acceleration were not significantly correlated, suggesting that they capture different aspects of aging.

After adjustment for chronological age, body mass index, sex, smoking, race, and study site, CXR-Age acceleration was associated with greater coronary artery calcium and higher 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk, lower pulmonary function, and poorer performance on all five physical-function tests, as well as greater disability. DNAm PhenoAge acceleration showed similar associations with coronary calcium, lung diffusion capacity, frailty, and disability, although several functional associations were limited to older adults. Horvath age acceleration had no significant associations with these outcomes. Stratified analyses found CXR-Age associations with functional decline among adults aged 45 and older.

Plasma proteomic analysis identified significant associations between CXR-Age acceleration and CDH13 and ApoD abundance and between DNAm PhenoAge acceleration and 13 proteins; CDH13 was associated with both clocks. No proteins were significantly associated with Horvath age acceleration. Manual review found that radiographs with the lowest CXR-Age acceleration were generally read as normal, whereas those with the highest acceleration often contained pulmonary or other thoracic abnormalities, although some lacked clear related findings.

The authors proposed that routinely obtained chest radiographs could support opportunistic biological-age assessment for screening and risk decisions. Limitations included the retrospective design, absence of longitudinal data, residual confounding, limited generalizability, use of only two representative epigenetic clocks, and the model's lack of interpretability. Prospective and interpretability studies were recommended.
