A German diplomatic note reported that Germany and its allies had rejected a December 12 proposal for immediate peace negotiations as insincere and meaningless, without offering counterproposals. Germany defended the proposal as sincere and feasible, argued that further bloodshed was indefensible, and maintained that an oral exchange could produce a just peace acceptable to all belligerents. It accused the enemy powers of hypocrisy, citing their alleged violations of international law and actions affecting Ireland, South Africa, North Africa, Russia, Greece, prisoners, colonial troops, and civilians in occupied territories. Germany also rejected Allied demands for reparation, recognition of nationality principles, and free small states, while attributing the war’s outbreak to Serbia, the Sarajevo assassination, Russian mobilization, and the policies of Britain, France, and Russia.

The paper introduces PATCH, a network-growth model combining preferential attachment, triadic closure, and homophily to study segregation, degree inequality, and group inequity in networks containing minority and majority groups. New nodes form either global links or links to friends-of-friends, with targets selected uniformly, by homophily, or by preferential attachment plus homophily. The homophily parameter controls in-group versus out-group preference, while the triadic-closure parameter controls the probability of local links.

Simulation results show that homophily is the primary driver of segregation and inequity. Homophilic preferences segregate groups and generally favor the majority group, whereas heterophilic preferences promote cross-group connectivity and favor the minority. Preferential attachment is the main source of degree inequality, often concentrating links among a few highly connected nodes. Triadic closure has context-dependent effects: when target selection is unbiased, it generally moderates segregation and inequity and can reduce inequality when preferential attachment is otherwise present. When biased by homophily or preferential attachment, its effects differ, although it does not amplify segregation under homophily. The group gaining greater overall visibility also tends to have greater internal degree inequality, indicating that the advantage primarily benefits a small number of its members.

Approximate Bayesian computation was applied to five decades of American Physical Society collaboration and citation networks and Computer Science Bibliography collaboration networks. Across all datasets and decades, models in which both global and local links were biased by preferential attachment and gender homophily best reproduced the observed statistics. The inferred networks showed mild gender homophily and moderate triadic-closure tendencies, generally increasing over time. Women’s representation increased but remained below parity, and women generally had lower degree visibility, except in the citation network from the 1990s onward.

The findings indicate that reducing network inequalities requires addressing link-formation mechanisms simultaneously; interventions affecting one mechanism may worsen other outcomes. The model’s limitations include identical homophily for both groups, fixed preferential attachment, omission of link dissolution or network exit, and no treatment of citation directionality.

Fifteen Sacred Heart Academy students, ranging from freshmen to seniors, traveled to Alajuelita, a poor neighborhood in San José, Costa Rica, with five chaperones from March 30 to April 7. Organized by Spanish teacher April Dice, the spring-break trip required participants to be enrolled in Spanish Two or have completed it and combined Spanish practice with community service. Students spent time with residents, brought meals to neighborhood children, played games and sang songs with them, visited a senior center, worked alongside American missionaries involved in local cleanup efforts, and hiked La Cruz de Alajuelita. Students reported improved Spanish skills, greater appreciation of the language, and personal growth from connecting with others and serving the community. Dice described watching her students grow and help others as rewarding and looked forward to future trips.

Jammu and Kashmir’s Legislative Assembly passed the 2018-19 budget of Rs 95,666.97 crore by voice vote, a 20% increase, comprising Rs 51,244.72 crore in revenue and Rs 44,422.24 crore in capital expenditure. The appropriation bill introduced spending reforms, including deadlines for releasing funds to departments and subordinate offices, mandatory BEAMS processing before payments, personal liability for treasury or PAO officials bypassing the system, and a 60-day procurement cap with disciplinary action for overruns. Lapsed fourth-quarter funds will first cover the state’s share of centrally sponsored schemes and PMDP utility-shifting and land-compensation costs. Departments are barred from engaging casual or need-based workers. The reforms aim to strengthen fiscal management, stabilize the economy, and increase public investment.

Dandelion seed tufts resist being blown loose from any one direction, so a clump often clings to the stem side opposite the breeze. After about three years of work, U.S. and Australian researchers — including Cornell fluid dynamicist Chris Roh, biophysicist Jena Shields and biomechanist Sridhar Ravi of the University of New South Wales in Canberra — identified microstructures that let batches of seeds catch upward gusts. Imaging shows each seed is tethered by an off-center strand surrounded by horseshoe-shaped shielding, lower on one side and taller on the other, which steadies the seed unless force tilts it toward the opening. Force-sensor tests found that releasing upslanting seeds took about an order of magnitude less force than plucking them downward, the first formal measurements of seed-release force. A low-pressure vortex above the tuft keeps it aloft. The study, "Letting go with the flow: directional abscission of dandelion seeds," was published Sept. 10, 2025 (doi: 10.1098/rsif.2025.0227).

SD Memory Card reads are block-oriented, with blocks up to 512 bytes and CRC protection. CMD17 reads a single block; CMD18 reads consecutive blocks until CMD12. Transfers are clock-synchronous, and payload data may include ECC. Sudden power loss does not destroy data except during host-issued writes or erases. Reads are rejected for block-length or address errors; hosts should ignore OUT_OF_RANGE after the final user-area block.

MAFLD, formerly NAFLD, is defined by hepatic steatosis with T2D, overweight/obesity, or metabolic dysregulation. Its global prevalence is 32.4%, rising to 55.5% among people with T2D. Concurrent T2D is associated with advanced liver disease, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and higher liver-related mortality. Because African evidence is sparse—estimated MAFLD prevalence among people with T2D is 30.4%, based on four studies—this study aimed to estimate MAFLD prevalence and its association with HbA1c in African populations with T2D.

This PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA-adherent systematic review searched six major databases, African databases, and reference lists through December 6, 2023. Eligible English-language observational studies included adults with T2D in African countries and provided or permitted calculation of MAFLD prevalence using a verifiable diagnostic method. Two reviewers screened studies and extracted data, with a third resolving disagreements; Joanna Briggs Institute checklists assessed bias. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled prevalence, while pooled correlations assessed associations with HbA1c.

Of 659 references, 232 were screened and 10 studies included: nine cross-sectional and one case-control, covering 1,667 participants across six countries. Samples ranged from 80 to 281; women comprised 61.1% in the nine studies reporting sex. Participants’ mean age exceeded 50, diabetes duration ranged from 4 to 10 years, and most were overweight or obese with poor glycemic control. MAFLD was diagnosed mainly by ultrasonography, with some use of the Fatty Liver Index or Hepatic Steatosis Index.

The Supreme Court announced that Collegium recommendations and reasons for judicial appointments, transfers and elevations, including names recommended or rejected, will be published online when sent to the government. The disclosure covers appointments to High Courts and the Supreme Court, permanent judge confirmations, chief justice elevations and judge transfers. The move responded to criticism that the Collegium lacked transparency, though it has drawn criticism from members of the judicial community.

Drug addiction remains a major public health concern, with opioid-driven overdose deaths exceeding 100,000 in 2022 and treatment dropout averaging 30% overall and reaching 91% in opioid addiction. Because self-reported craving and drug use can be affected by recall bias, limited self-awareness, demand characteristics, and social desirability, additional objective measures are needed. Urine toxicology is objective but binary and may not reflect changing use patterns. Cognitive-behavioral measures targeting drug-biased attention, choice, and reactivity may provide sensitive proxies for addiction severity and predict outcomes such as relapse, use, and treatment retention.

The study tests whether picture-viewing choice tasks and drug-word verbal fluency outperform demographics, subjective drug-use measures, and craving reports in predicting four-month treatment adherence among inpatient opioid use disorder. Participants were 59 inpatients with opioid use disorder at a residential rehabilitation facility and 29 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Treatment adherence was defined objectively as attendance at a follow-up visit after completion of a randomized treatment component. The authors hypothesized that opioid use disorder would show greater drug-biased choice and fluency than controls, that these measures would better predict treatment completion, and that drug-biased behavior would decline at follow-up.
The Greenwich Rotary Club presented Greenwich United Way with $5,000 for its Reading Champions program, funding tutor supplies, books, and year-end awards for participating children.

This medRxiv preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, used 7-tesla magnetic resonance spectroscopy to compare 16 brain metabolites in occipital and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex among 43 healthy controls, 42 first-degree relatives of people with psychotic psychopathology (PwPP), and 64 PwPP. The study used an 8-ms STEAM sequence, accounted for macromolecules, and applied rigid-baseline LCModel fitting without soft constraints.

Among six prespecified metabolites, occipital N-acetyl-aspartate (NAA) was lower in PwPP and relatives than in controls, although adjustment for age, sex, and BMI retained the difference only for PwPP versus controls. Prefrontal N-acetyl-aspartylglutamate (NAAG) was lower in PwPP than in the other groups, but this difference was no longer significant after demographic adjustment. Other prespecified comparisons, including GABA and glutamate, were not significant.

Post hoc analyses found higher prefrontal glucose in PwPP than controls after multiple-comparison correction, with relatives showing intermediate values; occipital glucose showed a similar but nonsignificant trend. Age, sex, BMI, tissue composition, and antipsychotic medication levels did not fully explain these glucose differences. Hierarchical clustering showed that glucose in both regions was associated with greater psychiatric symptom severity and poorer visual-task performance.

Repeat scans from 10 controls and 36 PwPP indicated fair-to-excellent longitudinal reliability across metabolites, with intraclass correlations of 0.44–0.96. No significant metabolite differences were found between PwPP with schizophrenia and those with bipolar disorder.

The TLV321x and TLV322x are single-, dual-, and quad-channel high-speed comparators with 40 ns propagation delay, 1.8–5 V supply range, and 40 μA quiescent current per channel. They feature low offset voltage, large output drive current, 1.8 mV internal hysteresis, and rail-to-rail inputs extending 200 mV beyond the supply rails. TLV321x devices have push-pull outputs, while TLV322x devices have open-drain outputs that support pull-ups to 5.5 V and wired-OR logic. A power-on reset holds the output low for up to 32 μs after the supply crosses 1.65 V. The devices are specified from −40°C to 125°C and are intended for current sensing, zero-cross detection, logic translation, and other speed-sensitive applications. The datasheet also covers unused-input handling, ESD precautions, hysteresis circuits, supply bypassing, high-speed PCB layout, and low-side current-sensing design guidance.

National Journal’s June 8, 2001, CongressDailyAM reported:

- House Appropriations subcommittee allocations for FY02 totaled $661.3 billion, generally close to President Bush’s $660.6 billion request but with notable differences, including $3 billion more for Labor-HHS, $1.1 billion more for VA-HUD and $1.2 billion more for Energy and Water. House leaders said they would support Bush’s roughly $7 billion FY01 supplemental request, including $6.1 billion for defense offset by $505 million in cuts, despite demands for $10 billion–$15 billion. OMB Director Mitchell Daniels favored staying within budget caps, while Roy Blunt warned that Bush might veto a larger supplemental.

- House Republicans said the Democratic Senate takeover would give them greater freedom to pass legislation, including energy, prescription drugs, campaign finance reform and possibly permanent tax cuts, before the August recess. Speaker Dennis Hastert also cited patients’ rights and presidential trade authority as priorities. Republican moderates said their views were being considered, while Representative Dick Gephardt said civility had improved but genuine bipartisan cooperation had not.

- Republican Representative Steve Largent announced plans to resign his Oklahoma House seat on Nov. 29 to pursue the governorship and requested a special election before then. The Republican field includes state Rep. John Sullivan, state Sen. Scott Pruitt and First Lady Cathy Keating; Tulsa school board member Doug Dodd appeared likely to become the Democratic nominee.

- Asa Hutchinson’s expected departure for a Drug Enforcement Administration post threatened to slow House business-liability legislation, particularly caps on punitive damages for small businesses. Democrats’ control of the Senate agenda was expected to complicate floor action, though bipartisan small-business support and President Bush’s backing for civil-justice reform could help.

- Labor Secretary Elaine Chao scheduled ergonomics forums in Washington, Illinois and California and a September policy initiative. Republicans praised the outreach, while Democrats questioned whether it would delay a workplace rule. Chao had not committed to issuing a new regulation after Congress overturned the Clinton administration’s ergonomics rule.

- FDA officials warned lawmakers that about two million international mail parcels containing regulated products enter the United States annually, overwhelming inspection capacity. Unreviewed drugs could be contaminated, ineffective, counterfeit or improperly stored. Democrats and Republicans agreed the danger warranted tighter regulation, even as Representative John Dingell noted that some consumers use foreign drugs because of U.S. prices.

- The House Energy and Commerce Committee was considering generic-drug patent reforms for a Medicare prescription drug bill. Chairman Michael Bilirakis said members would remain open-minded after a hearing, while Henry Waxman and brand-name drug manufacturers warned that reopening the 1984 law could jeopardize coverage for seniors.

- European officials said Bush’s Section 201 steel-import investigation could sour the upcoming EU-U.S. summit in Gothenburg. They opposed U.S. unilateralism, proposed an OECD-led fact-finding process and continued negotiations on the Kyoto Protocol, while saying an announcement on a new trade round would be premature.

- Senate Republican negotiators and Democratic leader Tom Daschle were close to agreement on an organizing resolution and formal assurances for prompt consideration of Bush’s nominees. Republicans had dropped filibuster threats in favor of negotiations.

- Bush planned to nominate Jo Anne Barnhart for a six-year term as Social Security Administration commissioner, subject to Senate confirmation. The position was expected to become especially sensitive amid debate over personal stock-market accounts in Social Security.

- Republican members of the Census Monitoring Board released a report calling the 2000 census highly accurate and questioning statistical sampling, which a Census Bureau panel had declined to recommend for congressional redistricting.

- Airlines announced voluntary customer-service commitments that would be included in passenger contracts. House Aviation Subcommittee Chairman John Mica scheduled a June 20 hearing to evaluate improvements, while legislation granting airlines limited antitrust immunity for schedule coordination awaited a likely House vote in early July.

- House Republicans introduced the National Monument Fairness Act, requiring public, governor and congressional input for presidential monuments larger than 50,000 acres and giving Congress two years to approve them before the proclamation sunsets.

- The congressional calendar included a Senate pro forma session and House committee hearings on the District of Columbia government, energy policy, drug access, census sampling, defense, emergency 911 systems and campaign finance reform, along with related hearings and events through Thursday.

The passage specifies SD Memory Card physical-layer behavior, including command switching, bus modes, CRC protection, timeout handling, command and response formats, status structures, and performance classes.

CMD6, introduced in Physical Layer Specification 1.10, is mandatory for version 1.10 and later cards but unsupported by earlier cards. Hosts can check the SCR register’s SD_SPEC field or CCC bit 10 before using it. CMD6 is valid in the Transfer state and returns an R1 response plus a 512-bit status block within a 100 ms timeout. Function switching takes effect within eight clocks. Selected functions remain active until a power cycle, CMD6 selects Function 0 in each group, or CMD0 resets the card.

CMD6 supports six function groups, each with sixteen functions and only one active function at a time. Function 0 is the default. Mode 0 queries supported functions, current selections, and maximum current or power consumption. Mode 1 changes functions. Busy functions cannot be changed and return their current function number. An invalid selection in Mode 1 causes all requested changes to be ignored. Defined groups cover access mode, command-system extension, driver-strength selection for 1.8 V signaling, and total power-limit control.

The default power limit is 0.72 W. Hosts select a higher limit according to card requirements, host power-supply capability, heat dissipation, and connector limits. In UHS-I mode, the power limit must be adjusted after selecting SDR50, SDR104, or DDR50; in UHS-II mode, it is set after initialization. A function lacking sufficient power fails initialization and is disabled. The returned status reports supported functions, resulting selections, and maximum consumption.

High-Speed mode provides a 25 MB/s interface by increasing the clock to 50 MHz. It is optional, and a host operating cards with different timing modes must connect only one card at a time.

The optional Command System function group assigns CMD34–37, CMD50, and CMD57 to standard, vendor-specific, or mobile-commerce behaviors. With the standard function selected, these commands are illegal; other SD Memory Card commands remain available regardless of the selected command set.

CMD8 checks whether a card can operate at the host’s supplied voltage. It is issued while the card is idle and before ACMD41. A compatible card returns R7 with the voltage range and check pattern echoed; an incompatible card does not respond and remains idle.

ACMD41’s CCS value identifies SDSC, SDHC, or SDXC cards. SDSC cards use byte addressing and CMD16-defined block lengths, while SDHC and SDXC cards use fixed 512-byte block addressing. SDHC and SDXC cards disable partial and misaligned access and do not support write-protected groups.

The host may stop or reduce the bus clock to manage data flow. After ACMD41, the clock normally must remain at 100–400 kHz, with polling at intervals below 50 ms if stopped. Eight clock cycles must follow the applicable command, response, data-block, or CRC-status endpoint before the clock is shut down. A busy card may continue programming without a clock, but a clock edge is required to terminate its busy signal.

CRC7 protects commands, responses other than R3, and CSD and CID registers. CRC16 protects data blocks and is calculated separately on each line in wide-bus mode. A CRC failure causes the addressed card to remain unchanged, omit the response, and set the CRC error bit. Illegal commands likewise cause no response or state change and set the ILLEGAL_COMMAND bit.

Read timeouts are the lower of 100 times the typical access time or 100 ms for Standard Capacity cards; High and Extended Capacity cards use at least 100 ms. Write timeouts are the lower of 100 times the typical program time or 250 ms. SDXC cards may indicate up to 500 ms busy in specified write circumstances, while Speed Class writes retain a 250 ms limit. UHS-II busy after a data burst may extend to one second. Erase timeouts use SD Status parameters when supported or may be estimated from block-write delay.

Commands are 48 bits long and are grouped into classes whose support is advertised through the CSD command-class bits. Responses travel over CMD and include CRC protection except for R3. Status information comprises the 32-bit Card Status, a 512-bit SD Status transferred with CRC16, and Task Status for queued operations. SD Status reports capabilities and performance data such as Speed Class, UHS Speed Grade, allocation-unit sizes, erase timing, Video Speed Class, Application Performance Class, and command-queue support.

Speed Class performance is organized into Allocation Units and 16 KB-multiple Recording Units. Speed Classes 2, 4, 6, and 10 define minimum write and read performance, including fragmented-AU movement performance. Class 10 is defined only for entirely free AUs. FAT-update timing is included so hosts can size buffers and account for metadata writes. SDXC extends the method to allocation units as large as 64 MB, requires sequential writes to entirely free AUs, uses exFAT FAT, Bitmap, directory-entry, and optional Continuous Information updates, and does not support Performance Move.

CMD20 supports SDXC Speed Class recording and is optional for SDHC. Its functions indicate Start Recording, Update DIR, and Update CI. A Speed Class host must issue Update DIR before Start Recording and Update CI immediately before the corresponding 512-byte CI write.

UHS Speed Grade defines Grade 1 as at least 10 MB/s and Grade 3 as at least 30 MB/s; a Grade 3 card also satisfies Grade 1 in both UHS-I and UHS-II modes. Video Speed Class defines grades 6, 10, 30, 60, and 90 for SDHC and SDXC cards. The passage states that Speed Class, UHS Speed Grade, and Video Speed Class methods are optional for cards in this specification version.

The lecture explains that the discrete-time Fourier transform may not converge because a sequence need not be absolutely summable. It introduces the Z-transform, \(X(z)=\sum_n x[n]z^{-n}\), with \(z=re^{j\omega}\), as the Fourier transform of the weighted sequence \(x[n]r^{-n}\). The Z-transform converges when that weighted sequence is absolutely summable; when \(r=1\), it reduces to the Fourier transform. Thus, the Fourier transform exists when the Z-transform’s region of convergence includes the unit circle.

Exponential sequences and sums of exponentials have rational Z-transforms expressible through zeros and poles. The region of convergence is part of the transform’s definition, so identical rational expressions can represent different sequences. It contains no poles and is bounded by them: finite-length sequences generally cover the entire z-plane except possibly zero or infinity, right-sided sequences have an exterior region, left-sided sequences an interior region, and two-sided sequences an annular region. Stability requires inclusion of the unit circle, while causality implies a right-sided response and an exterior region.

The Z-transform maps convolution to multiplication, and the transform of a system’s unit-sample response is its system function. For \(y[n]-\tfrac12y[n-1]=x[n]\), the system function is \(H(z)=1/(1-\tfrac12z^{-1})=z/(z-\tfrac12)\); its region of convergence determines whether the impulse response is stable and causal or unstable and anti-causal.

The MSPM0C1105 and MSPM0C1106 include zero-wait-state SRAM for volatile data such as the call stack, heap, globals, and code. SRAM is retained in RUN, SLEEP, STOP, and STANDBY modes but is lost in SHUTDOWN. Dynamic write protection is available in 1 KB increments, and placing code in SRAM can protect it from unintended overwrites while improving critical-loop performance and reducing power consumption.

The GPIO module supports up to 45 pins through Ports A and B, including atomic set, clear, and toggle operations, input filtering, wake from SHUTDOWN, and FastWake from STOP and STANDBY. The IOMUX provides programmable drive strength, speed, pullup/down, and pin multiplexing, with functions configured through PINCM registers.

The 12-bit ADC supports conversion rates up to 1.6 Msps with 10.6-bit ENOB using an external reference. It includes internal temperature-sensing, supply-monitoring, and analog-signal channels; selectable 1.4 V or 2.5 V internal references; external VREF+/VREF− support; and operation in RUN, SLEEP, and STOP, with triggers available from STANDBY. The temperature sensor produces a linear voltage output connected to an ADC channel and includes factory calibration data. The shared VREF module supplies selectable internal references to the ADC and comparator or accepts an external reference.

The comparator compares two input voltages and provides a digital result. It supports timer blanking sources, wakeup from all low-power modes, connection to the advanced-timer fault-handling mechanism, selectable input channels, and an 8-bit reference DAC.

The Low-Frequency Sub-System uses a typical 32 kHz clock for long-term timekeeping and contains the real-time clock and an asynchronous independent watchdog timer. The IWDT has an independent power and clock source, a 25-bit counter with open and closed windows, eight selectable periods, and generates a power-on reset if not serviced. The WWDT supervises code execution and can generate a reset or interrupt, supports eight periods, stops automatically in sleep mode, and can operate as an interval timer. RTC_B provides calendar counters, customizable alarms, periodic and interval wakeups, BCD or binary formats, leap-year correction, crystal-offset and temperature-drift calibration, and clock output for calibration.

General-purpose timers provide 16-bit up, down, or up/down counting, prescaling, quadrature encoder support, synchronization, cross-triggering, and interrupt or ADC trigger generation. Advanced timers add clock doubling, repeat counters, shadow registers, asymmetric PWM with programmable dead-band insertion, fault handling, synchronization, cross-triggering, and extra capture/compare channels.

Three UART peripherals support programmable baud rates, even, odd, stick, or no parity, LIN mode, DMA-compatible transmit and receive FIFOs, and loopback. I²C supports 7-bit and 10-bit addressing, controller and target operation, clock stretching, 100 kbps Standard mode, 400 kbps Fast mode, 1 Mbps Fast-mode Plus, SMBus 3.0, DMA, address-match wakeup, and glitch filters. SPI supports controller and peripheral roles, up to 16 Mbits/s, configurable chip select and prescaler, programmable frame sizes, DMA, and TI, Motorola, and National Microwire formats.

Security features include flexible code and data firewalls and CRC-16 with a customizable polynomial. The CRC module supports CRC16-CCITT and bit reversal.

The Arm-compatible two-wire SWD interface supports debugging of processor execution and device state, software-controlled peripheral behavior during debug, a boot-ROM and software mailbox, SWD disable or lockout, and password-authenticated debugging. A memory-mapped FACTORY region provides read-only device capability information and factory trim data, including DEVICEID and USERID fields.

The Tenth Circuit affirmed the Immigration and Naturalization Service’s decision to reinstate Alejandro Mendez Suarez’s 1996 exclusion and deportation order. Suarez, a Mexican citizen, was excluded and deported after presenting counterfeit documents, unlawfully reentered the United States in October 1999, and was arrested in Colorado in 2002. The INS reinstated his prior order under 8 U.S.C. § 1231(a)(5), and the district court transferred Suarez’s habeas petition to the Tenth Circuit for direct review.

The court held that the transfer was proper because Suarez was challenging the reinstatement order. It rejected his argument that reinstatement interfered with his Colorado bond and criminal defense, noting that the court could not grant relief on that issue and that the INS need not consider those consequences. It also found no improper retroactive application of § 1231(a)(5), because Suarez’s unlawful reentry occurred after the statute became effective. The record contradicted his claim that he voluntarily departed in 1996, and voluntary departure after an exclusion order would still constitute deportation or removal. Suarez was ineligible for adjustment of status under the LIFE Act because his prior misrepresentation made him inadmissible. Finally, the court found no due-process violation because Suarez did not contest the existence of the prior order or his unlawful reentry, and therefore could not show prejudice.

A PRISMA-guided systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 25 controlled observational studies examined mental health disorders in women with PCOS. PCOS was associated with higher prevalence of anxiety (PR 1.42), depression (PR 1.65), and eating disorders (PR 1.48) than in age-matched controls. Postpartum depression was more prevalent but not statistically significantly associated and was excluded from economic calculations. Estimated excess cases attributable to PCOS were 216,248 for anxiety, 262,176 for depression, and 48,764 for eating disorders. Their respective additional direct U.S. healthcare costs were estimated at $1.939 billion, $1.678 billion, and $644 million annually in 2021 USD, totaling $4.261 billion. Trim-and-fill analyses retained significance for anxiety and depression but not eating disorders, indicating less robustness for the latter association. Combining these findings with prior estimates, the annual direct U.S. economic burden of PCOS exceeded $15 billion in 2021 USD, with mental health disorders accounting for about 28%. The study also notes limitations including the small number of eligible studies, inclusion of some non-U.S. studies, and exclusion of indirect and intangible costs, and supports improved PCOS detection, clinical awareness, interventions, and research funding.
