Products sales were $96,458 million and Services sales $23,117 million, up from $20,766 million. By category, iPhone sales rose 6% to $69,702 million (driven by Pro models), Mac was relatively flat at $7,780 million, iPad fell 25% to $7,023 million, Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 11% to $11,953 million, and Services rose 11% on advertising, video and cloud services.

Total gross margin was $54,855 million (45.9%) versus $50,332 million (43.0%), with Products margin of 39.4% and Services margin of 72.8%, reflecting cost savings and mix. Operating expenses totaled $14,482 million, with R&D flat at $7,696 million and SG&A up 3% to $6,786 million. Operating income was $40,373 million; other income/(expense) net was negative $50 million; pre-tax income was $40,323 million; the tax provision was $6,407 million (15.9% effective rate); and net income was $33,916 million versus $29,998 million, with diluted EPS of $2.18 and basic EPS of $2.19. Total comprehensive income was $35,990 million.

Segment results: Americas net sales $50,430 million (+2%) with operating income $20,357 million; Europe $30,397 million (+10%) with $12,711 million; Greater China $20,819 million (−13%) with $8,622 million; Japan $7,767 million (+15%) with $3,819 million; Rest of Asia Pacific $10,162 million (+7%) with $4,579 million.

At December 30, 2023, total assets were $353,514 million, including cash and equivalents of $40,760 million and marketable securities of $32,340 million current and $99,475 million non-current. Total liabilities were $279,414 million, including $1,998 million of commercial paper, $10,954 million of current term debt, $95,088 million of non-current term debt and $8,264 million of deferred revenue (total deferred revenue of $12.5 billion, 66% expected to be realized within a year). Shareholders' equity was $74,100 million, with retained earnings of $8,242 million and accumulated other comprehensive loss of $9,378 million. Operating activities generated $39,895 million of cash; investing activities generated $1,927 million; financing activities used $30,585 million, ending cash of $41,974 million.

The company repurchased 118 million shares for $20.5 billion and paid $3.8 billion in dividends and dividend equivalents at $0.24 per share; $36.4 billion of the $90 billion authorization had been used. Manufacturing purchase obligations totaled $38.0 billion, of which $37.9 billion was payable within 12 months. Outstanding RSUs were 208,972 thousand with $27.4 billion of unrecognized compensation cost expected to be recognized over 2.9 years.

In legal matters, the Supreme Court denied both Epic's and Apple's petitions on January 16, 2024, ending the stay of the injunction against Apple's anti-steering provisions; the company implemented a compliance plan, which Epic moved to dispute. Separately, the ITC's limited exclusion order covering Apple Watch models with blood oxygen sensing was found by U.S. Customs and Border Protection on January 12, 2024, not to cover the company's proposed Series 9 and Ultra 2 redesign. Risk factors highlighted European Union Digital Markets Act compliance changes announced in January 2024 and ongoing antitrust investigations. No material changes were reported in market risk, critical accounting estimates or internal control over financial reporting; disclosure controls were deemed effective. ASU 2023-09 on income tax disclosures will be adopted in Q4 2026 and ASU 2023-07 on segment reporting in Q4 2025 retrospectively.

The author argues that opposition to school sex education often stems from fear, cultural anxiety, and misunderstanding rather than concern for children. In Ontario and Alberta, conservative Roman Catholics and evangelicals, alongside some Muslim and Sikh participants, have organized against new curricula, sometimes through demonstrations marked by anger, ignorance, and homophobic rhetoric. The author says modern sex education reduces shame, teaches children body ownership and the right to refuse, and helps them recognize and report abuse, countering claims that it sexualizes or grooms children. Schools should complement parents, and society should respond to change with trust, optimism, and faithfulness.

An October 23, 2001 email from Courtney Votaw ("Enron Mentions") forwards numerous articles on Enron and related business news.

**Litigation:** PR Newswire reported that Cauley Geller Bowman & Coates, LLP filed a class action in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas (Houston Division) for purchasers of Enron stock between January 18, 2000 and October 17, 2001, alleging violations of Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 through misrepresentations about the bandwidth trading market, overstated operating results from failing to write down investments in partnerships managed by CFO Andrew Fastow, and delayed write-downs of impaired assets. The complaint cited Enron's October 16 announcement of $1.01 billion in after-tax non-recurring charges ($1.11 loss per diluted share) for Q3 2001, elimination of more than $1 billion in shareholder equity, and insider sales of over $73 million during the class period; lead plaintiff motions were due by December 21, 2001.

**SEC inquiry and stock:** Enron said the SEC requested information on 1999–2000 transactions with limited partnerships managed by a senior officer (a $16 million pre-tax gain in 1999 and $36 million loss in 2000). Chairman/CEO Kenneth Lay said Enron welcomed the request and would cooperate fully; spokesman Mark Palmer called it an informal inquiry, "not an investigation," noting the arrangements were reviewed by auditors, attorneys and the board and disclosed in SEC filings; SEC spokesman John Heine declined comment. Shares fell $5.40 (over 20%) to $20.65 Monday, then 86 cents to $19.79 Tuesday, down 42% in a week and 76% year to date. Enron fell from second to tenth most highly rated S&P 500 stock per Thomson Financial/First Call after downgrades from A.G. Edwards and Edward Jones, while Lehman Brothers, Credit Suisse First Boston and Goldman Sachs kept top ratings.

**Conference call:** On a special call, Enron offered few new details and Lay sparred with investor Richard Grubman (Highfields Capital Management), who estimated Marlin II's water assets at $100 million, implying roughly $900 million needed to repay related debt; Lay accused him of driving the stock down. Enron said it would cut Q4 share count by 60 million following termination of the LJM2 financing (about 6.5% of diluted shares) yet kept 2001 earnings guidance of $1.80 and 2002 guidance of $2.15. Enron cited $3.35 billion in credit lines, with its debt-to-capital ratio estimated at 50–55% after the $1.2 billion equity writedown and covenants breached above 65%.

**Financing:** Bloomberg reported Enron asked Citigroup to arrange a $750 million loan in case it is cut off from money markets; it depends on a $3 billion commercial paper program, and Moody's had placed $13 billion of long-term debt on watch. Fastow said $3.5 billion was available on bank credit lines. Enron had bought back 62 million shares (the Wall Street Journal reported 55 million), reducing shareholder equity by $1.2 billion. Partnerships such as LJM Cayman, LJM2 and Whitewing ($1.4 billion of bonds; 250,000 convertible preferred shares) kept debt off Enron's books, with at least $3 billion in "off-the-books" financing; analysts questioned whether asset sales would cover the borrowings. An investor suit alleges the two Fastow-run partnerships cost Enron $35 million. Third-quarter loss was $638 million after $1.01 billion in charges.

**Texas Monthly feature:** "How Enron Blew It" (Mimi Swartz) traces Enron from a 1985 pipeline company to a trading colossus, citing a 1,700% stock rise, revenue growth from $40 billion to $100 billion, Skilling's Gas Bank, aggressive recruiting and uncapped bonuses, up-front mark-to-market accounting, the Performance Review Committee ("rank and yank") replacing 15% of a division's workforce yearly, Rebecca Mark's Azurix (IPO raised $695 million) which collapsed and was folded into Enron, the California energy crisis, the telecom collapse, and the stock falling from $80 in January to about $35. Skilling resigned abruptly after six months as CEO; Lay returned promising greater transparency and reform of the review system.

**Other items:** The Toronto Star reported WTO chief Mike Moore confirming the November 9–13 Qatar trade conference, 3M's third-quarter profit down 21% to $394 million, copper near a 15-year low at $1,366 a tonne, Groupe SEB's approved Moulinex takeover, Bombardier regional jet demand, Aliant Telecom cutting 140 jobs, and a 4.24 billion Swiss franc Swissair rescue package. AES Corp. asked Indian Prime Minister Vajpayee to act against Orissa state interference and unpaid 2.1 billion rupee bills, possibly withdrawing from the state distribution company, after Enron's September 14 letter threatening up to $5 billion in legal action over Dabhol.

A maths problem posed to 11-year-old Chinese pupils—whether a captain’s age could be deduced from 26 sheep and 10 goats—drew attention because it has no answer. Pupils gave humorous or defeated responses, and adults also failed. Shunqing Education Department said varied answers reflecting different personalities were the goal rather than a standard solution.

President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed September 19, 1901, a day of mourning and prayer throughout the United States for President McKinley, whose death he described as a crime against the nation. He urged citizens to gather in places of worship to honor McKinley’s life and submit to God’s will. The proclamation was issued on September 14, 1901, and signed by Secretary of State John Hay.

A May 16, 2001 compilation of press clippings focused on Enron, energy policy, and power markets. The New York Times and Bloomberg reported on the Bush administration’s Energy Development Task Force ahead of its 170-page report promoting domestic production of oil, gas, coal and nuclear power, renewable-energy tax credits and conservation. The task force met with more than 400 people from 150 groups but did not disclose whom officials contacted. Environmentalists, consumer advocates and congressional Democrats alleged industry favoritism, while Cheney’s staff and participating industry representatives disputed those claims. Conoco’s Archie Dunham, Enron’s Kenneth Lay and ExxonMobil’s Lee Raymond met with Cheney, while major environmental groups and California Governor Gray Davis did not receive comparable access.

Texaco was considering a shallow-water Gulf of Mexico terminal to regassify imported LNG and connect it to its offshore pipeline network. Initial capacity could reach one billion cubic feet per day and later double. Separately, Enron dropped litigation against NGX Canada, and a Globe and Mail report also named Canadian Enerdata as a defendant. The settlement brought EnronOnline trades into Alberta gas-price indexes and could support a combined “superindex”; reports differed on whether the dismissed suit was worth $64.6 million or $101 million.

A real-estate report said Houston’s downtown office vacancy rate fell to 6.26% from 6.65%, aided by energy-sector expansion, while national first-quarter property sales fell 11% to $11.6 billion. It also described Springfield’s new Basketball Hall of Fame project and the $96 million sale of Philadelphia’s Barbizon Hotel.

Energy shortages in Brazil and Chile highlighted their reliance on hydropower. Brazil prepared for consumption cuts of 15%–20% amid drought, inadequate state investment and slow privatization, while Chile’s generators sought additional thermal capacity and tariffs reflecting fuel costs. Enron had placed two of its three Brazilian energy projects on hold. Enron Japan proposed 10 reforms for the newly deregulated Japanese electricity market, including separating utility functions, restricting incumbents’ construction in their service areas and privatizing power development; it also sought approval for a thermal plant in Aomori Prefecture.

Saudi Arabia was expected to sign agreements on June 6 for three gas ventures valued at about $25 billion. Eleven companies, including a joint Enron-Occidental bid, were under consideration. In India, lenders to Enron-controlled Dabhol Power Company were expected to vote on terminating its electricity contract with Maharashtra, following payment defaults by the state electricity board and MSEB’s repudiation of a 1995 purchase commitment. The 740-MW first phase was due to expand to 2,184 MW. A Business Line editorial criticized the project’s high costs and said cancellation could leave substantial liabilities for Maharashtra.

Maharashtra’s Godbole committee was renegotiating the Dabhol agreement after three members resigned because of time constraints; a final report was due May 31, and officials were considering separating the LNG facility from the power plant. Former deputy chief minister Gopinath Munde urged an amicable settlement to avoid discouraging investment. In Karnataka, two 60-MW Sharavathi units were inaugurated, while the state outlined plans for about 2,000 MW of additional capacity through projects costing Rs. 10,000 crore. Chief Minister S. M. Krishna also cited litigation-related delays, cost concerns and environmental damage associated with power development.

Resource Generation (RG), a 20-year-old nonprofit, works with about 500 Americans ages 18–35 in the top 10 percent by wealth through 17 chapters. It helps members examine the sources of their wealth, its connection to inequality, and how to direct money, power and influence toward grassroots social-justice movements. RG teaches budgeting, accountability, evaluating organizations and social-justice philanthropy principles, while emphasizing that those most affected by injustice should help decide how funds are spent. It does not pool members’ money and also campaigns for structural changes involving health care, taxes and workers’ rights.

RG’s “money story” exercise encourages members to discuss openly how much wealth they have, where it came from and how it has benefited them. After participating, members’ annual giving rose substantially: Emily Bookstein from minimal giving to $15,000, Elizabeth Baldwin from $100 to $10,000, Hanna Mahon’s family foundation from under $100,000 to $1 million, and Adam Roberts from under $200 to $55,000.

The organization operates amid widening U.S. wealth inequality and links wealth accumulation to institutionalized racism. It promotes inclusion of people of color and support for grassroots anti-racist groups. Executive director Iimay Ho criticizes voluntary philanthropy as insufficient to restructure the economy, while Brookings Institution fellow Richard Reeves says discussing systemic advantages can undermine the idea that wealth simply results from hard work.

On March 7, 2018, NVIDIA’s Compensation Committee adopted its Fiscal Year 2019 Variable Compensation Plan, allowing eligible executive officers to earn variable cash compensation based on achievement of specified fiscal 2019 revenue goals. The goals include threshold, base operating plan, and stretch operating plan levels, and participants generally must remain employees through the payment date to qualify. Base-plan target awards are $1.1 million for Jen-Hsun Huang (110% of base salary), $300,000 for Colette M. Kress (33%), $650,000 for Ajay K. Puri (68%), and $250,000 each for Debora Shoquist and Timothy S. Teter (29%). The plan was filed as Exhibit 10.1.

The study examines the separation of Israel’s Druze school system from Arab education and its effects on Druze students’ matriculation eligibility and participation in higher education. Following Druze demands for educational autonomy, an independent unit developed Druze-specific curricula, textbooks, teacher training, facilities, and heritage programs. These aimed to foster Druze identity and loyalty to Israel. Matriculation eligibility rose substantially, reaching about 89% in 2022.

Interviews with nine Druze principals, supervisors, and trainee principals, analyzed thematically alongside matriculation data for 1976–2020, identified strong satisfaction with Druze educational achievements and a determination to continue improving them. Interviewees emphasized teaching staff quality, school leadership, sustained investment from early childhood, and liberal-modern social changes that expanded women’s education and employment as major contributors. Most did not view separation itself as the primary cause of improved results, although some credited it with greater cultural autonomy, tailored curricula, resources, and focused supervision; others characterized it as state “reeducation.”

The Druze curriculum was described as largely parallel to other systems, with distinctive elements in heritage, history, Arabic, Hebrew, identity, and civic education. Participants also identified a gap between strong high-school performance and students’ preparedness for university. They called for greater post-graduation follow-up, academic guidance, relevant matriculation preparation, and resources for higher-education readiness. The study recommends further representative research, careful evaluation of separation’s role, and a unified educational framework that combines common standards with cultural and religious distinctiveness. Limitations include the small convenience sample, possible subjectivity and researcher bias, and unavailable data for a separate Christian comparison group.

Williams Jones & Associates cut its Star Bulk Carriers stake by 52.6% in Q2, selling 35,000 shares and ending with 31,600 shares worth $311,000. GLG Partners and Capital Fund Management bought new stakes, while Goldman Sachs, Citadel Advisors, and Impala Asset Management increased their holdings. Institutional investors and hedge funds owned 75.03% of the stock. SBLK had a $651.91 million market capitalization, a 52-week range of $4.04-$13.40, and a consensus “Buy” rating with a $12.80 average target. TheStreet and Pareto Securities issued upgrades, while BidaskClub and Zacks downgraded the stock to “sell.” Star Bulk Carriers is an international shipping company operating 73 dry bulk vessels as of December 31, 2016.

The government assured the public that it is containing the bird flu outbreak in San Luis, Pampanga, with poultry movements restricted within seven kilometers, infected birds slated for culling, and local quarantine measures in place. Officials said the detected H5 strain is not transmissible to humans, though samples were sent to an Australian laboratory to test for H5N6, and recommended proper precautions and thorough cooking of chicken. The Health Department deployed epidemiologists to monitor farm workers and test anyone showing symptoms, while maintaining that no sustained human-to-human transmission had occurred.

Alex Caruso’s two-way stint demonstrates the Lakers’ successful use of the NBA’s 45-day system. After 42 days with Los Angeles, he has played 25 games, averaging 2.6 points and 1.9 assists; his best night was nine points and eight assists against the Knicks. He averaged 19 points and 7.4 assists for South Bay, second in the G-League’s Western Conference, and can rejoin Los Angeles after that season. His deal extends through next season. Coach Luke Walton said the arrangement develops players within the Lakers’ system and provides greater continuity than 10-day contracts.

A survey of 4,594 participants and an Omicron-parameterized branching-process model evaluated COVID-19 testing and isolation strategies for winter 2022/2023 in France, Belgium, and Italy. Adjusted survey results showed high intended testing among symptomatic people, high adherence to isolation, and nearly universal compliance with prescribed isolation duration once isolated. Willingness to receive an autumn booster among older adults was highest in Belgium, followed by Italy and France.

At an uncontrolled reproductive number of 1.6 and 75% isolation effectiveness, French and Belgian protocols were predicted to reduce transmission by 17–18%, while the Italian protocol reduced it by 24%. None would reduce the effective reproductive number below 1. The Italian protocol produced the greatest reduction because of longer isolation, averaging about 11 days versus about six days in France and Belgium, and resulted in less post-isolation transmission, but imposed greater social costs. Introducing test costs of up to €20 was estimated to reduce protocol effectiveness by about 60%. Belgium’s simpler fixed-duration protocol was predicted to perform similarly to France’s protocol while requiring approximately 30% fewer tests per infected person.

The modeled fall booster campaign increased inferred population protection against symptomatic infection, but reported uptake was substantially below survey expectations, especially in France and Italy. The authors concluded that simplified testing and isolation guidance could reduce resource use, while high booster coverage remained important for controlling the winter wave. Limitations included an age-unstratified model, no direct assessment of hospital capacity, fixed assumptions about isolation effectiveness, and possible self-selection bias in the survey cohorts.

Alcoa’s shares rose 68% after its October spinoff from Arconic and gained 36% in 2017 despite a fourth-quarter loss, prompting debate over whether the post-split producer is a buy. Rich Duprey highlights expected growth in bauxite production—from 45 million to 47.5–48.5 million bone dry metric tons—and nearly $600 million in 2016–2017 supply contracts, arguing that Alcoa’s position as the world’s largest bauxite producer could boost profitable third-party sales with limited capital spending. Jason Hall says Alcoa may be undervalued at a 12% discount to estimated asset value, but book value declined because of facility closures and an impairment, and further write-downs are possible. Low aluminum prices, dependence on foreign raw materials, global sales exposure, and potentially adverse U.S. trade policy also create risks. With profitability still uncertain after only two quarters as a standalone company, Hall is staying on the sidelines.

Mercer’s 231-city survey ranked Vienna first for quality of life for a ninth consecutive year, citing its culture, healthcare and moderate housing costs. Zurich ranked second, while Auckland and Munich tied for third and Vancouver led North America at fifth. Baghdad ranked last for a decade amid conflict; Sanaa and Damascus ranked slightly higher. London fell to 41st.

Playoff and Olympic formats differ, with Olympic teams effectively eliminated after the quarterfinals and both tournaments being longer and more draining. The coach is generally relaxed while players remain focused, but becomes sharp when they lose their edge, maintaining a largely wordless mutual understanding.

An internal Enron email dated March 19, 2001, from Miyung Buster to numerous recipients circulates eleven articles on California's electricity and energy crisis.

**Air pollution trade-off:** San Diego County's Air Pollution Control District Hearing Board voted 4-1 to let the former Encina (now Cabrillo) power plant emit several times more nitrogen oxides. County engineer Steven Moore said no added unhealthy ozone days would result if the plant burns natural gas all year, but significant ozone increases would occur if it switched to fuel oil, which is likely as gas supplies tighten.

**FERC refunds:** FERC found possible February overcharges of about $55 million by six suppliers (Dynegy, Williams Energy, Duke Energy, Portland General Electric, Reliant and Mirant), following a $69 million January order, requiring justification or refund of sales above $430 per megawatt-hour during Stage 3 alerts (January threshold: $273). Suppliers would likely receive credits rather than refunds; Dynegy faces $23.4 million and Williams $21.6 million. Gov. Gray Davis called the action "baby steps," while consumer advocates, Sen. Dianne Feinstein and Rep. Bob Filner criticized FERC for setting too high a baseline and excluding most sales. The state's grid operator said California may have been overcharged more than $500 million in December–January. Separately, PG&E said it would transfer $1.1 billion from a federal tax refund to its utility unit, and Davis announced more than $51 million over two years for consultants and conservation advertising.

**OPEC and policy:** OPEC's 4% output cut (1 million barrels a day, effective April 1) was called "disappointing" by Energy Secretary Spencer Abraham, who urged increased U.S. production and a national energy policy; Sen. Schumer proposed tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Bush favors opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. A Gallup poll found 31% viewing the energy situation "very serious" and 59% "fairly serious," with 56% favoring conservation over 33% favoring more production.

**Groups using the crisis:** Auto makers tried to weaken California's electric-vehicle mandate (reaffirmed unanimously by the Air Resources Board); the California Manufacturers & Technology Assn. asked Davis to reconsider the overtime rule; and the Westlands Water District cited power shortages in its suit to block Trinity River flows, drawing opposition from tribes and Trinity County officials.

**DWR power buying:** The Department of Water Resources, buying power for near-bankrupt utilities, was spending about $350 million a week and nearly $4 billion by month's end against a $10 billion authorization, operating from a secret Sacramento "Joint Operations Center" with limited market experience, withheld contract terms, and hired outside consultants from Navigant and Deloitte & Touche.

**Bankruptcy threats:** Coram Energy Group said it would petition to force Southern California Edison into involuntary bankruptcy, potentially followed by action against PG&E, jeopardizing the state's plan to buy the utilities' transmission lines. PG&E and Edison International stocks fell roughly 12% and 10%. Utilities carry more than $13 billion in debts; PG&E retained bankruptcy counsel and says it will pay down some debt.

**Blackouts and customer treatment:** PG&E's "Block 50" overhaul moved about 810,000 of 1.9 million exempt customers out and 690,000 in, leaving about 120,000 more customers blackout-vulnerable. A Chronicle column described restaurant owner Ken Zankel losing power after billing software errors and a mistaken shutoff notice.

**Commentary:** Mercury News chief editorial writer Phil Yost rejected claims that out-of-state generators constituted a "massive transfer of wealth," noting Calpine and LADWP are California-based, the alleged $15 billion profit is about 1.5% of the state's $1 trillion economy, and a Western regional market would be more efficient than a state-only one.

A Nov. 11, 2001 press-clipping digest chronicled Enron’s financial collapse and its agreement to be acquired by Houston rival Dynegy in a deal valued between $7.7 billion and $9 billion, with Dynegy assuming roughly $13 billion in Enron debt. Enron, once the dominant U.S. energy trader, admitted overstating profits by about $600 million over four years and restating its finances back to 1997, subtracting $586 million from net income and adding $2.5 billion to debt. It reported a $635 million third-quarter loss and a $1.2 billion reduction in shareholder equity.

The SEC’s formal investigation focused on the board-approved LJM1 and LJM2 off-balance-sheet partnerships, created under CFO Andrew Fastow to help Enron grow without added debt or diluted stock and to hedge business risks. Fastow’s dual role created an apparent conflict of interest. Enron established a special committee to investigate the partnerships and whether safeguards were properly implemented. Fastow and several other employees had departed, while treasurer Ben Glisan and general counsel Kristina Mordaunt were dismissed. Shareholders filed lawsuits against Enron, the partnerships and the company’s law firm. The SEC inquiry continued as Enron’s finances and executive conduct were scrutinized.

An editorial said the opaque partnerships concealed debt and risk, contributing to a cycle of falling earnings, investor distrust and weakening credit. It also cited unsuccessful investments in an Indian power plant, excess broadband capacity and the water company Azurix, and called for tighter regulation of accounting loopholes.

Enron’s collapse was viewed as a blow to Houston, which was also dealing with Compaq’s possible sale, Continental Airlines layoffs and the loss of American General’s headquarters. Experts said the acquisitions and downturns damaged the city’s business image but did not undermine its long-term appeal, infrastructure or reputation for innovation. Dynegy’s purchase was expected to preserve Houston operations and soften the loss.

California’s electricity crisis slowed nationwide deregulation, while lower gas and electricity prices, reduced price volatility and a weak economy hurt energy traders. Analysts nevertheless said deregulation was delayed rather than derailed and that energy companies could recover with the economy. Companies such as AES, Reliant and Constellation refocused or retrenched, while Commonwealth Energy diversified away from direct retail sales.

Wall Street scrutiny also focused on companies’ use of adjusted “pro forma” earnings that excluded substantial costs. Standard & Poor’s began including restructuring charges, stock-option expenses and operating write-downs in operating earnings. Enron served as a prominent example of opaque accounting, while Motorola’s reported $153 million pro forma loss contrasted with a $1.4 billion loss after charges. Investors and the FASB sought more consistent reporting, including use of EBITDA.

Meanwhile, the Dow rose 3.05% to 9,608, its first close above its Sept. 10 pre-attack level, helped by a half-point Federal Reserve rate cut and improving consumer sentiment. A Senate stimulus proposal offered about $70 billion in benefits and tax breaks but was criticized for special-interest provisions benefiting agriculture, Amtrak, film and commodity interests.

The professor reviews a Porter article arguing that corporate social responsibility should move beyond external compliance and stakeholder demands toward integration into business strategy. He summarizes four common justifications for CSR—moral obligation, license to operate, sustainability, and reputation—and explains their limitations: moral decisions are difficult to measure, community demands may ignore competitive capabilities, reputation benefits are hard to verify, and “long-term” sustainability goals are too vague and can postpone action.

Porter’s proposed framework considers generic social impacts, value-chain impacts, and the social dimensions of a company’s competitive context. Companies should consciously decline issues they cannot address, meet basic legal and ethical requirements, mitigate risks, and prioritize selected issues where sustainability can reinforce core competencies or create competitive advantage. Examples include Whole Foods, Siemens, GE, Toyota, Nestlé, UPS, and FedEx. The professor emphasizes embedding sustainability in the company’s “DNA” rather than pursuing rankings or responding temporarily to public pressure.

A life-cycle perspective is presented as essential for identifying priorities because many environmental and social impacts occur outside a company’s direct operations, particularly among suppliers, customers, and product users. For automobiles, about 70 percent of lifecycle emissions occur during use, making vehicle efficiency the main environmental priority while suppliers still require risk mitigation and standards compliance. Supply-chain depth should therefore depend on where significant impacts and business risks occur, available resources, and traceability. Agricultural companies such as Starbucks, Unilever, and Nestlé must reach deep into fragmented supply chains to protect product quality and brand promises; Starbucks’ CAFE Practices illustrate certification and training of coffee suppliers.

The lecturer outlines an implementation process: identify business pressures and material impacts, prioritize issues, measure resource use and environmental performance, establish goals, and connect targets to operational metrics. Measurements should be routine and credible, rather than annual estimates prepared only for CSR reporting. Carbon goals, for example, must be linked to controllable measures such as energy use, waste, or transportation activity. Targets should be ambitious but informed by baselines, pilots, capability assessments, and competitor benchmarks, with incentives or penalties tied to measurable results. Third-party verification may help protect integrity, especially in supply chains.

Supplier sustainability begins by requesting consistent data, allowing suppliers time to build measurement systems, and eventually incorporating environmental performance into contracts, scorecards, and procurement decisions alongside price, quality, and safety. The session concludes with instructions for students to compare assigned companies and assess whether their CDP rankings reflect the strategic principles discussed.

Erik Demaine introduces a class on geometric folding algorithms, covering the mathematics and computational methods of folding and unfolding geometric objects. Applications include robotics and programmable matter, computer graphics, mechanical linkages, manufacturing, nanotechnology, optics, medical stents and drug delivery, space deployment, protein folding, sculpture, origami design, and reconfigurable architecture.

The class studies three main structures: linkages made of rigid bars and hinges; paper, which may be folded but not stretched, torn, or cut; and polyhedra, including how to construct them from flat material and how to unfold their surfaces. Questions are divided into foldability problems, which ask whether a given structure can fold, and design problems, which seek a structure that achieves a desired shape or property. Results are characterized as universal algorithms, efficient decision algorithms, or computational hardness results. The course includes required lectures, a few problem sets, an optional open-problem session, and a project with a written report and presentation for credit; projects may be individual or collaborative.

For linkages, Demaine describes historical mechanisms, including Watt and Peaucellier linkages, that convert circular motion into linear motion or trace exact straight lines. Universal results allow linkages to trace piecewise-polynomial curves, including signatures, but remain open when self-crossing is forbidden. Rigidity is algorithmically decidable in two dimensions but remains difficult in three dimensions. Reconfiguration is generally hard; two-dimensional chains have universal results, while three-dimensional chains and two-dimensional trees can have locked configurations. Characterizing such locked structures remains open, although algorithms exist for unfolding many polygonal and tree linkages. Protein backbones resemble tree-like linkages and present related folding challenges.

For paper, determining whether a general crease pattern folds flat is NP-hard. Single-vertex patterns are understood, but efficient decision procedures for patterns such as \(2 \times n\) maps remain open. Computational origami design has universal results for arbitrary shapes, polyhedra, and two-color patterns. The Origamizer produces practical foldings of three-dimensional meshes, while the tree method optimizes paper use, an NP-complete objective handled practically with heuristics. A folding-cut theorem shows that one straight cut through folded paper can produce any desired collection of polygons. Curved creases, self-folding sheets, and universal hinge patterns can create programmable structures, although material thickness remains a major limitation; Britney Gallivan’s work established conditions for folding paper in half 12 times.

For polyhedra, it remains unknown whether every convex polyhedron has a nonoverlapping single-piece edge unfolding; nonconvex counterexamples exist. General unfolding is always possible for convex polyhedra and certain orthogonal or triangular surfaces, while other cases remain open. Demaine also describes reverse folding from a planar polygon into three-dimensional shapes and a recent theorem that any finite set of equal-area polygons can be connected as a hinged chain that folds into every target shape without collision, with extensions to three-dimensional forms under additional conditions.

Tamil Nadu’s sugar output is expected to fall by more than one-third in 2017/18, from about 1 million tonnes to 600,000, because of the state’s century-worst drought. Debt-strricken farmers and producers protested in New Delhi, while back-to-back droughts have damaged cane in Maharashtra. India’s 2016/17 sugar production was forecast at 20.3 million tonnes, 5% below the prior forecast. Uneven monsoon rains left southern India parched, though El Niño may spare India. Tamil Nadu’s 2016/17 cotton output is projected to fall 21% to 550,000 bales.

Tesla, Inc.’s unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2017 reported cash and cash equivalents of $4.01 billion, total assets of $25.05 billion, total liabilities of $18.89 billion, and stockholders’ equity of $4.99 billion.

Revenue for the quarter was $2.70 billion, compared with $1.15 billion in the prior-year quarter. Automotive revenue was $2.29 billion, energy generation and storage revenue was $213.9 million, and services and other revenue was $192.7 million. Gross profit was $667.9 million, operating loss was $257.5 million, and net loss was $397.2 million, or $2.04 per common share. Net cash used in operating activities was $69.8 million, net cash used in investing activities was $926.9 million, and financing activities provided $1.60 billion.

Following its November 2016 SolarCity acquisition, Tesla operates automotive and energy generation and storage segments and provides solar energy systems. It acquired Grohmann Engineering for $109.5 million in cash on January 3, 2017, recording preliminary goodwill of $40.1 million and intangible assets of $21.7 million. A terminated $25.8 million Grohmann incentive payment was expensed in the quarter. SolarCity purchase accounting remained subject to measurement-period adjustments, including an $11.6 million reduction to the initially recognized acquisition gain.

Tesla recorded $2.69 billion of resale value guarantee liabilities and potentially could have paid up to $977.4 million to repurchase vehicles under its leasing-partner guarantees. Total debt was $8.52 billion, and the company reported compliance with its financial covenants. During the quarter, it issued $977.5 million of 2.375% convertible notes due 2022, purchased convertible note hedges for $204.1 million, sold warrants for $52.9 million, and raised $399.6 million through a common stock offering.

The filing also disclosed warranties for vehicles and energy products, commitments under the Buffalo Gigafactory 2 lease, SolarCity-related litigation, an investigation concerning U.S. Treasury grants, and claims involving SolarCity securities and Tesla’s acquisition of SolarCity.

Metrocosm’s YouTube animation maps city growth from Eridu around 3000 BC using earliest recorded populations. A Yale-led team created an accessible dataset of city locations and populations back to 3700 BC by digitizing and standardizing historical research. Despite gaps in regional and early city coverage, it is far from comprehensive.

The paper proposes a bound-preserving adaptive coupling of cell-centered finite volume (CCFV) and discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods for steady convection-diffusion problems in two or three dimensions. CCFV provides local conservation and monotonicity but typically low accuracy, while DG offers high-order accuracy and sharp layer resolution but may produce unphysical overshoots and undershoots. The method monitors DG cell averages and replaces the approximation with CCFV in a neighborhood of any cell violating solution bounds beyond a prescribed tolerance. Cell averages remain unmodified, and conservative slope limiters can subsequently enforce bounds on the full solution. This hp-adaptive strategy integrates with standard adaptivity routines without altering the underlying CCFV or DG schemes or postprocessing cell averages.

The model problem is \(-
abla\!\cdot(K
abla u)+
abla\!\cdot(\vec eta u)+cu=f\), with Dirichlet and homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. The domain is partitioned into matching FV and DG regions with polynomial degree \(k\ge1\) in the DG region. FV meshes must satisfy two-point-flux-admissibility conditions, including orthogonal cell-center connections and uniform shape-regularity constraints. Related approaches include FV–DG limiters, artificial viscosity, flux-corrected transport, and nonlinear bound-preserving modifications, each of which may introduce cost, nonconservation, altered discretizations, or lack formal error analysis.

The lecture outlines a course on building secure systems through research-paper case studies and labs involving languages such as C, Assembly, Python, JavaScript, and others. The first lab focuses on exploiting buffer overflows in a web server; later labs cover defenses, code analysis, and browser-based worms. Students must read assigned papers, answer questions, and may use Piazza and recorded lectures.

Security is defined as achieving a system’s goal despite adversaries. The framework has three components: policy, which defines permitted behavior and may concern confidentiality, integrity, or availability; threat model, which states assumptions about attackers; and mechanism, which enforces policy under those assumptions. Security design is iterative, requiring developers to identify and repair weak assumptions or flawed mechanisms. Although systems have breaking points, careful testing can establish where security mechanisms work and fail.

Examples show how each component can fail. Weak recovery-question policies enabled account takeovers, while interactions among Amazon, Apple, and Gmail permitted a password-reset chain despite individually reasonable behavior. Threat models may wrongly assume secure user behavior, permanent cryptographic strength, trustworthy certificate authorities, or secure hardware and software supply chains. Mechanism failures include missing login throttling in iCloud, missing authorization checks at Citibank, an uninitialized Java random-number generator that enabled Bitcoin theft, and inconsistent SSL name encoding.

A C demonstration shows how an oversized input can overwrite a stack buffer, corrupt the return address, crash the process, or redirect execution to attacker-supplied shell code. Non-executable stacks raise the difficulty but can be bypassed through techniques such as return-to-libc attacks. The lecturer emphasizes testing edge cases, fixing unsafe code, and minimizing the trusted computing base so security depends on fewer components.

Tesla, Inc. filed an unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2018, reporting automotive and energy generation and storage operations. For the three months, revenue was $4.00 billion, gross profit was $618.9 million, operating loss was $621.4 million, and net loss was $742.7 million, or $4.22 per diluted share, compared with a $401.4 million net loss and $2.04 loss per share in 2017. For the first six months, revenue was $7.41 billion and net loss was $1.53 billion, or $8.42 per diluted share, compared with revenue of $5.49 billion and a $798.6 million net loss in 2017.

At June 30, 2018, Tesla reported $27.91 billion of assets, $22.64 billion of liabilities, $3.91 billion of stockholders’ equity, and $2.24 billion of cash and cash equivalents. Inventory rose to $3.32 billion from $2.26 billion at year-end, while operating lease vehicles fell to $2.28 billion from $4.12 billion. During the first six months, Tesla used $528.0 million in operating cash, $1.41 billion in investing cash, and received $770.3 million from financing activities; cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash declined by $1.18 billion to $2.78 billion.

Tesla adopted ASC 606 on January 1, 2018 using the modified retrospective method, reducing opening accumulated deficit by $623.2 million. The standard changed the accounting for certain vehicle sales with resale-value guarantees from leases or collateralized borrowings to sales with a right of return, affecting revenue timing and classifications. Tesla also planned to adopt the lease standard on January 1, 2019, expecting material effects, including recognition of right-of-use assets and liabilities.

The filing reported total debt principal of $10.91 billion and compliance with all debt covenants. Warranty reserves totaled $524.0 million at June 30, including $37.1 million added through the revenue-standard adoption. Tesla also disclosed supply-chain concentration risk and a 2018 CEO performance award covering 20,264,042 options across 12 market-capitalization and operating-milestone-based vesting tranches.

The passage criticizes Yale law professor Keith E. Whittington’s argument that, following Kirk’s assassination, professors should exercise discretion and avoid offensive or politically polarizing statements to preserve academic freedom. It rejects his claim that faculty speech must always remain germane and competent to avoid discipline, arguing that this standard could suppress even brief, off-topic expressions of emotion and permit viewpoint discrimination. Citing the AAUP’s 1940 Statement of Principles and its 1970 Interpretive Comments, the passage says discretion was intended as moral persuasion rather than grounds for punishment and that controversy is essential to free academic inquiry. It concludes that academic freedom should protect all professors, including those whose views are offensive or widely disliked, because free expression supports intellectual honesty and a free society.

Wyong Race Club and owner Gary Leafe are negotiating compensation after dogs attacked Eyes To Heaven on the track, severely injuring the filly. Leafe seeks $8,300 for three months of training and feed costs; the club wants a settlement but questions the calculation.

Hugh Bowman is seeking reductions to two suspensions so he can ride Winx in the Apollo Stakes, with appeals at Racing NSW and in New Zealand.

Michael Tubman marked his 70th birthday with part-owned Bye See’s Freshmark Handicap win. Gary Harley and Evan Holland were knocked down by Allez Rev after a Gosford race but escaped injury. Brad Widdup is expanding his independent stable, while Corey Brown explained taking Exceltic outside rather than through a gap in the Canonbury Stakes.

Gerald Ryan reports Menari is progressing toward The Galaxy, and Joe Pride plans a limited Terravista campaign beginning with the Lightning Stakes. Kinky Boom’s Caulfield win shortened its Golden Slipper price from $101 to $35.

At Microsoft Corporation’s 2018 Annual Shareholders Meeting on November 28, 2018, 6,722,310,265 of 7,677,511,729 shares entitled to vote were represented. Shareholders elected all 14 director nominees, receiving between 97.4% and 99.9% support. They approved named executive officer compensation on an advisory basis with 96.0% support and ratified Deloitte & Touche LLP as Microsoft’s independent registered public accounting firm for fiscal 2019 with 97.6% support.

Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2016 reported unaudited U.S. GAAP financial results. Quarterly revenue was $20.531 billion, compared with $21.729 billion a year earlier; nine-month revenue was $64.706 billion versus $71.400 billion. Quarterly net income was $3.756 billion, down from $4.985 billion, while diluted EPS declined to $0.47 from $0.61. Nine-month net income was $13.676 billion, compared with $15.388 billion. Operating income fell to $5.283 billion for the quarter and $17.102 billion for the nine months.

At March 31, 2016, cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments totaled $105.552 billion, total assets were $181.869 billion, total liabilities were $107.063 billion, and stockholders’ equity was $74.806 billion. Net cash from operations was $10.367 billion for the quarter and $24.861 billion for nine months. Microsoft repurchased $11.2 billion of stock through its repurchase program during the nine months and paid $8.185 billion in dividends.

The company reported three segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. For the quarter, their revenue was $6.522 billion, $6.096 billion, and $9.458 billion, respectively, with operating income of $2.994 billion, $2.188 billion, and $1.645 billion. Corporate and Other reported a $1.545 billion operating loss, largely from Windows 10 revenue deferrals.

Third-quarter operating highlights included a commercial-cloud annualized run rate above $10 billion, 22.2 million Office 365 Consumer subscribers, 110% Azure revenue growth, more than 270 million active Windows 10 devices, and 46 million Xbox Live monthly active users.

Microsoft used derivatives to manage foreign-exchange, equity, interest-rate, credit, and commodity risks and held substantial investments in securities and derivatives. Long-term debt had a carrying value of $40.9 billion and an estimated fair value of $43.5 billion. The company also disclosed $12.7 billion of tax contingencies and an unresolved IRS transfer-pricing matter.

The report described 14 acquisitions completed for $1.3 billion during the nine months, ongoing phone-business restructuring charges, approximately 55 other patent cases, antitrust matters, a Chinese regulatory investigation, and cell-phone litigation. Deloitte’s review found no material modifications needed to the interim financial statements.

Britain's Financial Ombudsman Service reported consumer credit complaints rose to 7,281 in the three months to June 30, up from 5,846 a year earlier, criticising lenders' poor affordability checks. Payday loans made up nearly half (3,126), followed by hire purchase (1,334). Full-year complaints leapt 89%, while PPI remained the most-complained product, with a claim deadline of August 29, 2019.

Using self-consistent quasiparticle GW with ladder-diagram vertex corrections (QSGŴ), the study investigates proximity-induced excitonic and magnetic effects in bilayer WSe₂/CrI₃ and ferromagnetically or antiferromagnetically coupled trilayer heterostructures. DFT-optimized structures include the C1 stacking arrangement, interlayer strain, and magnetic configurations. LDA predicts a type-II, 0.77 eV gap, whereas QSGW and QSGŴ predict type-I gaps of 2.33 and 2.21 eV, respectively, with both band edges dominated by WSe₂ states.

The calculations reproduce the WSe₂ A and B excitons and the principal CrI₃ Frenkel excitons near 1.45, 1.85, and 2.10 eV. They also predict robust bright interlayer excitons around 1.84 eV, between the A and B excitons, across all bilayer and trilayer magnetic variants. These states combine extended WSe₂ character with localized magnetic CrI₃ character, have binding energies near 400 meV, and are roughly twenty times brighter than intralayer CrI₃ Frenkel excitons, though about two orders of magnitude darker than the A exciton. Their prominent out-of-plane dipole distinguishes them from the nearby A₂s exciton near 1.83 eV.

Magnetic splittings of the A and B excitons depend strongly on Cr–W band alignment and magnetic configuration. Splittings range from tens to roughly 100 GHz in bilayer and antiferromagnetic trilayer systems to about 1000 GHz in the ferromagnetic trilayer; finite A and B splittings occur in the antiferromagnetic trilayer despite zero net magnetization. Interlayer spacing, strain, and interface coupling can substantially alter these values.

The results identify TMD–vdW-magnet heterostructures as platforms for bright, tunable interlayer excitons for photonic and spintronic applications. Radiative and nonradiative lifetimes were not calculated because the approach omits dynamical vertex effects and exciton–phonon coupling. Exploratory comparisons suggest CrBr₃ could yield brighter interlayer excitons but smaller magnetic splittings than CrI₃.

Finite-temperature molecular-dynamics simulations using an effective Hamiltonian, benchmarked against DFT, investigated Zr-substituted BaTiO₃ (BZT). DFT and simulations confirmed that the ordered 12.5% Zr superlattice has a rhombohedral ground state with polarization along [111]. At 1 K, induced nanodomains persist, and chemical doubling along [111] produces alternating topological textures: one half hosts the canonical −2 antiskyrmion composed of six −1/3 topological quarks, while the other hosts a +4 skyrmion composed of six +2/3 quarks. Both share the same vortex skeleton, with an integer charge offset of +1 per vortex across the chemical interface. A field-theoretic half-translation model describes this alternation, but the microscopic charge-transfer mechanism remains unresolved.

With random Zr substitution from 0% to 12.5%, stable, nontrivial textures remain at 1 K, but compositional disorder pins and distorts vortices, redistributes fractional charges, and produces irregular axial charge fluctuations and a patchwork, skyrmion-glass-like state. Nontrivial topology persists during heating until nanodomain collapse. Pure BT has the highest stability, with critical temperatures of approximately 65 K for 3.5 nm domains and 110 K for 6.5 nm domains. Random substitution lowers stability initially, with a minimum near 6–8% Zr and partial recovery toward 12.5%, reflecting competition between ferroelectric softening and disorder-assisted pinning.

In the ordered 12.5% superlattice, rhombohedral order remains stable above room temperature, with transitions near 320 K on cooling and 345 K on heating. Reversed domains do not persist without bias at 293 K, but a local [111]-directed field of 350 kV/cm writes and maintains nontrivial domains with uniform Q = +4 textures. These states are volatile and require continued field application. In random 12.5% BZT, the same field instead destabilizes a single domain and produces multidomain fragmentation.

The study identifies BZT as a platform for fractionalized ferroelectric topologies and proposes strain, electrostatic engineering, and compositional patterning as routes to improved room-temperature retention. Finite-size and disorder-dependent variability limit the quantitative thermal bounds, while experimental realization and interplane charge transport remain open questions.

Michael Liersch, head of goals-based advice and strategy at JPMorgan, says investors can succeed by planning, maintaining perspective, and staying the course. His five tips are:

1. Create a budget to understand how income is allocated among spending, giving, saving, and investing, then adjust as needed.
2. Reframe investing as a way to afford future goals rather than sacrificing current spending; view market declines as buying opportunities.
3. Invest for the long term, remain patient, and avoid panic selling or trying to time the market.
4. Seek a second opinion from someone who can challenge your views, such as a spouse, relative, or financial adviser.
5. Start with small steps, such as paying down credit card debt, adding money to an IRA, or automating savings contributions to build momentum.

Asian-Pacific stocks rose after U.S. officials downplayed conflict risks with North Korea, while Japan’s second-quarter growth beat expectations on strong household spending. U.S. stocks posted their largest weekly loss in months despite a Friday rebound, weighed down by disappointing earnings and geopolitical tensions. July inflation remained subdued, the dollar weakened, and markets largely discounted North Korean provocations. Trump said U.S. forces were “locked and loaded,” while Fed President Robert Kaplan said interest rates were appropriate pending clearer signs of higher inflation.

A May 24, 2001 compilation of Indian news reports chronicled the escalating dispute over Enron-promoted Dabhol Power Company and the Maharashtra State Electricity Board. Madhav Godbole, chairman of the state’s renegotiation committee, resigned after Sharad Pawar criticized the panel’s negative approach, but withdrew after Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh and the state Cabinet expressed confidence in him. The episode canceled a meeting with DPC, threatened the nine-party coalition and widened the ruling coalition’s rift. Pawar said his comments were personal and urged the panel to continue negotiations to reduce tariffs.

Godbole advocated a judicial inquiry into alleged favors to Enron, the contract’s legality and inflated demand projections. He said only a portion of Phase I was needed by Maharashtra, utilization averaged 30–40%, and the committee would continue examining Phase II and restructuring MSEB. A report excerpt said prolonged negotiations raised tariffs, the project’s base-load design was flawed, projected industrial demand failed to materialize, and Phase II absorption would require substantial tariff increases, greater consumption and reduced commercial losses.

The central government said it would facilitate a settlement but avoid a Centre-state dispute until Maharashtra decided whether to proceed or terminate the project. It pledged to consider worthwhile committee recommendations acceptable to DPC and MSEB, appointed A. V. Gokak to the panel, formed an interministerial group and assured lenders that the crisis would be addressed. NTPC was ruled out as a rescuer, while the Power Trading Corporation was considered for disposing of surplus power in deficit states.

DPC had issued a preliminary termination notice amid a dispute over power bills and a Rs 401 crore rebate claim. Maharashtra referred the disagreements to the state electricity regulator to defer arbitration. Domestic lenders suspended Phase II disbursements but remained optimistic about a government-mediated meeting; Indian lenders had provided about $1.4 billion of the project’s $3 billion financing. MSEB also faced a contempt petition for failing to provide confidential project documents to the NGO Prayas. Commentators said Dabhol had prompted wider scrutiny of private power agreements and underlined the need for distribution, tariff and contracting reforms.

Based on Pershing Square’s August 14, 2017 13F filing, Ackman’s U.S. long portfolio increased from $5.96 billion to $6.01 billion while remaining at seven positions. It stayed highly concentrated: Restaurant Brands International (~41%), Chipotle Mexican Grill (~20%), and Mondelēz International (10.41%) represented 71.06% collectively.

Principal changes included establishing a ~3% Automatic Data Processing stake at $97.30 per share, increasing Howard Hughes Corp. by one-third through warrant conversion, reducing Mondelēz, and selling the remaining ~5% Air Products and Chemicals position at about $145 per share. Restaurant Brands and Chipotle remained unchanged, while Platform Specialty Products was trimmed ~5%. Nomad Foods was also held. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were partnership holdings disclosed outside the 13F. Pershing Square’s only publicly known short was a 9% allocation to Herbalife.

The paper argues that the reproduction number \(R\), which tracks the growth rate of detected cases, can be biased when testing levels vary over time. Because testing determines how many infections and negative cases are observed, changes in case counts may reflect diagnostic activity rather than changes in viral transmission.

The authors present the acceleration index \(\varepsilon\), a unit-free elasticity defined as the proportional change in cumulative cases divided by the proportional change in cumulative tests. It can also be interpreted as the ratio of current to average viral speed, where positivity rates represent speed. Values above one indicate acceleration; values below one indicate deceleration.

The theoretical analysis relates the two measures as \(\varepsilon = R \times A/B\), where \(A\) is current infectivity intensity and \(B\) is current test intensity. They are equivalent only when test intensity tracks infectivity intensity through an appropriate time-dependent specification. If \(A>B\), the reproduction number underestimates viral acceleration; if \(B>A\), it overestimates acceleration. The acceleration index therefore nests the reproduction number as a test-adjusted special case.

French data from May 13, 2020, through October 26, 2022, covering pre- and post-vaccination periods and two later lockdowns, reveal substantial differences between the measures. The reproduction number often suggested improvement while the acceleration index indicated continued or renewed acceleration, particularly during 2022 and the Omicron wave. Following the second lockdown, the reproduction number suggested widespread deceleration, whereas the acceleration index showed that acceleration persisted in nearly all departments. Similar analyses for five additional countries showed that the direction and size of the discrepancy varied by country and period.

The authors conclude that authorities should track either the acceleration index alone or the reproduction number together with test and infectivity intensities. These approaches are formally equivalent, but the acceleration index is simpler and avoids explicitly controlling time-varying testing bias. An acceleration index above one also indicates that diagnostic capacity should increase so that test intensity can keep pace with infectivity intensity.

Limitations include uncounted and asymptomatic infections, dependence of accuracy on sufficient testing, and the resource costs of testing policies.

The Poland Local Board of Education dissolved teacher Cassandra Kibler’s contract amid an investigation into allegations of an inappropriate relationship with a student. Kibler had been on unpaid leave since April 2017, and her Ohio teaching license was revoked. The board also reviewed two proposals to reduce district operating costs through school consolidation and construction but took no action.

- California’s electricity crisis was attributed to deregulation combined with capped retail rates and utilities’ heavy reliance on volatile short-term wholesale markets. Generators, traders, aluminum producers, farms, and others profited from electricity scarcity, while consumers and utilities suffered sharply; Pacific Gas & Electric filed for bankruptcy. Enron reported a 75% rise in wholesale-services profits, though it said little came from California.
- Enron was considering buying U.K. power stations to meet supply obligations, profit from price swings, and provide risk-management services. Under the U.K. balancing system, spot prices ranged from £1,036 to negative £434 per megawatt hour. Possible acquisition targets included the Fiddler’s Ferry and Ferrybridge stations.
- Scottish Power was restructuring after falling pretax profit, a six-month Hunter power-plant outage costing about $160 million, market competition, and regulatory price controls. It was considering selling Southern Water, retaining its 50% stake in the unprofitable Thus telecommunications venture, and possibly acquiring Enron’s Portland General unit, while investors questioned the clarity of its strategy.
- Enron’s Dabhol Power Company in India remained in conflict with the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, which disputed the cost of power and had defaulted on some payments. Lenders to the $2.9 billion project sought lower interest rates and government intervention, threatened legal action, and sought $48 million in unpaid bills; the dispute threatened the second phase of the plant. Maharashtra also blocked roughly $300 crore worth of imported equipment over a customs-duty dispute.
- An Indian commentary said more than a decade of power-sector reforms had failed to reduce outages and had weakened state electricity boards. It urged the government to restore public-sector coal- and gas-generation investment and make state boards financially viable before relying on private investment.
- Northern Border Partners completed its roughly $100 million acquisition of the 350-mile Midwestern Gas Transmission system following Federal Trade Commission approval. General partners in Northern Border Partners were owned by Enron and Williams.
- BP Amoco was studying a roughly $200 million LNG terminal at the Port of Tampa, including storage, regasification, and a pipeline to utility customers. The project would require several years of approvals and compete with terminals planned by Enron, El Paso, and other energy companies.
- A federal appeals court ruled that Enron could fulfill its contracts to supply California public universities by buying power from investor-owned utilities rather than the spot market. Enron said the change would save it up to $12 million monthly, while California said it would increase state costs and planned to seek reconsideration.

Simone Askew became the first Black woman to lead West Point’s 4,400-member Corps of Cadets as first captain. The 20-year-old international history major led 1,200 new cadets during a 12-mile training march. She advises aspiring young women leaders to seek mentorship and remain open to learning. West Point graduate Pat Locke calls her a role model, while her mother describes her as a natural leader.

Syrian rebels faced a Wednesday deadline in talks with Russia to accept tough surrender terms for remaining territory in Daraa and Quneitra or face renewed military attacks. Russia, backing Assad’s forces’ two-week offensive, rejected rebels’ ceasefire proposal and required the army to return to pre-2011 positions, with local police taking over towns and no population transfers. Air strikes had paused, and more than 30 towns had returned to regime control. The offensive expanded regime control of Daraa province to about 60% and displaced 270,000–330,000 people, while Jordan and Israel kept their borders closed. More than 140 civilians were killed, including 11 family members killed by a land mine. World powers criticized the operation as violating a ceasefire, and the UN Security Council planned an emergency meeting.

Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2017 describes a technology company founded in 1975 and operating in more than 190 countries. Its strategy centers on an intelligent cloud and intelligent edge infused with artificial intelligence, supported by three ambitions: reinventing productivity and business processes, building its cloud platform, and creating more personal computing. Its products and services include operating systems, productivity and business applications, cloud services, developer tools, server products, video games, devices, training, consulting, online advertising, and intelligent devices.

Microsoft reports through three operating segments. Productivity and Business Processes includes Office Commercial and Consumer, LinkedIn, and Dynamics. Microsoft completed its $27 billion LinkedIn acquisition in December 2016, intending to accelerate Office 365, Dynamics 365, and LinkedIn growth. Intelligent Cloud includes SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center, Azure, and enterprise support and consulting services. Azure provides public, private, and hybrid cloud capabilities, including analytics, AI, machine learning, IoT, database, storage, and application-development services. More Personal Computing includes Windows, devices such as Surface and HoloLens, gaming through Xbox and related content and services, and search advertising. Microsoft sold its feature-phone business, including a manufacturing facility in Vietnam, in November 2016.

The company operates regional support centers and datacenters across the Americas, Australia, Europe, and Asia, localizes products internationally, and relies primarily on third-party manufacturers for devices. Research and development expense was $13.0 billion in fiscal 2017, representing 14% of revenue, with investments conducted through product groups focused on Office, AI and research, cloud and enterprise, Windows and devices, and LinkedIn. Microsoft also operates Microsoft Research and reported more than 66,000 issued patents and over 35,000 pending patents.

Products are distributed through OEMs, direct sales, distributors, resellers, retailers, and online channels. Volume-licensing programs include Enterprise Agreements, Microsoft Product and Services Agreements, Open and Open Value programs, Select Plus for government and academic organizations, and the Microsoft Online Subscription Agreement. Partner programs support cloud, software-service, and independent-software-vendor resellers. Microsoft’s customers include consumers, businesses of all sizes, public-sector organizations, developers, service providers, and OEMs; no individual customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in fiscal 2017, 2016, or 2015.

As of June 30, 2017, Microsoft employed approximately 124,000 people full-time: 73,000 in the United States and 51,000 internationally, including 40,000 in product research and development. Executive leadership included CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, President and Chief Legal Officer Bradford Smith, and executives responsible for marketing, global sales, human resources, and business development.

The report identifies extensive risks, including intense competition across platforms, business models, cloud services, devices, gaming, and advertising; uncertain returns on investments in new products and infrastructure; delays or defects in software and hardware; integration and impairment risks associated with acquisitions, including LinkedIn; inadequate intellectual-property protection; patent and licensing disputes; cybersecurity attacks, source-code exposure, service outages, and customer-data breaches; antitrust, privacy, trade, anti-corruption, tax, and other regulatory requirements; difficulty attracting and retaining talent; litigation; and component shortages or manufacturing disruptions. These factors could reduce revenue, increase costs, damage reputation or competitive position, impair goodwill or intangible assets, and materially affect operating results and financial condition.

The commissioner expressed confidence that Las Vegas is a strong NHL market, citing early fan enthusiasm and noting that league officials were not deterred by expansion there. Building, ownership, and economic issues caused delays, but the timing belongs to the team, with no negative effect on the NHL season or Seattle. He called the expansion team’s success positive for hockey, said its competitiveness does not disparage other teams, and cited scientists’ conclusion that there is insufficient information to draw a link under discussion. He also praised the franchise’s community outreach.

The study examined how three Ethiopian policy documents—the 2023 Education and Training Policy, 2020 General Education Curriculum Framework, and 2012 Guidelines for Curriculum Differentiation and Individualized Educational Programs—conceptualized curriculum differentiation and how principals and teachers in two Addis Ababa government secondary schools understood it. Using a case-study design, researchers reviewed the policy documents and interviewed two principals and 17 subject teachers from one regular school serving mixed-ability students and one special-day school admitting high academic achievers.

Policy intentions differed: the 2023 policy and 2020 framework emphasized differentiation through school types, streams, fields of study, and subjects, while the 2012 guidelines emphasized differentiating content, instructional processes, assessment, and learning environments in inclusive classrooms. Participants’ conceptualizations fell into five themes: gifted programs, placement into subjects, streams and schools, special curricula for groups, identification and accommodation of talents, and curricular planning or teaching strategies. The latter largely reflected limited awareness, while the strong focus on gifted and high-achieving students often differed from policy emphasis on inclusion. The study also found no clear system distinguishing high achievers from gifted or talented students.

The findings identified a tension between tracking and inclusion, with the absence of coherent policy guidance contributing to divergent interpretations and practices. Special-day and boarding schools had been expanded for high academic achievers amid emphasis on examination pass rates. The study recommended aligning policy documents, clarifying how gifted students are identified and selected, and offering more flexible subjects, tracks, difficulty levels, vocational options, arts, and assessments responsive to students’ interests, abilities, and career aspirations.

Former FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe was fired March 16, two days before his planned early retirement at age 50, following an Inspector General investigation into unauthorized media disclosures related to the bureau’s Hillary Clinton email probe. His firing may prevent him from receiving his Federal Employees Retirement System pension until age 57 and eight months and from obtaining health coverage for himself and his family. CNN estimated his pension at about $60,000 annually under an enhanced law-enforcement rate. Because McCabe fell short of the service required for early retirement eligibility, lawmakers proposed temporary federal jobs to restore eligibility, though a former law enforcement official disputed whether a short appointment would suffice. McCabe may appeal, and no criminal charges related to his firing are expected.

The St. Louis Blues have a strong, stable core, with nine key players signed through at least three seasons for a combined $47.425 million. Vladimir Tarasenko, Alex Pietrangelo and Colton Parayko anchor the group, while Alexander Steen, Vladimir Sobotka and Patrik Berglund face questions about age or performance. Jay Bouwmeester, Carl Gunnarsson, Robert Bortuzzo and Nate Prosser have contracts expiring soon, while Joel Edmundson is expected to become a restricted free agent. The Blues must also decide whether to re-sign Paul Stastny, whose deal ends after 2017-18, and whether to retain promising 21-year-old Robby Fabbri. Vince Dunn and Jordan Schmaltz could eventually strengthen the defense. Although the loss of David Backes and Troy Brouwer has left the team without a prominent surplus scorer, the Blues’ favorable contracts and strong organizational position suggest their core could continue to improve.

NVIDIA Corporation filed a Form 8-K on February 24, 2021, announcing financial results for the quarter and fiscal year ended January 31, 2021. The filing furnished a press release (Exhibit 99.1) and CFO Colette M. Kress’s commentary (Exhibit 99.2), which were not deemed filed and would not be incorporated by reference into other SEC filings.
The CBI began probing the alleged SSC CGL Tier II 2017 paper leak. The Supreme Court declined a monitored probe but allowed petitioners to seek remedies if dissatisfied.

NVIDIA Corporation filed an unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended July 28, 2019, its second quarter of fiscal 2020. The company reported 609 million common shares outstanding as of August 9, 2019 and classified itself as a large accelerated filer.

Second-quarter revenue was $2.579 billion, down 17% from $3.123 billion a year earlier but up 16% sequentially. Gross margin was 59.8%, compared with 63.3% a year earlier and 58.4% in the prior quarter. Operating expenses increased 19% year over year to $970 million. Operating income fell 51% to $571 million, while net income declined 50% to $552 million and diluted EPS fell 49% to $0.90. Sequentially, operating income, net income and diluted EPS increased 59%, 40% and 41%, respectively. For the first six months, revenue fell 24% to $4.799 billion, operating income fell to $929 million from $2.452 billion, net income fell to $947 million from $2.345 billion, and diluted EPS was $1.54 versus $3.74.

GPU revenue was $2.104 billion, down 21% year over year, while Tegra Processor revenue was $475 million, up 2%. By platform, Gaming revenue was $1.313 billion, down 27%; Professional Visualization revenue was $291 million, up 4%; Data Center revenue was $655 million, down 14%; Automotive revenue was $209 million, up 30%; and OEM and Other revenue was $111 million, down 4%. Gaming declines reflected lower desktop GPU and gaming-platform module shipments, partly offset by notebook GPU growth. Data Center weakness reflected lower hyperscale revenue, partly offset by enterprise growth from expanding AI workloads. Automotive growth primarily reflected a development-services agreement, AI cockpit solutions and autonomous-vehicle development agreements. Revenue from customers outside the United States represented 93% of total revenue, and one customer accounted for approximately 11%.

At July 28, 2019, cash and cash equivalents were $7.105 billion, marketable securities were $1.370 billion, total assets were $14.775 billion, total liabilities were $4.439 billion and shareholders’ equity was $10.336 billion. During the first six months, operating activities generated $1.656 billion, investing activities provided $5.040 billion and financing activities used $373 million. Cash and cash equivalents increased by $6.323 billion to $7.105 billion.

The company adopted the new lease accounting standard on January 28, 2019, recognizing $470 million of operating lease assets and $500 million of operating lease liabilities. Future minimum lease payments totaled $683 million, with a present value of $567 million and a weighted-average remaining term of 8.7 years.

NVIDIA agreed on March 10, 2019 to acquire Mellanox Technologies for $125 per share in cash, representing an approximately $6.9 billion enterprise value. Mellanox shareholders approved the transaction in June 2019; regulatory approval had been received in the United States and Mexico, while European and Chinese reviews were pending. A $350 million termination fee could apply in certain circumstances involving failure to obtain required approvals.

NVIDIA returned $195 million through cash dividends during the first six months and intended to return $2.11 billion of its previously announced $3 billion shareholder-return plan through repurchases and dividends. Repurchases were not expected before the Mellanox acquisition closed and could extend into fiscal 2021. The company also had $7.24 billion of remaining repurchase authorization through December 2022.

The filing disclosed securities and derivative litigation concerning statements about channel inventory and cryptocurrency mining’s effect on GPU demand, as well as litigation related to the Mellanox merger. NVIDIA had not accrued liabilities for these matters because losses were not considered probable. Disclosure controls were concluded to be effective, no material changes in internal control over financial reporting occurred, and there were no material changes in previously reported risk factors or market risks.
