MIT 6.832 Lecture 22 reviews model-free optimal control and introduces actor-critic methods. Policy-gradient algorithms directly perform local stochastic gradient descent on policy parameters, can scale well in some high-dimensional systems, and are described as having strong convergence guarantees. Their drawbacks include high-variance updates, poor performance as policy-parameter counts grow, sensitivity to smoothness and tuning choices, and the need for many samples or trials. Value-function and temporal-difference methods are relatively compact and data-efficient because they reuse estimates, and can outperform policy gradients when they converge well. However, their convergence guarantees are often weak when function approximation and changing policies are involved, and some methods diverge or oscillate. A central instability is that small changes in a value-function estimate can produce large changes in the resulting policy.

Actor-critic methods combine both approaches by representing the policy as an “actor” and a value estimate as a “critic.” Slower policy updates based on the critic are intended to preserve policy-gradient convergence while improving efficiency and reducing update variance. A value-function baseline compares observed reward with expected reward and can dramatically reduce estimator variance. If the baseline is uncorrelated with injected perturbation noise, it vanishes in expectation and does not affect convergence; even a poor baseline can preserve convergence, though a better estimate speeds learning. The lecture also connects actor-critic updates to the policy gradient theorem and cites work by Konda and Tsitsiklis, Sutton, and Peters.

A perturbation-based policy-gradient estimator can compare runs with and without added parameter noise, but this requires duplicate trials and resembles a deterministic update. Actor-critic methods instead estimate expected performance and compare it with a single sampled outcome.

The lecture presents Russ Tedrake’s “Toddler” robot as a model-free learning success story. Toddler is an underactuated walking robot with passive walking behavior and ankle actuation. It used online actor-critic learning, updating its policy after each footstep and penalizing deviation of its Poincaré return map from a desired deadbeat map. Without building an accurate robot model, it learned to step, walk, stabilize its limit cycle, and adapt to disturbances and changing terrain. Its learned controller was more stable than Tedrake’s hand-designed controllers. Learning typically took 10–20 minutes when policy and value estimates were learned simultaneously, but retaining a previously learned value estimate reduced convergence time to about two minutes. A very low-dimensional value estimate, with a discount factor of 0.2, was sufficient to reduce variance and accelerate learning. The lecture also briefly discusses walking-robot approaches, including passive walkers, Sony robots, and ASIMO’s energy-intensive strategy of avoiding underactuation by keeping its feet flat.

The lecture concludes with project logistics: written reports were due May 21, and 19 projects were scheduled for eight-minute oral presentations.

Kathrine Clark, proceeding pro se, appealed the modification of Ricky G. Rau’s custody and child-support order. After a bench trial, the trial court awarded Rau sole legal and physical custody of their three children. Because Clark provided no transcript and her brief failed to meet appellate rules, the majority applied the presumption of regularity, declined to construct arguments on her behalf, and affirmed. It also held that the order sufficiently addressed the children’s welfare through its finding of a material change affecting them and did not need to quote the best-interest standard verbatim.

The dissent argued that the order was facially deficient because it made no best-interest determination and that Clark’s arguments clearly raised the issue, permitting review despite her defective brief. It would have vacated the judgment and remanded for application of the proper legal standard. The dissent distinguished precedent relied on by the majority because its detailed custody order expressly found that the change would promote the children’s welfare.

Under a May bilateral trade deal, China agreed to accept U.S. beef and liquefied natural gas, while the United States began allowing exports of cooked Chinese poultry. The U.S. is not short of poultry—it is the world’s largest producer and second-largest exporter after Brazil—and the cooked-only restriction likely addresses avian-influenza concerns. Since 2013, China has reported 1,557 AH7N9 human cases and 370 deaths. Properly cooked poultry presents no viral or bacterial food-safety risk, but undercooking or cross-contamination can transmit Salmonella and Campylobacter; Chinese infection-rate data are unavailable. Other concerns include antibiotic residues and heavy metals. China’s rules are less robustly enforced, transparency is limited, and although Beijing announced stronger surveillance by 2020, contamination remains uncertain. USDA inspectors require equivalent foreign safeguards, government certification, regular inspections and annual on-site audits. Cooked poultry and restaurant use are exempt from country-of-origin labeling, so consumers may not know its origin. Market adoption will depend chiefly on price; China’s poultry industry is less integrated and technologically advanced than the U.S. industry, limiting short-term competition despite lower labor costs.

The article defines a bear market as one in which the market closes below its 200-day moving average and a bull market as one above it. Under this mechanical definition, bear markets occur about twice a year, average 25 trading days, and cover roughly 30% of the S&P 500’s time since 1960. It attributes poor investor results to behavioral biases such as buying high and selling low, illustrated by investors in the CGM Focus Fund losing 11% annually despite the fund’s 18.2% annual gain.

Traders are advised to prepare by backtesting strategies under strict rules, reviewing historical performance, and testing across different business cycles. They should maintain short strategies because they tend to work better during falling markets. The article also presents backtests showing that short strategies, and a long-only ATR swing strategy on QQQ, can perform well during bear markets. It emphasizes compounding, preserving capital, and the importance of the sequence of returns, while noting that the long strategy may underperform in strong bull markets.

Prepared traders should continue following their tested systems rather than reacting to fear or short-term news. Long-term investors are advised to keep investing because lower prices offer opportunities to buy, and the article describes stocks as a long-term inflation hedge with positive real returns. It also states that trend-following crypto strategies have held up in prior bear markets, assuming investor interest declines with crypto prices.

The passage describes NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPU architecture, its RTX 50-series GeForce products, and related rendering, AI, media, and power-management technologies. FLUX.dev is cited as requiring more than 23GB of VRAM at FP16 but less than 10GB at FP4; on an RTX 4090, FP16 image generation takes 15 seconds at 30 steps.

Blackwell’s fourth-generation RT Cores double ray-triangle intersection throughput and include Opacity Micromap Engine and Triangle Cluster Intersection Engine hardware. Mega Geometry enables full-fidelity ray tracing of modern level-of-detail systems such as Nanite by using Cluster-Level Acceleration Structures, GPU-driven APIs, and Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structures. CLAS structures can contain up to 256 triangles and reduce subsequent BVH-build processing by two orders of magnitude, while PTLAS updates only changed scene partitions. Mega Geometry also accelerates ray tracing of animated subdivision surfaces. It is supported through DirectX 12 with NVAPI, Vulkan extensions, and OptiX 9.0 on RTX GPUs from Turing onward. Blackwell also adds hardware-accelerated Linear Swept Spheres for strand geometry; common hair-rendering cases are about twice as fast as DOTS and require roughly one-fifth the VRAM.

SER 2.0 makes shader reordering logic twice as efficient and more precise, benefiting divergent ray-tracing workloads and neural shading. The programmable AI Management Processor uses a dedicated RISC-V processor to schedule GPU contexts, reducing CPU involvement and latency while coordinating AI and graphics workloads under Windows HAGS.

Blackwell adds 4:2:2 H.264 and HEVC encode/decode support. Its ninth-generation NVENC improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% in BD-BR PSNR, with an additional AV1 UHQ mode offering another 5% improvement and combined gains of up to 15%. The RTX 5090 supports three encoders and two decoders, increasing export speeds by more than 50% generation over generation. The sixth-generation NVDEC doubles H.264 decoding speed. DisplayPort 2.1b provides up to 80Gbps through UHBR 20, supporting 8K at 165Hz and 4K at 480Hz with DSC.

Blackwell’s Max-Q improvements include fine-grained clock, unit, and voltage-rail gating; separate rails for GPU cores and memory; frequency switching up to 1,000 times faster than earlier architectures; and sleep-state entry ten times faster than Ada. In a small-language-model inference example, these changes produced power savings of up to 50%.

DLSS 4 adds Multi Frame Generation, which can create up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame. Its AI model is 40% faster and uses 30% less VRAM than the preceding generation, while enhanced Flip Metering moves pacing to the display engine. New transformer-based models for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA use twice as many parameters and improve temporal stability, motion detail, anti-aliasing, and ray-traced image quality.

Cooperative Vectors for DirectX 12 and Vulkan, together with Slang features, allow Tensor Cores to be used from any shader stage. Blackwell neural-shader applications include RTX Neural Materials, Neural Texture Compression, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin, and RTX Neural Faces. Neural texture compression can provide up to seven-to-one VRAM compression over block-compressed formats; one demonstration reduced material storage from 1,110MB to 333MB. Neural Radiance Cache trains small networks on live game data to infer indirect lighting after one bounce, reducing ray-tracing work. RTX Skin applies ray-traced subsurface scattering, while Neural Faces uses a TensorRT-optimized generative model to infer realistic faces from rasterized faces and 3D pose data.

The full GB202 chip has 92.2 billion transistors, 192 streaming multiprocessors, 24,576 CUDA cores, 192 RT Cores, and 768 Tensor Cores; it powers the GeForce RTX 5090. GB203 has 45.6 billion transistors, 84 multiprocessors, 10,752 CUDA cores, 84 RT Cores, and 336 Tensor Cores, and is used by the RTX 5080 and 5070 Ti. GB205 contains 31 billion transistors, 50 multiprocessors, 6,400 CUDA cores, 50 RT Cores, and 200 Tensor Cores, and is used by the RTX 5070. The passage concludes with NVIDIA’s disclaimers that specifications may change, products are provided as-is, and suitability for particular applications requires customer validation.

Strength training improves muscle mass, strength, endurance, and independence, but correct technique, suitable loads, warm-ups, cool-downs, and gradual increases in intensity are essential for preventing injury. Common injuries include rotator cuff tears and tendinopathy, hamstring strains, herniated discs, tendonitis, tennis elbow, and golfer’s elbow. They may result from repetitive or sudden movements, overuse, poor form, or lifting weights beyond one’s current ability.

Preventive measures include maintaining good shoulder-blade posture, regularly stretching, warming up properly, modifying exercises that cause discomfort, and ensuring recovery between workouts. Warming up increases blood flow and prepares muscles for exercise, while cooling down helps blood vessels and the heart ease after activity. Static stretches are most useful after exercise; dynamic movements are preferable beforehand.

Stop exercising if pain persists rather than pushing through it. Rest, gentle activity, hydration, a good diet, and ice, compression, and elevation may aid recovery or initial treatment. Persistent pain warrants medical advice, and a qualified fitness instructor or personal trainer can help create an achievable, properly performed strength-training program.

The output diode’s voltage stress is \(V_{out}+V_{in,max}\), excluding parasitic spikes; the UC1825-SP design therefore selected a 60-V-rated diode. In a push-pull converter, each primary switching MOSFET experiences about twice the input voltage plus ringing when off, requiring a voltage rating approximately 2.5–3 times the input voltage.

Output capacitance is selected to support a full load-current step while meeting the ripple target. The example used approximately 1145 µF, six input-side ceramic capacitors, bulk tantalum capacitors, and a 500 nH output-filter inductor. A parallel 0.5-Ω resistor was specified to damp high-frequency peaking, with an efficiency tradeoff. Type IIB compensation was selected with a 5-kHz target crossover frequency; its zero was placed at least a decade below crossover, and its pole was optimized during testing. The sense resistor measures transformer ripple current and shuts down switching when peak current exceeds the set limit. The CS-pin threshold is approximately 1 V, and the shutdown current must exceed the design’s maximum expected current.

Tests cited include MOSFET voltage stress, output ripple, and a 0-to-10-A output transient using a 48-V input. The stated input operating range is 10–30 V from a well-regulated supply; remote supplies may require bulk capacitance in addition to ceramic bypass capacitors, with 100 µF given as a typical tantalum value. The controller can be used with push-pull, forward, half-bridge, or full-bridge topologies, with selection based on cost, size, and performance.

PCB-layout guidance calls for low-EMI inductors, feedback traces routed directly away from inductors and noisy power traces, input and compensation components placed close to the IC, and short, direct, thick power traces of at least 15 mil per ampere. Inductors, output capacitors, and diodes should be closely grouped. Power and signal grounds may be separated on multilayer boards, and switching-current loops should be arranged to flow consistently in the same direction to reduce EMI.

The output drivers support 2-A peak current and require careful grounding. A power-ground section for high-di/dt paths must connect to PGND, while VCC and VREF require direct bypass using low-ESR/ESL ceramic capacitors; the passage recommends 1-mF capacitors. MOSFET sources, input returns, and the bulk input capacitor connect to power ground, and the output is clamped to VCC and PGND with a high-current Schottky diode. No other circuitry should connect to power ground.

Additional sections cover documentation-update subscriptions, TI E2E support, ESD handling precautions, mechanical and orderable information, and the disclaimer that TI resources are provided as-is, leaving developers responsible for product selection, validation, testing, and compliance.

Human Rights Watch reports that Syrian refugees fleeing violence in north-west Syria face shooting, beating, detention, lack of medical care and forced return at the Turkish border, including incidents involving children and a woman who gave birth during a crossing. Amid escalating attacks in Idlib and elsewhere, monitoring groups reported civilian deaths, while 400,000 besieged residents of Eastern Ghouta face severe food and medicine shortages.

The filing included tax opinions from Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati and DLA Piper LLP and Tesla’s related press release.

Research published in Value in Health found that testing seven cancer-associated genes and providing risk-reduction management could cost-effectively extend life expectancy for women at risk of hereditary breast cancer. Using decision-analytic modeling, researchers compared seven-gene testing with standard BRCA1/2 testing. For 50- and 40-year-old women, the strategy cost $42,067 and $23,734 per life-year gained, respectively, and was considered cost-effective under World Health Organization guidelines. The study appeared in the April 2017 issue.

Police arrested Eric Robinson, 46, and charged him with first-degree murder for allegedly killing his roommate and dumping the body in a dumpster behind a shopping center. The killing occurred within 48 hours at the Plantation townhouse where Robinson, the victim, and a woman lived. Neighbors reported repeated altercations and said police had often been called. Robinson had recent domestic-violence, strangulation, and drug-possession arrests. The victim’s identity is being withheld pending notification of his family.

SOS Pressure Defense uses aggressive automatic contact switching to disrupt screens, deny passing lanes and quick shots, reduce fouls, and force turnovers and rushed shots. The basic “Screen-Over-Switch” sequence alerts the teammate, hedges into the offensive player’s path, and switches assignments.

Off-ball switching aggressively attacks passing lanes. Down and back screens begin with a contact switch, followed by “SNUGGLE” pass-denial positioning. The base-screen “Hi-Lo Switch Rule” calls for switching when the cutter goes baseline but not when the cutter goes over the screen.

On-ball switching differs by location. Above the extended free-throw line, defenders use an aggressive contact switch, followed by SNUGGLE denial, a SMOTHER position on the ballhandler, and a FRONT position on the screener. Below the line, defenders employ a baseline trap and “Triangle I” formation, then close out on the nearest offensive player when the trap is passed out of. Immediate automatic traps address occasional mismatches.

The passage is a continuation patent application claiming priority from earlier U.S. patent and provisional applications. Its drawings depict distributed storage systems, storage clusters, big-data analytics pipelines, and artificial intelligence and machine-learning infrastructure, including methods for GPU-storage interconnection, monitoring, optimization, query processing, data-transformation offloading and caching, and reproducibility.

The disclosed storage systems connect client computing devices to storage arrays through SAN or LAN networks. Storage array controllers perform reads, writes, erasure, monitoring, redundancy, compression, encryption, wear leveling, and device-management functions. NVRAM may buffer data before writes to persistent flash or disk storage and preserve data during power loss. Direct-mapped flash implementations let higher-level system software manage allocation units, data rewriting, erasure, and garbage collection across drives without duplicate lower-level drive-controller processes.

Storage clusters comprise distributed, hot-pluggable nodes or blades connected by internal and external communication fabrics. Data and metadata are striped using erasure coding and redundant copies, allowing continued operation after node or device failures and enabling proactive rebuilding. Authorities own ranges of data or metadata, determine data placement and erasure-coding schemes, and use replicated assignments so data can be located when an authority is unavailable. Placement may use pseudorandom functions such as CRUSH and can account for reachable nodes.

In the described elastic architecture, control, compute, and storage planes are separated logically. Authorities are stateless and may migrate between blades while retaining management of associated flash and NVRAM partitions. Updates are triplicated in NVRAM across separate blades, allowing survival of two concurrent blade failures without data loss. New or failed blades trigger automatic authority redistribution and load rebalancing; disjoint authority partitions reduce distributed locking. Authorities compress incoming data, preserve it temporarily in NVRAM, protect and persist it in flash, and reclaim obsolete data through garbage collection.

The systems may support protocols including NFS, SMB/CIFS, HTTP, IPv4, IPv6, Active Directory, LDAP, and cloud interfaces, along with access controls, audit logs, encryption-key rotation, and dynamic passwords. Storage systems may connect to public or private cloud providers through IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, AaaS, or storage-as-a-service models.

Shop & Save Market signed a letter of intent to open a grocery store in the former Dominick’s space at Jeffery Plaza in South Shore, the last vacant former Dominick’s within city limits. Owner Cezary Jakubowski said the deal is not final, but the store could open in 18–24 months. More than $10 million in city tax increment financing is planned, and the new store may have a different footprint. Shop & Save wants to buy the plaza, retain existing tenants and undertake extensive construction. South Shore has been classified as a food desert since Dominick’s closed in 2014.

The passage describes the device’s power-management, reset, clocking, interrupt, timing, and peripheral architecture. SmartReflex modules use external variable-voltage supplies to minimize power consumption in Core Logic Voltage Domains. Based on process, temperature, and performance requirements, they advise the host processor when to raise or lower each domain’s voltage. The host-to-regulator link can use GPIOs, I²C, SPI, or another system-selected method. Dynamic Voltage Frequency Scaling allows each domain to change operating performance points in real time without a reset; lower-frequency points use lower voltage ranges, although only specified combinations are supported and voltage differences between domains must remain below 150 mV. Adaptive Voltage Scaling is described as continuous, real-time voltage guidance within an operating point’s range, though its section is marked “Not Supported.”

Switchable SRAM blocks can enter shutdown mode, removing their supply voltage and losing their contents; they return to active operation when their power domain is turned on. Selectable ALWAYS_ON SRAM can be shut down through control-module registers. Some I/O groups independently support 1.8 V or 3.3 V, while each DDR interface independently supports 1.5 V or 1.8 V and has isolated supplies. PHYs must enter power-down mode before their associated power domains are switched off. Low-power standby requires all switchable domains off, the ARM Cortex-A8 running an IDLE loop at its lowest frequency, and unused functional blocks clock-gated.

Supplies are divided into four sequencing groups, and specified power-up and power-down orders must be followed. The 1.8 V supplies must be at least as high as the DDR supplies, and the 3.3 V supplies must never be more than 2 V above the 1.8 V supplies. Simultaneous ramp-down is permitted if the stated constraints are met. PLL and analog supplies should use suitable filtering, including ferrite beads and nearby capacitors. Recommended decoupling uses small 0.1 µF capacitors, at least one per two power pins, plus approximately one bulk capacitor of 10 µF or more per ten power pins. Excess capacitance must not alter startup sequencing, and the main reset should remain low until supplies are stable.

The device supports power-on, external warm, emulation warm, watchdog, software global cold, software global warm, test, and local resets. Power-on reset resets the entire chip, including test, emulation, and the EMAC switch, and requires supplies and used clock sources to be stable before deassertion. It places most pins in high impedance, resets modules through the PRCM, latches BTMODE, and starts the Cortex-A8 from the Boot ROM. External warm reset excludes test and emulation logic and can exclude the EMAC switch; emulator sessions remain active during it. Emulation warm reset is initiated through ICEPICK and otherwise follows warm-reset behavior. Watchdog reset follows warm-reset behavior and always asserts RSTOUT_WD_OUT. Software global cold and warm resets are initiated through PRCM control bits; the cold reset does not relatch BTMODE or reset the EMAC switch. Test reset is asserted through TRST, while local reset affects only the selected module. If reset requests coincide, only the highest-priority request is processed.

RSTOUT_WD_OUT reflects reset status and is three-stated while POR or RESET is asserted, allowing an external pull resistor to determine its level. BTMODE[11] controls whether it is asserted for POR and external warm reset, and its behavior differs for watchdog and other reset sources. Most I/O pins become high impedance during reset, with exceptions including emulation pins, isolated EMAC switch pins, and RSTOUT_WD_OUT during certain resets. DDR address and control pins are three-stated during reset and then take their internal-pull reset values. Each power domain has dedicated warm and cold resets triggered by specified global resets and by switching the domain off or on, respectively.

The PCIe subsystem supports isolated reset. Software must place it in an idle state before reset, then re-enumerate the bus and treat endpoints as newly connected. The EMAC switch can similarly remain operational during most resets, except power-on reset, when ISO_CONTROL is enabled; its switch function, reference PLL, selected registers, and pin multiplexing are preserved.

Device clocks are generated through reference inputs, PLLs, dividers, and PRCM multiplexing. DEV and AUX clocks can come from external crystals with internal oscillators or from 1.8 V LVCMOS-compatible sources. The DEV clock is normally 20 MHz but may range from 20–30 MHz under specified restrictions; AUX is optional and can also range from 20–30 MHz for audio or video PLLs. Crystal circuits require load-capacitor calculations and close placement. The PCIe PHY requires a low-jitter differential SERDES clock that is AC-coupled close to the device. Optional external clock inputs include AUD_CLKIN0–2, a 32.768 kHz CLKIN32, and two programmable clock outputs. The device contains 12 top-level and four embedded PLLs; all start in bypass mode after reset and require external filtered supplies. Their multipliers, dividers, and operating frequencies are constrained, and PLL_USB must operate at 960 MHz when USB is used. PRCM-generated SYSCLK and module clock frequencies must also remain within their specified limits.

The Cortex-A8 interrupt controller prioritizes up to 128 requests and generates IRQs or FIQs, although general-purpose devices do not support FIQ generation. The C674x DSP interrupt controller combines up to 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts and allows events 15–95 to be remapped among 24 multiplexed events. It also controls CPU exceptions, nonmaskable interrupts, and emulation interrupts.

AC timing data is referenced to device pins and uses a 4 V/ns input slew rate for 3.3 V signals, with a 1.5 V reference. Board-routing delays must be included in system timing analysis, and IBIS models are recommended for accurate I/O analysis.

The peripheral section describes two DCAN interfaces with CAN 2.0 support, configurable message objects, loopback, bus-off recovery, test-mode message RAM access, configurable CAN pins, and interrupts. The EDMA controller supports up to 64 channels and 512 parameter-table entries for transfers among memory and slave peripherals. Advanced Event Triggering provides hardware program breakpoints, data watchpoints, event or cycle counters, and state sequencing. Cortex-A8 and system trace collect and export real-time execution, timing, and data-access information through the Embedded Trace Buffer or a five-pin trace interface. JTAG supports emulation and boundary scan, and TRST has an internal pulldown for reliable initialization.

The EMAC switch is a three-port gigabit switch with two external ports supporting 10, 100, and 1000 Mb/s operation. It supports MII, GMII, RMII, and RGMII interfaces and uses MDIO to control and monitor multiple external PHYs. Its I/Os operate at 3.3 V and do not support 2.5 V signaling. Instead of using MTXER, the switch signals an underflow by intentionally inverting the frame CRC. MDIO continuously polls 32 addresses and supports PHY configuration, negotiation results, and status monitoring.

The GPIO subsystem contains four modules of 32 channels each, providing up to 128 configurable 1.8 V/3.3 V pins, programmable edge or level interrupts, independent set/clear operations, direct output-register writes, and open-drain support. The GPMC provides a glueless interface for NOR, NAND, SRAM, pseudo-SRAM, and custom logic, with an 8- or 16-bit multiplexed bus, up to eight chip selects, and 512 MB maximum addressing. The associated ELM extracts error addresses from BCH syndromes for NAND blocks and supports 4-, 8-, and 16-bit error-location processing.

The HDMI transmitter is HDMI 1.3a compliant and supports DVI-compatible RGB video, multiple color depths and resolutions, TMDS clocks up to 185.625 MHz, up to eight-channel uncompressed L-PCM audio, CEC, and a master DDC I²C interface. HDMI PCB guidance requires careful TMDS routing with approximately 100 Ω differential and 60 Ω single-ended impedance, paired vias with minimized spacing, pullups for DDC unless integrated in the ESD device, and suitable external ESD protection.

Whitworth University will reduce its advertised annual tuition from $54,000 to $26,900 next fall and base merit discounts solely on GPA, publishing the scholarship scale. Officials say the change responds to research showing students and parents want earlier, clearer information about college costs, not declining enrollment. Whitworth set its price by working backward from the scholarship scale, current student payments and need-based aid.

The change reflects growing criticism of colleges advertising high prices while offering opaque scholarships. Research cited says tuition resets have not increased overall enrollment but have raised the number of Pell-eligible students. However, some institutions continue using high prices to signal quality, creating what economist Phillip Levine called a prisoner’s dilemma. He also said universal adoption of net prices could raise antitrust concerns. Whitworth has received positive feedback from parents since announcing the change.

A study led by University of Guelph researcher Nigel Raine found that bumblebee queens exposed to field-realistic levels of thiamethoxam, a widely used neonicotinoid pesticide, were 26% less likely to lay eggs and establish new colonies. The parasite tested had little effect. Mathematical modeling suggested the pesticide could increase bumblebee populations’ long-term risk of extinction. Researchers said the findings may be conservative because they examined only one pesticide and one parasite, while disease and habitat destruction also threaten bumblebees.

Biotech headlines include TCGX’s $1.3 billion fund close, Europe’s major pharmaceutical policy overhaul, and telehealth’s shift toward drug-first thinking. The Texas Monthly article examines Enron’s rapid rise and decline under CEO Ken Lay and his successor, Jeff Skilling. After Enron’s 1985 acquisition, Skilling introduced the “Gas Bank,” enabling the company to buy, sell and guarantee gas prices. Enron combined trading expertise with a knowledge-based, aggressive culture that recruited highly educated employees, rewarded performance with uncapped bonuses and emphasized speed, risk-taking and job security above teamwork and loyalty.

Under Skilling, Enron became North America’s largest natural-gas merchant and expanded into electricity, bandwidth, broadband, financial trading and unconventional commodities such as coal, paper, steel and weather. Its growth relied heavily on subjective mark-to-market accounting, recognizing profits upfront, creating and dominating new markets, and abandoning projects when margins weakened. Internal forced rankings, monitoring and intense performance pressure fostered paranoia and competition, while employees described the company as increasingly mercenary and unsympathetic toward long-term commitments.

As CEO in 2001, Skilling faced criticism over Enron’s role in California’s energy crisis, continuing losses in India, the collapse of its telecommunications investments after the technology bubble burst, questions about accounting practices and executive stock sales. The stock fell from $80 in January to around $35. Although the economic downturn contributed, the article emphasizes the company’s aggressive culture and internal controls. Skilling resigned after six months; Lay returned as CEO, promised closer focus on Enron’s core business and reconsidered forced rankings. Skilling defended his legacy, saying Enron’s trading model represented a “second wave” that Houston still understood.

Tony Robinson has become patron of the John Cracknell Youth Enterprise Bank, which supports young people in Hull, the East Riding, Malton, Norton on Derwent, Pickering, and Scarborough. The trustee-managed bank, linked to the Hull Youth Enterprise Partnership, offers grants of up to £1,000 and has helped more than 400 young people fund purchases including computers, stationery, chocolate-making equipment, and dance costumes. Hull-born Robinson has championed small businesses for over 30 years and co-founded Enterprise Rockers CIC in 2012 to support micro-businesses.

According to police, Ankit killed Sheelu after she rejected his marriage proposal, then killed her cousin Shivani, who witnessed it, and burned both bodies. Police identified him through mobile-phone surveillance; he later confessed.

Coach DeBoer said his team improved stick coverage and defensive-zone awareness after giving opponents too much room early in the series, and credited his players' work. He declined to comment on Phil Kessel. DeBoer said the series is closer than it feels, with games decided by one goal or late losses, and that his group believes in itself and each other, knowing momentum can shift quickly. Bob Boughner reminded them of Steve Spott blowing a lead in the OHL finals. DeBoer praised Pavelski for taking responsibility and said San Jose expects to win on the road tomorrow despite the difficult environment.

The study introduces TOPIC (TOpology-constrained Prediction of Inorganic Crystals), a machine-learning-assisted algorithm for predicting lithium-oxide solid-state electrolytes with fully connected corner-sharing frameworks. TOPIC generates cation and oxygen frameworks under topology and coordination constraints, uses machine-learning interatomic potentials for optimization, places lithium through Monte Carlo simulations, and recalculates final structures with DFT. It successfully reproduced known oxide structures with up to 192 atoms per unit cell, including a modified prediction of cubic LLZO, and identified an unreported metastable LiTa2PO8 polymorph with nearly twice the conductivity of the known phase.

Screening showed that the lithium ratio is a key descriptor: low lithium content generally favors stable corner-sharing frameworks, which exhibited substantially higher ionic conductivity than non-corner-sharing structures. From 45 quaternary oxide compositions, the study identified 92 candidates predicted to exceed 0.1 mS cm−1 at room temperature and validated 15 using DFT-based molecular dynamics. Several candidates had known framework types, while others introduced novel prototypes. The NASICON-type Li4Hf2Si3O12 had a predicted conductivity of 14.09 mS cm−1 and a 6.5 eV band gap.

The analysis further found that increasing lithium content generally lowers migration barriers through structural distortion, although excessive lithium can block one-dimensional conduction channels. Aliovalent Hf doping opened three-dimensional pathways and reduced the activation barrier of Li2Ta2SiO8 from 0.562 to 0.352 eV. The reported structure library provides candidates and design principles for future searches, including untested three-coordinate polyhedra, La-containing garnets, quinary systems, and doped materials.

The article describes the David Swensen Portfolio, also called the Yale Model, a diversified strategy developed by David Swensen and Dean Takahashi. Swensen transformed Yale’s traditionally invested 60/40 endowment into one of the world’s largest and most successful endowments. The model allocates across stocks, bonds, and alternatives such as private equity, real estate, natural resources, and hedge funds, emphasizing low-cost index funds, passive investing, risk management, and undervalued or unconventional assets.

The portfolio is widely used by endowments, foundations, and high-net-worth investors, but its allocation should be adjusted for individual goals and risk tolerance. Investors can implement it with index funds or ETFs, including VTI, VNQ, VEA, EEM, IEI, and TIP, and rebalance regularly.

From 1985 to 2020, the Yale Model generated an annualized return of 12.5%, compared with 9.7% for the S&P 500. However, an article-based ETF backtest produced annual returns of 6.23% and underperformed the S&P 500, attributed to a large bond allocation and weak emerging-market performance. The backtest showed lower drawdowns than the S&P 500, with little difference between daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annual rebalancing.

The article explains that backtesting uses historical data to simulate portfolio performance, assess risks, and compare allocation or risk-management scenarios. It cautions that past performance is not guaranteed, the Yale endowment’s results may not apply to individual portfolios, and investors should consider their risk tolerance and consult a financial adviser.

A prospective, single-center observational study evaluated bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) in 157 patients hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure. BIS measured overhydration and the overhydration-to-extracellular-water ratio at admission and discharge, with analyses stratified by chronic kidney disease and HFrEF status. During 10.7 ± 7.1 months of follow-up, 51 patients experienced major adverse cardiovascular events and 45 experienced heart-failure hospitalization. CKD patients had higher admission fluid-overhydration measurements, while HFrEF patients had greater reductions in the ratio during hospitalization than non-HFrEF patients. However, neither baseline overhydration nor changes in fluid measurements significantly predicted MACE or heart-failure hospitalization in any subgroup. BIS therefore appears useful for monitoring fluid status, particularly in HFrEF, but its prognostic value in CKD and HFpEF remains uncertain. Limitations include the small, single-center cohort, absence of a non-BIS control group, reliance primarily on overhydration measurements, and limited follow-up.

The lecture contrasts wired communication, where the main impairment is additive white Gaussian noise, with wireless communication, where fading arises from changing propagation paths. In free space, far-field signals decay as \(1/r\), propagate at the speed of light, and experience antenna-pattern and propagation-delay effects. With fixed transmitters, receivers, and free space, the channel resembles a simple time-invariant noise channel.

A moving receiver introduces Doppler shift. A single Doppler shift can be tracked by the receiver’s frequency-recovery circuitry, but reflections create multiple paths with different, changing delays and Doppler shifts. Their interaction produces rapid periodic fading, called fast or multipath fading, and can prevent communication.

Detailed electromagnetic analysis is impractical for phones and base stations, so the channel is modeled through ray tracing. Each of \(J\) paths contributes a time-varying attenuation and propagation delay, with phase changes accounting for reflections. The output is a sum of attenuated, delayed versions of the input.

This model defines a linear but time-varying channel. Unlike a linear time-invariant system, a single input frequency can emerge as a modulated signal spanning multiple frequencies, so ordinary frequency-domain multiplication is inadequate. However, time-varying convolution remains valid, and the channel can be treated as a slowly varying filter. A baseband-equivalent model incorporates attenuation, delay, carrier frequency, and Doppler effects.

Because receiver frequency recovery tracks the average Doppler shift, the remaining channel variation depends on the spread between the paths’ Doppler shifts. This Doppler spread determines how long the channel appears stable and how rapidly channel measurements must be updated, making it a key parameter in wireless-system design.

- **Tensor Core performance:** The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU has 108 streaming multiprocessors (SMs) and 432 Tensor Cores, delivering up to 312 TFLOPS of dense mixed-precision FP16/FP32 performance. This provides 2.5 times the mixed-precision Tensor Core performance and 20 times the standard FP32 throughput of a Tesla V100. A100 Tensor Cores support FP16, INT8, INT4, binary, TF32, BF16, and IEEE FP64 data types.

- **Deep-learning computation:** TF32 is the default Tensor Core mode for AI training and provides up to eight times the FP32 throughput of A100 and up to ten times that of V100. FP16 or BF16 mixed-precision training offers up to twice the throughput of TF32, 16 times the FP32 throughput of A100, and 20 times that of V100. BF16 and FP16 can match FP32 training results without hyperparameter adjustment. A100 also provides higher-throughput FP16, BF16, and integer operations through wider thread-level data sharing, larger matrix instructions, and reduced register-file traffic.

- **HPC and FP64:** A100 Tensor Cores accelerate IEEE-compliant FP64 computation, reaching 19.5 TFLOPS—2.5 times the V100’s peak FP64 throughput. The cuSOLVER TCAIRS mixed-precision iterative-refinement solver supports TF32, FP16, and BF16. Across 37 SuiteSparse tests, TF32 produced the fastest and most robust results, with a geometric-mean speedup of 2.0 times over an FP64 solver; speedups reached four times for large complex matrices.

- **Structured sparsity:** A100 supports 2:4 fine-grained structured sparsity, requiring two nonzero values in each four-entry vector. Sparse Tensor Core instructions skip zero entries, doubling math throughput, while compressed weights reduce data footprint and bandwidth by half. NVIDIA’s pruning recipe trains dense networks, applies structured pruning, and fine-tunes the remaining weights; evaluations across numerous vision, detection, segmentation, language-modeling, and translation networks showed virtually no inference-accuracy loss.

- **Memory subsystem:** A100 includes 40 GB of HBM2 memory across five stacks, delivering 1,555 GB/s—more than 1.7 times V100 bandwidth. Its shared L2 cache is 40 MB, 6.7 times larger than V100’s, and provides 2.3 times the L2 bandwidth. Combined L1 cache and shared memory capacity is 192 KB per SM, compared with 128 KB on V100. SECDED ECC protects HBM2, L2, L1 caches, and register files. Compute Data Compression can improve DRAM read/write bandwidth by up to four times, L2 read bandwidth by up to four times, and effective L2 capacity by up to twice.

- **Data movement and execution efficiency:** Third-generation Tensor Cores share data across all 32 threads of a warp rather than eight, reduce register-file accesses, and issue fewer matrix instructions. A new asynchronous-copy operation transfers data directly from global memory to shared memory, bypassing the register file and optionally L1 cache. Hardware asynchronous barriers support thread-subset synchronization and overlap copies with computation. Maximum shared-memory allocation per SM increased to 164 KB from 96 KB on V100. Separate FP32 and INT32 cores can execute both instruction types simultaneously at full throughput.

- **MIG partitioning:** The Multi-Instance GPU feature can divide one A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated compute, L2-cache, memory-controller, and DRAM resources. These instances provide quality-of-service guarantees and fault isolation for concurrent virtual machines, containers, processes, and tenants. Compute Instances can further subdivide GPU resources and support Volta-style MPS. MIG vGPUs can be migrated between instances or GPUs to improve utilization, consolidate workloads, and permit maintenance without terminating jobs.

- **Interconnect and reliability:** Third-generation NVLink provides twelve links per A100 and 600 GB/s total bandwidth, twice V100’s aggregate bandwidth, while adding improved error detection, packet replay, and non-posted writes. A100 also supports PCIe Gen 4 with 31.5 GB/s per direction for x16 links, SR-IOV GPU virtualization, and fault attribution, isolation, containment, and remote page-fault reporting across NVLink-connected GPUs.

- **Additional hardware:** A100 adds a five-core NVJPEG decode engine capable of processing batches of up to five images, a hardware accelerator for optical flow and stereo disparity, and five NVDEC units rather than V100’s one. Global-memory FP16 atomic throughput is 11 times V100’s, while FP32 atomic throughput is 2.7 times higher. The GPU does not include display connectors, RT Cores, or an NVENC encoder.

- **CUDA 11 advances:** CUDA 11 adds support for third-generation Tensor Cores, sparsity, MIG, CUDA Graphs, L2 residency controls, asynchronous global-to-shared copies, and hardware asynchronous barriers. CUDA Graphs separate workflow definition from repeated execution and allow A100 to optimize uploads, launches, and dependency scheduling. L2 persistence controls reserve portions of the 40 MB cache for frequently reused data in 2.5 MB increments; the feature is disabled in MIG mode. Cooperative Groups adds asynchronous memory pipelines, hardware-accelerated reductions, and up to 30 percent lower grid-synchronization overhead.

- **DGX A100:** DGX A100 contains eight A100 GPUs interconnected by third-generation NVLink and six NVSwitches, providing 4.8 TB/s total bidirectional bandwidth. The 6U system delivers up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance and up to six times the AI-training performance of V100-based DGX-1. Its software stack includes CUDA, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and optimized containers for PyTorch, TensorFlow, MXNet, TensorRT, RAPIDS, and CUDA-X HPC. MIG can divide the system into as many as 56 hardware-isolated accelerators, and ConnectX-6 HDR InfiniBand adapters provide 200 Gb/s networking for large clusters.

Animal-rights protesters, including Liz White of Animal Alliance of Canada, picketed the park daily, logging hunters and carcasses, and support letters came from anti-racism groups, unions and some animal-rights organizations. On the second-to-last day, ministry officers found nails on a trail, apparently placed to puncture vehicle tires, and Ontario Provincial Police confirmed investigating a crime during the hunt's final two days; White denied involvement in the vandalism. Protesters and some community members, including Celeste Smith, disputed the harvest's framing, while First-time hunter Deyowidro't, who faced taunts for hunting, defended it as ancestral tradition rather than trophy killing.

The lecture reviews methods for folding polygons into convex polyhedra by gluing their boundaries to themselves. Such gluings are represented by gluing trees, which simplify the analysis of valid Alexandroff gluings. A cross-shaped polygon, for example, can be glued to form a cube; the gluing is noncrossing and places at most 360° of material at each point.

The main goals are deciding whether a folding exists, enumerating all foldings, and counting combinatorially distinct gluings. Combinatorial types are made finite by identifying gluings that differ only in metric details, such as the exact point where a vertex is attached along an edge.

For an \(n\)-vertex polygon, the number of general combinatorial gluing types is at most exponential. The gluing tree has \(O(n)\) nodes: most leaves correspond to polygon vertices, while at most four can be fold points because each contributes 180° of curvature and total curvature is 720°. Specifying whether junctions contain vertices or edges and locating the first polygon vertex adds only exponential factors. This bound is essentially tight: specially constructed spiky polygons have exponentially many gluings, including exponentially many edge-to-edge gluings.

Polygons of bounded sharpness have reflex angles bounded away from \(360^\circ\) by a fixed constant. Every leaf then contributes a fixed minimum curvature, so the number of leaves is constant. Consequently, such polygons have only polynomially many combinatorial gluings. Convex polygons are included among the bounded-sharpness examples.

Dynamic programming is used to enumerate gluings by solving subproblems associated with polygon intervals. For edge-to-edge gluings, enumeration requires exponential time in the worst case because exponentially many outputs may exist. A polynomial-time decision algorithm stores, for each subproblem, the solution minimizing the angle glued at its endpoints; checking all \(O(n)\) choices yields an \(O(n^3)\) algorithm. Whether a valid folding exists remains open for arbitrary gluings; the best known general decision algorithm is exponential.

Enumeration for arbitrary gluings additionally handles vertex-to-edge attachments and rolling belts. Solutions must then specify allowable intervals along edges because infinitely many metric gluings may exist. The resulting enumeration algorithm runs in exponential time generally and polynomial time for bounded-sharpness polygons. Implementations are available, and a separate Alexander-theorem algorithm can reconstruct the corresponding polyhedra.

Examples include a cross polygon with five edge-to-edge convex-polyhedron outcomes, while allowing arbitrary gluings yields 85 gluings representing 23 distinct polyhedra. Illustrations of an equilateral triangle and a square show additional finite outcomes connected by infinite families of rolling-belt gluings; among computed foldings of a square, an octahedron has the greatest volume.

Because #HV ignores interrupt shadows, a guest must execute HLT with interrupts disabled. The host should immediately re-enter the guest if interrupts or non-maskable events are pending, and the guest should check interrupt state upon resumption as if it had received #HV.

The #HV doorbell page is configured through VMGEXIT SW_EXITCODE 0x8000_0014, which provides actions to request a hypervisor-preferred guest physical address, set the doorbell page, and query whether one has been set. After mapping, the guest must access the page with C=0 in its PTE. Mapping and relinquishing the page must follow the specified RMP procedures.

The host must emulate APIC interrupt presentation, acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI semantics. It presents the highest-priority ready interrupt through PendingEvent.Vector while the vCPU is stopped and uses #HV and NoFurtherSignal to notify the guest. It also manages NoEoiRequired and performs implicit or explicit EOI cycles as appropriate.

The guest must atomically exchange PendingEvent with zero before acting on a vector, validate observed vectors, and defer dispatch until safe. For EOI, it atomically exchanges NoEoiRequired with zero; if the previous value was zero, it must write the X2APIC MSR through VMGEXIT. Non-maskable events must be handled even when EFLAGS.IF is zero, with the required PendingEvent flags cleared atomically.

ASTROCO, a conformer-style encoder for self-supervised learning of irregular stellar light curves, addresses Astromer/Astromer 2 transformers' limitations: equal treatment of all time steps, missed short-lived events (dips, flares, bursts), and uncontrolled influence of noisy or distant measurements. Each block combines multi-head self-attention, a depthwise convolutional sublayer with a Gated Linear Unit, and a gated feed-forward network, linked by residual connections and layer normalization. Magnitudes and uncertainties are projected and concatenated with sinusoidal time embeddings, then fused linearly, avoiding scale mismatch from additive fusion. Sequence embeddings mix features from all layers, including the input, via trainable softmax weights, followed by masked mean pooling. Pretraining masks 50% target time steps (~30% masked, 10% randomized, 10% unchanged but counted in the loss, BERT-style); masked/padded pairs are zeroed to prevent leakage. On MACHO R-band data, ASTROCO-S (5.9M parameters, 11.6 h on 4×A100) and ASTROCO-L (15.2M parameters, 1.2 d on 4×H200) achieve lower reconstruction error and higher macro-F1 than Astromer v1/v2 (5.4M parameters, 3 d on 4×A5000), and transfer to few-shot classification.

The ninth Carlsberg UK Northamptonshire Food and Drink Awards honored excellence in local produce, drinks, dining venues and culinary work at a November 15 dinner at Northampton’s Royal & Derngate. Antonio Carluccio OBE was absent following his death, with William Sitwell leading a toast to him. The Eat Out Eat Well scheme also recognized gold-scoring venues.

The passage outlines defensive strategies against the Triangle Offense, covering traditional NBA “show and recover” tactics and aggressive “SOS” disruption. Basic NBA defense packs the paint to force perimeter shots, denies cuts and screens, uses weak-side help, pressures post players, and closes out to shooters. Its four-phase sequence addresses corner cuts, post feeds and splits, corner screen-and-roll action, and weak-side two-man play.

SOS pressure can be applied full court to lengthen passing lanes and pull the offense from its normal positions. It includes wing-pass denial, aggressive post fronts, help rotations, post-split switches, and disruption of ball reversals and weak-side actions. “All Out” disruption begins with first-pass pressure and a trap, forcing players out of planned routes. Defenders rotate into help positions, deny post entries, close out to open players, and execute additional trap rotations after passes out of the trap or baseline drives. An optional corner-pass trap can extend the disruption.

Girlfriends’ Kenna McNeil said staff help students select flowers, ribbons, stones and other corsage items for several school proms. The shop has received close to 100 orders and began preparing around March 1 because flowers come from Arkansas and require lead time. Many students order about two weeks before prom, with 20–30 tux and corsage orders placed in recent days. McNeil enjoys seeing customers share photos of their prom accessories online. Staff are still working to make each order unique and attractive.

Defensive lapses led to quick goals the team could not erase, though the coach judged the play solid. After rebounding from a home loss to Buffalo, the team feels confident but must get the puck deep and grind it to the net against Buffalo’s defense.

Scores of Vietnamese fishermen clashed with police while seeking compensation from Formosa for a toxic-waste dump that killed tonnes of fish and devastated coastal livelihoods. Although Formosa paid Vietnam $500 million, fishermen said they had received nothing; some were detained or injured, and earlier lawsuits were dismissed.

The paper reviews twelve shared tasks organized by NFDI4DS, a German consortium supporting FAIR, transparent, and reproducible research data infrastructure. These community challenges compare methods using shared datasets and metrics and are hosted at venues including NSLP, SDP, CLEF, SemEval, and ISWC.

Seven tasks are completed: software mention detection (SOMD 2025), scientific-figure visual question answering (SciVQA), climate-change claim verification and literature retrieval (ClimateCheck), research-field classification (FoRC 2025), bilingual subject tagging (LLMs4Subjects), LLM-based ontology learning (LLMs4OL), and scholarly question answering over linked data (Scholarly QALD). Their results demonstrate progress in entity and relation extraction, multimodal QA, fact-checking, hierarchical classification, multilingual tagging, ontology construction, and knowledge-graph querying.

One task is ongoing: CLEF 2025 CheckThat!Lab Task 4 addresses detecting scientific claims and references in tweets and retrieving cited scientific papers, evaluated with macro-F1 and MRR@5.

Four tasks are under development: detecting machine-learning models and datasets in scholarly articles using GSAP-NER; extracting and linking entities from GitHub READMEs into the NFDI4DS knowledge graph (ReadMe2KG); producing calibrated uncertainty estimates for clinical prognosis from electronic health records (CURED, planned for 2026); and developing a FAIR meta-benchmarking platform for algorithm generalizability and domain adaptation (Algorithm2Domain). Collectively, the tasks support methodological progress, interdisciplinary collaboration, standardization, and long-term reuse of research outputs.

Hollywood's summer 2018 movie season opens with the potentially record-breaking "Avengers: Infinity War" (April 27), arriving as the year's box office is down nearly three percent following last summer's worst performance in over a decade. Franchise tent-poles dominate the slate, with Disney/Marvel's "Infinity War" and Universal's "Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom" (June 22) leading a long list of sequels and familiar brands including "Deadpool 2," "Solo: A Star Wars Story," "The Incredibles 2," "Ant-Man and the Wasp," "Mamma Mia: Here We Go Again!" and "Mission: Impossible — Fallout."

But Wall Street Journal reporter Ben Fritz, author of "The Big Picture," warns that oversaturation is possible: more franchise films compete for the same dollars, producing more flops. According to Box Office Mojo, 2017 ticket sales hit a 25-year low, and this year's revenue is concentrated, with "Black Panther" accounting for 23 percent of first-quarter ticket sales. Netflix also offers summer films, from the Sandler/Rock comedy "The Week Of" to "The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society."

Studios are touting slate diversity. Universal releases "Skyscraper" plus Focus Features titles including "Tully," "BlacKkKlansman," "Won't You Be My Neighbor" and a Pope Francis documentary. Warner Bros. has no major DC film, instead offering "Ocean's 8," "Tag," "Life of the Party" and "Crazy Rich Asians," with distribution president Jeff Goldstein saying the business is spread across 12 months. Female-led and gender-flipped reboots include "Overboard," "The Hustle," "Book Club" and "The Spy Who Dumped Me," alongside action fare "Mile 22" and "The Meg." Offbeat entries include "Uncle Drew," "Hereditary," Sundance breakouts "Eighth Grade," "Blindspotting" and "Sorry to Bother You," "The Happytime Murders," and "Hotel Artemis," an original thriller that writer-director Drew Pearce said could not have been made in the studio system, reflecting audience appetite for films with real personality that are "a little different and a little less cookie-cutter."

Digital leaders use relevant metrics to set ambitious goals and track project and individual progress. Data-driven evaluations, including 360-degree reviews, foster adaptation, innovation, experimentation, risk-taking, and team autonomy.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU architecture supports IEEE-compliant FP64 acceleration, delivering up to 2.5 times the FP64 performance of Tesla V100. Its new FP64 matrix multiply-add instruction replaces eight V100 DFMA instructions, while each of the GPU’s 108 streaming multiprocessors performs 64 FP64 FMA operations per clock, producing a peak of 19.5 TFLOPS. Mixed-precision Tensor Cores support TF32, FP16, and BF16 for HPC, iterative solvers, and AI. In cuSOLVER’s Tensor Core Accelerated Iterative Refinement Solver, TF32 produced a 2.0× geometric-mean speedup over the FP64 solver, compared with 1.9× for FP16 and 1.8× for BF16, with speedups up to 4× for large complex matrices.

A100 introduces fine-grained structured sparsity using a 2:4 pattern that permits two nonzero values in every four-entry vector. Sparse Tensor Cores skip zero entries, doubling mathematical throughput, while weight compression reduces data footprint and bandwidth by half. The prescribed inference process trains dense networks, prunes them, and fine-tunes remaining weights, yielding virtually no inference-accuracy loss across evaluated networks.

A100 combines 192 KB of L1 cache and shared memory per SM, up from 128 KB on V100, and includes separate FP32 and INT32 cores for simultaneous full-throughput execution. Its 40 GB HBM2 subsystem uses five stacks with eight dies per stack and provides 1,555 GB/s bandwidth, more than 1.7 times V100’s rate. The GPU has a 40 MB L2 cache, 6.7 times V100’s capacity, with 2.3 times the bandwidth. SECDED ECC protects HBM2, L2, L1 caches, and register files. L2 residency controls and compute data compression can improve reuse and provide up to fourfold gains in DRAM or L2 read bandwidth and twofold gains in L2 capacity.

For deep learning, A100’s third-generation Tensor Cores provide peak mixed-precision performance 16 times that of standard FP32 FMA operations. They share data across all 32 threads in a warp, issue eight times fewer instructions, and perform 2.9 times fewer register-file accesses than V100. Asynchronous copy instructions move data directly from global memory to shared memory, with a BYPASS variant that avoids L1 and the register file. Hardware asynchronous barriers support pipelining and finer-grained thread synchronization, while shared-memory allocation rises to 164 KB per SM. CUDA 11 adds support for third-generation Tensor Cores, sparsity, CUDA Graphs, MIG, and L2 residency controls. Task graphs reduce repeated launch overhead, and A100 adds launch and dependency optimizations. Cooperative Groups adds group-wide asynchronous-copy pipelines and hardware-accelerated reductions.

Multi-Instance GPU can partition an A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated compute and memory resources. Compute Instances can divide those resources further, support Volta-style MPS, and run multiple contexts simultaneously. MIG provides quality-of-service, fault isolation, and protection for multi-tenant workloads, and permits virtual GPUs to migrate between compatible GPU Instances. It is a compute-only feature.

Third-generation NVLink provides twelve links, 600 GB/s total GPU bandwidth, and peer-memory access at rates above PCIe. Its writes are non-posted and include error-attribution and recovery features. A100 also supports PCIe Gen 4 at 31.5 GB/s per direction for x16 connections and SR-IOV virtualization. New fault-handling technology supports error attribution, isolation, containment, and remote page-fault reporting across NVLink-connected GPUs.

Additional A100 hardware includes a five-core NVJPG JPEG decoder, an optical-flow and stereo-disparity accelerator, improved global-memory atomics, and five NVDEC units. FP16 atomic throughput is reported as 11 times V100’s, while FP32 atomic throughput is 2.7 times higher. A100 lacks display connectors, RT Cores, and an NVENC encoder.

DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs, six NVSwitches, 5 PFLOPS of AI performance in a 6U system, and up to 56 isolated MIG accelerators. Its third-generation NVLink fabric provides 4.8 TB/s total bidirectional bandwidth, and the system supports ConnectX-6 HDR InfiniBand adapters and Magnum IO scaling. The accompanying software stack includes CUDA 11, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, GPU-optimized NGC containers, and support for PyTorch, TensorFlow, TensorRT, RAPIDS, CUDA-X HPC, OpenACC, and CUDA.

An appendix explains neural-network pruning, the performance benefits of sparsity, and differences among fine-grained, coarse-grained, and structured sparsity. The document concludes with NVIDIA’s warranty, liability, licensing, trademark, and copyright terms.

The literature review identifies a fragmented evidence base on Asian higher education institutions’ global rankings, noting that most prior studies examined single countries, limited institutional samples, or particular ranking systems. It highlights persistent challenges including insufficient funding, uneven quality, limited research and innovation, weak industry collaboration, and inadequate internationalization.

Using a qualitative multiple-case and document-analysis design, the study examines THE World University Rankings from 2015–2025 for the top five institutions in each of ten countries: Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Pakistan, the Philippines, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam. Two external evaluators reviewed the analysis, and the study required no ethics approval because it involved no human or animal participants.

Chinese institutions showed the clearest sustained improvement. Tsinghua University rose from 49th to 12th, Peking University from 48th to 13th, Fudan University to 36th, and Zhejiang University to 47th by 2025; Shanghai Jiao Tong University entered the top 50 in 2024 before falling to 52nd in 2025. Japanese institutions were consistently ranked, with the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University remaining in the top 100. Tohoku University, the University of Osaka, and Tokyo Institute of Technology fluctuated substantially but returned to the top 200 in 2024–2025. Russian institutions generally maintained stable positions, led by Lomonosov Moscow State University, which remained in the top 200 and ranked 107th in 2025.

India showed an overall positive but uneven trend. The Indian Institute of Science appeared throughout the period, mostly within the 251–300 range, while Anna University and Jamia Millia Islamia improved over time. Mahatma Gandhi University and Shoolini University fluctuated and declined in 2024. Indonesia, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Thailand generally displayed stable-to-negative trajectories with substantial fluctuations. Indonesian institutions often remained in lower ranges or declined; Pakistani institutions showed inconsistent patterns; Philippine institutions were led by the University of the Philippines, whose rankings rose through 2021 before declining; and Thai institutions remained comparatively stable but with generally negative fluctuations. Bangladesh’s institutions were recent entrants, appearing mainly after 2020, with mostly neutral or slightly negative patterns. Vietnamese institutions generally declined, although Duy Tan and Ton Duc Thang universities reached the top 500 by 2023 before falling to the 601–800 range.

Overall, the study finds that most Asian HEIs trailed international counterparts and lacked stable ranking trajectories, while China, Japan, and Russia were the strongest performers and India showed improvement. Recommended policies include expanding global research, teaching, and academic-exchange networks; increasing institutional marketing; broadening funding opportunities; and establishing overseas offices with supportive legal and financial regulations. Limitations include examining only five institutions in ten countries and relying exclusively on THE rankings rather than systems such as QS or Webometrics.

The lecture reviews renormalization and renormalization-group evolution in SCET using the heavy-to-light \(b\to s\gamma\) current as an example. At one loop, the effective-theory result separates into infrared divergences matching those of QCD, ultraviolet divergences canceled by counterterms, and a remainder used in matching to the full theory. The operator’s momentum label \(\omega\) is fixed to \(m_b\) by external kinematics.

In general, SCET operators contain delta functions selecting large momentum labels carried by their collinear fields. These labels usually involve only external momenta, but in more complicated operators a Wilson coefficient may depend on loop momentum and enter an integral. When all operators occupy distinct collinear directions, external kinematics fixes their labels and the Wilson coefficient has a product rather than convolution form.

The renormalization-group equation for the bare Wilson coefficient yields the usual MS-bar evolution equation for the renormalized coefficient. Its anomalous dimension contains a regular term and a cusp term proportional to \(\log(\mu/\omega)\). The cusp contribution generates leading logarithms when the coefficient is evolved from the hard scale \(\omega\) to a smaller scale, while the regular contribution is needed at next-to-leading-log order. With a tree-level boundary condition \(C(\mu_0=\omega)=1\), a fixed coupling produces a Sudakov exponential containing \(\alpha\log^2(\mu/\omega)\) and hence Sudakov double logarithms. Including the running QCD coupling changes the exponent to a function of ratios of running couplings, while retaining an exponential series.

The Sudakov form reflects kinematic restrictions that confine radiation to the jet, while the effective-theory factorization scale separates hard and infrared physics. Its appearance through ultraviolet renormalization corresponds to infrared logarithms in the full theory. The cusp has a Wilson-line origin: after a field redefinition places ultrasoft effects in a Wilson line, the heavy-quark line contains a sharp kink. Renormalization of a cusp in a Wilson line produces a single logarithmic anomalous dimension, including at higher perturbative orders. A collinear Wilson line ending on a quark has similar structure.

Leading-log resummation uses tree-level matching and the one-loop cusp anomalous dimension. Next-to-leading-log resummation additionally requires the one-loop regular anomalous dimension and two-loop cusp anomalous dimension. Next-to-next-to-leading-log resummation requires one-loop matching, the two-loop regular anomalous dimension, and the three-loop cusp anomalous dimension. The cusp anomalous dimension is universal. The matching scale \(\mu_0\) may be any scale of order \(\omega\); varying it provides a probe of the accuracy of a truncated logarithmic expansion.

The momentum labels are fixed externally when an operator contains only one building block in each collinear direction. This applies, for example, to four distinct directions in a dijet process. If multiple quark fields lie in the same direction, one combination of their labels remains externally fixed, but their difference can enter loop integrals, producing convolution or integral forms in the anomalous-dimension equation. Such constructions reproduce familiar evolution equations, including DGLAP evolution of parton distributions and related equations for deeply virtual Compton scattering and the Brodsky-Lepage equation.

The lecture then turns to inclusive deep inelastic scattering, \(ep\to eX\), through virtual-photon exchange, using the Breit frame and separating hard and collinear fluctuations. Current conservation organizes the forward-scattering tensor into two structures, and integrating out the hard mode produces leading-power operators containing two collinear quark or gluon fields with corresponding Wilson coefficients. Parton distributions are defined as proton matrix elements of quark fields separated along a lightlike direction and joined by a Wilson line. Fourier transformation gives the momentum-space operator. In the forward proton matrix element, momentum conservation imposes a delta function relating the two field labels, while their sum gives a bounded momentum fraction; positive labels describe quarks and negative labels describe antiquarks. This operator will be combined with the hard coefficient to derive the deep-inelastic-scattering factorization theorem and its renormalization-group evolution.

The passage traces the rise of open-source software and its role in establishing container technology and collaborative approaches to distributed-system development. It defines patterns as technology-independent blueprints that guide the design of distributed systems. Patterns help developers learn from prior mistakes, establish a shared vocabulary, and create reusable components with stable, language-independent interfaces, improving both development speed and software quality.

Containers are presented as the foundation for distributed-system patterns. Dividing a single-node application into separate containers provides resource isolation, clarifies team ownership, separates concerns, enables component reuse, supports small focused teams, and makes testing, deployment, updates, rollouts, and rollbacks easier. These tightly coupled containers are commonly grouped in a Kubernetes pod, where they share resources such as filesystems, network namespaces, and process identifiers.

Three single-node patterns are described. The sidecar pattern combines an application container with a container that augments it, often without changing the application. Examples include adding HTTPS to a legacy HTTP service, synchronizing dynamic configuration through an API, exposing process and resource information through a `topz` interface, and building a simple platform as a service that deploys code from a Git repository. Reusable sidecars should be parameterized—preferably through environment variables—should expose stable APIs, and should be documented through Dockerfile directives such as `EXPOSE`, `ENV`, and `LABEL`.

The ambassador pattern places a proxy-like container between an application and the outside world. It can route requests to appropriate storage shards, discover and connect to environment-specific services, and split traffic between production and experimental implementations. Examples include using `twemproxy` with sharded Redis or Memcached and using nginx to direct 90% of traffic to production and 10% to an experiment while maintaining consistent user routing.

The adapter pattern converts differing application interfaces into a common interface. It can expose Redis metrics through a Prometheus exporter, normalize varied log formats with Fluentd, redirect logs to standard outputs, and provide richer database health checks without modifying third-party images. Adapters decouple applications from monitoring, logging, and health-check conventions while enabling reuse and protecting application containers from adapter failures.

The passage then introduces multi-node distributed systems and microservices. Microservices divide an application into small services communicating through APIs, enabling focused teams, independent releases, and independent scaling. Their looser coupling makes failures harder to debug and architectures harder to design, but common patterns provide proven practices and shared lessons.

A replicated load-balanced service is described as a scalable set of identical stateless instances behind a load balancer. Replication provides redundancy and supports horizontal scaling, while readiness probes indicate when instances can accept traffic. Session-tracked variants route each user consistently to one replica using IP hashing, cookies, or consistent hashing. A caching tier, such as Varnish, can improve latency and capacity, while nginx can provide SSL termination and reverse proxies can enforce rate limits.

Finally, sharded services divide requests or state among multiple shards, with a root routing requests to the appropriate shard. Sharding allows stateful systems to scale beyond one machine and uses memory more efficiently in caches, although shard failures create cache misses and added latency. Combining replication with sharding makes each shard resilient and independently scalable, but requires greater deployment complexity and overprovisioning. An ambassador or shared routing service can connect applications to sharded backends; the shared-service approach simplifies client deployment but requires independent scaling and adds a network hop.

U.S. stocks reversed early gains Thursday as Treasury yields climbed and technology shares fell ahead of major earnings, putting the S&P 500 on course for its first weekly decline in five. The Federal Reserve held rates steady but said inflation would rise this year and stabilize around 2%. Low unemployment claims, near seven-year-high factory prices and a 2% rise in fourth-quarter labor costs reinforced inflation concerns. The Dow gained 0.14%, while the S&P 500 fell 0.06% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.35%. Banks led gains. eBay jumped 13.8% after earnings and announced it would move away from PayPal as its main payments partner; PayPal fell 8.1%, while UPS dropped 6.1% because of higher shipping costs.
