Milan alleged violations of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause and the Eighth Amendment. Applying *Hewitt* and *Thompson*, the court held that inmates generally have no protected liberty interest in visitation privileges unless state law creates one through mandatory language and specific substantive predicates. Indiana Administrative Procedure 02-00-104 allowed denial of visitation without specific criteria, so Milan could not establish such an interest. Although the procedure required written notice and Nothstine admitted it was not provided, the court described the procedural issue as close and stated that, if his affidavit was true, the denial was justifiably reasonable. The court rejected Milan’s substantive constitutional claim and granted the defendants’ motion.

The paper examines e-learning ecosystem governance as a strategic requirement for organizations. It defines e-learning as the use of networked information and communications technology to extend and enrich learning, while noting continued difficulties integrating e-learning systems with content, business processes, and other organizational systems. An e-learning ecosystem comprises the learning community and enterprise connected through a learning management system, including stakeholders, learning utilities, environmental boundaries, and external and internal influences. Such ecosystems can align training with business objectives and improve return on investment, productivity, and employee performance.

The authors adapt an IT governance framework for e-learning governance, organizing it into structures, processes, communications and relational mechanisms, and pedagogies and instructional designs. They also adopt six dimensions from digital ecosystem governance: constitution and balance of interests, communication culture, credibility and trust, organization and synchronization, licensing and regulation, and technological standards. Regulatory, organizational, technological, and social conditions must be considered together because changes in one affect the others.

Information security governance is identified as essential because e-learning depends heavily on ICT and is exposed to security risks. Recommended measures include governance, policies and procedures, countermeasures, monitoring, risk assessment, and controls. Trust is also central, particularly trust in technological solutions, business activities, and knowledge. The paper concludes that further research is needed to understand the business benefits of improving e-learning governance practices in evolving digital business ecosystems.

Explainable AI can improve model understanding, resource efficiency, and risk mitigation, but faces challenges in evaluation, computational scalability, and real-world application. The passage proposes a concept activation vector (CAV) editing framework that trains logistic regression classifiers on LLM activation vectors to detect target concepts. Dynamically applying the resulting CAVs during inference can enhance or suppress concepts, support multiple simultaneous adjustments, resolve conflicts through optimization, and preserve fluent, coherent text while enabling interpretable output control.

A cloud-integrated storage appliance receives full or incremental backup snapshots, caches snapshot data locally, migrates closed snapshot data files to cloud storage, and retains snapshot metadata locally and in the cloud. For each defined data collection, metadata is stored in key-value stores as inode, directory, and data-map records keyed by monotonically increasing local snapshot identifiers. A global map links data collections, source and local snapshot identifiers, baseline relationships, and parent-child snapshot relationships.

A snapshot manager processes incoming snapshot components to create metadata records and snapshot data files, recording source-file and data-file offsets. During restoration, it resolves the requested snapshot, identifies its baseline, merges valid records back through preceding snapshots, builds restore maps, and supplies valid data blocks and descriptors to a restore target. File restoration incrementally searches directory metadata to locate the requested file, then reconstructs it from merged data-map ranges. Data files may be loaded locally or downloaded from cloud storage.

Snapshot reclamation marks snapshots for deletion and transfers still-valid metadata and data ranges to a succeeding valid snapshot, removing overwritten records and punching holes in partially overwritten data files.

The disclosure also describes synthetic baselines that reduce eviction of stable cached data. One method copies still-valid prior metadata to the newest snapshot and refreshes fingerprint and eviction-state data. A reverse-incremental method maintains a synthetic baseline, transfers overwritten ranges to a pre-baseline snapshot, incorporates new data, and updates snapshot mappings and eviction state. These methods are intended to reduce stable-data eviction and the restore delays and recovery-time-objective risks associated with retrieving evicted blocks from cloud storage.

NYPD officers shocked Dailene Rosario, a reportedly 14-week pregnant 17-year-old, with a stun gun in a Bronx apartment building after she allegedly shoved an officer into a doorframe during a fight involving her ex-boyfriend. Onlookers shouted that she was pregnant. Rosario is charged with resisting arrest, second-degree harassment and disorderly conduct; the NYPD says the incident is under internal review.

This protocol estimates the burden of disease (BoD) from COVID-19 in the Republic of Ireland from 1 March 2020 to 28 February 2021 using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), a metric that standardises morbidity and mortality into one measure, enabling comparison with other causes of disease and across regions and demographic groups.

Background: COVID-19 was confirmed worldwide by early March 2020; the WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March, and the Irish government, on National Public Health Emergency Team advice, closed educational, childcare and cultural facilities on 12 March, moving to full lockdown by 27 March, with varying restrictions thereafter. The passage also notes wide international disparities in COVID-19's direct population health impact and the uncertain profile of "Long-COVID" among people with initially mild illness, which will affect morbidity measures in future BoD studies.

Methods: data came from DATA.GOV.IE, which collates figures from the CSO, HPSC, HSE, Department of Health and DPER. Years of Life Lost (deaths × remaining life expectancy) used GBD 2019 life tables by sex, midpoint age-of-death assumptions per age group (80+ from Irish Life Tables) and CSO April 2020 population estimates; mortality data from the CSO (to 5 March 2021) plus DoH daily briefings to 31 March 2021 permitted reclassification, with ratios applied to unknown sex/age cases. Years Lived with Disability (cases × duration × disability weight) covered five health states: asymptomatic (zero weight, 3:1 ratio from seroprevalence), moderate, severe, critical and post-acute consequences (13.3% of symptomatic incidence, 28 days), with weights and durations mainly from GBD 2019 and severe/critical durations from Irish hospital data. DALYs = YLL + YLD. Ethical approval came from UCC's Social Research Ethics Committee.

The court granted in part and denied in part Defendant Samuel Felleke’s motion for summary judgment and denied Plaintiff Rebecca Shumye’s motion. It held that a Form I-864 is an enforceable contract requiring a sponsor to support the sponsored immigrant at at least 125% of the federal poverty level. The sponsor’s obligations continue unless the sponsor or immigrant dies, the immigrant becomes a U.S. citizen, permanently leaves the United States, or earns 40 qualifying quarters; divorce does not terminate them.

The court rejected Felleke’s argument that Shumye’s income should be aggregated across multiple years, holding instead that income must be evaluated separately for each year. Shumye conceded that her income exceeded 125% of the poverty level in 2000, 2001, 2002, 2004, and 2005, so Felleke received summary judgment for those years. Felleke’s evidence did not establish that her income exceeded the threshold in 2003, 2006, or 2007, and tax records supported a genuine factual dispute for 2003 and 2006. The court found the issue for 2007 premature because the motions were filed before that year ended.

In calculating income, the court held that the $49,000 divorce settlement was compensation for existing community property rather than income, and student loans were not income because they had to be repaid. Student grants and documented housing subsidies counted as income. The court declined to infer additional income from unexplained bank deposits because Felleke’s analysis was unsupported, and his calculations failed to account for identifiable deposits and other resources.

Shumye’s motion was denied because she failed to provide competent evidence establishing, without a genuine factual dispute, that her income fell below 125% of the poverty level or that Felleke breached his obligations in 2003, 2006, or 2007.

This excerpt contains Amazon.com, Inc.'s Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended June 30, 2016 (Commission File No. 000-22513), a Delaware corporation headquartered in Seattle. Amazon is a large accelerated filer, is not a shell company, and had 474,073,542 shares of common stock outstanding as of July 20, 2016.

Unaudited consolidated financial statements (in millions) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2016 and 2015 include statements of cash flows, operations, comprehensive income (loss), and balance sheets. For Q2 2016, net sales were $30,404 versus $23,185, operating income $1,285 versus $464, and net income $857 versus $92; diluted EPS was $1.78 versus $0.19. For the six months, net sales were $59,532 versus $45,901, operating income $2,356 versus $719, and net income $1,370 versus $35. Operating cash flow was $3,465 in Q2 2016 versus $1,997, with investing outflows of $2,439 and financing outflows of $1,039. At June 30, 2016, total assets were $65,076, total stockholders' equity $16,538, cash and cash equivalents $12,521, marketable securities $4,019, and long-term debt $8,212.

Segment results: North America net sales $17,674 (up 28%) with operating income $702; International net sales $9,844 (up 30%) with operating loss of $135; AWS net sales $2,886 (up 58%) with operating income $718. Sales growth was driven by increased unit sales (including marketplace sellers), price reductions, greater in-stock availability and selection, and AWS customer usage. No individual product or service exceeded 10% of net sales.

Notes address accounting policies, recent FASB pronouncements (revenue recognition, non-current deferred taxes, leases, stock-based compensation), fair value of cash and marketable securities ($16,996 total; no Level 3 assets), commitments and contingencies totaling $37,418 (including $8,154 operating leases and $7,996 capital lease obligations), long-term debt of $8.3 billion in unsecured senior notes plus a new $3.0 billion revolving credit facility entered May 2016 with no borrowings outstanding, and stockholders' equity including a February 2016 $5 billion repurchase authorization (no repurchases in Q2 2016), stock-based compensation expense of $768, and $4.5 billion of unrecognized compensation cost.

Contingencies include a voluntary report to OFAC and BIS regarding processing and delivering consumer product orders for certain individuals and entities in Iran, potential penalties, and patent litigation with Appistry, Kaavo, and Zitovault (several patents invalidated or complaints dismissed, with appeals pending). Tax contingencies were $1.6 billion; the IRS seeks approximately $1.5 billion in additional federal tax on 2005–2006 transfer pricing, contested in U.S. Tax Court; a French assessment of €196 million is being contested; and a European Commission state-aid investigation into Luxembourg tax decisions is open.

Management's Discussion and Analysis covers forward-looking statements, critical accounting judgments (inventory, goodwill, stock-based compensation, income taxes), liquidity and capital resources, and results of operations, including outbound shipping revenue of $2,000 versus $1,399 with net shipping costs of $1,362 versus $941, and operating expense growth in cost of sales, fulfillment, marketing, technology and content, and general and administrative.

Asian markets paused Tuesday after three sessions of gains as investors weighed stronger global growth hopes against a likely U.S. borrowing-cost increase. China’s unexpectedly generous November bank lending suggested possible improvements in retail sales and industrial output. MSCI Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan hovered near flat, while Japan’s Nikkei was steady after its highest close in 25 years. U.S. stocks rose, led by technology and energy companies, and the New York Port Authority explosion had no lasting market impact. The Federal Reserve was expected to raise growth and lower unemployment forecasts, potentially signaling four 2018 rate hikes instead of three; the ECB was expected to emphasize low rates. Forex trading was thin, with the euro steady near $1.1768 and the dollar near 113.48 yen. Gold weakened, while Brent and U.S. crude rose following a North Sea pipeline shutdown.

Texas Instruments’ mechanical, packaging, and orderable information for MSPM0C1105 and MSPM0C1106 provides current package and board-layout guidance, subject to change without notice. Linear dimensions are in millimeters and follow ASME Y14.5M; dimensions in parentheses are for reference. Packages require the thermal pad to be soldered to the PCB, and optional vias beneath paste should be filled, plugged, or tented. Stencil guidance includes 73%, 75%, or 78% printed solder coverage, laser-cut aperture designs for improved paste release, and possible IPC-7351/7525 alternatives. Package notes also cover seating-plane, mold-flash, solder-mask, thermal-pad, and board-assembly considerations, including that features may differ, no JEDEC registration existed as of September 2020, and mold flash, protrusions, or gate burrs must not exceed 0.15 mm per side.

Orderable-information footnotes define product status, preproduction-part limitations, RoHS values, lead or ball materials, moisture-sensitivity/reflow ratings, and part-marking formats. Carrier-tape drawings include pin-1 orientation and dimensional references. TI states that its technical, design, and safety resources are provided “as is,” are intended for skilled developers, and do not alter the company’s warranties or applicable sales terms.

The speaker reviews New Jersey’s uneven season, noting that the team often scored only two goals early on and blamed goaltender Martin too quickly. Ray Emery’s return to health led to victories and the starting role, while Martin remained a willing backup. The league is described as highly competitive, with Anaheim singled out as a strong, physical team with good goaltending and enthusiastic fans. New Jersey had generally handled demanding road games well, aside from one in Buffalo where it struggled to move the puck.

Brian Burke is praised for making bold trades, speaking candidly, and quickly assembling a team and coaching staff. New Jersey’s composure and leadership from Alfredsson, Phillips, and Redden are highlighted, along with the importance of goaltending, depth, tactical adjustments, four-line play, and using six defensemen in the postseason.

Several players are described as having improved. A tough, competitive player developed into a more complete contributor, a goaltender adapted from a down-butterfly style to a larger, more mobile approach, and another player developed into a dynamic two-way force. Anton earned increased responsibility after Chara’s loss and became a fearless leader in shot blocking.

After an earlier attempt to obtain Mike Comrie failed, New Jersey acquired him for immediate offense. Initially uncomfortable on the right wing and insufficiently competitive defensively, Comrie adjusted and became an important offensive threat and solid two-way player. The speaker also discusses changing practice and meal schedules because of a compressed schedule, reflects on leaving the organization after helping build and draft the roster, and remains proud of the players’ development. The passage closes by noting that scoring has increasingly required shots from the net, redirections, and effective shot blocking because defensive lanes are crowded.

The paper studies multi-agent learning in games with full-feedback rewards observed after a fixed delay of \(m\) steps. It shows that even minimal delay severely harms optimistic Follow the Regularized Leader (OFTRL): in an unconstrained Matching Pennies game with the Euclidean regularizer, any \(m\geq1\) causes OFTRL to incur at least \(\Omega(\sqrt T)\) regret and diverge from the Nash equilibrium, unlike undelayed OFTRL, which achieves \(O(1)\) regret and convergence.

To address this, the paper introduces Weighted OFTRL (WOFTRL), which weights the optimistic delayed reward prediction by an integer \(n\). A Taylor-expansion analysis shows that the optimistic weight and delay interact through \(n-m\): optimism improves prediction when \(n>m\), while insufficient optimism produces large, oscillating regret when \(n\leq m\).

When \(n=m+1\), WOFTRL satisfies an RVU inequality and achieves \(O(1)\) total regret with learning rate \(\eta=1/\sqrt{8\lambda L}\), where \(\lambda=(m+1)(m+2)/2\). The delay therefore requires a smaller learning rate and increases the regret bound. In poly-matrix zero-sum games, with a Legendre regularizer and sufficiently small learning rate, WOFTRL also achieves best-iterate convergence to a Nash equilibrium.

Experiments on Matching Pennies, Sato’s game, and weighted Rock-Paper-Scissors support the transition from \(O(1)\) to \(O(\sqrt T)\) regret around \(n=m\), with exceptions for large delays and finite learning rates. They also show convergence when \(n>m\) and divergence when \(n\leq m\). The results extend to Mirror Descent through the equivalence of generalized FTRL and Mirror Descent with Legendre regularizers. Future work includes proving last-iterate convergence under delay and studying stochastic or adversarial delays.

Molina Healthcare is characterized as a government-sponsored health insurer focused on Medicaid and dual-eligible populations, with strong contract wins and retention. It trades at a significant valuation discount—about 8–9 times earnings and 0.2 times EV/sales—and is presented as a structurally profitable compounder. Risks include policy changes, acquisition execution, medical-cost inflation, and cash-flow volatility, partly mitigated by state-level dynamics and contract discipline. The author discloses a beneficial long position in MOH and no compensation beyond Seeking Alpha.

The speaker accepts an honorary degree from Notre Dame, praising Father Hesburgh’s leadership and the courage of Bishop Donal Lamont, Paul Cardinal Arns, and Stephen Cardinal Kim in advancing human rights. He argues that graduates must accept responsibility for their futures and that personal courage is essential when confronting injustice and oppression.

His central argument is that the changing world requires a new American foreign policy grounded in democratic values, human dignity, openness, candor, and constructive global involvement. Although moral principles cannot alone produce quick results, he believes words and ideas influence history and can advance freedom. He also argues that democracies derive their strength and prosperity from protecting individual liberty and must continue to demonstrate that they are worthy of confidence.

He outlines five priorities. First, the United States should make human rights a fundamental tenet of foreign policy. Second, it should strengthen relations among democracies through economic cooperation, free trade, nuclear nonproliferation, development initiatives, and modernized defenses. Third, it should pursue an end to the strategic arms race through fair, reciprocal reductions, nuclear-testing bans, restrictions on chemical and space weapons, and eventual nuclear disarmament. He also advocates détente with the Soviet Union, mutual respect for different social systems, and cooperation in aiding developing countries.

Fourth, the United States should continue efforts toward Middle East peace by addressing security, borders, Palestinian self-determination, and the meaning of peace while holding parties to United Nations resolutions. Fifth, it should reduce nuclear proliferation and conventional arms transfers by limiting weapons sales, restricting advanced weapons and coproduction, and promoting peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

Beyond these priorities, the speaker calls for closer cooperation with newly influential countries in Latin America, Africa, and Asia; expanded international assistance to address hunger, disease, illiteracy, and repression; equitable trade; normalized relations with China; and a peaceful, timely transition to majority rule in southern Africa while protecting minority rights. He concludes that American foreign policy should reflect the country’s moral values, democratic confidence, material strength, and responsibility to humanity.

The September 28, 2000 VentureWire newsletter reported major private-company financing, transactions, governance changes, and executive appointments. Warburg Pincus closed a $2.5 billion international private equity fund for investments outside the United States. Primus Venture Partners raised $200 million for a fifth fund targeting online learning and early-stage companies. Gear.com’s president Ken Blue resigned, the retailer laid off 22 employees, and two executives became co-presidents. Goldman Sachs launched GSVentures with $250 million in initial capital to invest in financial-services and related technology companies. Hyperchip raised $67 million in Series C financing for new systems, while former astronaut Sally Ride resigned as Space.com’s president to pursue science education.

Numerous companies announced financing rounds. Caradisiac launched with $16 million, led by Renault; Eclaro raised $4.3 million; TurboGrad received $5 million; White Amber secured $20 million; Technology Strategy raised $14.5 million; Viathan obtained $17 million; 12snap raised $32.8 million; Avienda secured $30 million; Medpool.com received $10 million; and Summit Global raised $17.5 million. Other investments included $7 million for InterSense, $3 million for AniVision, $2.1 million in seed funding for Wishstream, and $1.5 million for Knoa Net. Ford took an undisclosed equity stake in Bios Group, and Indosuez Capital and Vestar Capital Partners invested in Internet Venture Works.

Asia Online withdrew its IPO, citing changed securities-market conditions. Zoho acquired National Content Liquidator for cash and stock in an undisclosed transaction and retained its employees, while Band-X acquired telecommunications publisher TeleGeography for undisclosed terms.

Several companies announced board additions, including Logictier, Clickability, DataRise, LinuxOne, Intellego, and AnywhereYouGo.com. Executive appointments included William Rumold at TriStrata, Joseph Laughlin at GlobalNetXchange, Bill Hale at LinkMe2, Bruce Chatterley at ViAir, Herb Lustig at Expanse Networks, and Ashok Siddhanti at zGraffiti.

Technology executives launched the Starting Point Partner angel fund, which planned to invest $200,000 to $1 million in early-stage infrastructure and technology companies. Common Angels closed a $10 million co-investment fund with 30 limited partners, making Centrata its first investment. AV Labs added former NetIQ executive Michael Rover as an investment principal. The newsletter also corrected MutualFunds.com’s domain-name appraisal to $1.25 million from $250,000.

A study of over 5,000 mothers linked parental obesity to age-three delays: obese mothers’ children were nearly 70% more likely to fail fine-motor tests, obese fathers’ children 75% more likely to fail social-competence tests, and extremely obese couples’ children nearly three times more likely to fail problem-solving tests.

NVIDIA’s GA10x Ampere architecture introduces third-generation Tensor Cores with TF32, BF16, and fine-grained structured sparsity support. Sparsity can double Tensor Core throughput, while TF32 provides up to five times the prior generation’s training throughput without code changes. These cores accelerate neural-network workloads including DLSS, AI denoising, Broadcast, and Canvas.

Full GA102 contains seven GPCs, 42 TPCs, and 84 SMs. Each SM includes 128 CUDA Cores, four third-generation Tensor Cores, a 256 KB register file, four texture units, a second-generation ray-tracing core, and 128 KB of configurable L1/shared memory. Both datapaths in each SM partition can process FP32 instructions, enabling 128 FP32 operations per clock across the SM. ROPs moved into GPCs, giving full GA102 112 ROPs rather than the prior generation’s 96. The GPU also has twelve 32-bit memory controllers and 6 MB of L2 cache.

Second-generation RT Cores double ray/triangle intersection testing, support hardware-accelerated ray-traced motion blur, and allow ray tracing to run concurrently with graphics or compute workloads. A new Interpolate Triangle Position unit can make accurate motion-blur rendering up to eight times faster than Turing. DLSS is enhanced with a 9x scaling factor, making 60 fps 8K ray-traced gaming feasible.

GA10x supports GDDR6X memory using PAM4 signaling, reaching data rates of 19.5 Gbps and up to 936 GB/s of peak bandwidth on the GeForce RTX 3090. Third-generation NVLink provides four x4 links and 112.5 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth between two GPUs; two A40 or RTX A6000 GPUs can combine 48 GB each into 96 GB. PCIe 4.0 with a x16 slot provides up to 64 GB/s peak bandwidth. NVIDIA RTX IO uses GPU-based lossless decompression and Microsoft DirectStorage to accelerate asset loading, reportedly up to 100 times over hard drives and traditional storage APIs while reducing CPU work, loading times, and stutter.

The A40 targets data-center visual computing, offering up to twice the FP32 and ray-tracing throughput and up to five times, or ten times with sparsity, the AI training throughput of Quadro RTX 6000. It includes 48 GB of GDDR6, PCIe 4.0, virtual GPU support, Quadro Sync, and compatibility with NVIDIA EGX. The RTX A6000 provides 10,752 CUDA Cores, 48 GB of GDDR6, hardware-accelerated motion blur and AI denoising, and can scale to 96 GB with a second GPU through NVLink.

Ampere GPUs support 4K at 120 Hz and 8K at 60 Hz through DisplayPort 1.4a and HDMI 2.1 with DSC, plus dynamic HDR and HDCP 2.3. Fifth-generation NVDEC adds hardware decoding for MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, and AV1, including 8K60 HDR AV1 playback with low CPU usage. Seventh-generation NVENC provides hardware encoding up to 4K H.264 and 8K HEVC.

The GeForce RTX 3090 uses GA102 with 82 SMs, 10,496 CUDA Cores, and 24 GB of GDDR6X. The RTX 3070 uses GA104, omits NVLink, and uses GDDR6. GDDR6X memory also includes Error Detection and Replay, which detects failed transactions and retries them. Reported architectural gains include up to twofold improvements in programmable shading, ray tracing, and AI, while Ampere GPUs are up to 1.9 times more power-efficient than Turing at equivalent performance.

Microsoft Research Asia’s Societal AI whitepaper defines Societal AI as the interdisciplinary study of AI’s societal effects and the transformation of AI research through collaboration between computer and social scientists. It argues that advanced AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), requires responsible, inclusive, and globally coordinated development to support harmonious, synergistic, and resilient integration into society. Drawing on workshops, research collaborations, and responsible-AI work begun around personalized recommendation systems, the paper presents ten evolving research questions.

These questions address:

- **Fairness and inclusion:** Ensuring AI works equitably across cultures, regions, languages, and demographic groups. The paper identifies training-data and language imbalances as causes of unequal performance and presents CulturePark, a multi-agent debate framework for augmenting low-resource cultural and linguistic data and fine-tuning culturally aware models.
- **Safety, reliability, and controllability:** Addressing unpredictable outputs, privacy leakage, malicious uses, and jailbreaking. Proposed defenses include embedding special tokens and adversarial training in white-box settings, prompt engineering in black-box settings, and self-reminder prompts that reduce jailbreak attempts.
- **Human-AI collaboration:** Studying fluid task allocation, interfaces, and evaluation, as well as collaboration among multiple humans and AI agents within organizations. It also highlights risks such as worker deskilling and replacement and calls for research on equitable transitions and skill development.
- **Evaluation of general-purpose AI:** Moving beyond static benchmarks through dynamically generated samples, varied difficulty levels, and multi-faceted capability analysis. The DyVal framework uses directed acyclic graphs to generate reproducible reasoning tasks and analyze specific abilities.
- **Interpretability:** Improving transparency and trust despite the lack of standardized evaluation methods, computational costs, and deployment challenges. A concept activation vector framework detects concepts in model activations and uses them to enhance or suppress behaviors such as toxicity or dishonesty while preserving fluency.
- **Value alignment:** Combining top-down moral guidelines with bottom-up learning from contextual human feedback. The paper describes research mapping LLM behavior to human value dimensions, generating evolving ethical test scenarios, and using complementary large and small models to evaluate value alignment.
- **Cognition, learning, and creativity:** Studying over-reliance, weakened independent skill development, and AI’s potential to personalize education and augment human reasoning. It urges collaboration among developers and educators so AI supports intellectual growth rather than replacement.
- **Work, collaboration, and business models:** Examining how AI may blur knowledge-based roles, transform the middle class, expand the gig economy, and enable network-based global innovation. It recommends institutional reforms, social protections, equitable access, and coordinated labor-market planning.
- **Social-science methodologies:** Using LLMs to synthesize research data, perform stance detection, sentiment analysis, and response coding, and propose theories. It stresses concerns about representativeness, bias, misinformation, and provenance, as well as the need for human oversight and interdisciplinary governance.
- **AI regulation:** Balancing innovation with protection of rights, safety, transparency, and accountability. The paper calls for forward-looking top-down frameworks shared by industry, academia, and policymakers, combined with bottom-up reporting by developers and users, transparent issue handling, and international cooperation.

Overall, the paper presents a practical foundation for responsible AI research while identifying unresolved challenges in institutional design, governance, evaluation, safety, and human development. It calls for AI systems that are controllable and explainable, supported by institutions capable of monitoring and correcting risks as AI becomes increasingly capable and autonomous.

According to Benjamin Graham, buying securities is not automatically investing. An investment must protect the purchaser’s capital and provide an adequate return; otherwise, it is speculation. The author’s profitable purchase of Ask Jeeves was therefore not an investment because he ignored downside protection when focusing on potential gains.

The passage advocates value investing through large margins of safety: buying companies at substantial discounts to intrinsic value, allowing for business deterioration or errors in valuation. Financially solid companies with clean balance sheets, little long-term debt, strong current-asset coverage, and ample liquid assets are preferred. Such discounts can arise from negative sentiment or temporary problems, and the price may rise toward intrinsic value as pessimism proves unwarranted or the company recovers. “Net net” stocks, which trade far below estimated business value and have conservative balance sheets, are presented as particularly promising when their balance sheets are not rapidly deteriorating.

The central conclusion is that investor status depends on a disciplined selection process focused on downside protection and likely profit, not on the type of security purchased.

Soccer free kicks restart play after fouls or procedural violations. The ball is placed where the infraction occurred, and the non-offending team takes possession. Defenders must remain at least 10 yards from the ball. Play begins when an offensive player touches the ball and it visibly moves, and the original kicker may not immediately touch it again. Direct free kicks may result in a goal without another player touching the ball; indirect free kicks require another player to touch it before it counts.

Free kicks in the defensive half generally retain possession through short passes, while those in the offensive third are used to create planned “set pieces” capable of producing a shot or goal. Defenses usually form a wall, so offensive plays must consider the distance and angle to goal, whether the kick is direct or indirect, and players’ abilities. Set pieces may be organized from eight general locations: outside, near, and far positions on either side and in the center. Walls commonly range from two to five players, depending on location and play.

Possible set-piece features include direct shots around or through the wall, simple touches, crosses, stepovers, misdirection, screening, a “committee” decoy, single or two-pass combinations, chips over the wall, ghosting runs, crashing attackers, and rebound or follow-up shots. Coaches are encouraged to study successful examples from games, books, and the web, then adapt plays to available personnel. Set-piece success depends on capable, responsible players who understand their assigned positions, the type of free kick, and when the referee has authorized play. A specialist may be used for bending free kicks, and left- or right-footed takers may be needed for different goal sides. Players should request the required 10-yard distance if defenders encroach and must wait for the referee to resolve it.

Most free kicks are ceremonial, allowing attackers to gather around the ball before executing a planned play. Quick free kicks take the restart immediately, usually on direct free kicks when the defense is unprepared or a goalkeeper is out position; the kicker must know the referee is ready.

Practice should progress from running plays without defenders, to mannequins, stationary defenders, live defenders, and full scrimmages with enforced rules. Coaches should correct mistakes, rotate players, develop contingencies for unavailable players, scout opponents for tendencies and weaknesses, avoid unnecessarily complicated plays, and ensure that indirect-kick designs include the required touch rather than assuming one will occur.

The Stack Zone Offense is a zone-based overload system that creates immediate matchup and adjustment problems through stack alignment, precise spacing, and constant movement. It assigns players defined roles so they can specialize, while coaches can reposition shooters toward open shots. The offense can quickly flop sides to attack the weakside, use multiple entries and late-clock specials, and generate offensive-rebounding opportunities. Mike Frink is credited with introducing this particular continuity.

The five core roles are: O1 as the point guard and offense director; O2 as the primary outside shooter; O3 as an active baseline player and offensive rebounder; O4 as a post player who can operate from either block and rebound; and O5 as a post player who can shoot or feed from the high-post area and pursue weakside rebounds.

Basic action progresses through four phases. Phase 1 uses overload reads, including feeding wing shooters, cutting along the baseline, posting entries, skip passes, and screens. Phase 2 adds pass-and-cut movement, high-post rolls, side-post feeds, weakside post attacks, and automatic skip passes when high-post entry is denied. Phase 3 reverses the ball when the baseline player cannot feed the wing or post, then reestablishes the overload on the opposite side; it also includes an automatic skip-pass response to an overplayed reversal. Phase 4 provides left-repeat pass-and-cut action.

Optional entries include flop and exchange actions that move shooters across the floor and reposition posts. Triple-stack alignments, contributed by Tom Newell, further complicate defensive assignments by shifting wing, short-corner, and middle positions. Additional variations include dribble entry, weakside flop, and post-roll actions.

Crunch-time specials include “Vegas,” using a weakside double screen and skip pass for O1; “Back,” using interchanging posts and weakside lob or reversal passes; and “Cat,” which immediately rotates into a 2-1-2 alignment against traps or double teams. The Cat uses sharp passing, post rolls after baseline-corner entries, and back cuts when the ball enters the middle. If a lob is unavailable in the Back special, the team returns to basic Stack overload action.

The document is an AMD AGESA™ host-environment interface and porting specification for host BIOS wrapper implementers. It defines the procedures, configuration parameters, build methods, binary integration, UEFI implementation, call-out mechanisms, and published entry points required to incorporate AGESA software into a platform.

The specification defines terminology for multiprocessor environments, including the boot strap processor (BSP) and application processors (APs), and requires published procedures to follow naming conventions: “Amd” for entry points and “Agesa” for call-outs. AGESA software uses three-level version numbering, while the interface uses two levels; interface changes add functions or features, whereas code-only releases are bug fixes. Source files include descriptive headers, and internal Doxygen documentation can be generated from the sources.

Host environments supply required platform parameters and may override optional defaults. An initializer creates and populates an interface structure, after which the host invokes the selected entry point, checks the returned status, and releases the structure. Errors are reported through status codes and a circular event log retaining the 16 most recent events. Status severity ranges from successful completion to fatal conditions that require POST to stop.

The build system centers on a platform-specific `<Plat>Options.c` file. Defaults and selected option procedures are compiled separately and linked with the main AGESA library. AGESA may be integrated directly with host sources or built as a relocatable binary module. Binary images contain `$AMD` and `$MOD` headers identifying modules, entry points, relocation data, image location, and size. Host calls pass through a bridge to an AGESA dispatcher, while AGESA call-outs return through a host router. The binary-module environment uses 32-bit protected flat addressing, with identity mapping required when paging is enabled.

Published entry points correspond to stages of the boot sequence, including ROM validation, recovery, processor initialization, memory initialization, suspend restoration, and OS handoff. `AmdInitReset` performs minimal processor setup and execution-cache allocation; `AmdInitEarly` performs fuller processor, HyperTransport, and power-management initialization; `AmdInitPost` locates, configures, and enables system memory. Hosts must not call unpublished internal functions or enable code-execution caching outside the provided AGESA procedures.

The UEFI porting section covers SEC, PEI, DXE, and runtime execution, including separate library targets, required build tools, processor and memory PEIMs, reset coordination, a DXE driver that publishes AGESA-generated tables through a protocol, and an iGPU VGA-control driver. The release package includes reference wrapper and option files, build-control files, binary compilations, specialized tools, and examples.

Host-provided services include structure allocation and release, event-log retrieval, DIMM data-eye results, APIC and PCI address lookup, processor and memory-address identification, FRU memory-device location, and MMIO range merging. AGESA also supplies stack-establishment and early-reset macros. During Cache-as-RAM operation, hosts must preserve required stack and MTRR state and must not modify cache controls before memory initialization completes.

The Supreme Court affirmed a decree ordering specific performance of a land-sale contract to Thompson, whose assignee brought the suit. Moore appointed an agent who verbally agreed to sell the land to Thompson. Moore later made a verbal agreement with Matthew Hunter, but then executed a title bond to Thompson and afterward conveyed the land to Hunter, who knew of the bond. Thompson tendered the purchase money and accrued interest and demanded a deed, but Hunter refused. Hunter later conveyed the property to Moses Hunter for $1,600, only $150 of which was paid.

Because the evidence supported two conflicting theories, the Court deferred to the trial court’s finding that Thompson had the prior equitable right and could obtain specific performance. A vendor may elect to treat an earlier verbal land-sale contract as void by making a valid later sale, protecting an intermediate purchaser under the statute of frauds. However, equity treats an enforceable contract as accomplished and relates it back only when the contract is valid and the vendee is entitled to specific performance. A vendor making that election cannot defeat an intermediate purchaser by a later conveyance unless the purchase money is paid in full without notice of the valid agreement.

The purchase money need not be deposited with the court; offering in the complaint to bring it into court when liquidated and obtaining a decree for performance is sufficient. Because Thompson tendered all due purchase money and interest, he was not chargeable with interest unless the vendor proved use of the money. The judgment was affirmed with costs.

This preprint study compared a syndromic multiplex PCR assay with targeted hybridization-capture mNGS for detecting respiratory pathogens in 29 nasopharyngeal samples from individuals suspected of acute upper respiratory infection. PCR detected at least one microorganism in 28 samples, identifying 15 agents: four bacteria and 11 viruses, with bacterial–viral coinfection in 10 samples. Using the Illumina/IDbyDNA Respiratory Pathogen ID/AMR panel and Explify Platform, mNGS identified 44 microorganisms—27 bacteria, 15 viruses, and two fungi—and found coinfection in 26 of 29 samples. It additionally detected 29 organisms outside the PCR panel’s targets.

For 33 shared targets, PCR and mNGS showed 98.33% positive agreement and 100% negative agreement; only one discordant sample was identified. mNGS exclusively detected 12 organisms classified as frequently associated with respiratory disease and three pathogenic organisms—Coxsackievirus A, SARS-CoV-2, and rhinovirus C. Both SARS-CoV-2-positive samples were confirmed by SARS-CoV-2-specific PCR.

Phenotypically, PCR results included no group 1 organisms, three group 2 organisms, and 12 group 3 organisms, while mNGS results included 14, 15, and 15 organisms in groups 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The authors concluded that targeted hybridization-capture mNGS may supplement PCR by detecting additional bacteria, viruses, and fungi and helping assess potential lower-respiratory trafficking. They noted that interpretation remains difficult because respiratory samples may contain colonizing organisms, and further clinical validation is required. No FDA-approved infectious-disease sequencing devices or kits were available at publication.
