Snow, ice and wind disrupted travel across southern England and northern Europe after Bath Rugby’s 24-20 Champions Cup defeat by Toulon, leaving many supporters stranded. Flights from Marseille, Nice and Amsterdam were cancelled, while London airports were affected. Some travelled via Munich, Brussels, Madrid, Italian cities and Paris, or were diverted to Bournemouth and Cardiff. Bath’s chartered flight reached Bristol, but supporters faced further cancellations, delays, missed connections, train disruption and a death on a rail line. A British Airways message reportedly cancelled the wrong flight, leading to manual recheck-in and a double-booking issue. Supporters also faced missed funerals, extra leave and pet-care arrangements. Some remained in Nice or Toulon awaiting later flights or trains.

China tightened rare-earth export controls, requiring licenses for goods containing rare earths worth at least 0.1% and for companies using Chinese extraction, refining or magnet-recycling technology. Shares of U.S. rare-earth and critical-mineral miners surged amid speculation that the Trump administration will expand investments in domestic supply chains. The administration has taken equity stakes in several miners, including MP Materials, while industry executives reported close contact with the White House. The restrictions preceded an expected meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the APEC summit in Seoul amid U.S.-China trade tensions.

After seven months out of action, a hockey player described negotiations to return to competitive hockey as deep and honest but lengthy. Selection for the Russian Olympic team, including three weeks of training with the Junior Whalers, helped restore his mental focus. When Carolina’s offer emerged, the Detroit Red Wings had seven days to match it. Despite financial concerns, Detroit matched the offer quickly. Eager to remain with his long-time teammates, the player returned on Friday, played despite exhaustion from the rapid events and travel from Japan, and was relieved to rejoin the team. He also credited the negotiations and the return of his teammates, including “Vladi,” whom he reassured in Russian after his arrival. The player expressed gratitude for Detroit’s effort to keep the team together and emphasized that playing hockey and producing were his primary goals.

The paper introduces Hybrid CA with Refinement (HCAR), a three-phase constraint acquisition framework designed to address over-fitted global constraints learned from limited examples. Earlier passive methods can infer overly specific constraints, active methods may require many oracle queries, and existing hybrid methods lack mechanisms to target passive-phase over-fitting.

Phase 1 analyzes a small set of positive solutions to detect structural patterns, optionally incorporate domain knowledge, instantiate global constraints such as AllDifferent, Sum, and Count, infer their parameters, and prune inconsistent fixed-arity candidates. Because limited examples may support coincidental patterns, these candidates can still over-fit; examples include a spurious Sudoku diagonal constraint and fixed cell values.

Phase 2 is the core query-driven refinement stage. Candidate global constraints receive machine-learning-based prior confidence scores and are tested through targeted oracle queries. Bayesian updates combine oracle evidence, while confidence thresholds determine acceptance or rejection. Rejected constraints may be refined through Subset Exploration, which removes strategically positioned variables while preserving constraint type and parameters to recover valid smaller structures. Adaptive query budgets redistribute unused resources among remaining candidates.

Phase 3 applies active learning to identify remaining fixed-arity constraints and complete the final model. Experiments on diverse benchmarks reported high accuracy and target-model coverage from limited examples with manageable query complexity, with interactive refinement playing a central role in reducing over-fitting.

This study examined perceived tenure and promotion research expectations for U.S. mathematics education faculty, focusing on how expectations vary by institution type, department type, and percentage of time devoted to research. Because written expectations documents may be absent or vague, the authors surveyed faculty perceptions.

From a pool of 15,938 identified faculty, 1,593 received surveys. After excluding respondents outside the target population and incomplete responses, 404 remained. The survey addressed demographics, expected annual publications, whether expectations were explicitly stated, and the necessity and perceived value of various publications and scholarly activities. Analyses included frequency counts, subgroup comparisons, multinomial logistic regressions, and post-hoc comparisons.

Overall, faculty typically expected to spend 20–40% of their time on research and publish about 1.64 papers annually. Research journal articles were consistently most valued. Books, book chapters, practitioner articles, and conference papers generally counted somewhat, while textbooks lacked consensus. Presentations were usually expected but counted modestly. Most faculty were expected to pursue external funding even if funding was not obtained. Professional development was neither required nor highly valued, and first authorship was considered important.

Expectations differed by Carnegie classification. R1 faculty generally devoted 40% of their time to research and were expected to publish about 2.25 papers annually; R2 faculty published about 1.5, and faculty at other institutions about one. R2 faculty were most likely to have their expected publication numbers stated in writing. R1 faculty placed less value on other publication types, more often required presentations and funding, and more often emphasized sole authorship. Faculty at other institutions placed comparatively greater value on presentations and professional development and were most likely to report no funding expectation.

Each 10-percentage-point increase in research commitment was associated with 0.184 additional expected papers. Higher-commitment faculty valued books, book chapters, and practitioner articles less, more often required funding, placed less value on professional development, and emphasized sole and lead authorship.

Education and mathematics departments showed relatively few differences. Mathematics departments expected 0.309 fewer papers, all else equal, but placed more value on conference papers and funding and less on professional development, presentations, and first authorship.

The authors concluded that expectations documents should explicitly state expected publication numbers, the value assigned to publication types, and whether activities such as funding, presentations, and professional development are required.

Two Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashes killed 346 people. Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea on October 29, 2018, killing 189 people 11 minutes after takeoff. Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed near Bishoftu on March 10, 2019, killing all 157 people aboard. In both accidents, the aircraft experienced an unrecoverable descent after takeoff.

Boeing initially emphasized Lion Air’s maintenance practices and pilot performance, but by November 2018 acknowledged that erroneous angle-of-attack data could trigger repeated uncommanded nose-down movements. The FAA required revised flight procedures, and all 737 MAX aircraft were grounded on March 13, 2019. The aircraft remained grounded for 21 months and returned to commercial service in November 2020. Before returning, Boeing recommended simulator training, and the FAA mandated ground and simulator training for MAX pilots.

The case traces the 737 MAX program to Boeing’s response to competition from Airbus’s A320neo. Boeing abandoned plans for a new aircraft and introduced the MAX under a compressed schedule. Employees described the development pace as “go, go, go,” with design work and technical drawings produced at roughly twice normal rates, tight budgets, and concerns about sloppy documentation and pressure against raising safety issues.

The Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, was developed to counter a nose-up tendency caused by the larger CFM LEAP-1B engines and their forward placement. Initially, MCAS required both a high angle of attack and high G-force and moved the horizontal stabilizer 0.6 degrees over ten seconds. Testing later showed the pitch-up condition could occur at low speeds. MCAS was therefore changed to move the stabilizer 2.5 degrees over ten seconds, omit the G-force condition, and reactivate every five seconds.

Although the aircraft had two angle-of-attack sensors, MCAS used data from only one, alternating between them. This created a single point of failure. An indicator and “AOA DISAGREE” alert could identify conflicting sensor readings, but the features were optional, tied together, and affected by a software bug. Lion Air’s replacement sensor was miscalibrated, and the aircraft lacked the equipment needed to display a warning.

FAA certification focused on significant differences between the MAX and earlier 737 models. Boeing described MCAS as a minor modification to existing trim systems and provided limited information about it, so it did not receive detailed review. Boeing did not formally document significant MCAS changes made during testing, including the stronger low-speed nose-down command and removal of the G-force requirement. Its safety analysis did not classify system-level risks as catastrophic. A Boeing chief technical pilot discovered the changes in a simulator and complained about them, while internal communications indicated that employees and test pilots had raised concerns before the crashes.

Boeing also sought to avoid simulator training, describing MCAS and other changes as minor differences that could be covered by computer-based training. The FAA approved a Level B training plan for already qualified 737 pilots, but it did not include pilot responses to automated MCAS activation. Many pilots later said they had received no prior instruction on MCAS or procedures for overriding it. Indonesia’s National Transportation Safety Committee identified inadequate training and flight-manual guidance as contributing factors.

The case describes a broader change at Boeing. Under Thornton “T” Wilson, Boeing had a prominent engineering, quality, and employee-family culture. Following Boeing’s 1997 acquisition of McDonnell Douglas, headquarters moved to Chicago, reporting shifted toward business leadership, and the company adopted outsourcing, lean manufacturing, computerization, and approximately 50,000 layoffs between 1999 and 2003. Longtime employees and outside observers described the resulting shift from an engineering-centered culture toward shareholder value, tighter control, and a climate that could discourage employees from challenging managers. A former employee’s account of defective 787 parts illustrated difficulty escalating quality concerns.

After the crashes, Boeing created a board-level safety review. Recommendations included having senior engineers report primarily to the chief engineer, establishing an independent safety group and permanent board safety committee, and examining cockpit design for pilots with less training. Multiple investigations followed; Boeing fired Commercial Airplanes CEO Kevin McAllister and CEO Dennis Muilenburg, who acknowledged that Boeing should have grounded the aircraft after Lion Air. An FAA personnel survey also found strong industry pressure, concerns about agency independence, and staff believing they could be overpowered by Boeing.

One estimate placed Boeing’s direct costs above $21 billion and lost sales at $67 billion for 1,200 aircraft. By mid-August 2022, Boeing’s share price was 52% below its pre-crash level, while Airbus’s was 20% higher. The case concludes with unresolved questions about engineering and management roles, the effects of schedule and cost pressure, the adequacy of self-regulation, and the reforms needed at the FAA and other agencies to prevent future disasters.

Keltner Channels, developed by commodity trader Chester W. Keltner in the 1960s, are three-line technical analysis tools that combine a central moving average—commonly a 20-period exponential moving average—with upper and lower bands set a multiple of the Average True Range (ATR) above and below it. A common setting uses a 2.0 ATR multiplier. The bands expand during high volatility and contract during low volatility.

Traders use the channels to assess volatility, trends, support and resistance, overbought or oversold conditions, breakouts, and potential entry and exit points. Strategies may trade mean reversion when price crosses a band or momentum when it breaks beyond one. The channels are also used in scalping and swing trading, and their settings should be tailored and tested for the asset, market conditions, and trading style.

Unlike Bollinger Bands, which use standard deviations and tend to respond more sharply to price changes, Keltner Channels use ATR and often three-price observations. A Bollinger squeeze inside a Keltner Channel indicates consolidation and a possible breakout. The passage describes Keltner Channels as non-repainting and potentially leading because their width reflects volatility.

One reported SPY backtest produced 288 trades, a 77% win rate, 6.3% CAGR, a 2 profit factor, and 15% time in the market. A momentum test using a 30-day period and 1.3 ATR produced 143 trades and a 3.6% CAGR. Results varied by market, and the indicator does not guarantee profitable trading or eliminate false signals.

The study investigates spin and orbital Edelstein effects in electron- and hole-doped monolayer 2H transition-metal dichalcogenides, including MoS₂, MoSe₂, MoTe₂, WS₂, WSe₂, WTe₂, NbS₂, and NbSe₂. A substrate or perpendicular gate field breaks the monolayer’s horizontal mirror symmetry, changing the point group from D₃h to gyrotropic C₃v and inducing chiral in-plane spin and orbital textures. An in-plane electric field then displaces the Fermi surface, generating net spin and orbital magnetizations through the spin and orbital Edelstein effects.

A minimal five-orbital Hamiltonian was constructed by Löwdin-downfolding chalcogen orbitals from a nearest-neighbor metal–chalcogen tight-binding model. Its parameters were fitted to DFT bands calculated with the PAW method and GGA functional, while explicitly including spin–orbit coupling and gate-field-induced orbital mixing. The field dependence was represented by parameters γ₁ and γ₂, which vary approximately linearly with the perpendicular field. Near band edges, the model reduces to an effective Hamiltonian containing kinetic, Ising, and Rashba terms. Retaining all five d orbitals is necessary because the electric field couples the l=1 sector with the l=2 and l=0 sectors. Orbital and spin moments were evaluated using the atom-centered approximation, and Edelstein susceptibilities were calculated from the Fermi-surface response in a relaxation-time approximation.

For hole-doped monolayers, holes initially occupy the K/K′ pockets, but the Γ pocket produces a much stronger response because γ₁ is larger than γ₂. The orbital textures of the two spin-split bands have the same chirality, so their orbital Edelstein contributions add, while their opposite spin chiralities cause substantial cancellation of the spin Edelstein response. Occupying the Γ pocket therefore sharply increases the orbital response and initially increases the spin response before cancellation becomes prominent. Because the required hole concentration can be high in some materials, small compressive strain can shift the Γ valence bands above the K/K′ bands. This allows the strongly responding Γ pocket to be occupied at low doping and substantially enhances both effects; for MoS₂, about 1% compressive strain is sufficient.

In electron-doped monolayers, electrons occupy the K/K′ conduction bands. Opposite spin chiralities largely cancel the spin Edelstein contributions, whereas unequal orbital-band weights prevent comparable orbital cancellation. Consequently, the orbital Edelstein susceptibility grows linearly with electron density and is several times larger than the spin susceptibility, even at low doping. Strain is not needed to obtain a large orbital response because the relevant conduction bands are already strongly field-dependent. The downfolded model is limited to small electron concentrations of roughly 0.02 electrons per unit cell because it does not reproduce the conduction-band K–Γ energy dip.

Across the studied materials, spin and orbital Edelstein susceptibilities reach approximately 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁷ μB V⁻¹m, one or two orders of magnitude above previously reported values for other systems. The responses scale approximately linearly with the gate field at low fields. The results identify doped, gated TMD monolayers as strong candidates for studying the orbital Edelstein effect and for spintronic applications.

On December 12, 2016, NVIDIA Corporation entered into a Termination Agreement with Goldman, Sachs & Co. to terminate 63,259,180.62 outstanding warrants for NVIDIA common stock. NVIDIA will deliver shares to Goldman, with the amount determined daily based on the stock’s daily volume-weighted average price from December 13, 2016, through January 31, 2017. The shares will be issued under Section 4(a)(2) of the Securities Act of 1933. The agreement is filed as Exhibit 10.1.

Past government shutdowns had little lasting impact on markets or the economy, costing an estimated 0.1 percentage point of GDP per week, with short-term losses generally recovered. This shutdown could differ because President Trump threatened permanent cuts to some federal employees, potentially worsening already-precarious employment conditions. A prolonged shutdown would also suspend key Labor Department activities, delaying and potentially reducing the quality of economic data. This could affect payroll figures, Social Security cost-of-living adjustments and Federal Reserve policy decisions. Furloughed federal employees and contractors would face the most immediate financial hardship, while the Washington, D.C. region could also be affected. Despite these risks, most economists expect the overall economic impact to remain relatively mild.

The Netflix documentary “Unknown Number: The High School Catfish” follows Michigan students Lauryn Licari and Owen McKenny as they receive escalating abusive, sexually graphic, and life-threatening messages from someone who appears to know them personally. After local investigations stall for 18 months, the sheriff sends the FBI 720 pages of messages and Owen’s phone for forensic examination.

The reviewer says the documentary handles cellphone forensics too briefly but illustrates how investigators may examine both mobile devices and cellular-provider records. Using the case to argue against excessive cellphone access in schools, the author highlights its potential links to cybercrime, investigations, and harm to students.

Oklahoma’s new one-year trial “bell to bell” policy prohibits phones, smartwatches, and other internet-capable devices in schools during the 2025–2026 school year, prompting backlash from some parents and students. The documentary’s culprit is unexpected, and the reviewer considers the story sad, thought-provoking, and worth watching.

The Bank of England allotted £5.085 billion in a six-month indexed long-term repo operation, its highest since March 2020 and more than double the previous week’s £2.352 billion. The facility offers secured funding against high-quality collateral as the BoE unwinds quantitative easing and shifts banks away from abundant reserves. Six-month demand remains below short-term repos, which drew £87.149 billion last week. The BoE must balance liquidity provision with keeping gilt markets functioning smoothly.

The Fabian Market Timing Model is a rule-based, long-term trend-following strategy for the S&P 500, developed by Richard Fabian in the 1960s. It uses the S&P 500’s 39-week moving average, with signals confirmed by the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the utilities sector, to reduce—but not eliminate—false signals. Buy and sell decisions are executed mechanically at the end of each week. Backtests showed returns closer to buy-and-hold, though the high CAGR was influenced by starting shortly after the dot-com bubble peak. The strategy’s main strengths were low volatility and maximum drawdown. Its central lesson is that disciplined adherence to a carefully chosen system is essential.

A House panel advanced a proposal to address South Carolina’s $24 billion pension gap by raising employee contributions from 8.66% to 9% and employer contributions from 11.56% to 18.56% by 2023, drawing objections from local governments. Separately, the House advanced legislation recognizing concealed weapons permits from all states. The Senate passed a bill authorizing Coastal Carolina University championship license plates, with proceeds supporting scholarships; a similar Clemson plate bill was introduced.

Chelsea will face Barcelona in the Champions League last 16 after finishing second in Group C behind Roma. The first legs are set for February 13/14 or 20/21, with returns on March 6/7 or 13/14. Barcelona topped Group D with 14 points and conceded once. Chelsea beat Barcelona 3–2 on aggregate in the 2012 semi-final. Lionel Messi, with 363 goals in 397 appearances since 2004, is the focus of the tie.

Tesla, Inc. filed a Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2021. The filing includes unaudited financial statements, related notes, and cautions that forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties, including those related to COVID-19, supply-chain constraints, competition, operations, demand, and financial results.

At September 30, 2021, Tesla reported total assets of $57.834 billion, total liabilities of $29.340 billion, and stockholders’ equity of $27.053 billion. Cash and cash equivalents were $16.065 billion; inventory was $5.199 billion; property, plant and equipment was $17.298 billion; operating lease vehicles were $4.167 billion; solar energy systems were $5.821 billion; and digital assets were $1.260 billion. Current debt and finance leases totaled $1.716 billion, while long-term debt and finance leases totaled $6.438 billion.

For the three months ended September 30, 2021, revenue was $13.757 billion, up from $8.771 billion in 2020. Revenue included $12.057 billion from automotive operations, $806 million from energy generation and storage, and $894 million from services and other activities. Gross profit was $3.660 billion, operating income was $2.004 billion, net income was $1.659 billion, and diluted earnings per common share were $1.44. For the first nine months, revenue was $36.104 billion, gross profit was $8.759 billion, operating income was $3.910 billion, net income was $3.301 billion, and diluted earnings per share were $2.84.

Nine-month operating cash flow was $6.912 billion. Investing activities used $5.952 billion, including $4.672 billion for property and equipment and $1.500 billion for digital assets. Financing activities used $3.946 billion, largely reflecting debt repayments. Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash ended the period at $16.694 billion.

Tesla operates two reportable segments: automotive and energy generation and storage. It designs, manufactures and sells electric vehicles and solar energy and storage products. The filing noted continuing pandemic-related logistics and supply-chain pressures, including port congestion, supplier delays and semiconductor shortages.

Automotive sales revenue is generally recognized upon delivery. Deferred automotive revenue, primarily related to Supercharger access, connectivity, Full Self-Driving features and over-the-air updates, was $2.22 billion, of which $1.39 billion was expected to be recognized within 12 months. Automotive regulatory-credit revenue was $279 million for the quarter and $1.151 billion for the nine months. Energy-related deferred revenue was $262 million.

Tesla purchased $1.50 billion of bitcoin during the first nine months and temporarily accepted bitcoin for certain product sales before suspending the practice in May 2021. Digital assets are accounted for as indefinite-lived intangible assets at cost, reduced for impairment and not adjusted upward for subsequent fair-value increases until realized gains arise. Tesla recorded $101 million of nine-month digital-asset impairments and a $128 million gain in March. At September 30, digital assets had a carrying value of $1.26 billion and fair value of $1.83 billion.

Inventory write-downs totaled $106 million for the first nine months. Construction in progress of $5.109 billion primarily covered Gigafactory Berlin and Texas construction, the Shanghai expansion, and manufacturing equipment and tooling. Capitalized interest was $52 million for the nine months. The accrued warranty reserve was $1.736 billion, reflecting $671 million of nine-month warranty provisions.

During the first nine months, Tesla converted $422 million of 2021 Notes, $416 million of 2022 Notes and $1.14 billion of 2024 Notes, issuing 5.3 million, 5.7 million and 16.8 million shares for the respective conversion premiums. It also repaid $1.80 billion of 2025 Notes, recording a $60 million debt-extinguishment charge, issued $1.08 billion and $904 million of automotive asset-backed notes in March and September, and repaid or terminated several other financing facilities.

Tesla adopted ASU 2020-06 on January 1, 2021 using the modified retrospective method, adjusting convertible-note accounting, additional paid-in capital, accumulated deficit and property, plant and equipment. The adoption reduced nine-month net interest expense by $196 million and increased nine-month diluted earnings per share by $0.19.

The 2018 CEO Performance Award had 12 vesting tranches tied to market-capitalization and operational revenue or Adjusted EBITDA milestones. All market-capitalization milestones had been achieved by the second quarter of 2021. Three-quarter CEO-award compensation expense was $190 million and nine-month expense was $665 million, including catch-up expenses of $116 million, $124 million and $124 million in the first three quarters.

Under its Gigafactory New York lease and related agreement, Tesla must meet employment and New York investment requirements, including incurring at least $5 billion in specified costs over ten years. Failure to meet annual requirements could require a $41 million program payment for each noncompliant year.

This interdisciplinary qualitative study examines how dialogic pedagogy can be understood and enacted in music and mathematics education. Using deductive, narrative, and hermeneutic approaches, it analyzes epistemological dialogue concerned with subject knowledge, ontological dialogue concerned with students’ lives and self-understanding, Bildung, musicking, and mathematizing.

Two cases are studied: a four-week choir project involving 40 pre-service music teachers, and a 45-minute upper-primary mathematics lesson involving 25 seventh-graders. In the music case, a teacher included a student’s suggested song, discussed its existential themes, and disclosed her brother’s death from AIDS. The episode combined subject learning with personal and existential engagement, while raising concerns about appropriate boundaries between personal and private disclosure. In the mathematics case, students discovered and tested a possible method for finding fractions between two fractions. The teacher acknowledged uncertainty, invited hypotheses, and followed students’ contributions, supporting mathematical reasoning, mathematizing, critical questioning, and student agency.

Across both cases, teachers promoted participation by listening carefully, taking up students’ ideas, sharing uncertainty, and allowing students to influence the activity while retaining subject expertise and leadership. Teachers and students appeared as whole persons, and classroom dialogue connected subject learning with personal, social, and democratic formation. The authors argue that these practices can support Bildung and democratic capacities, while emphasizing that such outcomes are not direct or predictable. They also note paradoxes: strategies invoking student voice may preserve teacher authority, personal engagement may intrude on students’ privacy, and educational goals may privilege particular cultural or social values.

The United States has a duty to help establish a lasting peace but must state the conditions for joining a league of peace. The war must end in terms creating a just, enduring settlement approved by mankind, not merely serving the combatants’ interests. Any covenant must include the peoples of the New World and reflect American political principles. Treaties alone cannot secure peace; lasting order requires an organized force representing a community of nations rather than rival power blocs. Assurances that the war’s purpose is not to crush opponents are interpreted as requiring “peace without victory,” based on equality, common participation, mutual benefit, and goodwill rather than humiliating terms imposed on the defeated.

A 19-year-old woman was sexually assaulted by a man aboard a train between Weston-super-Mare and Taunton on April 8; passengers intervened. British Transport Police are appealing for information from witnesses.

Lorna Gibson recapped trabecular bone and presented methods for modeling osteoporosis with random Voronoi honeycombs. A whale vertebra obtained from the Massachusetts Fish and Wildlife Department was introduced as a possible source of uniform trabecular-bone specimens for cutting and compression testing.

Finite-element analyses of two-dimensional Voronoi structures showed that their elastic and shear moduli closely matched closed-form analytical predictions. Structural randomness had little effect on modulus but reduced strength because varied strut lengths and orientations produced a broad distribution of strains and stresses. Low-density models failed by elastic buckling, while denser models failed through plastic yielding, with a transition near 3.5% relative density. Voronoi strengths were approximately 0.6–0.8 times those of regular hexagonal honeycombs and reached a minimum near 5% relative density, attributed to interaction between buckling and yielding.

Models examining bone loss compared thinning struts with removing them. Thinning caused predictable reductions in modulus and strength, whereas strut removal caused much larger losses. At the percolation threshold, a network separates into disconnected pieces and its stiffness and strength fall to zero. This threshold occurred after roughly 30–35% density reduction in two-dimensional models and 50% in three-dimensional models. A perturbed square-Voronoi model was adjusted to match the orientation of vertebral trabeculae and reproduced behavior similar to tested vertebral bone, including localized deformation bands.

The lecture also surveyed metal foams as potential porous coatings or substitutes in orthopedic and spinal implants. Discussed fabrication methods included replica processes, fugitive-phase processing, foaming agents, argon expansion, freeze casting, and laser-based powder-bed methods. Titanium and tantalum foams were highlighted because of their biocompatibility and corrosion resistance. Their measured properties showed substantial scatter but broadly followed expected foam scaling, with modulus related approximately to density squared and compressive strength to density to the three-halves power. Implant coatings primarily require porosity rather than a structure matching bone, although tissue-engineering scaffolds are often designed in the geometry of the anatomy they replace.

Finally, Gibson discussed the evolutionary development of mineralized skeletons. Early mineralized animal structures primarily used calcium carbonate, silica, or chitin, whereas bone consists of collagen and calcium phosphate. Ray-finned fishes were identified as the first vertebrates with bone, appearing about 450 million years ago. A study of an approximately eight-million-year-old *Oreopithecus* ilium digitally reconstructed from fossil fragments and compared its trabecular density and architecture with humans and three non-human primates. Its patterns were reported as more human-like, suggesting at least some bipedal behavior. Bone density was associated with stress magnitude, while trabecular orientation reflected principal stress directions. Solid bone properties can vary slightly among species, and osteoporosis may also involve age-related microcracks that further reduce strength. The next lecture was previewed as covering tissue-engineering scaffolds, osteochondral scaffolds, and cell mechanics.

The lecture reviews linearized general relativity, where spacetime is treated as a small perturbation of flat spacetime. The perturbation’s 10 components separate into six gauge-invariant degrees of freedom and four gauge degrees of freedom. Of the gauge-invariant components, the transverse-traceless metric perturbation \(h^{TT}_{ij}\) describes gravitational radiation and contains two physical degrees of freedom.

A wave propagating in the \(z\)-direction must have a spatial perturbation orthogonal to that direction. Although a single freely falling body appears stationary in coordinates that follow it, measurable effects arise when comparing nearby bodies. Their relative separation can be studied through light-travel-time measurements or geodesic deviation, which relates relative acceleration to spacetime curvature. A ring of test bodies illustrates the two fundamental polarizations: \(h_{xx}\) produces alternating stretching and squeezing along perpendicular axes (the “plus” polarization), while \(h_{xy}\) produces stretching and squeezing along diagonal axes (the “cross” polarization). LIGO detects these tidal distortions by timing laser light reflected between mirrors, using interference to measure changes in the light’s round-trip travel time.

The lecture then explains how to calculate the radiation field from a source. In Lorentz gauge, the linearized Einstein equations reduce to a wave equation for the trace-reversed metric perturbation, whose exact solution uses a retarded Green’s function. For a distant, compact source, the separation between source and observer may be approximated as constant, and only the leading multipole is retained. Applying the tensor virial theorem expresses the result in terms of two time derivatives of the source’s quadrupole moment. Projecting this result transverse to the propagation direction and making it traceless yields the quadrupole formula for gravitational waves. This leading-order result predicts that gravitational radiation is extremely small but carries substantial energy; a later lecture will address the energy form of the quadrupole formula.

The Fort Worth Court of Civil Appeals affirmed the judgment granting John and Mary Lee Geesbreght a divorce and awarding custody of their minor children to John, but reversed and remanded the property-division issues for a new trial. The court held that Tarrant County had jurisdiction because Mary Lee had appeared in the Texas case and waived her jurisdictional objection, and the children’s legal domicile remained in Texas despite their physical removal to Illinois. The jury found that awarding custody to John would serve the children’s best interests, made him managing conservator, and granted Mary Lee possessory-conservator rights and unlimited visitation. The court found no reversible error in the supplemental jury instructions or the custody verdict. On property, the trial court had valued John’s 500 shares in Emergency Medicine Consultants at $16,000 based on book value and omitted the corporation’s goodwill. The appellate court held that goodwill existed independently of John and that failing to consider it produced an inadequate property award to Mary Lee. Appeal costs were divided equally between the parties.

The study externally validated the Longitudinal Grade of Membership (L-GoM) model in Predictors 3, a community-dwelling, multiethnic cohort recruited through the WHICAP project in North Manhattan. The cohort was older, more female and Hispanic, and had lower education and less frequent APOE4 status than Predictors 2. Of 273 participants included in validation, 123 had mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and 150 had Alzheimer’s disease dementia; follow-up was annual.

The L-GoM model summarizes presentations across 11 clinical domains as a weighted combination of four latent disease subtypes. Subtype 4 represents disease severity and was the only subtype associated with significant mortality and need for full-time care (FTC); progression in the other subtypes ultimately leads toward subtype 4. Baseline scores generated individual predictions of survival and FTC prevalence for up to 7.5 years.

Survival predictions closely matched observed data overall. After excluding 32 participants whose AD diagnoses later reverted to non-dementia, all mortality observations were within confidence bands for both AD nonreverters and participants with MCI. FTC predictions were also generally close, with modest deviations for AD nonreverters and MCI groups. The model did not fit the AD reverters, whose survival was substantially higher and FTC need lower than predicted. The authors concluded that many reversion cases likely represented premature or incorrect AD diagnoses.

L-GoM scores differed significantly between MCI and AD, AD reverters and nonreverters, and by sex, ethnicity, and APOE status. The validation supports use of L-GoM across community-dwelling older adults of diverse backgrounds and extends its use to MCI. The web-based calculator implementing the model was also validated. Limitations include a small non-Hispanic nonwhite sample, validation concentrated among Caribbean-origin Hispanics, and the possible need to modify the model for other populations, instrumentation, or biological domains such as imaging, biomarkers, pathology, and gene expression.

Fibonacci trading uses Fibonacci ratios and tools—primarily retracement, expansion, fan, and channel tools—to identify potential support and resistance, plan entries and exits, and set stops or profit targets. Retracements mark levels such as 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, and 78.6% of a prior price swing, while expansion tools estimate the possible size of the next trend swing.

There is no universally best timeframe or retracement level. Day traders may use intraday charts, swing traders may use four-hour or daily charts, and higher timeframes may improve technical analysis. Market volatility also affects which levels price reaches. Backtesting is presented as the best way to evaluate a Fibonacci strategy.

Although Fibonacci trading is popular, the passage says its claimed success is largely anecdotal and lacks scientific support. The authors could not produce meaningful backtests because the strategy requires subjective rules, and they had not observed consistently successful Fibonacci traders. A cited study of Vanguard ETFs found that passive buy-and-hold outperformed an active Fibonacci-retracement strategy, though it still considered retracements potentially useful for identifying support, resistance, and profit targets. The authors advise caution, combining Fibonacci with other indicators, and avoiding strategies that have not been backtested. They consider Fibonacci unlikely to be a strong day-trading or crypto strategy without positive backtest evidence.

The passage defines day trading as buying and selling financial instruments within the same trading day to profit from short-term price movements. It can be profitable but requires substantial capital, numerous trades, constant market attention, quick decisions, discipline, and effective risk management. It describes 21 strategies:

- **Momentum:** Enter as prices rise and exit as momentum declines.
- **Range:** Buy near support and sell near resistance in less turbulent markets.
- **Scalping:** Seek small, rapid gains through trades lasting seconds or minutes.
- **Breakout:** Trade price moves beyond established support and resistance ranges.
- **Pullback:** Buy temporary declines within upward trends, using technical support to identify entries.
- **Reversal:** Attempt to profit when existing trends change direction.
- **Gap:** Exploit sharp price gaps caused by fundamental or technical factors.
- **News:** React to economic, earnings, and geopolitical news and its likely market effects.
- **Pattern:** Use chart patterns to anticipate price movements.
- **Seasonal:** Trade recurring annual patterns such as the January Effect or Santa Claus Rally.
- **Dark pool:** Trade in private markets where orders are not publicly displayed, accepting transparency and conflict-of-interest risks.
- **Statistical arbitrage:** Use mathematical models to exploit pricing inefficiencies between related securities.
- **Pairs:** Go long one correlated security and short another to profit from relative movements.
- **Order flow:** Analyze buy and sell order flow to anticipate prices.
- **Market making:** Provide liquidity by placing simultaneous buy and sell orders, accepting inventory and tail-event risks.
- **Short squeeze:** Trade forced short-covering that may drive prices upward.
- **Statistical volatility:** Use volatility-based methods to anticipate likely market patterns while adapting to changing conditions.
- **Market profile:** Interpret market data and price behavior to map possible movements.
- **Regime switching:** Adjust strategies as market trends or conditions change.
- **Volatility targeting:** Change position sizes to maintain a consistent portfolio risk level.
- **Phase analysis:** Trade according to phases of market cycles.

Strategies should be matched to market conditions and individual goals. Discipline, emotional control, predefined entries and exits, and logical analysis are emphasized. Technical analysis can help identify trends, support, resistance, and entry or exit points, but it is not infallible and should be combined with other analysis and backtesting.

Backtesting uses historical data to simulate a strategy under defined rules and assess past performance. It can reveal weaknesses and guide refinements, but it cannot guarantee future results because market conditions change and strategies can deteriorate over time. The passage cites a long-only SPY example with 165 trades, a 0.51% average gain per trade, a 60% win rate, 9% maximum drawdown, and 2.5% annual returns while invested only 2% of the time.

Day-trading risks include rapid losses from volatility, leverage, impulsive decisions, commissions, and potentially losing more than the initial investment through borrowed funds. FINRA requires U.S. pattern day traders to maintain at least $25,000 in equity. Although a skilled trader with a $10,000 account might earn $200–$300 through a 2%–3% daily return, the passage states that consistent 1% daily returns are unrealistic, most day traders do not profit, and as few as 10% make any money. It also states that almost all scalpers lose money.

Trading opportunities and risks vary by time: volatility and volume are typically highest during the first hour after opening and the final hour before closing, while midday conditions are often calmer. Holidays reduce volume and liquidity and may increase volatility. Seasonal changes can also affect volume, behavior, and opportunities. Astrology may be used by some traders, but its effectiveness is not scientifically proven.

Day-trading strategies can be adapted to stocks, foreign exchange, futures, and cryptocurrencies, provided each market’s dynamics are considered. Unlike day trading, swing trading holds positions for several days or weeks and avoids overnight and weekend exposure.

The passage compares the rapid spread of charter schools beginning with the “class of 1993” to the expansion of universal Education Savings Accounts (ESAs), or “divisible vouchers,” in a similarly paced “class of 2023.” The 1993 charter wave was largely politically blue, while the ESA wave and subsequent 2024–2025 adopters were entirely red. By 2025, the brief identified 11 states with universal ESAs and 12 if near-universal New Hampshire were included. Texas was considering joining them.

ESAs let parents use publicly funded accounts for private-school tuition, homeschooling, pods, curricula, and other educational goods and services. Their intellectual roots lie in Milton Friedman’s proposals for minimum-education vouchers and divisible vouchers. The brief interprets these policies as intended to reduce government’s role in education and produce taxpayer savings rather than guarantee high-quality schooling. U.S. voucher amounts are generally well below public-school per-pupil spending, unlike Sweden’s system, where vouchers reached parity with public-school spending. Other voucher advocates generally supported income-targeted aid and did not propose today’s flexible ESAs. Chile’s experience showed both the equity potential of higher voucher values and problems associated with supplemental “topping up.”

The passage identifies weak accountability as a central concern. Arizona inherited more than 170,000 unapproved expense orders, many lacking adequate receipts, while Florida approved purchases including kayaks, trampolines, theme-park tickets, televisions, and other items of questionable educational value. Pedagogical oversight is also limited: no state ESA program requires certified teachers; Arizona and Utah do not require student testing; and many programs do not require degrees, graduation reporting, or alignment with state academic standards. These gaps particularly affect homeschooled students and pupils in lightly regulated private schools or pods.

Financial concerns are equally prominent. Because private-school tuition often exceeds ESA allocations, families must supplement public funds, and private schools have responded to subsidies by raising tuition, as occurred in Iowa. Universal programs also subsidize middle- and upper-income families already paying private-school costs. Spending has risen sharply: Arizona’s voucher funding increased from $77 million in 2013 to just over $1 billion in 2025, Florida’s from $376 million to $3.7 billion, and Ohio’s from $150 million to just over $1 billion. The passage distinguishes immediate state costs from advocates’ projected long-term savings and argues that underfunding could impose larger long-term educational and social costs.

Based on studies of charter-school enrollment losses, the passage anticipates that districts receiving students through ESAs or vouchers will not realize savings proportional to lost revenue because schools have substantial fixed costs. It also warns that ESAs could disproportionately weaken small rural schools because students can leave for pods or homeschooling, potentially forcing consolidation or closure. Because rural schools serve as community and civic centers, their contraction could damage community life as well as education.

The passage also examines discrimination and student sorting. Safeguards are often absent: among states with private-school choice programs in 2020, few required schools to admit students without regard to religion, sexual orientation, or disability, and many did not publicly list participating schools. Indiana research found private schools pushing out low-achieving voucher students. As more higher-performing middle-income students use ESAs to leave public schools, difficult students may become concentrated in already-struggling schools. Religious schools receiving ESA funds may also restrict or dismiss faculty and staff on religious or sexual-orientation grounds. The brief notes that Supreme Court decisions permitting vouchers or tax-credit scholarships for religious schools did not cite European safeguards against such discrimination, including nondiscrimination requirements, common curricula, uniform per-pupil budgets, and uniform teacher pay.

ESA and universal-voucher programs are expected to continue expanding, supported by families already paying private-school tuition, religious schools, and the proposed Educational Choice for Children Act. Their growth may be constrained by lower private-school teacher salaries and the limited number of families able to homeschool or operate pods. Voters have rejected voucher referenda in several states.

The brief recommends repealing existing ESA programs. Where repeal is impossible, it urges lawmakers to reject expansion, impose budget and spending limits, restrict eligible purchases, strengthen monitoring and audits, require certified teachers and annual assessments, enforce civil-rights protections, and subject new programs to public hearings and, where feasible, referenda. State education agencies should publish participating schools, graduation rates, and access for students with disabilities, while local officials should document program effects, seek mitigating legislation, inform constituents, and adopt opposition resolutions where appropriate.

The Side Screen Offense is a two-player screen-and-roll isolation found throughout NBA playbooks. It can begin when a post steps out to set an on-ball screen, either after the point guard clears the wing or after a pass and basket cut. Most teams run it on the left for right-handed players and on the right for left-handed players, allowing penetration toward the vulnerable middle with the ballhandler’s stronger hand. Basic options include driving over the screen, pulling up, passing back to a rolling post after a switch, or kicking out when a weakside defender helps.

Successful execution depends on the ballhandler and screener functioning as one unit through footwork, timing, nonverbal communication, and experience. Defensive reads and counters include driving against a chase, dropping the ball to the post against baseline help, kicking out against a weakside sag, pulling up against a defender going under, driving opposite an early cheat, changing direction against a defender fighting through, popping the screener against show-and-recover defense, and using roll, post-up, or isolation actions against switches. Anticipated switches can be countered with a slip cut, denied screens with a lob pass, and traps with a string-out and 2-1-2 alignment.

Common entries include High Post Rub, Power/Motion, and Horns sets. Continuities include Flex, Triangle Game, single or double motion, weakside double screens, and baseline down screens, helping maintain balance, rebounding position, and late-clock organization.

The offense should be taught through whole-part-whole instruction, breakdown drills, and scrimmaging, supported by individual skill development. Coaches should scout opponents, anticipate defensive reads, vary alignments and entries, attack weaker defenders, and use Side Screens as the shot clock winds down. Defenders should also understand how to disrupt the action.

This continuation application incorporates by reference the contents of four earlier continuation patents and numerous provisional applications filed between November 2019 and October 2020. It describes hydraulic-fracturing fluid ends, which pressurize fluids and proppants for injection into wellbores and operate at pressures commonly ranging from 10,000 to 15,000 psi, with peaks up to 22,500 psi.

Traditional fluid ends use single alloy-steel housings with intersecting vertical and horizontal bores, creating highly stressed corners where fatigue cracks commonly form. Corrosion, erosion from proppants, and cyclic pressure can cause leakage and failure after only a few hundred operating hours, while a single fracturing operation may require up to 50 hours. Conventional power ends generally have longer service lives because they are not exposed to the same fluids and abrasives.

The disclosed fluid end uses multiple side-by-side, single-piece housing sections, preferably five, so an individual section can be replaced rather than the entire housing. Each housing has one longitudinal horizontal bore, eliminating the intersecting-bore stress points of traditional designs, reducing manufacturing time and cost, and permitting less expensive materials. Housings are attached to connect plates using stay rods, studs, washers, nuts, and alignment dowels.

Upper and lower intake manifolds can deliver fluids with different proppant concentrations, while discharge conduits and a discharge manifold carry pressurized fluid from the sections. The discharge bore may have an oval shape that becomes more circular under pressure, reducing housing stress and increasing flow.

Each housing also includes a removable stuffing box, retainer, plunger packing, packing nut, lubrication passages, seals, and a fluid-routing plug. The plug contains angled intake passages and offset discharge passages that direct fluid while reducing stress. Axially moving suction and discharge valves alternately open and close to route fluid into the pumping chamber and then toward the discharge bore. Tapered sealing surfaces, bevels, housing grooves, an expansion gap, and differently configured first and second seals accommodate pressure changes, reduce fatigue and erosion, and permit replacement of worn components. The drawings depict traditional equipment and embodiments of the modular fluid end and its components.

The lecture presents static fusion trees for predecessor and successor queries on a word RAM. They use linear space and polynomial preprocessing, and achieve search time proportional to \(\log_w n\), where \(w\) is the machine-word size. The construction resembles a B-tree with branching factor \(w^{1/5}\), allowing each node’s keys to be processed in constant time.

Fusion nodes rely on sketching, which extracts selected “important” bits from keys. These bits correspond to branching levels in the binary tree formed by the sorted keys; retaining them preserves key order. Because arbitrary queries may not follow the same branching paths as the stored keys, de-sketchification is required. A query is first located in sketch space, then its longest common prefix with neighboring keys identifies where it diverged from the key tree. A corrected query value is constructed by switching the incorrect branch and filling the remaining bits with zeros or ones. A second sketch-space search then yields the correct predecessor or successor rank.

A perfect sketch compresses only the important bits, but an approximate sketch is used in practice. It masks the important bits, multiplies the result by a specially constructed constant, and masks and shifts the product. The multiplier is chosen so that shifted bits do not collide, the important bits remain ordered, and the resulting sketch occupies an \(O(r^4)\)-bit region, where \(r\) is the number of important bits. With \(r=w^{1/5}\), all sketches for a node fit in \(O(w)\) bits and therefore in one word.

Parallel comparison locates a query sketch among many stored sketches at once. Repeating the query sketch in fixed-size fields, subtracting it from the stored sketches, and masking the result produces one comparison bit per key. The ordered transition from keys smaller than the query to keys larger than it identifies the insertion rank; multiplication can count the resulting one bits.

The lecture also constructs a constant-time method for finding the most significant set bit of a word on an ordinary word RAM. It divides the word into \(\sqrt w\) clusters, identifies nonempty clusters with masks and subtraction, compresses their status into a perfect sketch, and uses parallel comparison against powers of two to locate the first nonempty cluster and then its highest set bit. These sketching, comparison, and bit-scanning techniques together enable static fusion-tree queries in \(O(\log_w n)\) time.

The lecture explains how life cycle assessment (LCA) quantifies environmental impacts at the product or supply-chain level, complementing organizational-level carbon accounting. It uses a comparative study of hand-drying systems—Dyson Airblades, an Xlerator dryer, and several paper-towel products—to illustrate LCA methodology, assumptions, data limitations, and uncertainty.

The study compared systems based on a functional unit of one pair of dried hands. Its purposes included identifying impacts for Dyson engineers, comparing hand-drying options, informing product decisions, and supporting possible external claims. It used a cradle-to-grave boundary, standardized most manufacturing supply chains to China, used U.S. paper towels, and relied on bills of materials, bills of activities, third-party inventory data, and proxy data. Important uncertainties included drying times, product lifetimes, paper-towel quantities, electricity grids, manufacturing locations, transport, recycling, and waste treatment. Because Dyson commissioned the study and supplied detailed information about its own products, competitors had less access to comparable data and could challenge assumptions or commission another study.

Under ISO standards, LCA has four stages:

1. **Goal and scope definition:** Establish the product or service, purpose, intended application, audience, functional unit, system boundary, allocation rules, data assumptions, and whether the assessment is attributional or consequential. Attributional LCA describes the current, static system; consequential LCA models the effects of changes and indirect system-wide consequences. Comparative public assertions generally require third-party review.

2. **Inventory analysis:** Map the system and quantify inputs and outputs, including raw materials, energy, products, emissions to air and water, and waste. This requires bills of materials and activities, supply-chain information, manufacturing data, scrap rates, and databases such as ecoinvent. Missing product-specific data are replaced with proxies, averaged housing data, or other estimates.

3. **Impact assessment:** Classify inventory results into relevant impact categories and characterize them using equivalence or weighting factors. The study examined global warming potential, water use, cumulative energy demand, and the more comprehensive IMPACT 2002+ method. IMPACT 2002+ classifies midpoint effects such as carcinogens, ozone depletion, acidification, and resource extraction, then combines them into indicators for human health, ecosystem quality, climate change, and resources. Such aggregation embeds value judgments about trade-offs among impacts.

4. **Interpretation:** Relate results to the study’s objectives and evaluate robustness through sensitivity analysis, scenario uncertainty analysis using 20,000 Monte Carlo runs, and bill-of-activities uncertainty analysis. The most influential assumptions included drying time and electricity use. Despite overlapping outcome ranges, the Dyson Airblade had the lowest impact in most modeled scenarios—about 98%—although the Xlerator performed better under some assumptions.

SCOTUSblog’s “Relist Watch” examines petitions the Supreme Court has relisted for further conference consideration. It notes that relisting can signal a justice’s interest and increase the likelihood of review, although a case is generally more likely to be denied when a respondent waives a response.

The relisted cases involve:

- Parental rights: Parents challenge a school district’s transgender-support policies and its decision not to disclose students’ gender identities. The 10th Circuit held that the parents inadequately pleaded district responsibility for the challenged conduct.

- Religious accommodation: More than 1,000 New York healthcare workers challenge the state’s now-repealed COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The 2nd Circuit held that conflicting state regulations created an “undue hardship” under Title VII, while the workers argue that the Supremacy Clause requires federal religious-accommodation rules to prevail.

- App liability: A minor seeks to clarify whether Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act protects Grindr from claims involving defective design, age verification, geolocation, algorithmic recommendations, and sex trafficking.

- Jury trials and prison relief: California cannabis-code defendants ask whether the Seventh Amendment’s jury-trial right applies to state administrative proceedings. Separately, New Orleans officials seek to terminate a prison order requiring mental-health housing, raising what burden is required under Section 3626 of the Prison Litigation Reform Act.

- Arbitration: Flower Foods asks whether drivers who deliver locally bread that crossed state lines qualify for the Federal Arbitration Act’s exemption for workers engaged in interstate commerce.

- Criminal procedure: Relisted cases address the exceptions to appeal waivers, use of a screen for a child witness, alternatives to closing a trial to the public, congressional authority over intra-tribal conduct, and the effect of President Trump’s blanket pardon for January 6 defendants.

- FDA jurisdiction and property law: Stem-cell treatment companies ask whether processing a patient’s cells for reimplantation constitutes manufacturing an FDA-regulated drug. California’s unclaimed-property practices are challenged as violating due process and the Takings Clause.

- Civil rights and sovereign immunity: Other disputes concern qualified immunity for officers using body-weight pressure during a restraint, state liability for withholding forensic evidence under Brady, the Federal Tort Claims Act’s military-service exception, and alleged racial discrimination in striking Black jurors under Batson.

NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture combines real-time ray tracing, rasterization, AI, and simulation in a hybrid rendering model. The document describes enhancements to memory, display and video processing, GPU-to-GPU connectivity, artificial intelligence, geometry processing, shading, multi-view rendering, and VR support.

The NVIDIA Tesla T4 is presented as a Turing-based inferencing GPU for hyperscale data centers, enterprise solutions, and edge devices. It includes 2,560 CUDA Cores, 320 Tensor Cores, 16 GB of memory, and a 256-bit interface. It provides up to 130 TOPS of INT8 and 260 TOPS of INT4 inference performance, up to 40 times the inference performance of CPU-based systems, and more than 50 times their energy efficiency. It also offers up to twice the energy efficiency of the preceding Tesla P4. Its inferencing capabilities cover image classification and tagging, video analytics, natural language processing, speech recognition, and intelligent search.

Turing’s memory subsystem uses redesigned GDDR6 interfaces with 14 Gbps signaling and 20 percent better power efficiency than the GDDR5X used in Pascal GPUs. Package and board designs reduce signal crosstalk by 40 percent. Larger L2 caches and improved lossless compression increase effective bandwidth; the combination of greater raw bandwidth and reduced memory traffic produces an effective bandwidth increase of approximately 50 percent over Pascal. TU102 includes 6 MB of L2 cache, twice that of GP102.

The enhanced video engine supports additional formats, including HEVC 4:4:4 at 8, 10, and 12 bits and VP9 at 10 and 12 bits, and can decode more concurrent video streams than Pascal-based Tesla GPUs. Turing’s display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, 8K output at 60 Hz, Display Stream Compression 1.2, HDR, and BT.2100 tone mapping. Its enhanced NVENC encoder supports H.265 8K encoding at 30 fps and offers up to 25 percent H.265 and 15 percent H.264 bitrate savings. NVDEC supports the listed HEVC and VP9 formats.

Turing Multi-Process Service improves small-batch inference, launch latency, quality of service, and concurrent client handling. Tesla T4’s 320 GB/s memory bandwidth and doubled memory capacity relative to Tesla P4 allow hyperscale datacenters to nearly double VDI user density.

Turing replaces MIO- and PCIe-based SLI transfers with second-generation NVLink. TU102 has two x8 links and TU104 has one, each providing 25 GB/s per direction. TU102 therefore provides 50 GB/s in each direction, or 100 GB/s bidirectionally. Only two-way SLI is supported, while the added bandwidth enables new display topologies.

VirtualLink provides a single USB-C connection for VR power, display, and data while supporting HBR3 DisplayPort and SuperSpeed USB 3. It simplifies VR setups and enables use on smaller devices. Turing also expands resource management through bindless constant-buffer and unordered-access views and Tier 2 resource heaps.

Real-time ray tracing is enabled by dedicated RT Cores in each streaming multiprocessor. RT Cores handle bounding-volume-hierarchy traversal and ray/triangle intersection tests that otherwise require thousands of shader instruction slots per ray. Combined with denoising, efficient BVH structures, and compatible APIs, they make real-time effects such as reflections, refractions, shadows, and indirect lighting possible on a single GPU. The document states that Turing can exceed 10 Giga Rays per second and perform ray tracing about ten times faster than software-based ray tracing on Pascal.

The preferred approach is hybrid rendering, using rasterization where effective and ray tracing where it provides greater visual benefit, such as for reflections and shadows. Ray tracing can also be used for the entire workload in professional applications. NVIDIA Real-Time Ray Tracing Denoiser reduces the number of rays needed while maintaining image quality. Ray-traced shadows provide physically correct contact hardening, ray-traced ambient occlusion adds realistic definition, and ray-traced reflections avoid artifacts and limitations associated with screen-space reflections and static cubemap probes.

Turing introduces the RTX-OPS workload metric for mixed rendering workloads. Its example model weights Tensor operations at 20 percent, CUDA-core operations at 80 percent, RT-core operations at 40 percent, and INT32 operations at 28 percent. For the RTX 2080 Ti, these values produce a total of 78 RTX-OPS.

NVIDIA NGX is a Turing-only deep-learning stack that uses neural networks and Tensor Cores to accelerate graphics and other client-side functions. Its services are integrated through a thin API and managed through GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience. Models can use CUDA 10, DirectX, Vulkan, and TensorRT.

Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) trains against 64-times-supersampled reference images. Standard DLSS renders at lower input sample counts and infers target-resolution images with quality similar to temporal anti-aliasing while roughly halving shading work. DLSS 2X renders at target resolution and uses a larger network to approach the quality of 64-times supersampling. Other NGX services include Inpainting, which synthesizes replacement image content; AI Slow-Mo, which generates intermediate video frames; and AI Super Rez, which uses AI to enlarge images or video by 2x, 4x, or 8x, including real-time 1080p-to-4K video upscaling.

Mesh shading adds task and mesh shader stages that use cooperative thread models. Developers can submit many objects in a list, allowing task shaders to process the list, select levels of detail, and launch mesh shaders to produce triangles. This reduces CPU draw-call bottlenecks, supports more than an order of magnitude more objects at real-time frame rates, and enables dynamic geometric operations such as spherical cutaways in CAD models.

Variable Rate Shading (VRS) permits independent shading rates for each 16-by-16-pixel region. Developers can choose from several pixel-footprint options and control rates spatially or per primitive. Content Adaptive Shading lowers rates in areas with little changing detail, Motion Adaptive Shading reduces rates for moving objects, and Foveated Rendering concentrates detail near the viewer’s focus. VRS can also increase shading rates for multisampled anti-aliasing.

Texture Space Shading stores dynamically computed shading values in texture space and decouples visibility sampling from appearance sampling. Previously shaded texels can be reused within or across frames, improving temporal stability and allowing applications such as VR to stay within fixed rendering budgets. A stereo VR view can reuse shading from the first eye for the second.

Multi-View Rendering supports up to four hardware views per pass and up to 32 API-level views. Geometry is fetched and shaded once, while view IDs select view-specific transformations, attributes, and shader behavior. It expands Pascal’s simultaneous multi-projection capabilities and supports applications including stereo and wide-field-of-view VR, multi-character rendering, shadow-depth rendering, and cascaded shadow maps.

The TU104 chip contains six GPCs, 48 streaming multiprocessors, 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores. It is used in products including GeForce RTX 2080, Tesla T4, and Quadro RTX 5000. Tesla T4 uses a TU104 configuration with five GPCs, 20 TPCs, 40 SMs, 2,560 CUDA Cores, and 320 Tensor Cores. TU106, used in GeForce RTX 2070, contains three GPCs, 36 SMs, 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores, but does not support NVLink or SLI.

The document also explains ray-casting mechanics, BVH construction and refitting, denoising, and ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections. It states that the specification is provided as-is, is subject to NVIDIA’s sales terms and disclaimed warranties, reserves the right to change products and specifications, and does not warrant suitability for medical, military, aircraft, space, life-support, or other safety-critical applications.

This study assessed malaria and malnutrition risk factors and evaluated whether intermittent preventive therapy improved nutritional outcomes among school-age children in Muheza, northeastern Tanzania. It combined a cross-sectional baseline survey with a three-arm, randomized, open-label trial of 1,566 children aged 5–15 years. Participants received 12 months of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate-amodiaquine, or standard care and were followed for eight additional months. Baseline and longitudinal data were analyzed using logistic regression and linear mixed models.

At baseline, 27% of tested children had malaria. Among children aged 10 years or younger, 23% were underweight; 21% of all participants were stunted, and 28% were thin or severely thin. Malaria parasitemia was associated with 78% higher adjusted odds of stunting (AOR 1.78; 95% CI 1.36–2.33), with malaria attributed to 37% of stunting in the study population. Low socioeconomic status was associated with higher odds of being underweight (AOR 1.50), while recent malaria was associated with higher adjusted odds of thinness (AOR 1.37). Male sex was associated with higher odds of stunting.

Malaria prevalence was lower after 12 months in the treatment groups than in standard care, but nutritional status changed little. Neither preventive treatment significantly altered changes in weight, height, or BMI over time compared with control, and no treatment differences remained after treatment stopped.

The authors concluded that antimalarial drugs alone do not necessarily improve nutritional status and recommended integrated malaria-control and nutrition programs, including community collaboration to improve food availability in schools and provide sustainable nutrition education. Limitations included data originally collected mainly for malaria research, only one baseline measure of parasitemia limiting causal interpretation, inability to account for household clustering, and exclusion of children in grades 6–7. The preprint was not peer reviewed.
