COVID-19 was declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization on March 11, 2020, prompting Turkey to suspend in-person education and shift to virtual instruction through TRT EBA TV and other platforms. Students with disabilities in inclusive education settings faced challenges involving motivation, adaptation, socialization, individualized instruction, assignment tracking, family support, and access to devices and internet.

This qualitative study examined primary school teachers’ perspectives on these challenges and possible solutions during the pandemic. It used a phenomenology design and involved 10 general education primary school teachers from two Marmara Region provinces who had students with officially diagnosed disabilities. Data were collected through recorded, in-person, semi-structured interviews in 2021, lasting 28–35 minutes. The interview form was reviewed by four experts and piloted. Content analysis, in-vivo coding, and thematic analysis were used; transcription reliability was 98% and intercoder reliability was 90.17%.

Teachers contacted families, used EBA, Zoom, WhatsApp, hybrid schedules, and video submissions, and sought parental assistance with attendance and assignments. Although many students had high attendance with parental support, some attended only basic courses or could not participate because of internet, hardware, family-literacy, or support problems. Barriers to instruction and monitoring included large classes, insufficient teacher time, limited knowledge of students, difficulty implementing individualized education programs, weak home support, poor parent-teacher communication, limited contact with special education teachers, assignment-tracking difficulties, behavioral problems, and reduced social interaction. Reluctance to watch EBA TV, limited interaction, unengaging content, and difficulty obtaining or printing assignments were also reported. Nevertheless, some teachers successfully used EBA tracking and assessment features, daily parent communication, and family cooperation, and some students completed assignments and received high examination scores.

Applied responses included flexible schedules, hybrid instruction, home video monitoring, family guidance, and motivational calls. Suggested solutions included improving device and internet access, strengthening parent-teacher cooperation and home organization, supporting students’ social as well as academic development, keeping schools open, using EBA support centers for students and families, and coordinating with rehabilitation centers. Recommendations also included preparing accessible content, providing guidance and materials to teachers and families, and improving technological infrastructure. The study concluded that parental involvement was central to students’ participation and progress. Ethics approval was granted by the Eskişehir Osmangazi University Ethics Committee.

A phylodynamic and epidemiological study analyzed the Omicron BA.1 wave in England from November 2021 through January 2022 using 115,622 global SARS-CoV-2 genomes, including 48,615 English genomes, alongside mobility, case, and travel data covering 313 local authorities.

At least 6,455 independent introductions into England were inferred, 69.9% of which were singletons without observable local transmission. Importations increased exponentially until mid-December despite restrictions on arrivals from southern Africa, partly because source infections shifted toward major US cities; average weekly BA.1 importation intensity from 20 US cities was about four times that from South Africa during the restrictions. Although early introductions represented only about 6% of all introductions, they generated an estimated 80% of English BA.1 infections by the end of January. After Christmas, only about 25% of imported cases were followed by detectable local transmission.

Spatially, BA.1 spread rapidly from Greater London, with directional long-distance movements to other urban regions during early December. Continuous phylogeography and statistical modelling indicated that population size, distance, mobility, and London’s role as a travel hub shaped early expansion, while later spread increasingly involved movement toward regions with later epidemic peaks. Mobility reductions during Plan B restrictions and Christmas/New Year holidays contributed to geographically separated epidemic peaks. A statistical model estimated that each additional weekly case per 100 people in a hub reduced associated hub-to-home mobility by 11.97%, with a four-day lag, although long-distance travel was less affected than shorter-distance travel.

The findings indicate that targeted travel restrictions introduced after local transmission was established had limited effects, while behavioral responses to rising case numbers influenced the wave’s spatial expansion. Limitations include likely undercounting introductions, possible aggregation of unsampled lineages, and residual spatial and temporal sampling biases.

The paper adopts the UN definition of youth as ages 15–24 and distinguishes hard or technical skills from soft workplace skills. It defines experiential or work-integrated learning as learning through educational and practice settings and presents co-op as a form that integrates curriculum, work experience, and logistical coordination. Its central question is how co-op can improve school-to-work transitions and align Nigerian graduates’ skills with labor-market demand.

World Bank data for 1991–2021 show that Nigeria’s youth unemployment rate was historically below most comparison regions but rose to exceed all except South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa by 2021. Youth unemployment was generally at least twice the total unemployment rate, while the 2021 youth employment-to-population ratio in Nigeria and sub-Saharan Africa was about 20 percentage points below the total ratio. Informality, gender and regional disparities, and high NEET rates compound these challenges; Nigeria’s youth NEET rate was 28% in 2019, compared with 13% in OECD countries.

Co-op developed in industrialized countries and later spread to sub-Saharan African institutions. Alternating, parallel, sandwich, and “New American” models structure alternating periods of study and work or combine school and employment. Documented potential benefits include student skills, motivation, employability and earnings; employer recruitment and curriculum input; institutional industry links; and improved labor-market outcomes. However, research has often been limited or inconsistent, and program design and implementation strongly affect results. Studies from Canada and the United Kingdom generally associate work-integrated learning with better employment, lower unemployment, stronger job-field matches, and improved skills.

Practical co-op programs require academic eligibility, coordinated work terms, student fees, compensation, dedicated administrative units, quality assurance and accreditation. Nigerian policy responses include SIWES, the SURE-P Graduate Internship Scheme, and N-SIP’s N-Power initiative. These programs have supported skills and employability but face problems including weak industry integration, inadequate funding, poor placement matching, supervision gaps and administrative complexity.

The paper argues that a federally led, industry-integrated Nigerian co-op initiative could complement these programs, align curricula with employer needs, and support pilot implementation and public-sector work placements. It recommends an alternating model with multiple work terms, providing at least one year of career-related experience before graduation. It also cautions that governments cannot solve youth unemployment through training alone and calls for broader labor-market policies and research on governance, institution-specific models, costs and applicability to non-tertiary education.

The TLV321/2x comparators consume 40 µA per channel and provide 40 ns propagation delay for detecting fast voltage and current transients. TLV321x devices have push-pull outputs that source and sink current, while TLV322x devices have open-drain, sink-only outputs that can be pulled up to 0–5.5 V independently of the comparator supply.

Inputs may extend 200 mV beyond the supply rails but must not exceed them by more than 200 mV. Transient or fault current should be limited to 10 mA or less, and TI recommends series input resistance. Unused inputs must not be tied together because this can cause chatter; they should instead receive valid voltages that provide at least 50 mV differential input.

The devices include 1.8 mV of internal hysteresis. External hysteresis can be added through positive feedback using three-resistor inverting or two-resistor non-inverting networks. Output behavior depends on differential input voltage, with propagation delay influenced by overdrive; smaller overdrive, particularly below 100 mV, increases delay.

Internal ESD protection limits input excursions to 0.2 V beyond the rails. A power-on-reset circuit holds the output low for up to 32 µs after the supply crosses 1.65 V. Push-pull outputs must not connect to other outputs and unused ones must remain floating. Open-drain outputs support wired logic and level translation; TI recommends pull-up currents of 100 µA to 1 mA, and unused outputs may float or connect to V−. Series current-limiting resistors are recommended where output shorts are possible.

A low-side current-sensing application uses an amplifier and comparator to trigger when the amplifier output exceeds 1.1 V. High-speed layout practices are required, including placing a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass capacitor at the supply pin, minimizing input/output coupling, controlling trace impedance, and using series resistance to damp ringing. Additional sections address documentation updates, TI E2E support, ESD handling, revision history, and mechanical, packaging, and orderable information.

The passage describes NVIDIA’s GA10x Ampere architecture and its use in GeForce RTX 30-series, A40, and RTX A6000 GPUs. Each GA10x streaming multiprocessor contains 128 CUDA cores, four third-generation Tensor Cores, a second-generation ray-tracing core, a 256 KB register file, and 128 KB of configurable L1 cache/shared memory. Its four partitions use dual FP32 datapaths, enabling 128 FP32 operations per clock while retaining concurrent integer processing. Full GA102 GPUs contain seven GPCs, 112 ROPs, twelve 32-bit memory controllers, and 6 MB of L2 cache. FP64 support is limited to 168 units and one-sixty-fourth the FP32 rate.

Second-generation RT Cores accelerate BVH traversal and ray-triangle intersection at twice Turing’s rate and add hardware acceleration for ray-traced motion blur, including moving and deforming geometry. GA10x also supports concurrent ray tracing with graphics or compute workloads and simultaneous compute workloads. Third-generation Tensor Cores are individually twice as powerful as Turing Tensor Cores and add TF32 and BF16 support, fine-grained structured sparsity, and up to twice the effective matrix-operation throughput. Enhanced DLSS uses these capabilities to enable 8K gaming.

GA10x introduces GDDR6X memory using PAM4 signaling and Maximum Transition Avoidance encoding. It supports data rates up to 19.5 Gbps and peak bandwidth up to 936 GB/s. GDDR6X also adds Error Detection and Replay, which detects failed memory transactions and retries them. NVIDIA RTX IO and Microsoft DirectStorage enable GPU-based decompression and direct asset transfer from NVMe SSDs, reducing CPU load and accelerating game loading and streaming.

The architecture supports 4K at 120 Hz and 8K at 60 Hz through DisplayPort 1.4a and HDMI 2.1. Its fifth-generation NVDEC supports hardware decoding of MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, and AV1, while seventh-generation NVENC provides hardware encoding up to 8K HEVC.

The GeForce RTX 3090 uses GA102 with 82 SMs, 10,496 CUDA cores, and 24 GB of GDDR6X. The RTX 3070 uses GA104 with GDDR6 and lacks NVLink. The data-center-oriented A40 provides 48 GB of memory, PCIe Gen4, virtualization support, and NVLink scalability to 96 GB across two GPUs. The RTX A6000 likewise includes 48 GB of GDDR6, two-board NVLink scalability, hardware-accelerated motion blur, and AI denoising capabilities.

After praising Amy Barrett’s book on election law and originalism, the author accepts originalism as the interpretive method and applies it to Louisiana’s creation of a second majority-Black congressional district. The author argues that the “racial predominance” doctrine requiring strict scrutiny of race-based districting has no basis in the original public meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause or the Fifteenth Amendment. The latter, by its terms, addresses denial or abridgment of voting rights, not racial separation without vote dilution or any electoral infringement. Recognizing that precedent normally requires adherence, the author nevertheless argues that the racial-preponderance doctrine is unworkable and conflicts with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which permits remedies for vote dilution. A good originalist should therefore reconsider and abandon that doctrine, preserving congressional authority to address racially motivated districting through legislation. The author hopes Barrett and the Court will resolve the case with similar intellectual honesty.

The Investors Intelligence Sentiment Index, also called the Advisor Sentiment Index, is a weekly contrarian indicator created in 1963 by AW Cohen. It surveys more than 100 independent investment newsletters and reports the percentages of advisors who are bullish, bearish, or expect a correction. It also tracks the number of stocks above their 10- and 30-week moving averages. Extreme bullish readings—above 55%—may indicate excessive optimism and potential market weakness, while readings below 35% may indicate excessive pessimism and potential market strength. Weekly readings above 70% suggest an overbought market, and those below 30% suggest an oversold market.

Investor sentiment reflects investors’ overall market mood and may be estimated through price and trading activity or broad-market indicators. Unlike the AAII Sentiment Survey, which has polled individual investors about the market’s six-month direction since 1987, the Investors Intelligence Index focuses on professional advisors and commentators. Chartcraft publishes the index on its website, where subscriptions are available.

AMD Seamless Firmware Servicing (SFS) applies targeted, high-priority firmware fixes at runtime without requiring a system reboot. SFS patches are not persistent across warm or cold resets and must be reapplied after every reboot, including during OS boot, immediately after boot, or during normal operation.

SFS tracks three version types. The monotonically increasing SFS Patch Level (SFSPL) identifies the applied update package, with zero indicating an unpatched system, and prevents rollback. Individual firmware components have their own firmware and Security Patch Level (SPL) versions; newer packages advance these versions, although previously introduced functionality may be reverted. The monotonically increasing System Patch Level (SYSPL) tracks run-once code executed since the last reboot; its effects may be reversed, but its execution history cannot be erased. These levels, together with component versions, let the AMD Security Processor (ASP) ensure that patches match the system’s firmware and operational state and let the host OS query version information.

AMD cryptographically signs every SFS package, and the ASP verifies AMD’s signature before applying an update. Customers may optionally co-sign packages to retain approval authority over updates deployed in their datacenters. AMD describes the ASP as its root of trust for detection, while OEM/ODM designers own the root of trust for firmware updates and, unless AMD Platform Secure Boot is enabled, for their own firmware detection. Early OEM/ODM firmware restricts ROM access before untrusted code runs. When co-signing is enabled, the customer supplies an RSA public key to the ASP during early boot, before `BOOT_DONE`; the key cannot be changed afterward. The ASP then requires both AMD and customer signatures. Customers manage their signing keys, while AMD does not countersign them.

BIOS developers enable SFS through `APCB_TOKEN_UID_PSP_SFS_ENABLE` and optionally require co-signing through `APCB_TOKEN_UID_PSP_SFS_COSIGN_REQUIRED`; both options are disabled by default. Supported customer signing keys are 2048- or 4096-bit RSA keys, with RSA-PSS signatures using SHA-256 or SHA-384 respectively.

SFS application occurs at runtime. Updates must be applied sequentially, and on multi-socket systems the patch is communicated to the first socket’s ASP and applied to the appropriate additional sockets. Each package checks existing patch and firmware versions before determining applicability. Packages can modify registers or other values, replace a complete firmware image, or update parts of a firmware package. Validation occurs before updates are applied, and packages are responsible for confirming that required firmware versions exist to avoid dependency mismatches. If any portion cannot be fully applied, the package should not proceed, since the remaining option may be an undesirable forced reset.

A customer deployment agent prepares the required aligned command buffer, optional customer co-signing data, and the complete AMD-signed update package before sending its physical address to the primary ASP. The ASP protects the package memory from x86 access, verifies the customer signature when required, verifies AMD’s signature, loads and executes the patch, updates patch-level information, and returns status. Separate commands can report current firmware, SFSPL, SYSPL, and SPL information.

SEV updates are committed automatically and cannot roll back to earlier images without a reboot. With SNP enabled, pages used for an update must be HV-FIXED through `RMPUPDATE`. SEV or SEV/ES virtual machines may need to stop and restart during an SEV firmware update, while SEV/SNP virtual machines can continue operating. Updates run in parallel with x86 and DMA traffic and are designed to minimize performance impact, ideally without requiring OS quiescence.

SFS packages are binary objects aligned with AGESA releases and named using a family, AGESA release, and monotonically increasing package number. Each package applies only to a specific combination of firmware and system patch levels. Attestation data can be requested through sideband/SPDM or in-band/DPE interfaces, with SFS supplying required measurements; components prohibited from modification by an attestation scheme are not changed by AMD.

Passport applicants must take an oath of allegiance, provide a physical description, and submit an affidavit from at least one credible witness verifying identity and the stated facts. Native citizens may apply using the standard information. Persons born abroad to a native father must prove their father’s U.S. birth, residence, and citizenship at their birth. Naturalized citizens must submit their certificate or a certified court record and provide emigration, naturalization, residence, and identity details. The policy brief argues that UNESCO’s out-of-school children (OOSC) indicator is too narrow to measure educational exclusion because it tracks only whether school-aged children are enrolled in formal primary or secondary education. It overlooks attendance and learning, informal and non-formal pathways such as madrasas and community-based education, and the geographic, cultural, political, economic, and social causes of exclusion. Incomplete population data and the exclusion of marginalized groups also cause OOSC figures to underestimate exclusion.

Afghanistan illustrates these limitations. Formal schools have coexisted with historically rooted madrasa and masjid education, while conflict and geopolitical competition have shaped access, resources, curricula, and legitimacy. School enrollment rose from about 500,000 in 2000 to roughly 10 million in 2021, but education remained unequal. The Taliban’s ban on girls’ secondary education left about 80% of school-age girls out of school, affecting approximately 1.4 million students. Meanwhile, community-based classes, madrasas, online learning, radio, and television expanded without being captured by OOSC data.

Major barriers include geographic isolation and uneven resource distribution; the mobility, poverty, and work obligations of nomadic families; child labor; and inadequate facilities, staff, and learning materials for children with disabilities. Alternative pathways can help address these barriers, but the formal school system remains rigid and inflexible.

The brief recommends replacing OOSC with an out-of-education children (OOEC) indicator that captures formal, informal, non-formal, and technology-driven learning. It would legitimize diverse pathways, expose structural inequities, encourage culturally relevant reform, and support education systems as interconnected, resilient ecosystems aligned with SDG 4. Implementation requires data systems capable of tracking diverse learning experiences, credible credentialing across pathways, collaboration among education actors, and equitable resource allocation informed by cost data. Collaborative research, including the SPARKS initiative, can support this transition.

Archaeologists in Mexico are beginning a three-month excavation of a sealed tunnel system at Chichén Itzá, aiming to reach a previously unseen cenote beneath El Castillo. The team previously found two passages near the Ossuary that the Maya had deliberately blocked with stone. Cenotes—water-filled sinkholes and the Yucatán’s only freshwater sources—were central to Maya life and cosmology, viewed as entrances to the underworld and associated with offerings and human sacrifices intended to maintain balance with deities.

Researchers believe the hidden cenote may represent an “axis mudi,” or sacred center. Analysis of remains from Chichén Itzá’s Sacred Cenote found that about 80% of sacrifice victims were children ages 3–11, whose remains showed anemia and malnutrition. Researchers said the children may have been alive or already dead when deposited and called for further research.
Lab tests suggest jostling air-methane microbubbles create tiny lightning zaps that ignite seeping gas, potentially explaining ghostly will-o’-the-wisps.

Europe is positioning its Global Gateway initiative as an alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative in Africa, where nearly 600 million people lack electricity. A downloadable Take A Knee Chart is available in PDF and Google Sheets formats. Charts show player positions and movement order and support end-of-game clock management and practice in “kill the clock” situations. High school and college teams generally follow similar timing rules, including a 40-second play clock, but must account for incomplete passes stopping the clock and the absence of a two-minute warning.

The article examines distance education in Greek preschool education, focusing on kindergarten teachers’ familiarity, ICT literacy, experience, views, and prospects for post-pandemic use. It describes distance education as a technology-supported pedagogical process delivered synchronously, asynchronously, or in blended form. For preschoolers, technological tools are primarily supportive, while parental supervision and school–family cooperation are essential. Barriers include inadequate school infrastructure and internet access, unequal family resources, limited teacher training, and difficulties implementing ICT with young children.

A quantitative study was conducted during the 2020–2021 school year among kindergarten teachers in Epirus, Greece. Of 280 teachers in the target population, 84 were invited and 82 completed an anonymous Google Forms questionnaire between May 5 and June 4, 2021. The pilot-tested instrument combined demographic items, closed Likert-scale questions, and semi-closed and open questions; data were analyzed with SPSS 21. The sample was 96.3% women; 75.6% held bachelor’s degrees and 19.5% master’s degrees. Half reported basic ICT certification, while 35.4% reported enhanced certification.

Most respondents had little or no prior familiarity with distance education, and more than 90% had not incorporated it into kindergarten before the pandemic. Most also lacked experience with remotely delivered school programs or training. During implementation, 64.6% used synchronous and 35.4% asynchronous approaches. Webex was the dominant tool at 88.9%, followed by email at 60.5%; smaller proportions used e-class, Viber, Messenger, and other tools.

Teachers’ overall views of distance education for preschool were negative. Concerns included inadequate digital infrastructure and unequal internet or device access, preschool children’s limited independent use of technology, reduced effectiveness in developing social skills, restrictions on psychomotor activities, the need for adult supervision, weak student interest and participation, limited individualized learning, and insufficient inclusion of children with disabilities. More favorable but qualified views concerned flexibility, computer literacy, emergency use when attendance is impossible, teacher–parent cooperation, and blended learning. Nevertheless, distance education was generally viewed primarily as an emergency option rather than a strong ongoing preschool model.

A Kruskal–Wallis test showed that ICT certification level was significantly associated with pre-pandemic familiarity with distance education (p=.030); Level B certificate holders were more familiar than uncertified respondents (adjusted p=.025). Spearman correlation showed no significant relationship between years of service and ICT literacy (rho=.109, p=.331).

The authors recommend professional development in distance-education strategies and technology, modernization of school and family infrastructure, and interactive, age-appropriate learning resources accompanied by guidance and support for families. They caution that the age of preschool children and resulting digital inequality require careful integration. Because the sample was limited to Epirus, the findings cannot be generalized safely to all Greek kindergarten teachers.

ML²B is introduced as the first benchmark for evaluating large language models’ ability to generate complete machine-learning pipelines from multilingual natural-language descriptions. It addresses the English-only limitation of existing ML code-generation benchmarks by extending 30 real Kaggle competitions—24 public and 6 private—into 13 languages, yielding 390 evaluation instances. The tasks cover tabular, text, and image modalities across 12 domains. Public task descriptions were drafted through an LLM pipeline and manually reviewed, while private tasks were described manually. Standardized data cards, domain labels, and evaluation-metric metadata support reproducibility and reduce information leakage.

Descriptions, domains, and data cards were translated with GPT-4o, checked for artifacts, and assessed by native-language annotators with computing backgrounds. Performance is normalized as a Kaggle public-leaderboard percentile, with lower values indicating better results, to provide comparable rankings across competitions using different metrics and data scales.

The benchmark includes a main pipeline, isolated Docker runtime, and code grader. Submitted code is transformed using abstract syntax tree analysis, executed directly, and evaluated through required function interfaces. It supports a single-function MONO PREDICT format and a modular format with separate training, validation preparation, and prediction stages. The modular design delays access to prediction data, reduces preprocessing leakage, and enables static leakage analysis.

Five models are evaluated through AIDE and ML Master. Results show 15–45% degradation on non-English tasks, with English consistently producing the strongest rankings. Performance varies by language, domain, metric, and model. Low-resource languages such as Kazakh, Belarusian, and Romanian frequently produce nonfunctional code, while tabular classification and regression are less cross-lingual stable than image categorization and text classification. AIDE-tuned gpt-oss-120b and Gemini 2.5 Flash lead several slices, while hybrid systems such as gpt-4.1-mini with DeepSeek-R1 and gpt-oss-120b with Qwen3-Coder-30B partially mitigate weaknesses in harder domains and non-English tasks. No model is universally best.

Common failures include missing training entry points, runtime data loading, inconsistent preprocessing, altered function signatures, global dependencies, and invalid or deprecated library usage. Static analysis flagged potential leakage in 61 of 554 modular submissions; after identifying likely false positives and cases not involving prediction data, 33 submissions, or 5.9%, remained potentially leaky. Future work includes expanding private-task coverage, improving domain balance, adopting multilingual alignment and constrained tool-use methods, and strengthening secure interfaces and code auditing.
