This qualitative study examined how education for sustainable development (ESD) is understood and taught in South African Technology Education, guided by Kolb’s experiential learning theory. Semi-structured interviews and one-hour non-participant classroom observations were conducted with eight Senior Phase Technology teachers in Mpumalanga’s Ehlanzeni District. Interview transcripts were analysed inductively, while observation data were cross-referenced through triangulation.

Teachers demonstrated substantial knowledge of sustainability, including resource preservation, responsible technology use, renewable energy, societal well-being, and indigenous and traditional sustainability practices. However, their classroom teaching rarely incorporated these concepts, offered few ESD-related resources, or provided sufficient opportunities for learners to develop sustainability knowledge and skills.

The curriculum was found to offer several opportunities for ESD, including processing and recycling, waste management, renewable technologies, investigation of environmental impacts, responsible consumption, and sustainable design using recycled materials. Collaborative learning was identified as a promising approach because it supports knowledge sharing, diverse perspectives, creativity, problem-solving, cross-cultural collaboration, and the integration of indigenous knowledge. Nevertheless, demonstrations and lectures remained the dominant teaching methods, and collaborative learning was not consistently implemented.

The study recommends embedding ESD holistically across Technology Education, emphasising responsible citizenship, efficient resource and energy use, sustainable design and manufacturing, recycling, waste reduction, and responsible consumption. Teachers should use collaborative, hands-on activities and critical discussions about technology’s social and environmental effects. Limitations include the focus on one district, qualitative methods only, and the Senior Phase; broader provincial coverage, mixed-method research, and investigation of other phases were recommended.

This preprint describes the planned CBC2 prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 4 trial at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital in Bangkok. Beginning around January 2023, the study aims to enroll 90 women aged 18–70 with metastatic breast cancer who are receiving chemotherapy and have an Edmonton Symptom Assessment System score of at least 3. Participants will be randomized 1:1:1 to Ganja Oil, Metta Osot, or placebo oil and receive the assigned treatment nightly for 90 days. Assessments include baseline, an early safety visit, day 30, and day 90, with blood, saliva, stool, and skin samples collected before and after treatment. Withdrawal symptoms will be monitored for one month after treatment.

Outcomes will assess chemotherapy-related symptoms, quality of life, adverse effects, microbiome profiles, cytokines, bacterial metabolites, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacogenetics. Microbiome analyses will include alpha and beta diversity, while measured biomarkers include IL-17, interferon-γ, IL-10, TGF-β, LBP, sCD14, equol, short-chain fatty acids, and bile acids. The rationale includes pilot evidence of cannabinoid tolerability and symptom benefit, preclinical antitumor activity, and reported differences in microbial profiles among breast cancer subtypes.

Data will be analyzed by intention to treat using Stata 16, with chi-square tests, ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis tests, Shannon and Chao1 indices, and Jaccard/PERMANOVA analyses. The trial was approved by relevant institutional review boards and requires written informed consent.

Soccer’s position-numbering system, first used in England in the 1920s, assigned numbers from the back to the front and right to left within a 2-3-5 formation. With the 1950s “W-M” formation, inside forwards moved deeper, emphasizing the center forward, or “Number 9,” while set-back attackers became known as “Number 10s.” The center halfback also moved into defense.

From the 1960s, tactical experimentation and “Total Football” dissolved fixed numbering conventions, allowing players to choose numbers while roles overlapped and halfbacks became midfielders.

Beginning in 2012, U.S. Soccer standardized positions and numbers for a 4-3-3 formation, assigning goalkeeper, outside back, center back, defensive, central, and attacking midfield roles, wingers, and center forward. It also created position profiles based on technical, tactical, physical, and mental attributes. The text defines “False 9” as a center forward who drops into midfield to connect with leading midfielders and “Double-9s” as paired central strikers.

This application is a continuation of three prior “Microservices Architecture” patent applications, now issued as U.S. Patent Nos. 11,645,127, 11,467,888, and 10,860,390, each incorporated by reference. It describes cloud-computing systems and methods for implementing a configurable, scalable microservices architecture in data centers containing virtualized workloads, switching fabrics, orchestrators, distributed memory and storage, and specialized resources such as FPGAs, ASICs, GPUs, CPUs, resource pools, and virtual appliances.

The architecture exposes functions through a standardized microservices API, allowing applications to request services without knowing their implementation, location, or underlying hardware. Microservice-capable resources register their capabilities, invocation mappings, configuration, and connection capabilities with a service discovery function. A microservices driver queries this catalog, selects an available instance or provisions a new one, and translates generic API calls into optimized native invocations. FPGA provisioning may include obtaining and programming gate configurations through an orchestrator or specialized hardware.

The disclosure also describes message forwarders, unified addressing and access methods, service-path identifiers, active-message flows, and dynamic service chaining. Multiple microservices can be connected so that processing moves directly between instances without repeated returns to host software, reducing latency and request-response overhead. Load-balancing options include round-robin, weighted fair queuing, bus-state arbitration, deadline-based routing, hot-potato routing, and prioritization of hardware implementations.

Additional embodiments describe computing platforms with CPUs, memory, chipsets, communication interfaces, hypervisors, virtual network functions, and manageability engines that collect telemetry and support workload placement. An extensible ontological language can describe functions, parameters, performance requirements, and chained subfunctions, with compatibility to OpenAPI proposed. Example implementations focus on registering microservice accelerators, storing their metadata and spawn information, programming FPGA instances, and publishing registrations to microservices drivers.

Launched by CME Group in 2019, Micro E-mini S&P 500 Index futures (MES) are one-tenth the size of E-mini contracts, making them accessible to retail traders with smaller accounts. One contract equals the S&P 500 index value multiplied by $5; contracts expire on the third Friday of their delivery month at 9:30 a.m. ET. Quarterly contracts cover March, June, September, and December, with five consecutive quarters listed. Quotes are in dollars and cents per index point, and the minimum tick is 0.25 points, worth $1.25 per contract.

Regular trading runs from Sunday at 6 p.m. to Friday at 5 p.m. ET, with a daily maintenance break from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. ET. Traders must use a futures broker, fund an account, and meet margin requirements; the article states that approximately $1,060 in margin can suffice because of leverage. A trading strategy may use technical or fundamental analysis, precise entry and exit signals, position sizing, and risk management for speculation, diversification, or hedging. Historically, the contracts have performed better in winter and spring than in summer. Their recorded high was 4,808.25 in January 2022, while their low since launch was 2,174.00 in March 2020. Charts are available through CME, TradingView, Yahoo Finance, and paid platforms such as MultiCharts. ETFs tracking the futures market also exist. The contracts are not eligible for block trades.

May 2001 reports examined Enron’s business expansion, political influence and involvement in the Bush administration’s national energy policy. The Wall Street Journal said Enron had grown from a gas-pipeline operator into the largest U.S. gas and electricity trader, making its fortunes dependent on deregulation. Kenneth Lay’s eight-point agenda—opposing wholesale price controls, opening transmission lines to traders and easing construction barriers—was reflected in the administration’s policy. Enron also pursued favorable FERC appointments and maintained extensive ties to Bush officials, while benefiting from Lay’s access to President Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney.

Enron’s wholesale trading grew rapidly, and its net income nearly doubled from 1996 to 2000 as revenue rose to $100.8 billion. However, the company feared that rising Western electricity prices could produce price controls and derail deregulation. It therefore organized opposition to such measures in New York and California.

The Los Angeles Times reported that Bush’s more than 100 recommendations would generate extensive construction and investment and benefit major oil, gas, coal, utility, nuclear and construction companies, as well as some labor unions. Critics said consumers would receive little immediate relief from high energy prices, while renewable-energy industries and environmentalists objected to limited support for solar and geothermal power and the absence of stronger emissions-reduction measures.

Japanese utility officials opposed Enron’s proposal to separate electricity generation, transmission and distribution, warning that unbundling could leave no company responsible for reliable supply and produce California-style failures. Enron argued that liberalization would reduce high Japanese electricity charges and help manufacturers compete. Enron also planned to build a gas-fired plant in Japan.

Watchdog data cited by Agence France-Presse showed extensive energy-industry support for Republicans, including $25.5 million from oil and gas companies, $13.8 million from the nuclear industry and more than $1.4 million from Enron. Reuters reported broad approval from power suppliers but criticism from California, Democrats and environmentalists, who staged protests outside Cheney’s residence. Separately, Enron was reported to be withdrawing from the UAE’s Dolphin gas project, with its stake’s future ownership unresolved. In Mumbai, corporate relocation was strengthening western suburbs real estate, including an Enron lease of 100,000 square feet at Kamala Mills.

Davis also placed the California Independent System Operator under governor-selected leadership, pursued state ownership of utility transmission lines, created a governor-appointed state power authority, authorized up to $5 billion in commercial borrowing, suspended power-plant emission standards and assembled energy traders and consultants.

Consumer and business groups opposed elements of the proposals and threatened further legal or ballot action. The MOVE Index, known as the “VIX of the bond market,” measures U.S. interest-rate volatility using implied volatility from one-month OTC options. A strategy was backtested from 2002 using TLT, holding it when MOVE was below its historical mean of about 86 and selling when it exceeded that mean. The backtest produced somewhat linear but modest growth. Avoiding high-volatility periods slightly harmed 2008 returns but was beneficial in 2022, while the strategy’s maximum drawdown was roughly half that of buying and holding TLT. Overall, MOVE is a useful measure of bond-market volatility but appears ineffective as a standalone signal for trading bonds.

On-field vision—seeing, understanding, and responding to positioning and movement—is essential to elite soccer alongside ball skills. Pelé is said to have had 30% greater peripheral vision than average, while cited research indicates that at least 75% of learning is visual. Coaches recommend constantly scanning the field, knowing where all players are, raising the head quickly after receiving the ball, turning the head and body to widen the view, and moving into better positions. Players should identify multiple passing options, recognize runs and peripheral threats, avoid tunnel vision, anticipate defensive adjustments, and communicate verbally and nonverbally. Practice, experience, and familiarity with teammates make these skills more natural. To improve vision, players should receive the first touch away from the body; the passage recommends receiving a pass from the left with the right foot and vice versa. A 30-by-40-meter drill uses two jersey colors, requiring players to scan, exchange two-touch passes only with the other color, vary passing distances, and progress to one-touch passing while keeping their heads up. Visualization can also help improve on-field vision.

DAWN-PLASMA was a phase 2, multicenter, randomized, open-label proof-of-concept trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of convalescent plasma added to standard supportive care in hospitalized adults with COVID-19. Participants were randomized 2:1 to standard care plus convalescent plasma or standard care alone using a computerized system; the trial statistician remained blinded until database lock. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and ICH Good Clinical Practice guidelines, with ethics committee approval and informed consent obtained before enrollment.

Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years or older, male or non-pregnant female, with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and specified clinical or radiographic criteria. Exclusion criteria included mechanical ventilation before randomization, unacceptable safety hazards, prior grade 3 allergic reaction to fresh frozen plasma, treatment restrictions excluding intubation or ventilation, and recent anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody treatment.

The plasma intervention comprised 800–1,000 mL in four doses, with the first two units administered within 12 hours of randomization and the remaining two 24–36 hours after the first infusion. Plasma required a neutralizing-antibody titer of at least 1/160. The primary endpoint was the percentage of patients alive without mechanical ventilation on Day 15. Secondary endpoints included WHO clinical status on Days 15 and 30, sustained improvement or discharge, ventilation or death within 30 and 90 days, venous thromboembolism, transfusion-related effects, antibody-titer correlations with outcomes, safety, quality of life, laboratory results, and vital signs. Exploratory assessments included SARS-CoV-2 PCR, NT50 measurements, and outcomes according to pre-existing COVID-19 antibodies.

Between May 2, 2020, and January 26, 2021, 499 patients were assessed and 489 were randomized: 326 to convalescent plasma and 163 to control. Day 15 visits occurred for 434 patients and Day 30 visits for 423. The primary Full Analysis Set excluded one patient without confirmed COVID-19 and five patients who immediately withdrew consent without receiving treatment or providing post-baseline data. The Per Protocol Set excluded 26 plasma-assigned patients who received fewer than four units and three control patients who received convalescent plasma before Day 30.

In the plasma group, median time to first transfusion was five hours, median administered volume was 884 mL, and 80.7% of units had titers of at least 1/320. Six Full Analysis Set patients received no plasma, while 294 (91.9%) received all four units.

Effective diversification combines investments whose returns respond differently to market conditions, reducing the effect of poor performance on a portfolio. It requires considering asset selection, risk factors, financial goals, investment horizon, and liquidity. Five common mistakes can undermine diversification: failing to include all holdings, including employee benefits, stock options, and other overlooked assets; holding too many investments, which adds costs, reduces exposure to strong performers, and makes monitoring difficult; buying investments without understanding them, potentially resulting in losses or excessive concentration; choosing asset allocations that do not align with goals, such as insufficient income near retirement or inadequate liquidity; and allowing asset allocation to drift as different investments generate varying returns, without periodic rebalancing. Investors should also diversify within asset classes by considering equity market capitalizations and sectors, and debt credit profiles and maturities. Professional advisers or investment vehicles such as mutual funds can help investors lacking expertise or time.

The study addresses universities’ abrupt transition to remote teaching during the Covid-19 pandemic, when limited infrastructure, data-protection concerns, and the transfer of courses, curricula, schedules, and user records created substantial challenges. It reviews synchronous, asynchronous, and MOOC-based distance-education platforms, including Moodle, Coursera, and edX.

Using a developmental research model, the researchers created UZEP, an Internet-based synchronous distance-education platform implemented as Education as a Service in a cloud environment. It requires no client infrastructure or installation and integrates with university management systems through APIs and file-upload mechanisms. Its modules include learning management, virtual classrooms using BigBlueButton, online exams, homework and projects, digital-material sharing, announcements, surveys, and reporting. The exam module supports multiple question formats, randomized or equivalent question sets, anti-copying measures, monitoring, logging, and downloadable results.

UZEP was tested by 12 Turkish universities from October 2020 to February 2021, recording 78,732 users, 13,180 courses, 2,522 instructors, 11,314 exams, and 358,657 sessions. Expert, pilot, administrator, lecturer, and student evaluations found the platform easy to learn and use, quick to deploy, well integrated with university records, and functional for synchronous classes, assessment, and reporting. It was judged especially suitable for emergency deployment and for institutions with limited information-technology expertise. However, evaluations identified weaknesses in social and group-work tools, learning analytics, reporting, some assessment functions, and ease of using the learning-management component. Administrators, lecturers, and students generally reported positive but moderate satisfaction and requested stronger communication, collaboration, and assessment features. Limitations include reliance on self-reported questionnaires, comparison with only four platforms, and evaluation during the pandemic. Planned improvements include artificial-intelligence support for exam security and assessment, as well as social and interactive communication features.

The disclosure describes apparatus and methods for measuring the type, depth, extent, and progression of tissue damage around burns and other wounds. It is a divisional Australian patent application originating from PCT/US2018/016736 and claiming priority from U.S. Provisional Applications 62/454,487 and 62/521,926.

The disclosed technology measures electrical characteristics of tissue, particularly capacitance, and converts the measurements into sub-epidermal moisture (SEM) values associated with extracellular fluid accumulation or depletion. Toroidal sensors, including center and ring electrodes, generate an electrical field whose depth can vary with electrode geometry and operating characteristics. Electrode arrays can be selectively interconnected to form virtual capacitive sensors of different sizes and shapes. Drive circuits, processors, and stored instructions receive capacitance measurements, derive SEM values, compare them with reference values or thresholds, and identify tissue conditions.

For burns, the disclosure distinguishes necrotic tissue, a surrounding zone of stasis, and an outer zone of hyperaemia. Necrotic tissue has reduced moisture and no oxygen perfusion. Tissue in the zone of stasis has reduced perfusion and SEM, may develop substantial edema, and may recover if further cellular damage is prevented. Tissue in the hyperaemic zone remains perfused, generally heals, and may have elevated SEM. SEM profiles relative to normal tissue can indicate the depth and severity of damage, identify transitions between tissue zones, and mark the outer edge of necrotic tissue.

Apparatus for mapping damage may include electrode-bearing substrates, virtual capacitive sensors, visual indicators, projectors, cameras, printers, and storage devices. LEDs or other indicators can display different tissue classifications or boundaries. Marking elements and perforations can enable marking the skin, while an optical system can project lines, dots, colors, or shaded regions onto the wound and surrounding tissue. Camera images and SEM measurement records can be stored to provide a pictorial and measurement history of wound progression.

Another disclosed apparatus determines burn depth by measuring capacitance and comparing the measurement, or a difference from unaffected tissue, with stored capacitance-depth data. SEM values can also be compared with stored SEM-depth data to identify burn depth.

The methods may be applied through single-sensor or multi-sensor measurements over defined anatomical regions and measurement patterns. Measurements can be repeated over time to assess changing edema, tissue damage, and healing, including after skin closure. Delta values, regional thresholds, chronological thresholds, trends, statistical quality metrics, and alerts can be used to identify significant changes. SEM monitoring may also be used to evaluate wound-healing therapies and guide continuation, modification, replacement, or cessation of treatment. Although described primarily for thermal burns, the disclosed sensing and mapping approaches are stated to apply to cuts, ulcers, gangrene, pressure ulcers, and other tissue injuries.

This continuation application claims priority to U.S. Provisional Application No. 62/334,529 and describes low-latency MAC protocol data unit assembly for 5G flexible radio access technology (5gFLEX). A wireless transmit/receive unit (WTRU) may receive or determine physical-layer transmission parameters before an uplink grant, including modulation and coding scheme, resource ranges, transport-block sizes, HARQ parameters, and power or timing information. It may also decode downlink control information (DCI), identify decoding parameters such as aggregation level, CRC length, robustness, and DCI format, and use configured mappings to determine QoS, spectrum operation mode, HARQ feedback, resource, timing, and transmission parameters.

To reduce grant-to-transmission latency, a WTRU may incrementally create fixed-size data blocks, segment higher-layer data, and perform CRC insertion, encoding, or modulation before receiving a grant. Upon grant reception, it may select and multiplex prepared blocks according to flow, logical channel, service, QoS, TTL, priority, grant restrictions, and size differences. Data blocks may carry individual CRCs, allowing a network to acknowledge a transport block or selectively trigger retransmission based on the number or proportion of erroneous blocks. Aggregated data-block ACK/NACK feedback may support fast retransmissions.

The disclosed 5gFLEX environment supports varied use cases, waveforms, spectrum and bandwidth configurations, spectrum operation modes, variable TTIs, multiple duplexing schemes, spectrum aggregation, and both network-based and WTRU-based scheduling. Example system diagrams describe WTRUs and UTRA, E-UTRA, and IEEE 802.16 radio access and core-network architectures.

Union benefit funds sued Waterworks, Inc. under ERISA to compel an audit. The court denied both parties’ cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes over what agreement resulted from a 2004 meeting and whether Waterworks’ subsequent conduct demonstrated an intent to be bound by the union’s collective bargaining agreement. Although Waterworks submitted contribution reports referencing the CBA and paid amounts consistent with it, it did not sign the reports’ acceptance clauses and claimed union representatives agreed it was not bound. Plaintiffs’ LMRA-based inference did not resolve this factual dispute. The court also found plaintiffs’ late-raised argument about the union representative’s authority waived and, alternatively, creating a factual issue concerning apparent authority.

NVIDIA Corporation’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 30, 2022 describes a Delaware corporation headquartered in Santa Clara, California, with common stock traded on Nasdaq under “NVDA.” The filing reports approximately $467.25 billion in non-affiliate market value as of July 30, 2021, and 2.51 billion shares outstanding as of March 11, 2022.

NVIDIA presents itself as an accelerated-computing company that expanded from PC graphics into artificial intelligence, scientific computing, data science, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and virtual and augmented reality. Its platform strategy combines GPUs, networking, systems, CUDA software, algorithms, libraries and services. The company states that it has invested more than $29 billion in research and development since its founding, introduced the GPU in 1999 and CUDA in 2006, and that GPUs and networking power more than 70% of, and eight of the top 10 systems on, the TOP500 supercomputer list.

The company operates in two reporting segments: Graphics, covering gaming, enterprise workstation graphics, vGPU, automotive infotainment and Omniverse; and Compute & Networking, covering data-center platforms, Mellanox networking, autonomous-driving solutions, cryptocurrency processors, Jetson robotics and AI software. Its principal markets are Gaming, Data Center, Professional Visualization and Automotive. Business strategies include advancing its accelerated-computing and AI platforms, extending graphics and virtual-world technologies, providing end-to-end autonomous-driving systems under DRIVE, and licensing intellectual property.

On February 8, 2022, NVIDIA and SoftBank terminated NVIDIA’s agreement to acquire Arm because regulatory challenges prevented completion. NVIDIA expected to record a $1.36 billion charge in the first quarter of fiscal 2023 for the related prepayment.

NVIDIA uses a fabless manufacturing model, relying on external suppliers for wafer fabrication, assembly, testing and packaging, including TSMC, Samsung and numerous contract manufacturers. It sells through partners, original equipment manufacturers, system builders, distributors, cloud providers, electronic channels and direct enterprise sales. The filing identifies intense competition, rapidly changing technology and standards, demand-forecasting uncertainty, long and complex supply chains, third-party manufacturing dependence, product defects and cybersecurity threats as material risks. Fiscal 2022 demand exceeded supply in several areas and did not follow historical seasonality.

The filing also discusses intellectual-property protection, government regulation, environmental and social governance, climate-related risks and human capital. NVIDIA reported 22,473 employees in 32 countries, including 16,242 in research and development, a 4.9% turnover rate and a workforce that was 80% male and 19% female. The company stated a goal of matching 100% of global electricity use with renewable purchases or generation by fiscal 2025 and planned the Earth-2 climate-modeling supercomputer.

Among specific risk disclosures, NVIDIA reported that on February 23, 2022, criminal threat actors used stolen credentials and deception to obtain unauthorized network access, misappropriate proprietary information including source code and leak some information online. The company rotated credentials, hardened its network, investigated the data taken and notified law enforcement and other authorities.

Former Army Black Hawk pilot and West Point mechanical engineering graduate Sungi Cho founded a company after developing the 3D-printed Warbelt Hanger, a $10.99 attachment for organizing warbelts and loadouts. His products expanded from military customers to law enforcement. Cho later launched the MOLLE Backer, a $10.99 two-pack base mount compatible with hard and soft MOLLE systems, aimed at military, outdoor, and trade users.

After leaving the Army for an MBA at MIT Sloan, Cho brought 15 printers to Massachusetts and hired two part-time engineering students. MOLLE Backer demand stabilized at 1,800 units, or 900 two-packs, per month. Facing growing orders, Cho evaluated replacing 3D printing with stronger, more efficient injection molding. Ten printers could produce 1,800 salable units monthly, while a third-party manufacturer could complete an 1,800-unit order in nine hours. Printing cost $0.50 per unit in PETG, $0.09 in scrap, and $0.04 in electricity; injection molding cost $0.20 per unit in plastic, $0.006 in scrap, and $0.75 to a third-party manufacturer, excluding inserts. Both methods incurred $0.48 for threaded inserts, $0.50 for screws, and $0.11 for packaging. Monthly labor totaled 56 hours at $20 per hour. The $11,487 mold cost substantially exceeded the $1,716 printer cost. Cho remained unsure how to structure the financial analysis and had not yet considered all nonfinancial factors.

The passage explains options trading in EEM, including its benefits and risks. Options can profit from rising or falling markets and provide leverage, but they involve potential losses from adverse price movements, time decay, liquidity problems, and volatility. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses and is not recommended for beginners without a margin of safety.

Black-Scholes is presented as the main method for analyzing option prices and potential risk and reward, incorporating the underlying asset’s price, time to expiration, strike price, and implied volatility. Technical tools such as trendlines, support and resistance levels, and chart patterns can supplement this analysis, and traders are encouraged to backtest ideas.

Common strategies discussed include long calls and puts, covered calls and puts, straddles, strangles, collars, and butterfly spreads. Risk management involves position sizing, stop-loss levels, hedging, and monitoring delta. Hedging uses offsetting positions to reduce potential losses.

Broker fees, commissions, liquidity, and bid-ask spreads affect trading costs and vary by contract and activity. Minimum deposits generally range from $500 to $2,000, while margin requirements generally range from 10% to 50%. Options typically expire on the third Friday of their expiration month. Tax treatment depends on the trader’s country and may include capital gains taxes, stamp duty, or local taxes.

The options chain displays contract prices, bids and asks, implied volatility, and delta. Traders should select a reputable broker offering competitive fees, strong service, a user-friendly interface, and suitable margin and liquidity terms.

The ADS868xW devices are fully integrated, fully differential 16-bit SAR data-acquisition devices with an integrated analog front end, programmable gain amplifier, ADC driver, and buffered precision reference. They support programmable input ranges, input and AVDD alarms, and a multiSPI digital interface.

The analog input has independently programmable high and low alarm thresholds with shared hysteresis. The high alarm asserts when the digital output exceeds its threshold and resets at or below the threshold minus the hysteresis value; the low alarm asserts below its threshold and resets at or above the threshold plus the hysteresis value. The AVDD alarm has fixed design trip points, typically asserting above 5.3 V or below 4.7 V.

The multiSPI interface includes input and output shift registers, configuration registers, and a protocol unit. It supports four legacy SPI-compatible protocols, single- or dual-SDO output, and source-synchronous operation with internal or external clocking. Dual-SDO mode uses SDO-0 and SDO-1 and transfers data in half the required clock cycles. Source-synchronous mode supplies a clock on RVS.

For daisy-chained operation, devices share CONVST/CS and SCLK, pass data through SDO-0 and SDI, and require identical configuration values with SDO_CTL_REG bits 7–0 set to 00h. The host receives device N’s data first, followed by devices N−1 through 1. An optimal frame contains 32 × N SCLK capture edges.

The device operates in RESET, ACQ, and CONV states. An active-low asynchronous RST input can trigger either an application reset, which restores configuration-register defaults, or a power-on reset, which resets internal circuitry. ACQ acquires the analog signal and supports low-power NAP mode. A rising CONVST/CS edge initiates conversion using an internal clock; further transitions are ignored until conversion ends, after which the device returns to ACQ. The host can monitor RVS for completion or wait for the maximum conversion time.

The device has nine documented configuration registers: DEVICE_ID_REG, RST_PWRCTL_REG, SDI_CTL_REG, SDO_CTL_REG, DATAOUT_CTL_REG, RANGE_SEL_REG, ALARM_REG, ALARM_H_TH_REG, and ALARM_L_TH_REG. Writes to protected RST_PWRCTL_REG bits require first writing 69h to address 05h.

A data-transfer frame begins when CONVST/CS goes low and ends when it rises. Output data load into the 32-bit output shift register, while received data shift into the input register. A 32-clock frame is optimal; shorter frames invalidate writes and are treated as NOPs, although output data remain valid, while in longer frames the final 32 received bits form the command. Commands execute when CONVST/CS rises. Subsequent output can contain conversion results, register-read data, or fixed patterns, with optional device-address, input-range, AVDD-alarm, input-alarm, and parity flags.

An application example combines an ADS8681W with an MUX36D08 to provide eight software-configured voltage or current channels. It supports common industrial ranges including ±2.5 V, ±5 V, ±10 V, 0–5 V, 0–10 V, 4–20 mA, and 0–20 mA. The ADS868xW settles to 1% accuracy in under 5 µs and has input bandwidth up to 400 kHz at −3 dB. A thermistor example demonstrates using programmable alarm thresholds and hysteresis to improve temperature monitoring and avoid false triggering.

AVDD and DVDD are separate, independently adjustable supplies. Recommended decoupling includes close-placed 1 µF capacitors, at least 10 µF near the supplies, 1 µF and 10 µF REFCAP capacitors, and at least 4.7 µF at REFIO when using the internal reference. Programmable NAP and power-down modes reduce consumption; power-down powers down analog blocks while retaining the interface and registers. PCB guidance includes separating analog and digital routing, using short ground paths, avoiding vias between supply pins and bypass capacitors, and decoupling reference connections directly.

This retrospective study evaluated whether diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps could noninvasively predict TERT promoter (pTERT) mutation status in glioblastoma using a 50-layer ResNet. Among 266 patients, conventional MRI sequences achieved approximately 50–52% accuracy, while ADC maps reached 78.63% accuracy (AUC 0.865). Combining DWI and ADC maps (DWI*) performed best, with 85.20% slice-level accuracy (AUC 0.934) and 86.6% patient-level accuracy.

Using the entire tumor as the region of interest outperformed tumor core and enhancing tumor ROIs. Age, necrosis volume, and tumor location were associated with pTERT mutation, but an SVM model using these clinical features achieved only 70.91% accuracy (AUC 0.735), and adding them did not improve the DWI* ResNet model. The authors concluded that DWI combined with ADC maps has greater predictive value than conventional structural MRI and may support preoperative pTERT assessment. Limitations include the small retrospective cohort, predominant use of cross-sectional slices, restriction to pathology-confirmed WHO grade IV glioblastoma, and the need for larger external validation.

This protocol outlines a scoping review of antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome (MS) among community-dwelling adults. It will examine modifiable determinants, including diet and physical activity; non-modifiable determinants, including age, gender, ethnic background and family history; non-pharmacological interventions used to prevent or treat MS; and the preferred setting and timing for delivering interventions.

The review will follow Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and the PRISMA-ScR checklist, using a PICOTS framework. Searches will cover multiple bibliographic databases, ClinicalTrials.gov, Google Scholar and grey literature from January to April 2023, continuing until saturation. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed-method studies and evidence syntheses will be eligible. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, while one reviewer will screen full texts with a 10% sample checked by another. Data will be extracted into a standardised form, with a 10% sample independently checked.

Included evidence will undergo narrative synthesis and be mapped by population, determinants, interventions, delivery context, study origin and research methods. Formal quality appraisal will not be conducted; instead, JBI evidence levels will be assigned. Stakeholders, including patients and family members or carers, will be consulted about determinants and intervention feasibility. The review aims to identify evidence gaps and inform future research, with results disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conferences.

The Colorado Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for Shelter Mutual Insurance Company. Samuel and Mary Breit sought $200,000 under two Shelter policies providing $100,000 each in uninsured motorist coverage after third-party coverage paid $100,000 for injuries exceeding $200,000. The court held that identical, unambiguous anti-stacking provisions limited aggregate liability to $100,000. The “Other Insurance in the Company” clause barred stacking policies issued by the same insurer, while the separate “Other Insurance” clause limited recovery to the highest applicable coverage and apportioned liability among different insurers. These provisions addressed different situations and did not conflict, unlike the policy at issue in Compton. The court also found the reasonable-expectations doctrine inapplicable because the policy language was clear, and the Breits’ appeal was not frivolous.

Cervical cancer is preventable, yet its burden is concentrated in low- and middle-income countries because screening and precancer treatment are often inaccessible. Current treatments such as ablation and excision require trained providers and functioning health systems. Self-administered intravaginal 5-fluorouracil (5FU) is being investigated as a potentially scalable treatment, but African women’s experiences and acceptability after actual use had not previously been described.

A 2023–2024 Phase I pilot trial in Kisumu, Kenya, enrolled 12 women living with HIV aged 18–49 who had biopsy-confirmed CIN2/3 and received ablation or excision 4–12 weeks earlier. Participants self-administered 2 grams of intravaginal 5FU at home every other week for eight applications and attended alternate-week clinic visits for safety and adherence assessments. Acceptability was assessed through questionnaires and in-depth interviews with all 12 participants, examining content, complexity, comfort, credibility, and delivery. The trial previously found the regimen safe, with primarily grade I adverse events; all participants tolerated all doses, and 96% adherence was supported by three measures.

Participants initially reported uncertainty, worry, or fear but ultimately all considered 5FU safe and felt confident using it correctly. All preferred self-administered 5FU to the ablation or excision they had previously received. Qualitative findings emphasized its ease, privacy, convenience, reduced pain and fear, and minimal disruption to daily work and responsibilities. Study education, clinic support, and pelvic-model practice increased confidence and helped participants manage side effects. Reported adverse effects included vaginal discharge, itching, and discomfort during urination.

Challenges included measuring the correct two-gram dose, identifying the cervix, initially using tampons, negotiating condom requirements for dual contraception, and finding privacy at home, particularly in single-room households. Partner discussions about contraception were sometimes difficult, although partnered participants reported eventual support. Repeated education was important for overcoming these barriers. The study concluded that self-administered 5FU had high acceptability as an adjuvant treatment among these women and supported further research on topical therapies as primary, interim, or additional treatment in settings with substantial access gaps. The small, single-site pilot limits generalizability, and larger randomized and multisite studies are needed to confirm efficacy and broader acceptability.

The Trump administration has shifted day-to-day control of career and technical education from the Education Department to the Labor Department, while retaining federal oversight. Officials say the change will align education with workforce needs, increase accountability, reduce state administrative burdens and boost young adults’ participation in the labor force.

Supporters from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and state workforce leaders say better employer alignment could improve job placement and expand access to apprenticeships, training and valued credentials. Alabama’s coordinated education-workforce system is cited as a model.

Critics, including career-education advocates and Democratic lawmakers, question the move’s legality and view it as another step toward dismantling the Education Department. They warn that staffing shortages may weaken guidance to states and schools, reduce support for students with disabilities and encourage short-term credentials that do not lead to higher-paying jobs or advancement opportunities. Others fear CTE’s reputation as a college pathway will be overshadowed by its association with low-wage vocational tracks.

Uncertainty remains over staffing, legal requirements and whether programs will prepare students for both immediate employment and longer-term careers.

This withdrawn, non-peer-reviewed preprint evaluates six machine-learning models for pancreatic cancer diagnosis using synthetic data containing demographic, clinical, and symptom variables. The data were split 80% for training and 20% for testing, with no resampling. All models achieved similar accuracy (76.05%–76.35%) but very low sensitivity, reflecting severe class imbalance. SVM had the highest sensitivity (1.90%), followed by logistic regression and neural networks (1.47%); Random Forest and Decision Tree detected no true positives. SuperLearner achieved the highest precision (66.67%) but only 0.42% sensitivity. Gene-expression heatmaps, PCA, and correlation analyses of metastasized cancer and normal colon tissues showed group separation and were proposed as possible sources of discriminatory features. Recommended improvements include resampling, cost-sensitive learning, threshold tuning, feature engineering, explainable AI, integration of imaging and genomic data, real-world validation, and collaboration between data scientists and clinicians. The study concludes that balancing sensitivity and precision remains essential for clinical adoption.

The Indiana Supreme Court reversed the grant of partial summary judgment in David Shaner’s wrongful-death action arising from Laura Shaner’s death following dialysis complications after surgery. David sought both final-expense damages and survivor damages, including loss of consortium, earnings, services, love, companionship, and support.

After David died intestate without known heirs, successor administrators of Laura’s estate continued the claims. The trial court and Court of Appeals held that survivor damages could not proceed because David had no heirs and any award would merely benefit the State, making it punitive.

The Supreme Court held that Indiana’s wrongful-death and survival statutes provide that a properly asserted survivor-damages claim does not abate when the surviving spouse dies, regardless of whether the spouse has heirs. It therefore rejected summary judgment and distinguished its reasoning in *Bemenderfer v. Williams*.

However, the court found that Laura’s estate administrators had not established standing to pursue David’s survivor-damages claim because those damages were payable exclusively for David’s benefit. The trial court was remanded to determine whether a legal representative or successor in interest could continue the claim and whether David’s estate could be reopened.

The device provides an active-high alarm output on ALM/SDO-1/GPO when configured via SDO_CTL_REG. The lecture contrasts tournament and cash-game poker before focusing on tournament preflop strategy. Tournaments use fixed entry fees, increasing blinds, elimination after losing all chips, and payouts based on finishing position. Players cannot choose tables or rebuy, survival is the main objective, and results are highly variable, with many losses followed by occasional large payouts. Cash games have fixed stakes, allow players to leave, rebuy, and choose opponents, and involve more metagame and player targeting. The instructor prefers tournaments for the class because they require less metagame, cover more varied situations, and are more exciting. In MIT Poker Club play, cash tables use play money, while only tournaments count toward standings.

Preflop play is emphasized because it determines the cards available for the rest of the hand. The instructor reviews approximate equities and broad patterns: a larger pair generally has about an 80% chance against a smaller pair; a pair against one overcard is often around 70/30; two overcards against a pair can be close to an even chance; and with four unpaired cards, the higher-card hand is often roughly a 60/40 favorite. Examples include AKo against QQ at 43%, AKs against 22 near 50%, and A2o against 109s at 51.6%. Suitedness matters more when a hand is behind because it provides more flush and straight possibilities, while it changes the equity of an already strong hand less. Suited hands also have better implied odds.

The central practical lesson is not to avoid routine preflop all-ins. As a rough rule, with antes, a player who intends to enter a hand should shove below about 12 big blinds; without antes, the threshold is closer to 10. Small blind all-in ranges can be wider than button ranges because position no longer matters once both players are all-in. The lecture demonstrates this with an exploitative model in which the blind calls 25% of hands. T8o has 36% equity against that range, and 32o has 28%, yet both shoves are profitable under the model because the opponent folds so often. The calculation also shows that if the small blind only shoves strong hands, a 25% calling range can be reasonable, meaning that one player’s strategy must be incorrect.

An iterative best-response example illustrates how strategies adjust to one another and converge on Nash equilibrium. In a 15-big-blind situation with antes, the equilibrium strategy has the small blind shoving about 66.8% of hands and the big blind calling about 38.5%. This equilibrium is difficult to exploit; exploitative deviations should move in the direction indicated by the opponent’s actual tendencies.

Concrete ranges can be learned through theory, memorization, and interpolation. Position has a larger effect than stack depth: moving earlier in the action reduces the number of shoves, while having fewer big blinds increases it. Illustrative values include 43.9% from the button at 10 big blinds, 38.8% from the cutoff at 7, and 24.1% under the gun at 3. Forced-all-in ranges under the gun are 6.2% at 15 big blinds, 13.4% at 10, and 33.3% at 5.

Short stacks favor all-ins because many hands have poor implied odds and little room to maneuver. Small pairs can be shoved even at moderate depths, and A2 suited benefits from removing an ace from opponents’ possible holdings. Suited connectors such as 7-6 suited are stronger with deeper stacks because they can make more straights and flushes and induce weak hands to fold; A4 offsuit instead depends heavily on late position and calls from weaker opponents. All players’ stack sizes matter, especially short stacks in the blinds, because they are more likely to call and reduce the incentive to steal blinds.

Calling all-ins is also emphasized. Even a hand such as 9-8 suited can be worth calling against a 10-big-blind shove because the required equity is about 37%, and folding may be the larger mistake. With only four big blinds, nearly any hand has sufficient equity to call, and the instructor estimates playing about 95% of hands. With roughly 10 big blinds, a player should generally shove or fold rather than make a small raise that allows an opponent to force an all-in.

For deeper re-raise situations, the instructor recommends a re-raise of roughly 2.5 times the original raise, unless that size would commit more than about one-quarter of the stack, in which case shoving is preferable. Calling an existing preflop raise with a hand such as AJs or AQs can be reasonable because it prevents the raiser from gaining an all-in option. Against limpers, the response should be a raise, adding approximately one big blind to the normal raise size for each limper; with a short stack, shoving may be preferable. The lecture closes by noting that although giving opponents extra options is normally undesirable because weak hands can call and strong hands can force all-ins, deliberately offering options through tiny bets can work against opponents likely to make mistakes.

The E-mini S&P MidCap 400 futures track the S&P MidCap 400 index, formed in 1991, which measures the performance of 400 mid-sized US companies with market capitalizations between $3.6 billion and $13.1 billion. The index is market-cap weighted and is recalculated quarterly in March, June, September and December. Inclusion criteria require a company to be US-based, listed on an exchange, and have a minimum investable factor of 0.10. The index ticker is MID.

**Contract specifications:** Two futures contracts exist at CME — the standard and the e-mini, with ticker EMD. One contract unit equals $100 times the index value, quoted in dollars and cents per index point. The minimum price fluctuation is 0.1 index point ($10) for outright Globex trading and 0.05 index point ($5) for BTIC and calendar spreads; the block minimum is 50 contracts for BTIC. Contracts follow quarterly cycles (Mar, Jun, Sep, Dec) with five consecutive quarters listed, are financially settled by cash based on the special opening quotes of the index, and trading terminates at 9:30 a.m. ET on the third Friday of the contract month; BTIC terminates at 4:00 p.m. ET on the preceding Thursday.

**Trading hours:** Globex trades Sunday through Friday, 6:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET the next day, with a one-hour maintenance break from 5:00 to 6:00 p.m. ET Monday through Thursday. BTIC trades 6:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET, and ClearPort runs 6:00 p.m. to 5:15 p.m. ET with a 45-minute break.

**Price data:** As of December 1, 2022, the futures traded at $2585.8, making one contract worth $258,580. The index's all-time high was 2925.93 in November 2021 (the futures' all-time high was 2924.2 that month), and its all-time low was 119.43 in June 1991.

**ETFs and CFDs:** The most liquid ETF is IJH (Invesco), traded since summer 2000 with average daily volume near 1 million; SPMD and the equal-weighted EWMC also track the index. CFDs offered by brokers such as IG can track the futures or index and have no expiry, unlike futures.

**Strategy and seasonality:** Two backtests are described — a volatility strategy with poor results and an overnight strategy (March 2022) with 362 trades, 0.31% average gain per trade, 5% CAGR, 60% win rate and 1.63 profit factor. Both performed better on SPY and QQQ than on IJH, suggesting profitable, uncorrelated midcap strategies are harder to find. Seasonally, the index tends to perform better in winter and spring than in summer and fall.

**Other details:** Trading requires registration with a futures broker, funding, and only initial margin since futures are leveraged. The main risk is adverse price movement calculated on full contract value — at 20x leverage, a 1% adverse move equals a 20% account loss. Prices are influenced by component stocks, interest rates, economic news and the US dollar. Charts are available via TradingView, CME, Yahoo Finance and MultiCharts.

A Russell 2000 Death Cross occurs when its 50-day moving average falls below its 200-day moving average and is commonly viewed as bearish. The most recent cross occurred in 2022, after which the S&P 500 fell. Despite these results, sizable drawdowns made the signal imperfect. The backtest used cash indexes rather than ETFs, and the signal may be less reliable for the S&P 500 than for the more volatile small-cap Russell 2000.

The lecture examines how demand estimates, ownership structures, and supply-side restrictions can be combined to study competition. For a multi-product firm, an ownership matrix and demand derivatives define an “omega” matrix that enters firms’ first-order conditions. Inverting these conditions recovers marginal costs given estimated demand, observed prices, and a conduct assumption. If marginal costs are completely unrestricted, however, any model can be rationalized and is not testable without additional assumptions. Imposing a cost function, such as costs depending on commodity and advertising prices, allows demand and supply to be estimated jointly. Supply-side moments and overidentifying restrictions can then test conduct assumptions and reject demand parameters that imply implausible costs, such as negative marginal costs.

The lecture reviews the BLP automobile study, which uses 1971–1990 U.S. data, including 2,217 model-years and list prices. Product counts rose over time, domestic brands’ shares declined largely because of increased Japanese imports, and cars became smaller, possibly in response to the 1970 oil shock. Simple logit-based OLS and IV regressions are recommended as preliminary checks before estimating the full random-coefficient model. OLS price coefficients are biased toward zero when firms price unobserved product quality, while IV produces more negative coefficients and fewer implausibly inelastic demand estimates. A simple hedonic cost regression explains much of the observed price variation. BLP’s random coefficients capture substantial preference heterogeneity, including mixed preferences over fuel efficiency, and yield substitution patterns that differ markedly from logit, especially in responses to the outside option. Supply-side restrictions help improve the precision of demand estimates. Limitations include ignoring used-car-market responses, dealership and franchise constraints, negotiated transaction prices, and financing, insurance, and other purchase add-ons.

Nevo’s cereal study tests whether high accounting margins reflect collusion or multi-product firms’ incentives to avoid cannibalization amid heterogeneous consumer tastes. It estimates a random-coefficient logit demand model with product fixed effects and demographic-based preference variation. Product fixed effects add parameters, can absorb variation used in BLP instruments, and are best handled through an inner-loop regression. Instruments include other-market prices for the same firm, regional cost shifters, and brand indicators that may capture advertising and unobserved brand competition. Fixed effects, instruments, and demographics yield more negative price coefficients, while demographic interactions explain variation that BLP could represent only as unobserved heterogeneity.

Using cereal panel data, Nevo compares model-implied markups with accounting margins, including a 46 percent retail margin. Estimated markups range from 31 to 46 percent depending on the treatment of advertising. He rejects joint profit maximization by the 25 estimated brands but cannot reject separate brand-level pricing or models using the observed ownership structure. A simple logit model produces much lower markups and would not reject collusion. The comparison depends on whether accounting costs represent the relevant economic costs, and the study does not model advertising or other product characteristics as endogenous.

The lecture then introduces the common ownership hypothesis: diversified institutional investors may give competing firms incentives to soften competition by weighting competitors’ profits in managers’ objectives. Accounting-based evidence shows that institutional ownership and inferred profit weights placed on other firms’ profits have increased over time, and major cereal producers share common institutional owners. Backus, Conlon, and Sinkinson develop a structural test that inverts firms’ first-order conditions, imposes a flexible cost function, and uses GMM moment restrictions and a Rivers–Vuong nonnested test to compare conduct models. In the cereal case, the results reject common ownership in favor of own-profit maximization and also reject perfect competition and full monopoly using optimal demand-side instruments. The lecture notes that this is a case study, the general hypothesis remains debated, and a convincing mechanism by which institutional investors induce firms to soften competition is unresolved.

The Ichimoku Kinko Hyo is a technical-analysis system attributed to Goichi Hosoda and his assistants. It identifies support and resistance, trend direction, and momentum by plotting averages that form a projected “cloud.” Its five components are Tenkan-Sen, a nine-period midpoint; Kijun-Sen, a 26-period midpoint; Senkou Span A, the average of Tenkan and Kijun shifted forward 26 periods; Senkou Span B, a 52-period midpoint shifted forward 26 periods; and Chikou Span, the closing price shifted back 26 periods.

Price above the cloud indicates an uptrend, while price below it indicates a downtrend. A thick cloud reflects high volatility, and a thin cloud reflects declining volatility. Tenkan/Kijun crossovers provide trend signals, Chikou confirms or may precede price movements, and Senkou lines mark support and resistance. Traders can use these signals individually or combine them into strategies, which should be backtested and forward-tested; daily bars are suggested, but the appropriate timeframe must be tested.

The article emphasizes sound trading rules, discipline, and risk management. Backtests across several assets generally produced lower risk-adjusted returns than buy-and-hold, although the strategy reduced drawdowns and spent less time in the market. The principal risk is that Ichimoku signals may be inaccurate or unreliable, making caution and thorough testing essential.

The passage profiles 13 publicly traded restaurant comparables, including Brinker, Buffalo Wild Wings, Cheesecake Factory, Chipotle, Cracker Barrel, Darden, DineEquity, McDonald’s, Panera, Shake Shack, Sonic, Texas Roadhouse, and Zoë’s Kitchen. The 60/40 portfolio allocates 60% to equities and 40% to bonds, using assets that are often uncorrelated so bonds can cushion equity losses during slowdowns. It can be implemented globally or with ETFs such as SPY and TLT or VTI and BND, rebalanced one to four times yearly, or through a managed fund. The passage cites an 8.8% average annual return since 1926 and notes that returns were positive in 35 of 42 years.

During 2022, rising inflation and aggressive Federal Reserve rate increases caused stocks and bonds to fall together, illustrating that bonds are not always a safe haven. The portfolio was down 17.77% year-to-date as of September 17, with a Sharpe ratio of -0.76. Nevertheless, the passage says double-digit declines have occurred previously, the strategy is not dead, and abandoning it or attempting market timing is unwise.

Alternatives include an 80/20 portfolio, the All-Weather Portfolio, trend-following strategies, gold, a small 1–2% cryptocurrency allocation, international equities, tail-risk strategies, and Thomas Carlson’s “Defence First” strategy. A backtest adding the KMLM commodity trend-following ETF to create a 60/20/20 portfolio produced the strongest performance from 2021 through the article’s publication.

The Rhode Island Supreme Court affirmed Andrew A. Bucci’s conviction for providing legal advice to Robert Oliva while suspended from the practice of law. After a de novo jury trial in Superior Court, Bucci was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment.

The Court rejected Bucci’s argument that the evidence showed only that he obtained another attorney to represent Oliva. Recorded conversations demonstrated that Bucci personally advised Oliva on criminal litigation strategy, including search-and-seizure law, grand jury procedure, venue, witness interviews, and restitution. Although another attorney appeared in court, Bucci directed that attorney and continued managing the litigation.

The Court also held that the statute prohibiting suspended attorneys from furnishing legal advice did not require proof of any pecuniary benefit.

Finally, the Court concluded that Rhode Island’s two-tier criminal system permitted a more severe sentence following a de novo trial. Under Colten v. Kentucky, the due-process restriction applied by the U.S. Supreme Court in North Carolina v. Pearce did not bar Bucci’s six-month sentence. Any claim concerning the legality or propriety of the sentence had to be raised through a Superior Court Rule 35 motion and could not be considered on direct appeal.

GAIS, a nonprofit serving 200 farmers in Gbudue, urged South Sudan’s government to restrict imported seeds and support local producers. This study examined whether group-based versus individualized cortical parcellations affect estimates of functional connectivity (FC) differences between patients with early psychosis and healthy controls. Using Human Connectome Project–Early Psychosis data, the researchers compared the 100-region Schaefer atlas with individualized parcellations generated by the Group Prior Individualized Parcellation algorithm. After quality control, the sample included 112 patients and 55 controls; analyses were repeated with a 200-region atlas and global signal regression.

Individualization reallocated more than 40% of cortical vertices and produced slightly more functionally homogeneous parcels. Both methods identified widespread FC reductions in patients. However, group-based parcellation yielded significantly larger case-control differences and implicated more dysconnected edges in the Network Based Statistic component: 2,712 versus 2,461 edges, approximately 9% more. The edge-level t-statistic matrices were only moderately correlated between methods, and 643 edges differed between their significant components, indicating that conclusions about affected edges and regions varied substantially by parcellation method. In contrast, network-level patterns were highly consistent, especially for raw edge counts, and the control network was most affected.

Parcel-size changes did not differ significantly between patients and controls, although larger between-group size changes were moderately associated with greater FC differences. The authors conclude that group-based parcellations inflate estimated FC disruptions, while individualized parcellations provide more conservative and refined estimates without materially altering broader network-level findings. Limitations include the relatively low-resolution surface mesh, antipsychotic medication exposure, and heterogeneity between affective and non-affective psychosis.

The lecture reviews linear systems \(Ax=b\), where MATLAB’s backslash solver requires about \(O(n^3)\) operations and typically achieves machine accuracy. Ill-conditioned systems may admit multiple machine-accurate solutions and can amplify small changes in \(b\). For nonlinear equations, Newton–Raphson repeatedly solves linear systems; convergence depends heavily on the initial guess. Methods such as dogleg and trust-region approaches may require many iterations. MATLAB’s `fsolve` reformulates \(f(x)=0\) as minimizing \(\|f(x)\|\), while `fmincon` similarly searches for stationary points by minimizing the squared norm of a gradient.

Explicit ODE methods are straightforward but can be numerically unstable. Implicit methods require nonlinear solves at every time step, making the cost roughly the number of time steps times nonlinear iterations times \(O(n^2)\) for Jacobian formation. Large iteration counts and step counts can produce substantial computation, although modern computers generally handle the assigned problems.

The lecture also introduces functionals, which accept functions rather than only numerical inputs. Examples include gradient and Jacobian operators. In density functional theory, molecular energy is treated as a functional of electron density; related approaches use material density in solution-phase problems.

Numerical integration is presented as a basis-function approximation problem. An approximate function \(\tilde f(t)=\sum_k c_k\phi_k(t)\) is fitted and integrated analytically. Using fewer basis functions than data points yields approximation, while matching the number of points gives interpolation and forces the fit through the data. Interpolation is appropriate for highly accurate data but may improperly fit noise from experiments or stochastic simulations. The interpolation coefficients satisfy a linear system \(Mc=y\), whose matrix must be nonsingular; linearly independent or orthogonal basis columns provide this property. Monomial bases are simple but produce exponentially worsening condition numbers, while Lagrange and Newton bases offer alternative coefficient calculations. Higher-degree polynomial interpolants can also exhibit large oscillations.

Gaussian quadrature chooses evaluation points and weights so that \(n\)-point rules integrate polynomials exactly through degree \(2n-1\). A three-point rule is exact through degree five and has sixth-order scaling, compared with Simpson’s rule, which is exact through degree three and has fourth-order scaling. Seven-point Gauss quadrature is exact through degree 13. A 15-point extension can provide an additional comparison estimate for assessing accuracy and is more efficient than repeatedly subdividing Simpson or trapezoid rules.

For multidimensional integrals, nested quadrature makes the required function evaluations grow exponentially with dimension. This “curse of dimensionality” makes high-dimensional electronic-structure integrals impractical by straightforward quadrature and motivates methods with better scaling.

The lecture reviews the Hawking–Page transition as a competition between thermal AdS and large-black-hole phases in a single CFT, including their different energy and entropy scalings and the heuristic analogy to confinement and deconfinement. It then introduces entanglement entropy for a system divided into \(A\) and \(B\): one traces out \(B\) to form the reduced density matrix \(\rho_A\), then computes its von Neumann entropy. For pure states, \(S_A=S_B\) by Schmidt decomposition; zero entropy indicates a product state, while nonzero entropy indicates entanglement. For mixed states, the entropies need not agree and include classical statistical uncertainty. The lecturer also discusses ordinary and strong subadditivity inequalities.

For many-body systems with local Hamiltonians, the leading entanglement entropy of a region obeys an area law, scaling with the size of the region’s boundary and inversely with a short-distance cutoff. Locality implies that the leading entanglement comes from degrees of freedom near the boundary, although longer-range entanglement produces subleading terms. In \(2+1\)-dimensional topologically ordered systems, a shape-independent subleading constant detects otherwise hidden long-range correlations. In \(1+1\)-dimensional CFTs, the entropy has the logarithmic form \(S_A=(C/3)\log(L/\epsilon)\), where the central charge \(C\) characterizes the theory’s degrees of freedom.

Finally, the lecture presents the Ryu–Takayanagi holographic formula,
\[
S_A=\frac{\operatorname{Area}(\gamma_A)}{4G_N},
\]
where \(\gamma_A\) is a minimal bulk surface anchored on the boundary of \(A\). The surface depends on the bulk geometry corresponding to the chosen CFT state. Minimal-surface arguments reproduce strong subadditivity and the \(1+1\)-dimensional entropy formula; in a finite-temperature black-hole geometry, a sufficiently large interval produces a surface near the horizon and recovers the black-hole entropy. The lecture concludes that this relation links entanglement and quantum information to spacetime geometry, connecting quantum field theory, many-body physics, black holes, and string theory.

Existing research on LLMs in finance has focused on specialized models, instruction tuning, RAG, prompting, and multi-agent architectures for tasks such as sentiment analysis, summarization, and forecasting, but offers limited guidance on integrating and maintaining LLM systems in real financial workflows. This study examines the software engineering challenges of incorporating open-source and commercial LLMs into domain-specific report analysis and compares their complexity, performance, and maintainability.

Using an exploratory Design Science Research field study with Getinge AB’s finance department, the researchers reviewed relevant literature, conducted focus groups and workflow analysis, and defined tasks for identifying drivers of changes in order intake and net sales. Sensitive financial data and inconsistent formats from spreadsheets, presentations, ERP systems, databases, and meetings required tailored preprocessing; synthetic or anonymized data were used where external sharing was prohibited.

Two prototypes were developed. A local Ollama-based system tested lightweight open-source models, eventually using LLaMA 3.1 in a four-agent pipeline for data interpretation, trend analysis, report writing, and validation. Small models often failed to follow instructions and hallucinated, while chained agents propagated and amplified errors; larger models were slower on CPU-only hardware. A commercial GPT-4o API system used a structured single prompt and was later refined into separate analyst and report-writer prompts. GPT-4o required little setup and generally captured most trends without extensive decomposition, but sometimes missed important drivers, mixed positive and negative trends, cited multiple main drivers, or copied example phrasing too rigidly. Prompt chaining improved analysis but did not consistently produce constraint-compliant final summaries.

Evaluation compared 20 summaries from each prototype with expert-written versions, using feedback from two financial-reporting professionals. Both produced professional, useful draft summaries but required manual refinement. Problems included omitted trends, redundant or irrelevant content, unclear selection rationale, incorrect regional attributions, inconsistent structure, and lack of numerical context. GPT-4o was preferred for its concise reporting style, while the local model offered descriptive summaries potentially suitable for internal use. Neither was considered dependable for finalized reporting without human validation.

The study identifies three central challenges: task-specific prompts and output constraints, heterogeneous data preparation, and sensitive-data deployment restrictions. Local models provide privacy and control but require greater engineering, infrastructure, and post-processing effort; GPT-4o simplifies integration and maintenance but introduces compliance, provider-dependence, and vendor-lock-in concerns. Limitations include the small expert sample, qualitative evaluation, transformed and dated data, single-company context, and model non-determinism. Future work should examine modular rule-aware prompts, prompt asset management, multi-agent fault isolation, and hybrid deployments combining local processing for sensitive tasks with external models for complex operations.

Four central challenges are identified for quantum electrodynamics and quantum optics in attosecond strong-field physics: generating massively quantum states of light; entangling light with electronic states in complex materials; characterizing and applying the resulting states; and simulating attosecond QED with quantum platforms. Proposed approaches include multimode squeezed and structured light, resonant HHG, conditioning and post-selection, and cold-atom or trapped-ion simulators.

Recent advances support these goals. Fully quantized theoretical models, QFT-based post-selection, and hybrid semiclassical–quantum approaches can describe entangled light–matter final states. Attosecond metrology, ultrafast streaking, pump–probe methods, and measurements of photon statistics, coherence, and Wigner functions enable time-resolved studies of quantum correlations. Structured driving fields, bright squeezed light, and entangled-photon sources offer new routes to high-photon-number states and control beyond low-depletion regimes. Two-dimensional, correlated, and topological materials provide platforms where harmonic emission can encode quantum pathways, correlations, and phase information. Quantum simulators based on shaken traps and Kramers–Henneberger transformations offer controlled settings for testing strong-field dynamics. Quantum tomography, homodyne detection, entanglement witnessing, multidimensional spectroscopy, state reconstruction, and machine-learning inversion are extending characterization to the ultrafast domain.

Overall, the field is moving toward treating intense laser fields, light, and matter as fully quantum entities. The anticipated roadmap includes scalable quantum light sources, attosecond-scale entanglement applications, quantum simulation platforms, and potentially ultrafast quantum processors.

The DAWN-plasma study was a prospective, multicenter, randomized, open-label phase II proof-of-concept trial comparing standard of care plus convalescent plasma with standard of care alone in hospitalized adults with COVID-19. It was conducted under the Declaration of Helsinki and ICH Good Clinical Practice guidelines, with ethics approval and informed consent obtained. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients alive without mechanical ventilation at Day 15. Secondary endpoints covered clinical status, oxygenation, ventilation, hospitalization, mortality, sustained improvement, thromboembolism, transfusion reactions, neutralizing-antibody titers, quality of life, safety, laboratory measures, and vital signs.

Between May 2020 and January 2021, 499 patients were assessed and 489 were randomized 2:1 to convalescent plasma plus standard of care (n=326) or standard of care alone (n=163). The full analysis set excluded one patient without confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and five who withdrew immediately after randomization without receiving treatment or providing post-baseline data, leaving 483 patients. The plasma group received four units totaling 800–1,000 mL, with a median of 884 mL; the first transfusion occurred a median of five hours after randomization. Most administered units had neutralizing-antibody titers of at least 1/320, while titers below 1/160 were prohibited.

The primary endpoint did not differ between groups: 83.7% of the plasma group versus 84.1% of controls were alive without mechanical ventilation at Day 15 (odds ratio 0.99; p=0.976). No significant between-group differences were found for secondary endpoints, including mortality and outcomes at Day 30, and per-protocol results were similar. A prespecified subgroup analysis showed an interaction with age. Neutralizing-antibody titers increased by Day 6 regardless of treatment, and higher titers at baseline and Day 6 were associated with better outcomes, but the intervention did not affect the antibody increase.

Adverse-event frequencies were similar between groups. Overall, 139 patients experienced adverse events, 49 experienced fatal adverse events, and 100 experienced serious adverse events. Five adverse events led to treatment discontinuation, all in the plasma group, while two led to study discontinuation. Fourteen adverse events in 12 patients and seven serious adverse events in seven patients were considered treatment-related. Transfusion-related side effects occurred in 19 of 320 plasma recipients, with no TRALI cases reported. Laboratory measures and vital signs showed no meaningful between-group differences. The investigators concluded that early transfusion of high-volume, high-titer convalescent plasma did not change the clinical course of hospitalized COVID-19.

Fanconi anemia (FA) patients have a high incidence of oral potentially malignant lesions (OPMLs) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), often at young ages, creating a need for noninvasive surveillance. This multicenter prospective longitudinal study assessed cancer-gene mutations in saliva and plasma from 16 FA patients at two Spanish hospitals between November 2018 and December 2021. Eleven patients had hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and five had not. Repeated samples were analyzed by next-generation sequencing using the Oncomine Pan-Cancer Cell-Free Assay.

Mutations were detected in 15 liquid-biopsy samples from nine patients; no copy-number variants were found, and most mutations involved TP53. Among 14 patients with follow-up, seven developed oral lesions or carcinomas. Six of these seven had detectable mutations before clinical diagnosis, with a median lead time of 205 days. Mutations were absent from samples of five patients who remained free of lesions or tumors. Mutation status was associated with significantly different oral lesion/tumor-free survival and classified patients with 92% accuracy, 86% sensitivity, and 100% specificity. One patient with leukoplakia had no detectable mutation, and one low-frequency IDH2 mutation was attributed to possible clonal hematopoiesis.

The findings support saliva and plasma mutation analysis as a noninvasive method for identifying FA patients at elevated risk of OPML or OSCC and for guiding closer surveillance. Larger, longer studies are needed to validate the approach and determine whether it improves early diagnosis.
