Karen White joined Pequot Capital as a principal, and Jeani Delagardelle joined Sprout Group as a venture partner focused on healthcare investments.

Corrections stated that Global Factory raised $13 million rather than $12 million, NewsMarket’s reported $3 million was a seed round rather than Series A, and Screen4Me.com board member Peter Trost was CEO and president of BrannRMG, not Holland & Knight.

Stone tools found at India’s Attirampakkam site were dated to 385,000–172,000 years ago, suggesting migration from Africa may have occurred earlier than thought. Their makers and the extent of African versus local influence remain unknown and require further study.

UNL is investing in agricultural and environmental studies through new facilities, interdisciplinary research and a strategic plan. Its agriculture and natural-resources programs account for 48.5% of $295 million in campus research spending, while enrollment rose 78% from 2006–16. East Campus improvements include housing, recreation and a new Veterinary Diagnostic Center; a five-year, $20 million National Science Foundation grant will study root and soil microbes, with support from faculty across Nebraska institutions and Doane University.

Buffalo County Historical Society opened a climate-controlled, 6,000-square-foot Family History Center at Trails & Rails Museum. The building supports artifact preservation and exhibits, while a $1.2 million campaign seeks another $660,000 for expanded display space.

Lincoln Public Schools has the smallest student-teacher ratios among Nebraska’s 10 largest districts. Research cited in support of small classes links them to better outcomes, particularly for low-income and minority students. Continued small classes require resources, but may reduce future social and educational costs.

Alliance’s car-built Carhenge, created by Jim Reinders in 1987, has become a tourism and folk-art attraction as the city prepares for the Aug. 21 eclipse with concerts, sports, a powwow and other events.

AMR is described as a major global health threat linked to approximately 700,000 deaths in 2019, with deaths projected to reach 20 million by 2050 and economic costs exceeding $2.9 trillion. Contributing factors in India include over-the-counter antibiotic access, weak regulation, low awareness, inappropriate prescribing and self-medication, misdiagnosis, inadequate hygiene and healthcare infrastructure, and excessive agricultural antibiotic use.

This cross-sectional study examined AMR among clinical isolates at ACS Medical College and Hospital in Chennai from November 2023 to May 2024. It enrolled 346 participants and analyzed urine, blood, sputum, wound/pus, and other swab specimens. Tissue samples and patients previously receiving antimicrobial therapy were excluded. Cultures were processed aseptically, and antibiotic susceptibility was tested using the Kirby-Bauer disk-diffusion method on Mueller-Hinton agar according to CLSI guidelines.

Of 346 specimens, 264 (76.3%) showed positive growth, while 82 (23.7%) showed no growth. Gram-negative bacteria accounted for 75.4% of positive cultures. Participants were predominantly older adults aged over 45 (56.6%) and female (52.3%). Urine was the largest specimen category (42.4%).

The most frequently isolated organisms were E. coli (28.8% of positive cultures) and Klebsiella species (26.9%), followed by Staphylococcus (13.2%) and Pseudomonas (9.5%). E. coli predominated in urine cultures, Klebsiella was prominent in sputum and urine, Staphylococcus was most frequent in wound samples, and Salmonella was detected only in blood samples.

Among 76 E. coli isolates, resistance was particularly high for polymyxin B (98.7%), cefoperazone/sulbactam (97.4%), cefuroxime (93.4%), and cefotaxime (92.1%). Amikacin and gentamycin showed higher sensitivity rates of 71.1% and 63.2%, respectively, while several other antibiotics produced intermediate responses. The authors stated that these patterns could complicate treatment and support locally tailored antimicrobial stewardship.

Limitations included the six-month duration, small sample size, cross-sectional design, rapid changes in AMR, urban focus, lack of clinical outcome and comorbidity data, and failure to focus specifically on hospital-acquired infections. Recommendations included multidisciplinary stewardship teams, resistance surveillance, ongoing clinician education, locally based guidelines, diagnostic testing, controls on non-prescription antibiotic sales and self-medication, clinical decision-support tools, accountability, and regular evaluation of stewardship outcomes. Future research should address resistance mechanisms, long-term stewardship, host and microbiome factors, alternative therapies, and improved surveillance.

This continuation application describes industrial automation systems and cloud-based industrial data services. Embodiments register industrial assets on a cloud platform with asset identities, hierarchical asset models referencing device data tags, and available data-service applications. Asset owners select applications through client devices, while gateways collect tagged industrial data for processing according to the selected application.

Industrial devices and controllers support basic information data types (BIDTs), including State, Rate, Odometer, and Event types. Users configure BIDT metadata to define states, value ranges, rollover or interval rules, triggering tags, units, update rates, and related data sources. Gateway devices discover BIDTs and their metadata and organize them through user-defined asset models representing facilities, production lines, machines, equipment, and devices.

Application server systems, either on-premises or cloud-based, aggregate asset models from multiple gateways into plant models and generate contextualized presentations for authorized clients. Presentations can include BIDT-specific widgets, historical trends, event logs, and role-specific views for operators, engineers, plant managers, or OEMs. A gateway device registry authenticates registered gateways using device information and certificates, and issues expiring communication channels for secure data transfer to customer cloud platforms.

The study used finite-element growth-and-remodeling simulations to generate synthetic thoracic aortic aneurysms caused by combined impairments of elastic-fiber integrity and cellular mechanosensing. From 100 random insult distributions and five combinations per distribution, 500 dilatation–distensibility map pairs were produced; 450 were used for training and 50 for testing. CNN- and FNN-based DeepONets, UNet, and a Laplace Neural Operator were evaluated using dilatation alone or both dilatation and distensibility, represented as heat maps or grayscale maps.

Most networks predicted the spatial insult profiles within 10% relative L2 error. Adding distensibility reduced errors by roughly half across all architectures and was particularly important for distinguishing aneurysms with similar maximum dilatation. CNN-DeepONet and UNet performed well even with dilatation alone, whereas LNO had the largest errors in that setting. With both inputs, UNet achieved the best overall accuracy, followed by LNO, and accurately represented non-insult regions. Heat-map versus grayscale format had relatively little effect on most networks.

The findings indicate that full-field measurements of aortic dilatation and distensibility could help identify disease mechanisms and mechanical vulnerability more effectively than maximum aortic size alone. Limitations include the use of synthetic data, one initial geometry and material parameter set, mechanically stable aneurysms, and omission of aortic curvature, unstable growth, dissection, rupture, and human patient data.

Joe Hadzima outlines major legal issues facing startups, emphasizing that law is fact-specific and the lecture is educational issue-spotting rather than legal advice. He organizes these issues by the business lifecycle: intellectual property, legal entity, people, and financing.

Intellectual property is a potential startup asset that can support financing and demonstrate technological management. He describes trademarks as source identifiers that can be protected through use and registration, copyrights as automatic rights in original expression that generally belong to the author unless created as employment, and trade secrets as confidential competitive advantages protected through nondisclosure and restricted access. Contractor-created work requires an assignment of ownership, and open-source licenses must be followed. Patents provide stronger, costly, country-specific rights to exclude others for 20 years. Patentability generally requires novelty, utility, eligible subject matter, non-obviousness, and an enabling description; public disclosure or sale can create filing deadlines. Provisional applications can establish priority for a year without being published, but later applications cannot add subject matter omitted from the provisional. The United States now uses first-to-file rules, and founders must ensure inventions are properly assigned to the company.

The lecture also covers university technology licensing. The Bayh-Dole Act placed administration of federally sponsored research at universities, and MIT’s Technology Licensing Office handles invention ownership, prosecution, and licensing. Startups commonly obtain an option and then a license, commonly paying royalties, assuming some patent costs, or giving MIT a minority equity stake. Founders should resolve ownership and licensing issues early, before investors conduct due diligence.

For financing-oriented technology companies, Hadzima presents the Delaware corporation as the default because of its flexible corporate law and specialized courts. Incorporation limits shareholder liability, so founders should incorporate early. An S-corporation election may avoid double taxation if eligibility requirements are met, but typical venture financing ends that status. Section 83 of the Internal Revenue Code can cause founders and employees receiving restricted stock to owe ordinary income tax on its fair-market value when the stock is received. Issuing stock before investment and making a timely Section 83(b) election can help address this problem.

People and equity issues include founder ownership splits, board composition, fiduciary duties, stock-transfer restrictions, and founder agreements. There is no universal equity formula; splits should reflect past and future contributions, sacrifice, intellectual-property ownership, and outside opportunities. Employee stock may not motivate people automatically, so companies should calibrate equity grants carefully. Hadzima cites a rough first-financing employee pool of 12%–18%. He discusses restricted stock, incentive stock options, non-qualified options, their different tax treatment, and typical vesting of 25% after a one-year cliff followed by monthly or quarterly vesting over three years. Plans should also address repurchases, forfeiture, acceleration, and departures.

Finally, securities laws require registered offerings or valid exemptions, including compliant private placements; violations can create criminal and personal liability. Business plans should not contain offers to sell securities. Hadzima briefly reviews capital structures, convertible notes, and venture financing terms. He explains liquidation preferences, including straight and participating preferred stock, and anti-dilution protection, including full-ratchet and weighted-average approaches, emphasizing how each affects founders’ ownership and potential proceeds.

The author approves the 1877 electoral counting act as a constitutional and orderly means of resolving the disputed presidential election. The bill assigns questions over single returns to Congress and provides for a tribunal of inquiry to decide disputed double returns, with decisions standing unless both Houses concur. Because all states have voted and a tie is impossible, one candidate must have been elected, making a lawful, accepted resolution essential to national peace and economic activity. Although the bill may not be ideal for future disputes and permanent general legislation may eventually be needed, it is presented as an appropriate response to the current crisis and as a safeguard against an irregular struggle over the presidency.

The paper examines the relationship between digitalization and sustainable development, as well as how national cultural characteristics relate to digitalization. It reviews industrial and digital transformation, sustainable development’s economic, social, environmental, and cultural dimensions, and the intermediary role of macromarketing. Using 2014–2017 data for 28 EU countries, the study compares the Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI) with measures of competitiveness, innovation, GDP, entrepreneurship, country contribution, Sustainable Development Goals, and Sustainable Society Index. It also tests correlations with Hofstede’s cultural dimensions.

Results show strong positive correlations between digitalization and economic and social measures, including competitiveness, innovativeness, entrepreneurship, health and well-being, and Sustainable Development Goal performance. Digitalization is negatively associated with environmental well-being, including climate, energy use, renewable energy, and consumption. Although the findings support the stated hypothesis, the authors note that correlations do not establish causality.

Culturally, digitalization is associated with lower power distance and uncertainty avoidance and with higher individualism and indulgence. Masculinity and long-term orientation show no significant relationships with DESI. The paper concludes that cultural differences affect digitalization and that macromarketing can support its adoption, but also that greater attention to environmental impacts is needed. Limitations include the EU-only sample, incomplete or irregular sustainability measures, and reliance on Hofstede’s framework; future research should examine more countries, alternative cultural models, and policy-oriented macromarketing tools.

The Sansa Fuze manual describes a portable digital audio/video player with a 1.9-inch color screen, integrated FM radio where applicable, built-in microphone, internal storage, and microSD/microSDHC expansion. It supports MP3, WAV, WMA, secure WMA, Audible audiobooks, podcasts, MPEG-4 video, and JPEG photos; additional formats and photo/video transfers are handled through Sansa Media Converter. Its nonreplaceable rechargeable battery provides up to 24 hours of audio or five hours of video playback.

Controls include a power switch, thumbwheel, Hold switch, and playback buttons. The Hold switch disables controls to prevent accidental operation while playback continues. The power switch turns the player on or off and resets it when held for about 10 seconds. The thumbwheel navigates menus, adjusts volume, and controls track progress.

The player can be charged through a computer’s USB port, an optional AC adapter, or an optional car adapter. The computer must remain on for USB charging, and media cannot be played while connected to a computer. Firmware updates and Sansa Media Converter are available from SanDisk’s support website. Formatting deletes all player content.

Music can be transferred by drag-and-drop or with Windows Media Player, while Audible files require Audible Manager. Windows Media Player supports library selection, playlists, and synchronization. Photos and videos are converted and transferred with Sansa Media Converter, which can crop, rotate, resize, and transfer media to internal storage or a memory card.

Music, audiobook, podcast, and voice-recording playback is supported through categorized menus. Playback options include repeat, shuffle, MusicEQ, ratings, Go Lists, deletion, chapter mode, and audiobook speed control. Video playback supports pause, seeking, scanning, bookmarks, ratings, brightness adjustment, and deletion. Photos can be browsed and shown in slideshows with options for shuffle, looping, slide duration, music, Go Lists, and deletion.

FM radio supports frequency searching, manual presets, automatic scanning, regional and mono/stereo settings, and recording of tuned stations. Up to 30 preset stations can be stored. The built-in microphone can record the user’s voice, interviews, or speeches.

System settings include wallpaper color, display art, backlight timeout, power saver, language, date and time, brightness, factory reset, device information, USB mode, formatting, and press-and-hold behavior. Content can also be deleted directly on the player or through a computer.

Troubleshooting guidance covers file transfers, supported bit rates, formatting, firmware updates, photos and videos, podcasts, missing metadata, memory-card compatibility, and resetting the player. SanDisk provides technical support, how-to videos, firmware utilities, and a one-year limited hardware warranty. The software license permits limited personal use, disallows modification and reverse engineering, provides no implied warranties, limits liability, and governs use in high-risk activities. Users remain responsible for complying with copyright and intellectual-property laws.

The Sixth Circuit affirmed the trial court’s judgment, finding no error in its jury instruction addressing the inconsistency between interrogatory No. 4 and the general verdict and concluding that substantial evidence supported the jury’s verdict.

Ari Ne’eman compares RFK Jr.’s statements linking autism to vaccines and acetaminophen with the Soviet Union’s ideologically constrained research on intellectual disability. He recounts how President Kennedy’s 1963 President’s Panel on Mental Retardation visited the USSR to study disability services. Soviet officials rejected genetics, intelligence testing, and socioeconomic explanations, pressuring researchers to assign organic diagnoses, sometimes using EEG findings to attribute disabilities to brain injury. Despite similar classroom populations, Soviet prevalence estimates were far below U.S. estimates, leading the delegation to identify diagnostic practices as a likely explanation.

Ne’eman traces rising U.S. autism diagnoses to broader DSM criteria, diagnostic substitution from intellectual and learning disabilities, and improved access to diagnosis, including reduced racial and socioeconomic disparities. He says a 2006 Pediatrics study found evidence supporting substitution rather than an unprecedented autism epidemic but faced backlash from vaccine-linked advocacy. He criticizes the Trump administration for reviving similar claims, weakening scientific independence, and seeking cuts to Medicaid and parts of the Developmental Disabilities Act, warning of harm to autistic people and disability services.

The Houston Astros defeated the Chicago White Sox 7-1 Sunday for their sixth straight win and a three-game sweep, outscoring Chicago 27-2. Jose Altuve’s go-ahead single triggered a five-run seventh inning, Marwin Gonzalez hit a two-run double, and Evan Gattis homered for the first time this season. Lance McCullers allowed one run and eight hits in six innings. The Astros next face the Los Angeles Angels in a three-game series, with Gerrit Cole starting Monday. Chicago fell to 4-14, losing seven consecutive games and 12 of 13. White Sox starter Reynaldo Lopez, battling a stomach ailment, allowed one run in five innings. Reliever Danny Farquhar remained in critical but stable condition after collapsing Friday, and his No. 43 jersey was displayed in the bullpen.

Sarah Blakely and her husband paid more than $300,000 for a modest Toronto house, renovated it and sold it seven years later for over $1 million after local values tripled. They plan to buy a larger home in Ottawa mortgage-free, citing lower costs, retirement savings and proximity to family.

Real estate agent Josie Stern says Toronto’s market is beginning to cool as buyers await possible government affordability measures, though strong demand and limited supply still favour sellers. The average Greater Toronto Area sale reached $916,567, up 33.2 percent from a year earlier, with bidding wars once common.

Many sellers are cashing out and leaving Toronto for less expensive housing in Burlington, other Golden Horseshoe communities and Nova Scotia. Hamilton-Burlington home prices rose 22.6 percent in the first two months of 2017 compared with a year earlier, while a Nova Scotia mansion’s online popularity drew inquiries from several provinces.

In Vancouver, sales remain strong in much of the city, but a 15 percent foreign-buyers’ tax has weakened interest in west-side luxury homes. Stern supports crackdowns on speculators but warns sellers may regret leaving if they cannot afford to rebuy.
More than 50 patients and attendants narrowly escaped a Lucknow hospital fire; no injuries were reported. Over 24 ICU patients were moved to nearby hospitals, and an inquiry was ordered.

Defending champions India face Bangladesh in the second Champions Trophy semi-final at Edgbaston on 15 June. India’s batting has performed well in most group matches, while both teams boast pace bowlers and spinners. The day match starts at 3 PM IST, broadcast on Star Sports and streamed on Hotstar.

- COP cards operate in CMD42 version 1.0 compatibility mode until a COP Unlock command is accepted, after which CMD42 version 2.0 processing is enabled. COP-related behavior depends on the Force Erase Password (FEP), its length register, and password commands’ COP bit. Setting FEP stores a new password and length, disables Force Erase and Reset PWD, and does not change the current lock state. Password replacement data can contain both the old and new passwords; an incorrect old password produces `LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED` without changing the password. Resetting FEP requires the correct password and clears FEP and FEP_LEN without altering PWD, PWD_LEN, or the lock state.

- After power-on or CMD0 reset with FEP set, a COP card enters the locked state and rejects other CMD42 operations until COP is unlocked. Normal Force Erase requires the ERASE bit to be the only set bit and works only on a locked card; success erases all card content, including PWD and PWD_LEN, and unlocks the card. The secure area is not erased, and temporary and group write protection remain during erasure before being cleared. FEP Force Erase additionally requires the COP and ERASE bits and a password matching FEP; it erases card content and unlocks the card while retaining FEP and FEP_LEN. ACMD6 is rejected while locked, and other commands not accepted in the locked state are treated as illegal.

- CMD42 must use a sufficient block length. Invalid password lengths and execution errors set `LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED`, while `CARD_IS_LOCKED` reports the resulting lock state through CMD42 or a following CMD13. Three lock/unlock card types are distinguished, and hosts are warned not to issue invalid parameter combinations, force erase while permanent write protection is set, or set FEP on a COP card when the password is unknown.

- CMD55 causes the next command to be interpreted as an application-specific command. Undefined but legal ACMDs are handled as regular commands, illegal ACMDs do not alter card state, and APP_CMD status indicates how the command was interpreted. ACMD41 has a specified exception, and several ACMD numbers are reserved for SD proprietary applications.

- CMD6 switches among functions in six function-group positions, with defined groups for access mode, command-system extension, driver strength, and power limit. Function 0 is the default and 0xF retains the current function. Mode 0 queries supported functions, selections, busy status, and maximum power or current; Mode 1 changes functions and cancels the entire switch if any selection is invalid. The command returns an R1 response and a 512-bit status block, with a 100 ms timeout. Mode 0 is used to check whether functions are busy before applying Mode 1. The default power limit is 0.72 W, with higher limits dependent on the power function and card type. In UHS-II mode, access-mode and driver-strength groups are unused, command-system support is optional, and power-limit support is mandatory.

- Selected functions return to their defaults after a power cycle, CMD0, or selection of Function 0. CMD6 may select High-Speed mode, which provides up to 25 MB/s using a 50 MHz clock, but only one card may be connected when cards use different timing modes. Command-system functions can assign CMD34–37, CMD50, and CMD57 to standard, vendor-specific, or mobile-commerce behavior.

- CMD8 checks whether a card can operate at the host’s supplied voltage and must precede ACMD41 during initialization. An accepted voltage produces an R7 response echoing the voltage range and check pattern. SDSC cards use byte addressing and CMD16-defined block lengths, whereas SDHC and SDXC cards use block addressing with fixed 512-byte memory-access blocks; the latter disable partial and misaligned access.

- The host may lower or stop the bus clock under specified conditions, subject to initialization and clock-edge requirements. CRC7 protects commands, most responses, CID, and CSD, while CRC16 protects transferred data blocks. A CRC failure or illegal command produces no response or state change and sets the corresponding card-status error bit.

- Read and write operations have defined timeout behavior. Standard-capacity reads use the lower of 100 times the typical access time or 100 ms, while high- and extended-capacity cards use at least 100 ms. Standard-capacity writes use the lower of 100 times the typical program time or 250 ms. High-capacity cards normally limit write busy to 250 ms, while SDXC cards may indicate up to 500 ms in specified circumstances. UHS-II busy signaling after a Data Burst may last up to one second, and hosts are recommended to use write timeouts greater than 500 ms.

- Commands are fixed 48-bit codewords with start, transmission-direction, six-bit index, optional 32-bit argument, CRC, and end bits. The Card Command Classes in CSD identify mandatory and optional command support. UHS-II definitions differ for several commands, including restrictions on CMD13 during transfers and use of TLEN and CMD12. Responses include R1, R1b, R2, R3, R6, and R7 formats. Card Status reports errors and current state, SD Status is a 512-bit structure reporting capabilities and performance information, and Task Status reports queued-command status; CMD13 selects card or task status through its argument.

- The performance section defines Speed Class 2, 4, 6, and 10, UHS Speed Grade 1 and 3, and Video Speed Class 6, 10, 30, 60, and 90. User areas are divided into Allocation Units and Recording Units, with Recording Units based on 16 KB units and unable to cross Allocation Unit boundaries. Fragmented-AU performance combines free-unit write performance and internal move performance; Class 10 is defined only for entirely free Allocation Units. Read performance is measured through random Recording Unit reads and must meet or exceed write performance. The FAT update cycle consists of two FAT-table writes and one directory-entry write, and its duration is used when evaluating the performance impact of inserting updates during recording.

The passage examines two 2018 documents—the Baku Declaration of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) communiqué—and their implications for India and the Global South. The Non-Aligned Movement represents 120 countries, while the Commonwealth comprises 53 countries, including many small states. India was represented at the Baku meeting by External Affairs Minister Sushma Swaraj, whereas Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended the CHOGM, where he sought to deepen India’s relationship with Britain after Brexit. The passage notes questions about India’s Global South priorities following Modi’s absence from the 2016 NAM summit.

Both documents condemned protectionism and supported a fair, rules-based multilateral trading system, the Doha Development Round, trade facilitation and capacity-building for developing countries. However, the author argues that South-South cooperation has largely become an expression of solidarity rather than a means of challenging structural inequalities in global trade. He questions whether non-alignment’s promise of policy autonomy can be sustained amid continuing barriers to developing countries’ exports, limited market access and the abandonment of the earlier Charter for a New International Economic Order.

The Baku Declaration strongly supported ending Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory since 1967, including East Jerusalem; condemned settlements, demolitions, detentions, blockades and violence against Palestinians; and called for an independent Palestinian state within pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. It also condemned changes to the occupied Syrian Golan and demanded Israeli withdrawal. The declaration additionally emphasized tolerance, respect for diversity and opposition to racism and discrimination, which the author presents as a challenge to India amid criticism of its treatment of minorities and Dalits.

The CHOGM communiqué reaffirmed support for free trade and WTO measures while setting a goal of expanding intra-Commonwealth trade and investment to US$2 trillion by 2030. It highlighted the disproportionate exposure of small states and Small Island Developing States to external shocks, climate events, unsustainable debt, limited development financing and financial “de-risking.” It called for debt management, greater financial inclusion and international efforts to preserve vulnerable states’ access to finance, although the author questions whether existing global economic governance can deliver these outcomes.

On refugees and migrants, the CHOGM welcomed the New York Declaration, supported safe and dignified returns, and expressed solidarity with Bangladesh following the influx of more than one million Rohingya from Myanmar. It called for an end to violence, accountability and sustained return under UNHCR oversight. The passage criticizes India’s deportation policy and legal position that refugee obligations did not apply because India was not party to the 1951 Convention and its 1967 Protocol, describing these positions as damaging India’s humanitarian image.

The author concludes that, despite welcome commitments on trade, migration, occupation, intolerance and international crimes, the documents leave deeper questions about technology transfer, market access, currency transactions and policy autonomy unresolved. He urges Global South countries to pursue alternatives to the economic constraints associated with the “Washington Consensus.”

LeBron James, a four-time NBA champion and the league’s highest-paid player, earned $479.5 million over 21 seasons and signed a two-year, $97 million Lakers extension that brought his guaranteed career salary to $532 million. He earned $126.9 million in 2022—$36.9 million from the Lakers and $90 million from endorsements and other ventures—and reached an estimated net worth of $1 billion in 2022. His sponsors include Nike, AT&T, Walmart, Intel, Kia, Beats by Dre and PepsiCo, while his family also signed Nike endorsement deals. His Instagram presence, with 158 million followers, reportedly generates about $428,000 per sponsored post.

James has invested in Blaze Pizza, Lobos 1707 tequila, Liverpool FC, Fenway Sports Group, Canyon Bicycles and a Manhattan office building. His media company, Uninterrupted, received a $16 million investment from Warner Bros., while a minority stake sale in SpringHill valued the company at $725 million. Although often rumored to own Klutch Sports Group, no evidence was found that he is an owner.

His wealth funds luxury cars, including Porsches, a Rolls-Royce Phantom and a custom Kia, as well as a $9 million Miami home he sold for a $4 million profit, a 30,000-square-foot Akron compound and a $23 million Los Angeles mansion. He bought his mother a Porsche and his wife a Ferrari Testarossa. Despite being described as frugal, he spends heavily on personal training, recovery, nutrition and tattooing.

James founded the fully funded I Promise School in Akron, pledged about $41 million through his family foundation to send more than 1,000 students to college and supported the More Than a Vote campaign.

James, 41, is in the final year of his Lakers contract and has hinted at retirement. His October 2025 “The Decision” tease caused a reported 20-fold jump in Lakers ticket sales, but he revealed it was a Hennessy Cognac advertisement. He previously played alongside his son Bronny in October 2024, becoming the NBA’s first father-son duo to play together.

The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of Hilite International’s judgment as a matter of law and held the asserted claims of Melchior’s ’017, ’506, and ’254 patents invalid. The majority held that Danckert anticipated claim 22 of the ’017 patent because it disclosed hydraulic cam-phaser operation responsive to torque reversals and satisfied every claim limitation; “direct transfer in a closed line” was neither a claim limitation nor part of the district court’s construction. The ’506 and ’254 claims were not anticipated by Danckert because they require additional features, but were obvious over Danckert in view of Shirai, which supplied those features. Melchior had argued only lack of anticipation and did not challenge the obviousness rationale on appeal. The court declined to address Hilite’s other appellate issues. Judge Newman concurred in the no-liability judgment, disagreeing with the anticipation holding but finding no substantial evidence of infringement because the parties stipulated that no infringement occurred while the external oil pump operated and the record contained no evidence of contrary operation during transition.

St. Jude researchers identified the kinases Mst1 and Mst2 as regulators of distinct dendritic cell functions and T-cell responses. Using the data-driven NetBID algorithm, which integrated gene expression and proteomics data, the team found that Mst1/2 and the Hippo signaling pathway control differences between dendritic cell subsets. CD8α+ dendritic cells were more metabolically active than CD8α− cells, and altering their metabolism affected T-cell priming. Mst1/2 also used the NF-κB pathway to trigger production of interleukin-12, supporting CD8α+ dendritic cell function and CD8 T-cell responses. The study, published in Nature, provides clues for cancer or immune-disorder treatments through modulation of dendritic cells and suggests NetBID can identify hidden drivers in other datasets.

Apple Inc. filed a Form 8-K on January 27, 2021, reporting its financial results for the first fiscal quarter ended December 26, 2020. The Form 8-K was signed by Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Luca Maestri.

The passage reviews digital technology and flipped learning (FL) in school physical education (PE) and physical education teacher education (PETE). Although digital competence is part of Norway’s national curriculum, teachers often lack sufficient technological and pedagogical competence, and research on digital technology in PE remains limited. FL is defined as providing course concepts before class through videos so that class time can focus on active, practical, collaborative learning. Previous studies suggest potential benefits for engagement, motivation, autonomous learning, and understanding, but little research has examined FL in Norwegian PETE.

Using a qualitative, constructivist grounded theory approach, researchers studied 22 PETE students—11 male and 11 female, with an average age of 24.2—through five semi-structured interview groups. FL was implemented in 11 lectures across dance and motor-learning units over two semesters. Students viewed short preparation videos before active, student-centred classroom sessions.

Five themes emerged: expectations, simple input, deep learning, a supportive learning environment, and challenges. Videos concentrated essential information, lowered the effort required to prepare, supported repeated and self-paced learning, and increased students’ preparation and participation. Peer expectations encouraged preparation and discussion, while advance preparation reduced uncertainty and increased confidence before practical dance activities. FL also shifted the teacher’s role toward mentor and facilitator, with students collaboratively constructing knowledge. Reported challenges included limited opportunities to ask questions during preparation, technical access problems, and the perceived time required for flipped activities.

Overall, students viewed FL as useful and applicable across theoretical and practical PE contexts, perceiving benefits for motivation, engagement, learning, and future teaching practice. The study notes limitations concerning unexamined perceptions and recruitment from a single institution and recommends further research on digital technology, teacher TPACK, and student learning in PETE and school PE.

Roman pottery on Chapel St Leonards beach near Skegness may indicate a lost Roman settlement, the third Roman artefact found there in recent months after a coin and brooch fragment. Other finds include medieval and Iron Age objects. Lincolnshire County Council asks residents to report coastal discoveries so they can be recorded.

The Alabama Supreme Court answered the certified question in the negative, holding that an insurance policy’s definition of “insured” as an employee acting within the scope of duties does not conflict with a provision covering constitutional or civil-rights violations and therefore does not create ambiguity requiring construction against the insurer.

Shrader and Livingston alleged that City of Attalla police officers sexually abused them after arrest and pursued § 1983 and related claims. After settling those claims, they sought coverage under EMCC’s linebacker policies. The policies covered personal injury, including constitutional or civil-rights violations arising from law-enforcement activities, but limited insured status to employees acting within the scope of their duties. The district court found the policies unambiguous and the alleged abuse outside the officers’ scope of duty.

The court distinguished the earlier Titan decisions. Titan I concerned a conflict between provisions covering unintended injuries and intentional offenses, while Titan II relied on the law of the case rather than deciding whether a scope-of-duties limitation could restrict civil-rights coverage. The linebacker policy contains no comparable intentional-versus-unintended conflict.

The court explained that conduct “under color of law” under § 1983 and conduct within the scope of employment overlap substantially, including when officers improperly exceed their authority while performing official duties. Because some civil-rights violations can satisfy both requirements, the scope limitation does not eliminate all coverage for constitutional or civil-rights violations. The coverage is therefore neither illusory nor ambiguous, and Alabama law permits insurers to define insured status narrowly when the policy is unambiguous and must be enforced as written.

The study proposes a “compromised airway epithelium” hypothesis, under which short-term outdoor temperature drops may further weaken airway defenses, worsen COVID-19 symptoms, and increase severity. Using official temperature and hospitalization data for Tomsk, Russia, from January 1 to March 31, 2022, during the Omicron wave, the authors conducted an adapted case-crossover analysis using hospitalizations and pneumonia as proxies for severity.

Seventeen hospitalization surges were identified. Fourteen followed temperature drops exceeding 3°C within a 1–2-day lag; temperature was classified as the primary trigger in eight instances and an additional factor in six. Three surges occurred without notable temperature changes and were attributed to other factors. The authors note that temperature and humidity jointly affect airway supersaturation, aerosol deposition, cooling, and immune responses, while other environmental and behavioral factors also contribute. Limitations include the use of a single city and wave, absence of direct severity measures, and potential confounding. The findings may support forecasting hospitalization increases and preparing healthcare systems, but further mechanistic and mathematical research is required.

Call to the Pen’s weekly minor league baseball recap highlighted Braves right-hander Mike Soroka, a 19-year-old promoted to AA, who went 2–0 with 11⅔ innings, a 0.77 ERA, 0.43 WHIP, no walks and a 34.15% strikeout rate in two starts. Notable offensive feats included Kyle Tucker’s seven RBI for high-A Buies Creek and Jose Medina’s three home runs for low-A Lake County. Standout pitching included Dane Dunning’s eight scoreless innings with 13 strikeouts, Josh Staumont’s six shutout innings with 12 strikeouts, nine perfect innings by Visalia and a combined no-hitter by Kane County. Leaders were Ian Happ with six home runs, Jorge Mateo with nine stolen bases and Mike Clevinger with 25 strikeouts. Phillip Wellman also earned his 1,000th managerial win with AA San Antonio.

Using U.S. markets as a proxy, historical evidence suggests that wars and geopolitical conflicts do not necessarily produce poor stock returns or greater volatility. After Pearl Harbor, the Dow initially fell nearly 20% but recovered within months and rose more than 60% before World War II ended. Following Iraq’s 1990 invasion of Kuwait, stocks initially sold off, had fully priced in the war by October, and rose sharply when Iraqi forces were expelled.

A study of U.S. stocks from 1890 to 2017 found that wartime and conflict periods had less volatility than periods with fewer geopolitical problems. Higher government defense spending was associated with lower volatility, with a negative correlation of 0.26, possibly because spending and monetary expansion supported economic activity and reduced uncertainty about corporate profitability.

These findings apply to conflicts fought away from domestic soil. Wars affecting a home country can cause severe economic and market disruption, as illustrated by Germany after World War II and Russia following its 1917 revolution.

Among other assets, gold has often risen during geopolitical uncertainty and may also respond to anticipated money printing; wars can increase the money supply and inflation. Commodities, including oil, often benefit from disrupted supply chains but are difficult to predict and have had poor long-term returns compared with stocks.

Peter Joseph Saville, a dentist who served thousands of Worthing patients for more than four decades at his West Park Lane practice, died peacefully at home on June 27, aged 90. His granddaughter remembered him as kind, gentle and energetic.

Born in Ilford in 1928, he trained at Guy’s Hospital and served in the Army Dental Corps in Cyprus and Egypt. He married Josephine in 1954, moved to Worthing and established his own practice. His RAF navigator brother Bernard was killed in action.

Saville played cricket, hockey, golf, tennis and squash, founded The Manor Sports Club squash section and held leadership roles in local organisations. A devout Catholic and Eucharistic minister, he visited Lourdes as a carer and pilgrim, belonged to the Catenian Association for over 50 years and supported charities.

He is survived by Josephine, six children and eight grandchildren. His funeral mass is at Saint Mary of the Angels, followed by burial at Durrington Cemetery.

Nobel Prize-winning biochemist Peter Agre will give a free public University of Louisville lecture May 9 on science diplomacy, human rights, and disease worldwide. The 12:30 p.m. talk is part of a distinguished lecturer series co-sponsored by UofL’s Chemistry Graduate Student Association and Clariant.

Gold prices firmed ahead of Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen’s congressional testimony, with spot gold nearly unchanged at $1,225.06 an ounce. Investors weighed possible additional rate hikes as U.S. inflation expectations rose for a second straight month and the dollar stayed nearly flat. SPDR Gold Trust holdings increased 0.49%. The European Commission warned of euro-zone economic strain, while Venezuela’s gold holdings fell 23% in 2016.

The study demonstrates a nanoscale chirality-selective thermal switch formed by combining ferromagnetic [Co/Pt] multilayers with chiral α-SiO₂. Ultrafast demagnetization of the ferromagnet transfers spin angular momentum to the lattice, generating chiral phonons whose angular-momentum sign follows the initial magnetization direction. These phonons transfer energy and angular momentum into adjacent chiral α-SiO₂, producing a chiral phonon diode effect in which thermal conductivity depends on both magnetization direction and crystal handedness.

Time-resolved magneto-optic Kerr effect measurements showed that reversing magnetization changed the apparent α-SiO₂ thermal conductivity by about 7% at room temperature, with the trend reversed between left- and right-handed crystals; non-chiral amorphous SiO₂ showed negligible dependence. The resulting thermal on/off ratio was approximately 1.07 under direct optical excitation and about 1.02 when an aluminum transducer weakened demagnetization. The switch remained functional down to 50 K, where reduced phonon-phonon scattering increased the on/off ratio to about 1.2.

First-principles-based molecular dynamics and phonon-dispersion calculations linked the effect to angular-momentum-polarized phonons in α-SiO₂, with low-frequency phonon structure governing the direction-dependent heat transfer. The results establish a simple ferromagnet/chiral-material platform for electrically insulated nanoscale thermal switching and thermal regulation.

The Debrief, a digital media brand launched in 2014 to address issues relevant to young women, announced its closure because it could not see a viable future. Many writers were expected to move to sister publication Grazia. The site conducted campaigns on contraceptive mental health and agency fees and received numerous awards, prompting heartbroken reactions from readers.

Students earned academic honors, leadership positions, residency placements and service opportunities. At Misericordia, occupational therapy student Molly Noon was inducted into Pi Theta Epsilon and named to the dean’s list; Immaculata graduate Abigail Kauffman received a senior leadership award. Geisinger College of Medicine students received residency placements in obstetrics-gynecology, pediatrics and psychiatry. At King’s, Hayley Hammer joined Psi Chi, Lyle Luckenbill became student government treasurer and Molly McMullen completed a communications internship. Kutztown inducted Gregory Schuettler into Alpha Epsilon Lambda. At Susquehanna, Ashley Machamer presented research at an Eastern Psychological Association meeting and Kelsey Miller became Kappa Delta president. Occupational therapy master’s student Shelby Weikel joined the University of Sciences’ pinning ceremony. Students from Wilkes performed trail cleanup and animal rehabilitation in Costa Rica, while Susquehanna students taught English in the Dominican Republic.

Successful school-based mental health programs combine strong family-school-community partnerships with central roles for school staff and teachers, who observe behavioral changes and make referrals. They integrate credentialed community clinicians into schools and actively promote their availability through classroom presentations, events, social media and other outreach, reducing stigma and helping students access care.

Maryland’s model arose in the late 1980s after school health centers recognized that students’ physical complaints often reflected social and emotional problems. Low follow-up among referred students—because of transportation, childcare and stigma barriers—prompted the University of Maryland to expand on-site mental health services through contracted community providers rather than assigning more duties to school employees.

Minnesota adapted this approach under Mark Sander, created a funding model allowing insurers to pay for clinicians’ school-based work, and expanded support across the state. Its programs now use public and private insurance plus $20 million in state funding. Although successful programs can adapt to local needs and resources, their shared emphasis on collaboration, accessibility and integration has made school-based mental health a national leader in the field.

Entering Week 5 of the 2025 NFL season, the Steelers hold sole possession of first place in the AFC North after the Bengals’ loss to Denver. The Steelers were the division’s only Week 4 winner, while the Browns and Ravens struggled and the Bengals dealt with injuries and poor quarterback play. The Steelers have a bye.

The Economist’s “Carrie Bradshaw index” ranks major U.S. cities by the salary needed to afford a typical studio apartment while spending no more than 30% of gross income on rent. It compares median wages with threshold wages; scores above one mean most people can afford a studio. Coastal cities are least affordable, while Sun Belt and Midwestern cities fare better. New York ranked most unaffordable for the third year, and 59 cities scored above one.

College adviser Jaime Smith’s book offers practical guidance for community college students transferring to four-year institutions, covering course equivalency, housing, costs, major admission, scholarships, and cases involving military, financial, disability and academic circumstances. The reviewer recommends consulting local transfer advisers about articulation agreements, major-credit limits and scholarships because websites may omit important details. The book’s main weakness is its vague treatment of completing an associate degree: many statewide agreements require it, and without a degree, receiving schools may accept only selected credits, increasing the risk of credit loss. A completed degree can also resolve concerns about low grades or dual enrollment and preserve a credential if studies are interrupted. Overall, the book is considered accessible, useful and practical.

**Summary**

Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) reduces heterosexual HIV acquisition risk by 50%–60% and was adopted by Uganda's Ministry of Health in 2007 following WHO/UNICEF guidance, which recommends 42 days of abstinence after circumcision for complete wound healing. VMMC is free in Uganda with PEPFAR support via the CDC, and men receive pre-procedure counseling plus follow-up at 24 hours and 7 days. Cross-sectional studies indicate 25%–50% of circumcised men resume sex early (early sex resumption, ESR), raising risks of HIV acquisition and transmission to female partners, wound disruption, bleeding, swelling, and pain. Associated factors previously reported include older age, lower education, unemployment, marriage, and multiple sex partners, but temporal trends in prevalence were unknown.

This study used cross-sectional data from four survey rounds of the Rakai Community Cohort Study (RCCS), an open population-based cohort of about 20,000 consenting participants aged 15–49 in 40 communities in greater Rakai, surveyed every ~18 months. Rounds spanned June 2013–January 2015, February 2015–September 2016, October 2016–May 2018, and June 2018–October 2020. Men aged 15–49 reporting circumcision were included, with censoring across surveys and restriction to recent circumcision (≤3 years). Frequencies, proportions, and modified Poisson regression (adjusted prevalence ratios) were used per round in Stata 14. Ethics approval came from UVRI's REC, the Western IRB, and Uganda's National Council of Science & Technology; data were de-identified with written informed consent.

Results: overall ESR prevalence declined from 45.1% (2013/15) to 21.8% (2015/16), 21.8% (2016/18), and 14.9% (2018/20). ESR was consistently higher among men aged 35–44, currently married men, those with multiple partners, and men with primary education; it was higher among fishermen in the first three rounds. Unadjusted analyses showed higher ESR among HIV-positive men in 2015/16 and 2016/18, multiple partners in 2016/18, primary education in 2018/20, and no formal education in 2016/18. Multivariable analysis confirmed higher ESR among primary-educated versus post-primary men in 2018/20 (aPR 2.38), married versus never-married men in three rounds, and men with multiple partners in 2016/18 (aPR 1.76); men ≥45 had lower ESR in 2018/20, and occupation and HIV status were not associated across rounds. Pooled data confirmed elevated ESR among ages 20–24 and 35–44, currently and previously married men, men with multiple partners (aPR 1.36), and men with primary education (aPR 1.29), while adjusted HIV status and fishing occupation were not significant.

Discussion: The twofold decline may reflect strengthened counseling from 2016, yet prevalence remains above the WHO target. Married men may face pressure from wives; counseling wives and targeting older men, multiple-partner men, and men with lower education were recommended. Limitations include self-reported, likely under-reported sexual resumption and inability to determine HIV status at VMMC uptake.

Ronald E. Gabler was convicted by a jury of aggravated assault for attacking Thomas R. Duff and was denied a new trial. The evidence showed that Gabler followed his estranged wife to Duff’s home, confronted Duff, and beat, choked, kicked, and dragged him, causing injuries requiring hospitalization.

On appeal, Gabler claimed ineffective assistance of counsel because trial counsel did not investigate Duff’s medical records or interview his physicians and did not object to testimony that Gabler had previously beaten his wife. Applying the two-prong test of *Strickland v. Washington*, the court found no deficient performance and no reasonable probability of a different outcome. Counsel’s decision not to introduce medical evidence was reasonable trial strategy intended to limit references to Duff’s injuries, and the evidence showed the alleged assault was mutually combative. Medical testimony would not have negated the State’s proof that Gabler used his fists in a manner likely to cause serious bodily injury.

The court also found no prejudice from counsel’s failure to object to character evidence. Gabler had repeatedly placed his own character at issue, insisted over counsel’s advice that his minister testify, and was cross-examined about counseling Gabler’s wife. The court separately declined to review an unspecified Georgia constitutional claim because Gabler cited no particular provision and made no distinct argument. Although Gabler did not challenge the sufficiency of the evidence, the court reviewed it and concluded that it supported the conviction. The judgment was affirmed.

This medRxiv preprint reports a Phase 1/2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of seven-day oral mifepristone (600 mg/day) in 32 non-abstinent individuals with alcohol use disorder who were not seeking treatment. After a three-week washout, participants completed a laboratory session involving yohimbine (32.4 mg), cue reactivity, a priming alcohol dose, and open-bar alcohol self-administration. Outcomes included safety, alcohol craving and consumption, cortisol mediation, and moderation by family history density of alcoholism.

Mifepristone was generally safe when combined with yohimbine and alcohol. No serious adverse events occurred; three non-serious events occurred, all during placebo. Mifepristone did not alter alcohol pharmacokinetics or subjective stimulation and sedation, and outpatient adverse events did not differ between conditions. Diastolic blood pressure was lower with mifepristone, while heart rate did not differ significantly.

Compared with placebo, mifepristone reduced cue-elicited salivary output during both alcohol trials. Self-reported craving and urge were lower during the first alcohol trial but not the second. Cortisol levels were higher with mifepristone, but cortisol changes did not mediate the craving, urge, or salivary effects. Neither laboratory nor outpatient alcohol consumption was significantly reduced.

Participants with high family history density had greater craving, urge, and salivary output and lower cortisol. Mifepristone reduced craving and urge primarily among those with low family history density, while reducing salivary output in both groups. Limitations included the small preliminary sample, few female participants, no placebo-controlled yohimbine condition, and no measurement of mifepristone blood levels. Overall, the findings support the safety of the mifepristone–alcohol combination and suggest a possible effect on laboratory alcohol craving, warranting larger studies, potentially using higher doses and response biomarkers.

The lecture advances from tree-level QED diagrams to loop diagrams. Unlike tree-level processes, where intermediate momenta are fixed by external momenta, loops introduce a free momentum that must be integrated over the full range. These integrals commonly diverge because they naively extrapolate QED to arbitrarily high energies and short distances, beyond where the theory can be tested. Cutoffs cannot be assigned confidently because QED’s validity scale is unknown.

In the late 1940s, Schwinger, Feynman, and Tomonaga developed methods that yielded physically sensible results despite these divergences. Dyson later simplified and clarified their work, helping establish Feynman-diagram techniques and the renormalization program. Wilson’s renormalization group in the late 1960s and 1970s supplied a deeper physical understanding of it.

Loops add two major conceptual features. First, they incorporate vacuum fluctuations through virtual photons and electron–positron pairs. Tree-level diagrams can be derived by perturbatively solving equations of motion and include quantized particles, but not the full quantum fluctuations represented by the path integral. Second, interactions make physical masses, charges, and fields differ from the corresponding bare parameters in the Lagrangian.

The simplest loop examples illustrate these effects. A virtual-photon correction to the electron propagator shifts the electron’s pole, changing its bare mass to a physical mass, and modifies the propagator’s residue, leading to electron-field renormalization. A virtual electron–positron loop in the photon propagator leaves the photon massless, as required by gauge invariance, but renormalizes the photon field through a factor \(Z_3\). A vertex correction similarly renormalizes the electric charge. Gauge symmetry requires the bare charge and photon field to renormalize in a coordinated way.

The vertex correction also produces an anomalous electron magnetic moment. A derivation from the Dirac equation shows that its nonrelativistic limit yields a Pauli interaction,
\[
\frac{e}{2m}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{B},
\]
which corresponds to \(g=2\). Schwinger’s 1948 one-loop calculation found the anomalous factor \(1+\alpha/(2\pi)\), in excellent agreement with experiment. Higher-order calculations involve progressively more diagrams: seven at the next order, 72 at the following order—which took 25 years and was completed in 1996—and 891 at the next. Experiments measure the anomalous factor with precision around \(10^{-12}\), allowing stringent tests of QED, whose theoretical and experimental results agree extremely well.

Bulk RNA sequencing of 38 granulomatous myopathy muscle biopsies from three cohorts revealed marked IFN-γ pathway activation and increased expression of immune-cell, cytokine, chemokine, TNF-family, checkpoint, interleukin, and TGF-β markers, alongside reduced muscle-structure and mitochondrial markers. Spatial transcriptomics localized CD4+ T-cell infiltrates, plasma cells with local immunoglobulin production, IFN-γ targets, IL1B, TNF, TGFB1, and key disease-specific genes to non-caseating granulomas. Intersection of differential-expression analyses identified 1,293 specifically upregulated and 256 downregulated genes, largely associated with active granuloma macrophages and correlated with disease-activity markers. CHIT1 was the most significantly upregulated gene and was elevated in granulomas and giant cells at RNA and protein levels. A support vector machine model achieved 99.6% AUC and 98.6% accuracy, supporting the gene set’s potential for diagnosis and activity monitoring. Limitations included excluding infectious or genetic granulomatous causes and validating most markers only at the RNA level.

This medRxiv preprint compared REM sleep microstructure in 20 patients with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), 20 patients with Parkinson’s disease and RBD (PD+RBD), and 20 controls using polysomnography. PD+RBD was associated with less REM sleep, longer REM latency, shorter REM bouts, and a higher normalized bout frequency. REM arousals were highest in iRBD. REM sleep without atonia was higher in iRBD than in PD+RBD and controls, while both patient groups exceeded controls. The proportion of phasic REM sleep was higher in iRBD than in controls and PD+RBD, which did not differ significantly from each other. Phasic REM generally increased after the first quarter of the night, with the largest increase in PD+RBD.

PD+RBD had lower sawtooth-wave density than controls and shorter sawtooth-wave segments than both other groups. Both patient groups showed altered sawtooth-wave spectral distributions, with less predominance of low-frequency activity and a shift toward higher frequencies. During NREM-to-REM transitions, controls predominantly showed muscle-atonia onset first, whereas STW onset was more common in iRBD and PD+RBD. Transition duration increased progressively from controls to iRBD and was longest in PD+RBD.

The findings indicate that RBD-related REM abnormalities extend beyond loss of muscle atonia and dream enactment to broader changes in REM organization. Limitations include small samples, no PD-without-RBD group, medication effects, limited electrode coverage, cross-sectional sampling, and laborious manual STW analysis. The prognostic relevance of these measures for phenoconversion remains to be investigated.

The lecture reviews optimal control for the double-integrator system \(\ddot q=u\), comparing hand-designed linear feedback and pole placement with bounded-control, minimum-time bang-bang control. The bang-bang policy has a nonlinear switching surface and is analyzed through Pontryagin’s minimum principle, which formulates constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers and provides necessary local optimality conditions.

Dynamic programming is then introduced for additive discrete-time costs. The principle of optimality yields a recursive cost-to-go function, and its continuous-time limit produces the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation. Unlike Pontryagin’s principle, the HJB sufficiency theorem can certify that a policy is globally optimal when it minimizes the HJB expression with a corresponding value function.

Applied to linear systems with quadratic costs, the HJB derivation produces a linear-quadratic regulator: the optimal control is \(u^*=-R^{-1}B^TS(t)x\), where \(S(t)\) satisfies an algebraic Riccati equation. The infinite-horizon steady-state solution yields a time-invariant LQR gain; MATLAB’s `lqr` routine computes it. A double-integrator example produces an elliptic value function and an oscillatory closed-loop trajectory converging to the origin. HJB could not certify the minimum-time solution because its value function is not smooth, while Pontryagin’s principle remains applicable along trajectories. The lecture concludes that these analytical methods extend to linearized complex systems but generally break down for nonlinear dynamics, motivating algorithmic approaches.

A June 1, 2001 news digest focused heavily on California’s electricity crisis, international energy projects, and Enron-related developments.

With Democrats controlling the U.S. Senate, senators planned legislation to cap wholesale electricity prices in California and other Western states. President Bush opposed caps, arguing they would neither reduce demand nor increase supply. Gov. Gray Davis and Democratic Sens. Jeff Bingaman and Carl Levin sought federal intervention and investigations into energy companies, citing high regional rates, price differences between gas at the border and in Southern California, and campaign donations from major power suppliers. Bush ordered increased federal monitoring for price gouging and designated Pat Wood as his California liaison. Polling found 70% of Californians favored federal price caps, while nationwide assessments of Bush’s energy policy were less favorable.

California investigators began examining whether unregulated electricity trading floors, repeated electricity transactions and possible information sharing contributed to rising prices. A state Senate panel also investigated whether power companies used unnecessary plant shutdowns to tighten supply. Enron, Mirant, Duke Energy, Dynegy, Williams and Reliant were among the companies involved. Industry representatives denied wrongdoing and said trading also helped balance supply and demand, although some supported additional oversight. Separately, state regulators were nearing completion of probes into alleged manipulation, including artificial shortages that allegedly drove wholesale prices as high as $1,900 per megawatt hour. Five lawsuits sought damages, and regulators were inspecting records concerning plant operations.

California legislators considered keeping Southern California Edison solvent by shifting much of the cost of its unrecovered wholesale power purchases from residential customers to large commercial users. One proposal would classify about 3,600 high-usage businesses as non-core customers and finance roughly $5.5 billion through surcharges. Enron was also lobbying for direct-access contracts that would allow large customers to buy power from suppliers such as Enron. Business groups warned that additional rate increases could cost the state billions in economic activity.

In a Financial Times commentary, John Dizard predicted that California’s Democratic-controlled legislature would approve a bailout for Edison International. The utility had $3.5 billion in undercollected wholesale costs, while the state had spent nearly $8 billion buying power after utilities exhausted their borrowing capacity. The proposed rescue involved a state loan secured by Edison’s transmission system, additional holding-company support and a dedicated charge to ratepayers. Edison’s shares had risen nearly 70% that year but remained down 46% year over year.

India’s government was working on a package to resolve the seven-month dispute between Enron-backed Dabhol Power Company and the Maharashtra State Electricity Board over power costs and unpaid bills. No party favored closing the $3 billion project, but no immediate solution or timetable had been established. The government explored selling Dabhol power to electricity-deficient states, while an Economic Times commentary argued for broader electricity-market reforms and renegotiation of the contract. Financial restructuring could lower Dabhol’s roughly Rs. 4-per-unit rate by about 30%, but the project was not viable at current tariffs without changes.

Fitch placed India on negative outlook because of fiscal deficits above 9% of GDP, government debt exceeding 60% of GDP, slow privatization, weak public finances and deterioration in the foreign investment climate. Fitch also cited outstanding guarantees equivalent to 9% of GDP, including Enron’s use of a central-government guarantee for payment arrears owed by the Maharashtra State Electricity Board.

Foreign companies were increasingly buying their Indian affiliates to take them private, boosting shares of other multinational-linked companies by as much as 40% or more. Analysts cited easier foreign investment, reduced disclosure requirements and companies’ desire for full ownership as factors.

ExxonMobil and Royal Dutch/Shell were expected to lead Saudi Arabia’s South Ghawar and Shaybah gas projects, while Exxon had already been selected to lead the Red Sea venture with Occidental Petroleum and Enron. The Saudi government was opening three major gas projects to foreign investment, but final leadership roles and stakes remained subject to approval. Separately, Cogentrix Energy began construction of an $800-megawatt, $490 million natural-gas plant in DeSoto County, Mississippi, with Enron subsidiary NEPCO as engineering and construction contractor; the plant was expected to operate in 2003.

Thomas E. White became the 18th secretary of the Army after previously serving as vice chairman of Enron Energy Services.

Hedge funds are privately offered investment pools managed by professionals for accredited investors and institutions. They seek to maximize returns and reduce risk through strategies such as long and short positions, leverage, derivatives, and varied risk-management techniques. They generally invest in liquid assets, unlike private equity funds, and can use broader and more aggressive mandates than publicly available mutual funds and ETFs.

Common strategies include long/short equity, event-driven, global macro, relative value, and fixed-income arbitrage. Niche funds focus on areas such as real estate, insurance-linked instruments, and cryptocurrency. Long/short equity strategies buy undervalued securities and short overvalued ones, while merger arbitrage takes opposing positions in companies involved in a merger to exploit price inefficiencies.

Successful hedge funds often combine systematic and discretionary approaches. Correlation among strategies is important: uncorrelated, even mediocre strategies may improve a portfolio and reduce drawdowns. Individual backtest performance alone is therefore less significant than compatibility with other strategies.

The article also discusses operating a “one-man hedge fund,” emphasizing professional planning, meticulous record-keeping, adequate capital, meaningful diversification, and substantial dedication. Typical minimum hedge fund investments range from $100,000 to $500,000. Potential advantages include higher returns, diversification, professional management, and access to unique investments. Risks include liquidity, leverage, counterparties, ineffective strategies, high fees, and performance restrictions. Hedge funds usually report quarterly performance, and investors are advised to consult a tax adviser about tax implications.

Canadian researchers writing in Archives of Sexual Behavior report that facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR) may relate to infidelity. Their study combined two: 145 heterosexual students measured for facial dimensions and sex drive, and 314 students at another university who also answered questions about attitudes toward infidelity. Men with high FWHR scored higher on sex drive and propensity for infidelity, and high-FWHR students took relationship bonds less seriously. Researchers caution the small, unusual subject group limits firm conclusions.

The study examines how ultraviolet femtosecond-laser irradiation of 190-nm niobium films creates laser-induced periodic surface structures (LIPSS) and alters their superconducting behavior. By varying pulse energy, researchers fabricated square films and narrow bridges with ripples parallel or perpendicular to the transport current. SEM, TEM, XRD, resistivity and susceptibility measurements, SQUID magnetometry, magneto-optical imaging, and time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau simulations were used to correlate processing conditions, microstructure, and superconducting properties.

Increasing pulse energy progressively increased surface roughness, reduced film thickness, nucleated LIPSS at roughly 0.7–0.8 times the optimized pulse energy, and produced complete ripple coverage at the optimized energy. The approximately 260-nm-period ripples formed perpendicular to the laser polarization, while excessive energy created holes. Irradiation also enlarged grains near ripple peaks and contracted the niobium lattice parameter by about 1.05% for fully patterned films.

The intrinsic superconducting properties changed moderately and largely independently of ripple orientation. The critical temperature decreased from about 8.93 K in pristine films to 8.53 K with fully formed LIPSS, and the upper-critical-field boundary shifted downward by approximately 50 mT. The reduced lattice parameter correlated with the reduced critical temperature.

Flux pinning became strongly anisotropic and depended on field, temperature, and current direction. Currents flowing along the ripples generally supported higher critical current densities than currents across them, with optimized samples outperforming pristine films particularly below about 100 mT and between 6 and 8 K. Magneto-optical imaging and transport measurements confirmed the anisotropy, which approached isotropy near the upper critical field.

TDGL simulations indicated that thickness undulations of up to roughly 100 nm create channels that favor vortex occupation and increase the parallel critical current density by about a factor of two. They also reproduced a nonmonotonic field dependence associated with collective vortex motion at lower fields and individual vortex hopping at higher fields. Overall, the results show that laser-processing parameters can controllably tune niobium’s structure, intrinsic superconducting parameters, and anisotropic critical-current behavior.

A non-peer-reviewed medRxiv preprint introduces PHIVE, an unsupervised, physics-informed variational deep-learning framework for rapid metabolite quantification in high-resolution whole-brain MRSI. PHIVE uses a convolutional encoder and physics-informed decoder to learn latent model parameters, reconstruct spectra, and simultaneously estimate CRLB, aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainty. It also supports conditional spline baselines with varying stiffness and uses an ensemble of five independently initialized models to quantify uncertainty.

The study analyzed 7T MRSI data from 12 healthy volunteers: eight subjects (122,473 spectra) for training and four (39,051 spectra) for testing. PHIVE was compared with LCModel using six metabolite ratios, Bland–Altman analysis, correlation, coefficient of variation, and paired t-tests. PHIVE processed each whole-brain dataset in 6 milliseconds versus approximately 2 hours for LCModel, a six-order-of-magnitude reduction. Metabolite maps showed substantial agreement with LCModel, with reported R² values ranging from 0.27 to 0.86. PHIVE generally had lower coefficients of variation, particularly for Glx and mIns. It produced slightly higher mIns estimates, while most other reported differences were not statistically significant. Uncertainty was generally higher in low-SNR regions, including the brain periphery and ventricles.

Limitations include the absence of absolute ground truth, a small single-center healthy sample, lack of frequency-correction preprocessing, lower agreement for tCho and mIns, potential interpretability concerns, and no longitudinal validation. Baseline stiffness also materially affected metabolite estimates, and optimal stiffness selection requires further study.

The passage calls for expanded U.S. research and development to strengthen national defense and preserve peace, restoration of an effective intelligence community, and elimination of congressional reporting requirements for covert CIA operations.
