This medRxiv preprint reports a phase 2/3, observer-blind, randomized, controlled trial of SII-NVX-CoV2373 in India. Approximately 920 children aged 2–11 years and adolescents aged 12–17 years were assigned 3:1 to receive two 0.5-mL doses of vaccine or placebo on days 1 and 22. Safety was followed for 180 days, and immune responses were compared with vaccinated Indian adults from the same study.

The vaccine was safe and well tolerated. Two serious adverse events occurred among adolescent vaccine recipients, both judged unrelated to vaccination; no serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest occurred among younger children. Most solicited and unsolicited adverse events were mild and resolved without sequelae, although injection-site pain, tenderness, headache, fatigue, and fever were common.

Both pediatric cohorts met the prespecified non-inferiority criteria for anti-spike IgG and neutralizing antibodies compared with adults. After dose two, seroconversion exceeded 98% and remained above 90% at day 180. Antibody titers were higher in children than in adults and declined by day 180 while remaining substantially above baseline and placebo levels. A subset showed responses against Delta, Omicron BA.1, and Omicron BA.5.

The study did not assess vaccine efficacy directly and excluded participants with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. The authors concluded that SII-NVX-CoV2373 could support pediatric vaccination, noting the need for continued vaccination of susceptible young and newborn cohorts. The study was funded by Serum Institute of India, with several authors employed by SIIPL or Novavax.

The U.S. pet retail market had 18,370 stores and $25.2 billion in sales in 2017, with brick-and-mortar traffic pressured by grocers, mass retailers, and online competitors. Consumer demand for natural, premium products and services was growing, while major chains PetSmart and Petco pursued premium merchandise, services, and acquisitions.

Mud Bay began in 1988 when Elsa Wulff opened a small farm store near Olympia, Washington. Joined by her children Lars and Marisa, the business focused on natural dog and cat food, highly trained staff, educational materials, and unusually attentive customer service. It acquired eight stores from the insolvent Bosley Pet Food Marts in 2000, converted them to its natural-product model, and returned to profitability. By the end of 2013, Mud Bay operated 27 stores, generated $38.4 million in revenue, and employed 261 people. Its mission combined the health of pets, the happiness of pet owners, and building a strong company.

Mud Bay’s customer model emphasized consultative selling, extensive nutrition and behavior training, free samples and information, and helping customers even when that meant sending them elsewhere or sacrificing a sale. Its employee model included open-book management, profit sharing, flexible scheduling, internal promotion, extensive training, and a culture intended to help employees develop. Nevertheless, in 2014 Mud Bay had 48% staff turnover, low profit margins, and wages that made retaining employees difficult.

Beginning in 2014, executives and employees developed a “Good Jobs Vision” through small-group discussions and a 20-person strategic planning team, known as “The Twenty.” Its goal was for Mud Bay to become one of the Pacific Northwest’s best-loved retailers by 2017. Five strategies supported this goal: investing in staff; offering fewer products at everyday low prices; standardizing processes and empowering continuous improvement; improving efficiency through cross-training and operating with slack; and partnering with animal-welfare organizations.

Mud Bay subsequently raised wages, increased medical-insurance eligibility, introduced an Employee Stock Ownership Plan in 2015, added an Employee Assistance Program in 2017, and expanded employee and leadership training. It did not implement a 401(k) match, paid parental leave, or pet insurance. The company reduced active SKUs from 3,750 to 3,180, created store-based category expert teams, and lowered prices. It made some progress standardizing returns, inventory, merchandising, and delivery processes, reducing problem deliveries from 8.6% in 2016 to 4.8% in 2017, but hiring practices and other processes remained inconsistent. Mud Bay also lacked a formal employee idea system and did not fully implement task-based staffing or systematic “slack.” The company expanded animal-welfare events, donations, outreach staffing, and opened a small-format “Mudlet” whose operating profits were donated to the Seattle Humane Society.

By 2018, Mud Bay had 45 stores, prices averaging about 7% below its principal brick-and-mortar competitors and roughly equal to major online competitors, and highly rated online reviews. From 2014 to 2017, sales grew 70%, average same-store growth exceeded 9%, and sales per labor hour rose from $116.86 to $132.07. Employee turnover fell from 48% to 31%, the share working at least 30 hours rose from 69% to 82%, average hourly store wages rose from $12.12 to $15.06, and employees collectively owned 4.8% of the company. At the same time, higher labor and benefit costs, lower prices, and expanded overhead reduced net profit margin from 2.18% to 1.99%.

Mud Bay also struggled to complete all planned initiatives because of limited time, money, leadership capacity, and systems for evaluating results. Lars described reduced profitability as the cost of building a stronger, more stable organization intended to remain healthy and profitable over the long term, but insufficient profit prevented the 2018 budget from being finalized.

To address operating margins, COO Tracy Yamane proposed closing stores at 8:00 p.m. rather than 9:00 p.m. Monday through Saturday. The proposal would save labor, give employees more time outside work, eliminate short “clopenings,” increase midday staffing overlap, and remove unpopular midday shifts. Marisa supported it, while Lars opposed it because earlier closing might inconvenience customers, conflict with Mud Bay’s commitment to gracious service, and cause lost revenue to exceed labor savings. Before deciding, Mud Bay’s information team analyzed sales by half-hour across six weeks in three seasons, including sales immediately before and after store hours. The annual planning team reviewed the analysis, but the passage does not state a final decision.

This qualitative study examined education students’ and lecturers’ experiences of the effectiveness of Physical Education teacher training in distance mode at North-West University in South Africa. Data were collected through open-ended questionnaires with 17 third-year distance students and semi-structured interviews with four lecturers, then analysed inductively.

Five themes emerged. First, lecturers were widely regarded as professional, accessible, attentive and supportive, although students noted the absence of physical contact and “real interaction.” Second, lecturers’ passion for Physical Education encouraged enthusiastic teaching, while students reported increased subject knowledge, competence and confidence. Third, major obstacles were inadequate prior knowledge of Physical Education and sport, limited technological skills and internet access, and inefficient assignment administration, record-keeping and feedback at the management centre. Fourth, videos supported practical learning by allowing students to observe, repeat and reflect on movements, but insufficient videos and delayed feedback on practical submissions limited their ability to correct mistakes immediately. Fifth, most students considered the course content interesting and reported more positive perceptions of Physical Education, including recognition of its contribution to holistic development and its value within Life Orientation.

Recommendations include increasing face-to-face lecturer–student contact, providing additional technology training, expanding the use of videos and other media for practical instruction, strengthening interaction functions in learning management systems, and improving university management and administrative systems for assignments.

Rieva Lesonsky explains that all businesses manage documents through printing, filing, copying, storing and scanning, and poor management can waste time and money, hinder customer service and expose sensitive information. A Xerox survey found that about 40% of business processes remain document-driven; improving document management can reduce supply costs, streamline workflows, support business growth and boost productivity. The survey also found that 97% of businesses know their print costs and 81% plan to improve document management.

Recommended measures include tracking printing expenses, scanning documents to cloud services through Xerox ConnectKey-enabled multifunction printers, securely importing documents into workflows, and enabling mobile scanning, faxing and cloud storage. ConnectKey apps also support direct sharing from the cloud and customized destinations such as email, FTP, shared folders and USB devices. Printing restrictions can add PIN requirements, identify users, limit color printing and reduce waste, while automatic low-toner email notifications help maintain supplies.

Blackwell’s AI Management Processor (AMP) is a fully programmable GPU context scheduler implemented with a dedicated RISC-V processor at the front of the GPU pipeline. It offloads GPU task scheduling from the system CPU, matching Microsoft’s HAGS model to reduce latency, improve multitasking, smooth frame pacing, and coordinate AI and graphics workloads.

Blackwell adds hardware encode and decode support for YUV 4:2:2 video, which retains more color information than 4:2:0 while requiring less data than 4:4:4. Ninth-generation NVENC improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% BD-BR PSNR, supports 4:2:2 H.264 and HEVC encoding, and adds an AV1 Ultra High Quality mode for a further 5% improvement. The RTX 5090 supports three encoders and two decoders, while Blackwell’s sixth-generation NVDEC doubles H.264 decoding speed. DisplayPort 2.1b provides up to 80 Gbps through UHBR 20, supporting 8K at 165 Hz or 4K at 480 Hz with DSC.

Max-Q power improvements include advanced clock, unit, memory, and voltage-rail gating. Separate rails allow GPU cores and memory to be controlled independently, while clocks adapt to workloads up to 1,000 times faster than previous architectures. Blackwell enters its deepest sleep state 10 times faster than Ada; in a small-language-model inference example, these power-management features produced savings of up to 50%.

DLSS 4 introduces Multi Frame Generation, which can create up to three additional frames for every traditionally rendered frame. Its AI model is 40% faster than the prior method, uses 30% less VRAM, and runs once per rendered frame. Enhanced Flip Metering moves pacing to the display engine for more consistent timing. DLSS Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing now use transformer-based models with twice as many parameters, improving temporal stability, motion detail, lighting, ghosting, and anti-aliasing.

Blackwell also advances neural shading by making Tensor Cores accessible through shaders via the DX12 and Vulkan Cooperative Vectors API and Slang. Potential uses include neural texture compression, RTX Neural Materials, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin, and RTX Neural Faces. Neural Materials approximate complex optical layers in real time. Neural Texture Compression reduces texture data while maintaining quality; a cited demo reduced storage from 1,110 MB to 333 MB. Neural Radiance Cache infers multiple lighting bounces from limited ray tracing, while RTX Skin applies real-time subsurface scattering. Neural Faces uses a TensorRT-optimized generative model to transform a rasterized face and pose data into a more natural-looking face.

The Blackwell GPU family includes GB202, the flagship configuration with 92.2 billion transistors, 24,576 CUDA Cores, 192 RT Cores, 768 Tensor Cores, and a 512-bit memory interface, used in the RTX 5090. GB203 has 45.6 billion transistors, 10,752 CUDA Cores, 84 RT Cores, 336 Tensor Cores, and a 256-bit interface, serving the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti. GB205 has 31 billion transistors, 6,400 CUDA Cores, 50 RT Cores, 200 Tensor Cores, and a 192-bit interface, used in the RTX 5070. NVIDIA states that specifications may change and are provided without warranties or implied intellectual-property licenses.

Only U.S. citizens may be issued passports, which the Secretary of State and authorized diplomatic or consular officers may grant under presidential rules. Issuance to eligible, law-abiding citizens is generally permitted but not mandatory. Applicants must establish citizenship, U.S. domicile, and an intent to return and reside in the country. Expatriation bars issuance, though temporary foreign residence does not constitute expatriation when a genuine intent to return remains. Because no legislative definition exists, decisions depend on individual circumstances, including ties to the United States, health, finances, foreign activities, and future plans. Permanent foreign residence and domicile also preclude a passport. Citizens residing in countries with U.S. extraterritorial jurisdiction may remain abroad indefinitely and receive passports if their pursuits are legitimate and do not harm relations with the host government; special recognition is extended to certain American communities in Turkey and their descendants.

ITV presenter and former news anchor Matt Barbet is launching the Home Roads podcast on June 8 via iTunes and Acast. Inspired by bike-ride conversations, it features cyclists sharing favourite routes and discussing their lives, careers, successes, and failures. Initial guests include Alex Dowsett, Sarah Storey, Nicolas Roche, and David Millar, with Ben Saunders, Simon Warren, Simon Mottram, and Philippa York to follow.

A city court reserved its order on Congress leader Shashi Tharoor’s anticipatory bail plea until the next day in the death case of his wife, Sunanda Pushkar. Delhi Police opposed the plea, citing risks of flight, witness influence, and interference with the investigation. His counsel argued he should receive protection because he was not arrested before the charge sheet was filed. Police named Tharoor the sole accused, alleging cruelty and abetment of suicide; he remains unarrested.

The article presents the 200-day moving average (200 DMA) as a widely used trend-following indicator that averages an asset’s closing prices over 200 trading days. A close above the average generally indicates an uptrend, while a close below indicates a downtrend. The article uses a simple crossover strategy, buying when price moves above the 200 DMA and selling when it falls below, and notes that simple and exponential moving averages produce broadly similar results.

Its main strength is defensive: it can reduce exposure before bear markets, limit drawdowns, and help preserve capital. Backtests cited for the S&P 500 since 1960 show returns broadly comparable to buy-and-hold but with substantially lower drawdowns, although taxable capital gains may result. Paul Tudor Jones likewise describes the 200 DMA as a way to avoid severe losses and exit declining markets.

The strategy is not a silver bullet. In prolonged bull markets without significant recessions, whipsaws, commissions, slippage, and missed gains can cause substantial underperformance. From March 2009, the tested strategy produced an 8.5% CAGR versus 12.8% for buy-and-hold, although its maximum drawdown was lower, at 19% versus 34%. Since 1960, the strategy reportedly crossed above its average 187 times, but only 28% of those trades were winners, with a maximum of nine consecutive losing trades.

Variants include Jeremy Siegel’s rule of buying at least 1% above the 200 DMA and moving to Treasury bills at least 1% below it, trend filters, and 50/200-day or three-average crossover systems. The article also discusses volatility differences above and below the average and advises backtesting to determine the best period, averaging method, and rules. Overall, it describes the 200 DMA as a simple, universal tool for filtering noise and avoiding trouble, not as a guaranteed path to outperforming buy-and-hold.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU is an Ampere-architecture, Compute Capability 8.0 accelerator for deep learning, HPC, and general data-center workloads. It increases DRAM bandwidth to 1,555 GB/s through a five-site HBM2 subsystem—over 1.7 times V100—while providing 2.3 times V100’s L2 read bandwidth. Its 40 MB L2 cache is nearly seven times larger than V100’s. Cache-residency controls, including persistent caching for reused data and producer-consumer buffers, reduce writebacks and redundant DRAM traffic. Compute Data Compression can save up to 4× DRAM read/write bandwidth and 4× L2 read bandwidth.

The new Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) capability can partition an A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated compute, L2 cache, memory-controller, and DRAM paths. This provides defined quality of service, fault isolation, and predictable performance for multiple clients. GPU Instances can contain multiple Compute Instances, which independently context-switch and support Volta-style MPS for combining CPU processes in a CUDA context. MIG supports vGPU migration between instances and GPUs for workload consolidation, service, and power savings. L2 cache set-aside functionality is disabled when MIG is active.

Third-generation NVLink provides 12 links per A100, 50 Gbit/s per signal pair, and 600 GB/s aggregate bandwidth, compared with 300 GB/s on V100. It supports peer-memory access, non-posted writes, error attribution, packet replay, and remote page-fault reporting. PCIe Gen 4 provides 31.5 GB/s per direction for x16 connections, while SR-IOV allows a PCIe-connected GPU to be shared by multiple processes or virtual machines. A100 also adds technologies for error detection, isolation, containment, attribution, and recovery.

Additional A100 features include a five-core NVJPG hardware JPEG decoder, a hardware optical-flow accelerator supporting optical flow and stereo disparity, and five NVDEC units rather than V100’s one. Global-memory atomic throughput is 11 times higher for FP16 and 2.7 times higher for FP32 than V100.

CUDA 11 adds support for third-generation Tensor Cores, sparsity, CUDA Graphs, MIG, and L2 residency controls. CUDA Task Graphs separate workflow definition from execution, reducing repeated CPU launch costs and enabling A100 to optimize uploads, dependencies, and execution order. A new asynchronous-copy API directly transfers data from global to shared memory without register staging; BYPASS and ACCESS variants control L1 usage. Hardware asynchronous barriers separate arrival from waiting, support fine-grained thread synchronization, and allow copies to overlap with computation. Cooperative Groups adds group-wide asynchronous-copy pipelines and hardware-accelerated reductions. L2 persistence can reserve cache space in 2.5 MB increments and can be configured through streams, graphs, address windows, or per-access controls.

DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs with six NVSwitch devices, offering 4.8 TB/s total bidirectional bandwidth, up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance in a 6U system, and up to 56 isolated MIG accelerators. It supports third-generation Tensor Cores with TF32 precision and sparsity, eight 200 Gb/s Mellanox ConnectX-6 adapters, and scaling through Magnum IO and large clusters. NVIDIA reports up to six times the V100-based DGX-1 AI training performance. Its software stack includes CUDA 11, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and the NGC Private Registry with optimized containers, models, scripts, Helm charts, and SDKs.

The appendix explains neural-network sparsity, in which pruning removes low-contribution weights or connections to reduce computation, memory traffic, energy use, and network size. Fine-grained structured sparsity, supported by A100 through 2:4 patterns, maintains balanced workloads while skipping zero-valued connections; NVIDIA reports virtually no accuracy loss in its evaluated networks.

The lecture reviews slender adorned chains, fatter linkages, and hinged dissections, focusing mainly on hinged dissections. Although many individual animations exist online, no general software tool for animating them is available. Suggested projects include building an animation engine, implementing slender adorned folding through CDR or linear programming, designing new dissections, and developing the 128-piece alphabet-based family of hinged transformations.

A universality construction shows how any polyomino of a given size can be hinge-dissected. Squares are divided into triangular halves, and an induction based on the shape’s dual graph and spanning tree constructs a cyclic hinged chain, which can be opened into a path. Similar constructions apply to polyiamonds, polyhexes, and polyabolos. The method also generalizes to arbitrary polyforms with matching edges and to three-dimensional forms, such as regular tetrahedra. Refinements into slender pieces establish that many of the resulting open chains can move continuously.

Physical and biological examples include salt-actuated pieces that spontaneously fold from a square to an equilateral triangle and DNA origami, which uses complementary DNA strands to produce fixed shapes. A related ball-and-socket chain mechanism can continuously fold into arbitrary paths while avoiding collisions. MIT prototypes of chain-folding robots remain electrically connected throughout motion, unlike modular robots whose units must repeatedly attach and detach.

The lecture also explains the classical dissection from one rectangle to another by tiling copies of one rectangle and superimposing them with a slanted rectangle. This “piece-lie” or tessellation-superposition technique can also produce hinged dissections such as the square-to-equilateral-triangle transformation. Hinged versions of the square-to-triangle design can form a table, although collision-free motion requires careful choreography. Existing furniture includes a configurable Dudeney cabinet and a proposed house that can change with the seasons.

A standard construction that repeatedly repairs hinges may double the number of pieces for every polygon edge visited, yielding an exponential worst case. A proposed pseudopolynomial alternative applies to polygons whose vertices lie on a grid and aims for a number of pieces polynomial in the vertex count and grid ratio. Its approach triangulates the polygons using equal-area grid triangles, turns the triangles into slender chains, performs triangle-to-triangle conversions while preserving hinges, moves hinges with local gadgets, converts triangles to equal-height rectangles, and combines rectangle transformations through “pseudocuts.” Keeping recursive depth constant is intended to prevent exponential growth.

For higher-dimensional dissections, equal volume alone is insufficient. Dehn’s invariant, formed from edge lengths and dihedral angles over the rational multiples of π, must also match. Dehn showed this condition is necessary, and Sydler proved that equal volume and equal Dehn invariant are sufficient for three-dimensional dissections; the same result holds in four dimensions, while the conditions in five or more dimensions remain unknown. Matching Dehn invariants is decidable, but efficient algorithms for comparing them and constructing dissections remain open. The lecture concludes that the techniques for converting ordinary dissections into hinged ones are expected to extend to three dimensions, though this has not yet been formally written up.

Researchers at the Universities of York and St Andrews found that New Caledonian crows and kea parrots solved tasks better after exploring relevant objects beforehand. Play with colored blocks and ropes helped them later select suitable tools, indicating incidental “latent learning” about object properties. However, they did not change their behavior after learning the objects could be used as tools, suggesting exploration was not deliberate information-seeking.

- Non-automatic exits (NAEs) are exit events other than automatic exits. In SEV-ES guests, hardware raises a VMM Communication Exception (#VC), whose error code equals the event’s VMEXIT code. The guest inspects the cause, places required state in the Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB), invokes VMGEXIT, and resumes after the following VMRUN. The #VC handler returns with IRET, which normally must not be intercepted.

- The GHCB protocol defines versioned NAE events and the minimum guest state supplied to, and result state returned by, the hypervisor. SW_EXITCODE generally maps to SVM intercept exit codes, with user-defined codes allowed where needed. Guests may handle #VC directly or para-virtualize the originating instruction and invoke VMGEXIT. Hypervisors must handle direct VMGEXIT requests even when no #VC occurred and validate them before responding.

- The GHCB VALID_BITMAP identifies valid fields. Guests must normally mark SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, and SW_EXITINFO2 valid; hypervisors must mark SW_EXITINFO1 and SW_EXITINFO2 valid. Each side resets the bitmap before setting relevant bits. A field’s bit is calculated from its byte offset divided by eight. Software must disable interrupts and preemption while updating the GHCB, setting its MSR, or accessing returned data. For NMIs, a separate GHCB or save-and-restore procedure is recommended.

- Hypervisor errors are reported through SW_EXITINFO1; a nonzero lower 32-bit value indicates an error. SW_EXITINFO1 equal to 1 requests exception injection, with the EVENTINJ value in SW_EXITINFO2. Other conditions include malformed VMGEXIT input, an unregistered GHCB address, an invalid shared buffer, missing valid input fields, or invalid event data.

- Event-specific processing includes:
  - **IOIO_PROT:** The guest decodes the faulting I/O instruction or para-virtualizes it, constructs SW_EXITINFO1, and supplies any decrypted string buffer through the shared GHCB buffer and SW_SCRATCH. Multiple VMGEXIT calls may be needed for strings.
  - **MSR_PROT:** The guest identifies whether the fault came from RDMSR or WRMSR and supplies the state defined for the corresponding NAE.
  - **VMMCALL:** Register support is hypervisor-specific; otherwise, only the registers listed in the NAE table are supplied.
  - **#NPF/MMIO:** Nested-page-table reserved bits identify MMIO accesses. MMIO reads and writes use separate NAEs, with guest physical addresses, transfer lengths, and decrypted-buffer addresses conveyed through the defined fields. Transfers may span multiple VMGEXIT calls.
  - **Page State Change:** SEV-ES and SEV-SNP guests can request page changes through a structure in the shared buffer, which holds up to 253 entries. Requests can make pages private or shared and update SNP RMP ownership; PSMASH and UNSMASH are SNP hints. Progress is recorded through the current-entry and current-page fields so processing can resume after interruption.
  - **SNP Guest Request:** The guest provides shared request and response pages, and the hypervisor translates and validates them before calling firmware and reclaiming the response page. The firmware return code is placed in SW_EXITINFO2; zero indicates success. Rate limiting is recommended, and retries must preserve message sequencing because the sequence number contributes to the AES-GCM IV.
  - **SNP Extended Guest Request:** This extends guest requests with returned certificate data identified by GUID, including VCEK and VLEK certificates. The guest supplies enough shared pages for the certificate table and data; otherwise, the hypervisor returns the required page count in RBX and an error value in SW_EXITINFO2.
  - **AP Creation:** An SEV-SNP guest can create, update, or remove an AP’s vCPU state at a specified VMPL. The guest must use RMPADJUST for the VMSA page, and the hypervisor validates the VMPL and APIC ID. Deferred and immediately runnable creation forms are defined, and the guest tracks its VMSA pages. With the SNP AP Creation feature, vCPU hotplug can be supported.
  - **#HV Doorbell Page:** Under Restricted Injection, a guest can obtain, set, query, or clear a per-vCPU doorbell page used for host notifications.
  - **#HV Send IPI and #HV Timer:** These events let an SEV-SNP guest send IPIs and access emulated APIC-timer functionality when Restricted Injection is enabled.
  - **APIC ID List:** A guest can request the APIC IDs assigned to it. It supplies contiguous shared pages, and the returned list contains a four-byte count followed by four-byte APIC ID entries.
  - **SNP Run VMPL:** A guest can ask the hypervisor to run the current vCPU at another VMPL, with each VMPL potentially having its own VMSA.
  - **SNP TIO Guest Request:** This binds and uses trusted devices in an SNP guest’s private address space. The guest supplies unencrypted PCI, MMIO-range, and TDISP information; optional shared data pages can carry a measurements nonce and receive measurements, certificates, and a TDISP attestation report. The hypervisor must report when insufficient pages are provided.
  - **Secure AVIC:** Guests can register or unregister a private APIC backing page for a specified vCPU; the hypervisor ensures a registered page remains present while that vCPU runs.
  - **Termination Request:** A guest can request termination, optionally supplying termination information and a reason code. An unsupported NAE is reported through the Unsupported Event exit code.

- SEV-ES guests identify hypervisor and SEV support through additional CPUID properties, including the encryption bit position and the reduction in physical-address-space bits. Traditional INIT-SIPI booting is difficult because measured guest register state cannot be changed afterward. Alternative AP reset-hold mechanisms park APs and later restore reset state; an encrypted, page-aligned UEFI AP jump table can convey reset-vector information between firmware and the OS. SEV-SNP can instead use AP Creation with an RMP-adjusted VMSA, which permits the guest to control when an AP becomes runnable.

- For NMI handling, the hypervisor must not intercept IRET but must intercept #DB. The guest can use the debug-exception interception to confirm that NMI handling is complete before another NMI is injected.

- Hardware debug-register virtualization is supported when indicated by SEV_FEATURES and the hardware capability; the hypervisor clears debug-register intercepts and hardware saves and restores their state. Without that support, DR7 reads and writes are intercepted, with writes cached by the #VC handler rather than applied to the real register. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported by this specification.

- The Restricted Injection host-notification format uses a host-owned doorbell page containing a 16-bit PendingEvent field and a NoEoiRequired byte. PendingEvent identifies interrupt vectors, NMI, #MC, and a NoFurtherSignal condition. Guests access the page with C=0.

- The host is expected to emulate APIC presentation, acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI semantics. It presents the highest-priority ready vector, may replace an unacknowledged vector with a higher-priority one, and sets NoFurtherSignal when notification is outstanding. The guest must atomically retrieve and clear pending information, use an explicit APIC EOI when necessary, validate observed vectors, and follow the specified HLT convention. A non-cooperative host may cause denial of service but must not compromise host integrity.

The coach praised his team’s effort after reducing five defensemen midway through the second period, noting that the forwards and the five-man defensive group handled the workload effectively. He highlighted the third period as their best, Max and Jannik’s speed, and Raffi’s timely physical play. He described both teams as fast, physical, and offensively dangerous and said their contrasting goaltending styles might require clarification.

Raffi was praised for his emotion, work ethic, and preparation, despite sometimes playing outside the rules. Manny remained day to day and was not skating. The coach also discussed his limited playing career, decision to coach, excitement about an opportunity to win the Stanley Cup, and a disciplined approach of focusing on one game at a time. He expressed confidence in Boston’s strength and balance, praised a young player’s upside, and said the team used its time off effectively through on- and off-ice preparation.

Joan Jordan, a 45-year-old Irish software engineer, was diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in 2010 after being paralysed down one side of her body. She stopped working before diagnosis and faced repeated job rejections after disclosing her condition. Now working 15 hours a week with the European Patients' Academy, she has written a book, "huManS Multiple Sclerosis," and seeks a sponsor to print more copies. Separately, MS Ireland, with Novartis, launched a report, "Making Ireland the Best Place to do Multiple Sclerosis Research," recommending an MS Research Community, better data sharing, patient involvement, funding models, and improved dissemination of findings; Joan spoke at Trinity College for World MS Day.

Saskatchewan Roughriders receiver Duron Carter continues to play cornerback, while returner Christion Jones is gaining emergency defensive-back reps. Jones, a backup receiver with tailback experience, says he is prepared for either role. He ranked third in the CFL in punt- and kickoff-return average and led the league with 531 combined return yards. Coach Chris Jones says the team limits his workload but would use him at defensive back if needed.

The manual covers the SanDisk Sansa Fuze portable media player, including safety, setup, features, file management, playback, support, warranty, and software licensing.

The player has a 1.9-inch color screen, built-in microphone, optional FM radio, internal memory, and a microSD/SDHC expansion slot. It supports MP3, WAV, WMA, secure WMA, Audible audiobooks, podcasts, JPEG photos, and converted MPEG-4 video. Battery life is stated as up to 24 hours for audio or five hours for video.

Safety guidance emphasizes moderate headphone volume, particularly because prolonged loud exposure can cause temporary or permanent hearing loss. Headphones should not be used while driving, cycling, or operating motorized vehicles. The player must be kept away from moisture, cleaned with a soft lint-free cloth, and its nonreplaceable battery must not be disassembled, crushed, short-circuited, or incinerated. Users are responsible for proper disposal and compliance with copyright and intellectual-property laws.

Controls include a power switch, hold/lock switch, thumbwheel, and navigation buttons. The player can be turned off with a two-second hold and reset with a ten-second hold. It charges through a computer USB port, AC adapter, or car adapter, although some low-power USB ports may be inadequate.

The patent application is a continuation of U.S. Patent Application Ser. No. 16/192,068, “Address Obfuscation for Memory,” filed Nov. 15, 2018, and describes techniques for obscuring the relationship between logical and physical memory addresses.

A configurable mapping function converts logical addresses used by a host or external controller into physical addresses identifying memory cells containing requested data. The function may be implemented through mapping subcomponents that independently apply operations such as pass-through, inversion, XOR, XNOR, OR, AND, NAND, or address swapping to individual or multiple logical-address bits. The number of possible mappings can be extremely large; twenty-bit addresses with four selectable operations per bit can produce more than one trillion configurations.

Mapping functions may be fixed during manufacturing using fuses, trim parameters, or fuseloads, or selected dynamically using random-number generators, unique device, die, or array identifiers, linear feedback shift registers, asynchronous oscillators, schedules, or trigger events such as boot, reboot, access-count thresholds, host commands, or detected row-hammer activity. Functions can vary over time and among devices, dice, arrays, or other memory entities. A security key may enable direct addressing for manufacturer testing and debugging, with that mode disabled before shipment.

The disclosure describes how address obfuscation complements wear-leveling. Wear-leveling transfers data among physical cells to distribute access wear while logical addresses remain fixed. If a cell fails, changing logical addresses of failed accesses can reveal the wear-leveling movement pattern, particularly when the same mapping is used across devices. Different or changing initial address mappings produce different failure sequences, making knowledge obtained from one device, die, array, or time less useful for attacks on others. A scratch cell outside the logical-address domain supports movement when the physical-address space is larger than the logical-address space.

A representative system includes a host, external memory controller, memory device, device and local controllers, memory dice, memory arrays, selection components, mapping components, and communication channels for commands, addresses, clocks, and data. Memory cells may be accessed through word lines, digit lines, row and column decoders, and sense components; read operations may require rewriting or refreshing cell contents.

The described operation selects a mapping function, receives an access command containing a logical address, determines the corresponding physical address, and accesses the data at that physical address.

The passage argues that schools’ repeated emphasis on “skills,” such as critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration and digital literacy, has displaced teaching knowledge about the world, including history, geography, science, mathematics, languages, literature and the arts. It contends that complex skills require subject knowledge: students cannot think critically about, communicate meaningfully about, or comprehend unfamiliar material without first learning its content. It also challenges the characterization of memorization as antiquated and the belief that information can simply be looked up, using string theory to show that understanding even one topic can require extensive study.

Citing research across education and social sciences, the author presents broad background knowledge as essential to strong reading and complex thought. The passage describes declining knowledge emphasis amid grade inflation, reduced graduation-testing requirements and uneven learning outcomes, while noting efforts to adopt knowledge-rich curricula and warning that AI could support or weaken them. Ultimately, it argues that substantial knowledge is necessary for critical thinking, educational equity and fully examined lives.

A secondary analysis of the 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey assessed demographic factors associated with insecticide-treated net (ITN) ownership and use among children under five and pregnant women. The survey covered 13,727 households and 14,476 women aged 15–49. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were used.

Overall, 56% of households owned at least one ITN, averaging 1.3 nets per household; 25% had sufficient nets if each covered two people. Ownership was higher in rural than urban households and highest in the North West and North East, while the lowest and second wealth quintiles had higher ownership than the highest quintile.

About 41% of children under five slept under an ITN. Usage was associated with age, residence, geopolitical zone, and household wealth, but not sex. Younger children, rural residents, children in the North West or North East, and children in lower wealth quintiles were more likely to use ITNs.

Among pregnant women, 49.6% used an ITN. Usage was associated with geopolitical zone and household wealth; women in the North East and North West and those in lower wealth quintiles were more likely to use nets. Women with no or primary education were also more likely to use ITNs than those with more than secondary education, while residence was not significantly associated with use.

The study concluded that despite progress, ITN coverage among children under five and pregnant women remained below the National Malaria Strategic Plan target of 80%. It recommended ongoing monitoring, expanded distribution and healthcare access, and stronger health education to address regional and socioeconomic disparities.

Researchers analyzed 39 Ediacaran fossils from about 560-million-year-old seafloor deposits off Newfoundland and concluded that some forms previously considered pseudofossils were spongelike animals, possibly ancestors of modern sponges. One creature, named for Johnny Rotten because of its spiky appearance and for the Beothuk “jiggamint” fruit, had fingerlike tubes projecting above pores on its upper surface, suggesting it filtered food from the water. Reaching nearly 53 centimeters, it was rounded at one end and pointed at the other, likely had a domed body that collapsed after death, and probably lived atop other organisms, potentially taking shape from the surface beneath it. Its sponge-like pores indicated that it was an animal rather than decomposed organic matter.

A University of Queensland study found that Black, Western Green and Jameson’s mamba venoms cause a dual neurological attack. Postsynaptic neurotoxicity initially causes limp paralysis that current antivenoms can treat, but presynaptic toxicity then produces painful, uncontrolled spastic paralysis, explaining why some patients initially improve before symptoms return. Venom function also varies geographically, particularly among Black Mambas in Kenya and South Africa, complicating treatment. Researchers say specialized antivenoms informed by the full range of venom activity could improve treatment and snakebite care. The work was conducted with the Monash Venom Group.

This systematic review examines the effectiveness, benefits, and challenges of artificial intelligence in higher-education assessment, grading, and feedback. Guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, it considers how AI can align technological capabilities with pedagogical goals and subject-matter requirements. Twenty studies published between 2010 and 2023 were selected through searches of PubMed, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, ERIC, and Scopus. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts, and full texts, extracted data using a predefined form, assessed study quality, synthesized findings thematically, and reported the selection process with a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.

The review found that AI can improve the efficiency, scalability, consistency, and objectivity of assessment. Machine-learning systems can process large volumes of student work rapidly, automate grading, reduce educators’ workloads, and provide timely formative feedback. AI grading can match human graders in accuracy for objective STEM assessments, but its reliability for subjective work involving critical thinking, creativity, communication, and unconventional reasoning remains uncertain. AI-generated feedback can be rapid, detailed, personalized, and adaptive, helping students identify learning gaps, adjust their strategies, track progress, and become more engaged and self-regulated. It can also support diverse learners by tailoring materials, explanations, and learning pathways.

Persistent concerns include algorithmic bias, data privacy and security, inadequate transparency, infrastructure and training gaps, uneven access, academic-integrity risks, and the need for educator and student adoption. Bias may arise from training data, system design, or societal prejudices, requiring diverse datasets, transparent design, regular audits, and ongoing monitoring. The review concludes that AI should complement rather than replace human judgment, with educators retaining responsibility for interpreting results and providing contextualized feedback. Future research should validate AI assessment across disciplines and populations, examine long-term effects on learning and retention, and develop ethically sound policies, interdisciplinary guidelines, professional development, and inclusive implementation practices.

NVIDIA Corporation filed an unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended May 1, 2022, its first quarter of fiscal 2023. Revenue was $8.29 billion, up 46% year over year, with gross profit of $5.43 billion and a 65.5% gross margin. Operating expenses rose to $3.56 billion, primarily including a $1.35 billion charge for terminating the proposed Arm acquisition. Operating income was $1.87 billion, net income was $1.62 billion, and diluted earnings per share were $0.64, down from $0.76 a year earlier.

Graphics revenue increased 34% to $4.62 billion, while Compute & Networking revenue rose 66% to $3.67 billion. Revenue by market was $3.62 billion for Gaming, $3.75 billion for Data Center, $622 million for Professional Visualization, $138 million for Automotive, and $158 million for OEM and Other. No customer represented at least 10% of revenue.

As of May 1, 2022, NVIDIA held $3.89 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $16.45 billion of marketable securities. Total assets were $45.21 billion, total liabilities were $18.89 billion, and shareholders’ equity was $26.32 billion. The company generated $1.73 billion of operating cash flow and $2.61 billion of investing cash flow, while financing activities used $2.45 billion. During the quarter, NVIDIA repurchased $2.00 billion of stock and paid $100 million in dividends. Its board subsequently expanded the repurchase authorization to $15 billion through December 2023. Long-term debt totaled $10.95 billion, and no commercial paper had been issued under its $575 million program.

NVIDIA and SoftBank terminated the agreement under which NVIDIA would have acquired Arm because of significant regulatory challenges. The related prepayment was written off, resulting in the $1.35 billion acquisition termination cost. NVIDIA also disclosed long-term purchase commitments of $11.44 billion, operating lease obligations, and continued stock-based compensation expense of $578 million.

Legal disclosures included a $5.5 million SEC settlement related to prior cryptocurrency-mining disclosures. A securities class action had been dismissed, with plaintiffs appealing as of the filing date, while related derivative lawsuits remained stayed. No loss accrual was recorded for these proceedings.

Management identified demand forecasting, cryptocurrency-market volatility, long manufacturing lead times, inflation, China pandemic restrictions, and the war in Ukraine as material risks. It paused direct sales to Russia and reported continuing supply constraints, particularly for networking products. Management stated that existing cash, marketable securities, and commercial paper arrangements were sufficient for operating and foreseeable capital needs.

Management concluded that disclosure controls were effective as of May 1, 2022, and that no changes in internal control over financial reporting materially affected or were reasonably likely to materially affect financial reporting. NVIDIA was also implementing a phased upgrade of its enterprise resource planning system.

On April 20, 2010, two explosions aboard Transocean’s Deepwater Horizon rig forced 126 workers to abandon the drilling platform in the Gulf of Mexico. Eleven people died and 17 were injured. The rig burned for 36 hours and sank on April 22, taking with it well equipment intended to prevent a blowout. By July 15, nearly five million barrels of oil had spilled, at an estimated rate of 53,000–62,000 barrels per day, making it the largest marine oil spill in U.S. waters. Gas alarms on the rig had been disabled because high gas levels were triggering false alerts.

BP’s history included state ownership, privatization, extensive cost cutting, mergers, and an effort to present itself as an environmentally focused company under the “Beyond Petroleum” brand. CEO Tony Hayward pledged greater safety leadership while promoting a less risk-averse culture and aggressive growth. BP’s decentralized “asset federation” model gave site managers substantial authority and tied compensation to asset performance, but reportedly discouraged the sharing of risk-management practices and provided limited centralized oversight.

Safety failures preceded the disaster. The 2005 Texas City refinery explosion killed 15 people and injured 180. A Baker Panel report attributed responsibility to senior BP executives, identified maintenance and safety cutbacks, and said BP lacked a consistent corporate commitment to process safety. The 2006 Prudhoe Bay pipeline leak spilled more than 200,000 gallons after corrosion and regulatory warnings. Although BP subsequently announced safety investments and organizational reforms, 97% of willful OSHA refinery violations issued from June 2007 to February 2010 involved two BP-owned refineries.

BP held a 65% interest in the Macondo well, 52 miles south of Venice, Louisiana, at nearly 5,000 feet below sea level. Drilling began on February 3, 2010, on Transocean’s $560 million rig. The project had been expected to take 51 days and cost $96 million, but by the disaster it was on its 80th day and over budget. The rig had not entered dry dock for nine years, a 2009 audit identified 390 urgent repairs, and its drilling-control computers frequently froze. Many BP managers involved in Macondo had held their positions for only weeks or months, while 11 companies participated in constructing the well casing.

The case focuses on three decisions to suspend the well. First, BP selected faster, less expensive long-string casing, which provided two barriers against gas flow rather than the liner-and-tieback option’s four, despite internal warnings about the added risk. Second, BP used six centralizers even though Halliburton’s model indicated a significant risk of cement channeling and recommended at least 21. Halliburton formally reported a “SEVERE gas flow problem,” but the accompanying email did not state the danger, and BP managers later testified that they had not read the relevant page. Third, BP performed only a partial circulation of drilling mud—30 minutes instead of the estimated six to 12 hours—and declined to conduct a cement bond log that could have detected a failed cement bond, despite warnings and a loss of 3,000 barrels of mud. Congressional investigators also questioned BP’s failure to install a lockdown sleeve.

The disaster damaged Gulf wetlands, affected 25 national wildlife refuges and all five Gulf states, killed wildlife, and severely affected fishing and tourism. BP established a $20 billion Gulf Coast Claims Facility; by February 2011, it had received more than 500,000 claims and paid over $3.6 billion. A federal deepwater drilling moratorium temporarily reduced industry spending, production, and employment, while estimates placed regional job losses from energy, fishing, and tourism at 250,000. The case concluded that the three principal decisions, BP’s organizational culture, and its contractor relationships may have contributed to the blowout, with cost reduction and expediency taking precedence over caution while official investigations continued.

In his inaugural address, the speaker calls for candid, vigorous leadership to overcome the nation’s economic crisis. He argues that widespread unemployment, reduced purchasing power, frozen trade, lost savings, and agricultural hardship stem not from a fundamental lack of national resources but from failed financial leadership and an excessive focus on profit. He urges greater honesty, honor, and responsibility in banking and business.

The immediate priority is to put people to work through direct government employment, public projects, and greater use of natural resources. He also advocates redistributing population, improving agricultural values, preventing foreclosures, reducing government costs, coordinating relief efforts, and planning transportation, communications, and utilities. Banking, credit, investments, and currency require effective regulation and safeguards against speculation.

Domestic recovery must take precedence over international trade restoration, though he supports world trade through international economic readjustment. National recovery should rest on interdependence, unity, disciplined leadership, and the “good neighbor” policy. He will seek cooperation from Congress and the states, using constitutional powers and, if necessary, broad emergency authority comparable to wartime powers. Concluding that the people demand direct action, he accepts their mandate with confidence in democracy and national renewal.

The lecture examines limited attention in decision-making, treating attention as fixed for now and deferring its potential malleability to a later lecture. Experiments on change blindness, the gorilla test, and dichotic listening show that people can direct attention yet retain little information when competing stimuli or mental tasks divide their focus. Attention may also be constrained by physical surroundings, sleep, noise, health worries, multitasking, poverty-related deprivation, and temptation.

Inattention occurs even in high-stakes settings. EntreMed’s stock rose only gradually after positive cancer-treatment results were published and later featured on the New York Times front page; the subsequent replication failure produced a large delayed decline. Investors also confused similarly named companies and stock tickers. Researchers can identify inattention by making available information salient, providing reminders, or simplifying information and observing changes in behavior.

A simple model separates a product’s visible value from an opaque component, with an inattention parameter θ. Chetty and co-authors applied it to sales taxes, which are often revealed only at checkout, while ordinary price changes are visible on store tags. In a three-week California grocery-store experiment, after-tax price tags for randomized goods made taxes salient. This reduced average sales by 2.2 units from a baseline of 25, an 8.8% decline. Using the estimated price elasticity, the authors inferred θ ≈ 0.75: consumers reacted to sales-tax changes only about one-quarter as strongly as to other price changes. Separate evidence from excise and sales taxes likewise found almost no response to nontransparent sales taxes. Salient excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco can deliberately encourage behavior changes associated with externalities or harms to consumers’ future selves.

The lecture then asks how inattention could cause large welfare losses. Beliefs guide what people attend to, so an incorrect model can prevent relevant information from ever being noticed. In Indonesian seaweed farming, experienced and literate farmers knew line lengths and spacing but neglected pod size. Inducing experimentation alone had little effect, whereas explicitly presenting results and recommendations caused large gains. This evidence shows that people can persistently overlook available, potentially important information, fail to learn, and incur substantial losses.

MACD and RSI are popular momentum indicators that can be combined to analyze trends, overbought and oversold conditions, and potential market movements. MACD is based on a 12-period EMA minus a 26-period EMA, with a 9-period EMA serving as the signal line; it is primarily used for trend analysis but can whipsaw in range-bound markets. RSI, developed by J. Welles Wilder, ranges from 0 to 100, with readings above 70 traditionally indicating overbought conditions and readings below 30 indicating oversold conditions.

Traders can use MACD to identify trend direction and RSI to identify price swings, or use one indicator to confirm signals from the other. Long and short rules can be based on MACD crossovers combined with RSI movements from overbought or oversold regions. Customized strategies may use a slower MACD for trend direction and a faster RSI for mean-reversion trades.

Because the indicators may provide redundant signals and results vary by asset and parameters, clear trading rules and backtesting are essential. One tested strategy combined MACD, RSI, and a mean-reversion filter. On SMH from 2001 onward, it recorded 235 trades, a 73% win rate, and an average gain of 0.88% per trade after 0.03% commissions and slippage, with the strongest performance in semiconductors.

**California power crisis coverage:**
- A Bloomberg primer by David Wilson documented the crisis: PG&E Corp. (Pacific Gas & Electric) and Edison International (Southern California Edison), the state's two largest utilities, face more than $11.5 billion in power-related debt and multiple January payment defaults, driven by a 1996 deregulation law that froze retail rates until March 2002 while power prices quadrupled in 2000 and natural gas rose as much as 25-fold in December. S&P cut Edison to "D" and others to "CC"; Moody's cut parents to "Caa3" and units to "Caa2"; Fitch cut Edison to "CC." Bank of America and J.P. Morgan arranged $4.2 billion in loans but refused PG&E access to part of a $1 billion credit line. Bond insurers MBIA (over $1 billion guaranteed) and Ambac (about $150 million) are exposed; Ace Ltd. holds about $14 million in reinsurance and $125 million in credit-default swaps. State agencies played distinct roles: the PUC granted 10 percent rate increases versus the 26–30 percent sought; the Power Exchange suspended the utilities' trading privileges after missed payments. Two-thirds of state plants are over 30 years old; reserve alerts culminating in a Stage 3 alert led to the first blackouts on Wednesday. Gov. Gray Davis declared an emergency and the legislature approved $400 million for state power purchases; a Davis bill would allow $3.5 billion annually at $55/MWh versus the $72 average, plus refinancing of power-purchase debt. Richardson's electricity order, extended twice, expired the following Tuesday; on his last day he signed a natural gas order, with Clinton finding a gas supply emergency in central and northern California. Outcome was doubtful, as four suppliers were prepared to force bankruptcy filings.
- A second Bloomberg report said California averted a third straight morning of blackouts; the PUC blocked utilities from unilaterally cutting service; $400 million may last under seven days; Kinder Morgan's pipeline disruption threatens gasoline shortages; six suppliers representing 36 percent of PG&E's daily gas supply may stop deliveries, with only 60 percent of next month's gas secured; Bush spokespeople and FERC oppose price caps while Davis and Sen. Feinstein favor them. Edison defaulted on $32 million in commercial paper, may default on $223 million more by Jan. 31, forfeited contracts after missing a $215 million payment and suspended $596 million in bondholder payments; PG&E defaulted on $76 million in commercial paper. PG&E stock rose 44 cents to $10.19; Edison fell 6 cents to $8.94.
- A Reuters analysis (Thomasch and Stempel) said deregulation ended utilities' safe-haven status; PG&E and Edison shares fell more than 60 percent since early November, erasing about 15 percent of the S&P utilities index; first mortgage bonds bid at 80–82 cents and unsecured bonds at 45–50 cents; bondholders rank ahead of shareholders in bankruptcy; Bill Gross called utilities no longer safe, conservative vehicles; PG&E and Edison may fail or be bailed out; Reliant, Duke and Southern Energy face large credit exposure; and years of energy problems were predicted.

- EOTT Energy Partners declared a fourth-quarter 2000 distribution of $0.475 per common unit ($1.90 annualized), payable Feb. 14, 2001 to unitholders of record Jan. 31, 2001; Enron Energy Corp. is general partner.

- Enron Energy Services and Owens-Illinois announced a 10-year energy management agreement covering 53 facilities in 20 states with projected purchases exceeding $2 billion; Enron manages energy at over 28,500 customer sites, reported $40 billion revenue in 1999 and $60 billion for the first nine months of 2000; Enron shares closed at $70-7/8 and Owens-Illinois closed unchanged at $6-7/8.

The flexbone is a run-heavy offense evolved from the wishbone, emphasizing option plays and misdirection. It often moves two A-backs closer to the line of scrimmage to create additional passing threats and is sometimes called the triple-option offense.

Effective personnel include a decisive, athletic quarterback who can run, pass adequately, and threaten defenses with play action; a powerful, athletic fullback who excels at inside running and blocking; quick, agile A-backs who can block, run, and catch; strong wide receivers who can block and threaten deep; and athletic offensive linemen who understand assignments and excel at cut and combo blocking.

The offense’s rarity often leaves defenses with little preparation time. Multiple running threats create assignment confusion, support ball control and long possession, and can wear down opponents and capitalize on weak tackling. Its primary weaknesses are limited passing volume, difficulty moving quickly or overcoming large deficits, extensive practice demands that leave less time for pass development, and execution problems in bad weather caused by the timing required for mesh reads and pitches.

Common formations include the double slot, using pre-snap motion and counter motion; trips, which shifts an A-back across the formation; and receivers over, which creates an extra blocker while making a receiver ineligible. Key running plays include the triple option, with fullback dive, quarterback keeper, and pitch options; the midline option, which has no pitch and relies on a quarterback-fullback mesh and defensive-tackle read; and the rocket toss, a quick outside run with a pitch to a moving A-back. Common passing concepts include play-action post wheel, toss boot, and four verticals.

Navy, Army, and Air Force have traditionally used versions of the flexbone. Paul Johnson also used it at Georgia Southern, Navy, and Georgia Tech; his 2009 Georgia Tech team won the ACC championship. The offense remains widely used at smaller high schools and lower college levels, and Harding University won the Division II national championship in 2023.
