The initiative draws parallels with Luther’s use of inexpensive pamphlets and the printing press to spread reformist ideas rapidly. Reactions are mixed: some users welcome the approach, while older churchgoer Ingeborg Brunner prefers traditional worship and congregational singing.

- NVIDIA’s Ampere-based A100 Tensor Core GPU targets AI, HPC, and data-center workloads. It uses third-generation Tensor Cores and supports TF32, FP16, BF16, and IEEE-compliant FP64. TF32 is used by default without script changes; FP16 or BF16 mixed precision provides the highest training throughput.

- A100 delivers peak mixed-precision Tensor Core performance up to 16 times standard FP32 FMA operations. Its FP64 Tensor Cores provide up to 2.5 times V100’s FP64 performance, with peak throughput of 19.5 TFLOPS from 108 streaming multiprocessors.

- CUDA 11’s cuSOLVER includes the Tensor Core Accelerated Iterative Refinement Solver, supporting TF32, FP16, BF16, and FP32. Across 37 SuiteSparse problems, TF32 produced the fastest and most robust mixed-precision results, with geometric-mean speedups of 2.0×, 1.9×, and 1.8× over the FP64 solver for TF32, FP16, and BF16, respectively. Speedups reached 4× for approximately 40K complex matrices.

- A100 introduces fine-grained structured sparsity using a 2:4 pattern, allowing two nonzero values in every four-entry vector. Sparse MMA instructions skip zero entries, doubling Tensor Core compute throughput. Pruning and fine-tuning retained weights halves storage and bandwidth requirements and produced virtually no inference-accuracy loss across the evaluated networks. Sparsity for training requires early introduction and remains an active research area.

- A100 combines 192 KB per SM of L1 cache and shared memory, supports simultaneous FP32 and INT32 execution, and uses asynchronous global-to-shared-memory copies and asynchronous barriers to reduce data-movement overhead. Third-generation Tensor Cores share data across 32 warp threads rather than eight on Volta, issue eight times fewer matrix-multiply instructions, and perform 2.9 times fewer register-file accesses.

- The GPU includes 40 GB of HBM2 memory delivering 1,555 GB/s, plus a shared 40 MB L2 cache with 2.3 times V100’s L2 bandwidth. ECC protects HBM2, L2, L1 caches, and register files. L2 residency controls, cache management, and Compute Data Compression improve reuse and can reduce DRAM traffic while increasing effective L2 capacity and bandwidth.

- Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) can divide an A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU instances, each with dedicated compute, cache, and memory resources. GPU and Compute Instances provide quality of service, fault isolation, simultaneous context execution, Volta-style MPS support, and vGPU migration while retaining the CUDA programming model.

- Third-generation NVLink provides 12 links and 600 GB/s total GPU bandwidth, compared with six links and 300 GB/s on V100. A100 also supports PCIe Gen 4 at 31.5 GB/s per direction for x16 connections and SR-IOV virtualization. Enhanced error detection, attribution, isolation, containment, and remote fault reporting improve availability in multi-GPU and multi-tenant systems.

- Additional hardware includes a five-core NVJPEG decoder, an optical-flow and stereo-disparity accelerator, and five NVDEC units. Global-memory atomic throughput improved by 11× for FP16 and 2.7× for FP32 over V100.

- CUDA 11 adds support for task graphs, asynchronous copy, asynchronous barriers, L2 persistence controls, Cooperative Groups, hardware-assisted reductions, and MIG. L2 persistence can be allocated in 2.5 MB increments, although set-aside functionality is disabled in MIG mode.

- DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs and six NVSwitches, providing 4.8 TB/s total bidirectional interconnect bandwidth and up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance in a 6U system. It can expose up to 56 isolated MIG accelerators, includes eight 200 Gb/s Mellanox ConnectX-6 adapters, and uses the CUDA Toolkit, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, NGC containers, and GPU-accelerated libraries for deep learning, analytics, and HPC workloads.

The Larry Swedroe Portfolio is an evidence-based, diversified strategy designed for long-term growth with limited volatility and drawdowns. Its typical allocation is 30% stocks and 70% bonds: 15% US small-cap value, 7.5% international small-cap value, 7.5% emerging markets, and 70% intermediate bonds. Swedroe favors low-cost, passively managed index funds and ETFs, broad diversification, a long-term perspective, and avoiding market timing and active management.

His bottom-up value approach seeks undervalued companies with strong balance sheets, consistent earnings, and good management while avoiding overpaying. Small-cap value stocks may offer higher returns, greater growth potential, and diversification benefits but also carry higher volatility and loss risk.

The portfolio is intended as a set-and-forget strategy, reviewed and systematically rebalanced annually or when an asset class deviates from its target by roughly 5%. A backtest using VIOV as a US small-cap value proxy, covering only 2012 onward, reports a 3.71% annual return. The passage also cites a presumed 30-year annualized return of 6.28% and a 5.46% standard deviation, while noting that lower rates provided a tailwind. The large bond allocation is expected to reduce both returns and volatility relative to stock-heavy portfolios.

The passage reviews Berkshire Hathaway’s share-repurchase program, initially authorized in 2011 at up to 110% of book value and raised to 120% in 2012. Berkshire bought $1.3 billion of stock in 2012—9,475 Class A and 606,499 Class B shares—but made no purchases from 2013 through 2016, despite briefly trading near the threshold. The author argues that the fixed 120% limit has become increasingly conservative because Berkshire’s intrinsic value has risen well above book value as unrecorded gains at controlled companies accumulated. Berkshire had ample liquidity, and Buffett said the 120% level clearly benefits continuing shareholders. The author recommends a modest increase and strongly considering repurchases if price-to-book again reaches the low-to-mid 120% range. The writer discloses a long position in BRK.B.

European stocks headed for a fifth consecutive day of losses and their biggest weekly decline since November 2016, with the STOXX 600 down about 1.8%. Rising bond yields and a stronger euro pressured equities, while investors awaited U.S. payroll data and weighed the risk of unwinding leveraged trades. Germany’s DAX fell more than 5% in eight sessions after leading European markets earlier in 2018. Deutsche Bank reported a €497 million 2017 loss, its third consecutive annual loss, while Caixabank and Sabadell results were described as underwhelming. A Bank of America Merrill-Lynch technical indicator issued a “Sell” signal, although some analysts maintained the global synchronized-growth investment case. European fourth-quarter earnings were forecast to rise 11.9% year over year, with results from major technology companies influencing European shares.

The Florida appellate court reversed summary judgment for The Personal Service Insurance Company and vehicle owner George Johnson, Jr. Under Florida tort law, an owner who entrusts a vehicle to another may be personally liable for the driver’s negligence. Because the accident occurred in Florida but the surety bond issued in Ohio, the court applied Ohio contract law. It held that Personal Service, as a matter of law, was liable for a judgment obtained against Johnson arising from the ownership and use of the vehicle. The court rejected Personal Service’s reliance on decisions limiting its liability and remanded the case for further proceedings.

The paper examines how an Australian university addressed insufficient arts-education competencies among pre-service primary teachers, focusing on the effects of limited curriculum time. Grounded in Ball’s education policy sociology and informed by qualitative methods, it analyses three contexts: policy influence, policy-text production and policy practice. The literature review traces neoliberal restructuring and curriculum rationalisation, which reduced arts education to one of 32 primary programme courses, despite national and international recognition of arts education’s academic, creative, cultural and social benefits. Persistent barriers include inadequate time, resources, specialist preparation, teacher confidence and competing assessment pressures.

Critical discourse analysis examines how language, power and stakeholder negotiations shaped the 2019 Arts Specialism curriculum text and related documents. NAAE initiated advocacy involving ACDE, AITSL and other stakeholders, while government policy requiring primary teacher specialisations provided support. Standards developed with NAAE emphasised expert content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge and effective classroom teaching.

The resulting four-course specialism covers dance, drama, media arts, music and visual arts through experiential study, creative production and school-based projects. Each course is 12 weeks and allocates 120 hours to pre-service teachers, totalling 600 hours. Delivery formats include portfolios, projects, presentations, performances, displays, placement activities and reflective evaluation. COVID-19 required online and community-based adaptations, while partnerships with schools, arts organisations and a First Nations dance artist supported culturally responsive learning.

Pre-service teacher feedback indicated stronger content and pedagogical knowledge, confidence, agency and school-based teaching experience, with regional projects also receiving positive feedback. Challenges persist concerning curriculum time, coordination, staffing, costs, resources and industrial-relations requirements. The paper concludes that stakeholder-supported curriculum development offers a promising model for improving arts teacher preparation, while recommending expansion across institutions, stronger policy support and longitudinal research on graduate careers and school-based curriculum implementation.

Centuries-old tales describe children reportedly raised by wolves, apes, or sheep; many are considered apocryphal or hoaxes, but some remain intriguing. Sir Kenelm Digby’s 1644 account of Jean de Liège says the Belgian boy lived alone in the woods for about 16 years, developed exceptionally sharp senses, was hairy and speechless when captured at about 21, and later learned to speak. The passage notes no evidence that wild living causes hair growth and suggests the story may involve hypertrichosis. Nicholas Tulp’s 1672 “sheep-boy” was said to have been raised among Irish sheep, bleated rather than spoke, and ate only grass and hay. A nineteenth-century Texas legend recounts a “Wolf Girl” who escaped captivity and reportedly resurfaced in 1852 with two pups. Whether such “humanimals” still exist remains controversial.

A free, five-week chronic-pain self-management course starts in Montrose in May, delivered weekly by Pain Association Scotland for Angus Health and Social Care Partnership. Open to Angus residents aged 18 or over regardless of the cause or stage of their pain, it covers understanding pain, stress, pacing, flare-ups, relaxation and medication through interactive discussion and peer support. It does not replace medicine or directly relieve pain, but aims to improve coping and quality of life. Participants reported better coping and positive effects on relationships.

The passage says iPhone’s closed ecosystem provides stronger privacy and security than Android, though at the cost of openness and innovation, and acknowledges that iPhones remain vulnerable to malware and exploits. iOS 10.3.1 features include password, PIN, and fingerprint encryption; two-factor authentication prompts; automatic data erasure after ten failed login attempts; and secure iCloud backups. Apple also provides built-in anti-malware layers, unlike Android’s reliance on third-party antivirus software. Find My iPhone enables remote location, locking, and data erasure. App permissions require explicit approval and are more tightly restricted than on Android. Apple controls both hardware and software and regularly patches supported devices, while Android’s fragmentation and manufacturer customization make consistent patching difficult.

U.S. homebuilder sentiment fell to 68 in April from 71 in March, though it remains favorable. New-home sales stayed robust, reaching a 592,000 annualized rate in February—nearly 13% above a year earlier—helped by low mortgage rates and a solid job market.

For NMI injection, the hypervisor must intercept #DB but not IRET and must use the guest’s “NMI Complete” message to determine when another NMI may be injected. A guest can implement this by setting a per-CPU flag, using a #DB interception before IRET to issue “NMI Complete” via VMGEXIT.

SEV-ES supports virtualized hardware debug registers when the hardware provides “DebugVirtualization,” enabled through the SEV_FEATURES bit in the VMSA; the hypervisor must clear debug-register intercepts. Otherwise, it must intercept DR7 reads and writes, cache written values in the #VC handler, and return cached values on reads. SMM is unsupported, as is nested virtualization under SEV-ES and SEV-SNP.

SEV-SNP guests use a shared #HV doorbell page to receive host notifications, with the format aligned to APIC behavior. PendingEvent occupies bytes 0–1, NoEoiRequired occupies byte 2, and bytes 3–63 are reserved. PendingEvent contains a vector, NMI and virtual #MC indicators, a NoFurtherSignal bit, and reserved bits. The backing page must remain host-owned, and guest accesses must use C=0.

The host must emulate APIC presentation, acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI semantics. It presents the highest-priority ready interrupt through PendingEvent.Vector, using #HV to notify the guest when required. It records presented vectors, uses NoEoiRequired to avoid unnecessary VM exits for EOIs, and handles acknowledgments and subsequent EOI cycles. Non-maskable events set the corresponding PendingEvent bits and NoFurtherSignal.

Upon receiving #HV, the guest must atomically exchange PendingEvent with zero before acting on a vector. It may defer dispatch until safe and must validate vectors against expected interrupts. EOI is completed by atomically clearing NoEoiRequired when its previous value was nonzero; otherwise, the guest must perform an explicit X2APIC EOI MSR write through VMGEXIT. Even with EFLAGS.IF clear, the guest must handle pending non-maskable events and may clear their flags and NoFurtherSignal without clearing a pending maskable vector.

Because #HV bypasses interrupt shadows, a halting guest must execute HLT with interrupts disabled and must not inspect pending interrupts first. The host must immediately re-enter a halted guest when events are pending, and the guest must inspect interrupt state immediately after resuming.

Doorbell configuration uses VMGEXIT SW_EXITCODE 0x80000014 to obtain the preferred address, set the page for a vCPU when Restricted Injection is enabled, or query its assignment.

Basketball coaches should prepare for last-shot situations because a single possession, followed by the next period’s opening possession, can create a six-point swing or more. When leading or trailing by fewer than eight points with under 30 seconds left, teams should generally hold for the final shot. The best player should receive the ball and take an open shot, while teammates read defensive overplays and attack the offensive boards, since putbacks often decide close games. Plays should remain simple, and teams should practice different scenarios with the game clock to develop timing, spacing, execution, confidence, and conditioning.

At 10 seconds, players should be positioned; at eight seconds, the play should begin; at three to five seconds, the shot should be taken; and if the opponent rebounds with zero to two seconds left, they should lack time to advance the ball. Players must master skip and baseball passes, half-court shots, tipping, and intentional free-throw misses that hit the rim.

Coaches should preserve at least two timeouts, take one with one to three seconds remaining, and prefer inbounding to half court before calling timeout when possible. Other strategies include countering breaks after opponent scores, taking shots aligned with the basket, counting down the clock with the bench, ensuring proper clock administration, practicing plays from both sides, and assigning a skilled inbound passer.

Situational guidelines vary by time and court location, using endline fly, sideline, baseline, quick-break, or predetermined last-shot plays. After missed free throws or rebounds, teams may timeout; after made shots, they may execute quick-break plays. Own free throws may be intentionally missed to secure an offensive rebound. Maximum dribbles are one at three seconds, three at five seconds, and five at seven seconds.

As tensions rise on the Korean Peninsula, former Canadian diplomat Marius Grinius says Canada’s inconsistent engagement with North Korea has cost it diplomatic influence. John Bishop, a veteran of the 1951 Battle of Kapyong, doubts Canada could again play a pivotal regional role, while veteran Doug Finney urges action to protect civilians and preserve Canada’s Korean War legacy. North Korea’s nuclear and missile testing has prompted sharp U.S.-North Korean warnings of possible conflict. Humanitarian concerns include widespread undernourishment and limited access to clean water in North Korea. Scholar Tina Park argues Canada should uphold its responsibility to prevent crimes against humanity and support long-term stability on the peninsula.

October’s night sky features a supermoon on October 6, when the full moon coincides with its closest approach to Earth and may appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than usual. International Observe the Moon Night occurs October 4. The Draconid meteor shower, originating from debris from comet 21P Giacobini-Zinner, peaks around October 8 and may produce up to 10 meteors per hour, though supermoon brightness may hinder viewing. The Orionid shower peaks October 21 with about 20 meteors per hour and runs from September 26 to November 22. Dark skies during the new moon offer the best viewing opportunities.

This MIT OpenCourseWare lecture (18.06-style linear algebra course) opens with the instructor noting a typo correction posted for homework 1, explaining that course staff review problems and issue corrections when needed. He then reviews formal systems for reordering in systems of equations: permutation matrices, which swap rows when multiplied on the left and swap columns when multiplied on the right by the transpose, are unitary (P·Pᵀ = I), and can reorder both sides of a system. Such reordering is essential for Gaussian elimination, either to minimize numerical error through pivoting or to minimize fill-in; he illustrates this with a research system of ~40 million equations and unknowns that could only be solved with reordering. This is a form of preconditioning.

He turns to sparse matrices, describing a diffusion example using the game Plinko, where a chip falls through pegs with 50/50 left-right probability. A sparse matrix with two half-valued diagonals (built with spdiags) spreads the probability distribution level by level, eventually flattening toward a uniform, binomial-like distribution; a uniform distribution is an eigenvector of A². This motivates the lecture's main topic: eigenvalues and eigenvectors — eigenvectors are vectors that are only stretched when multiplied by a matrix, and the eigenvalue is the amount of stretch. Eigenvectors are not unique (only their direction matters), but the stretch factor is unique. Eigenvalues are found from the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI) = 0, a polynomial of degree N. Diagonal and triangular matrices have their diagonal entries as eigenvalues; eigenvalues of a real matrix may be complex but appear in conjugate pairs; the determinant is the product of eigenvalues and the trace their sum. He applies this to a chemical reaction rate matrix, where a zero eigenvalue corresponds to the steady state and other eigenvalues to rate processes, and demonstrates finding eigenvectors by Gaussian elimination, with the number of freely specifiable components giving the geometric multiplicity, compared with algebraic multiplicity (multiplicity of a characteristic polynomial root). When geometric and algebraic multiplicities agree for all eigenvalues, the matrix has a complete set of eigenvectors and can be diagonalized: A = WΛW⁻¹, which lets systems of equations be solved via Λ⁻¹ and linear ODEs decouple into independent equations. He notes W⁻¹ equals Wᵀ for symmetric matrices with normalized orthogonal eigenvectors, mentions the Lanczos/Krylov algorithm for computing eigenpairs efficiently, and previews alternatives (Jordan normal form, Schur decomposition, and next lecture's singular value decomposition) for matrices lacking complete eigenvector sets.

Taylor Swift has repeatedly broken music and chart records throughout her career. At 17, she became the youngest artist to write and perform a No. 1 country song with “Our Song.” She was the youngest CMA Entertainer of the Year winner in 2009 and, with “Fearless,” the youngest Grammy Album of the Year winner in 2010 before Billie Eilish surpassed that record. Swift became the first woman to win the Grammy twice for “1989,” the first to win three times for “Folklore,” and, with “Midnights,” the first artist to win four times. She also holds the most American Music Awards, with 40, and the most Billboard Digital Song Sales No. 1 hits, with 29.

Swift has the most Grammy Song of the Year nominations in history, including a later nomination for “Fortnight.” “Red (Taylor’s Version)” spent a record 99 weeks atop the Billboard Top Country Albums chart, while “All Too Well (10 Minute Version)” became the longest song to reach No. 1. She has won the most VMAs for Video of the Year and is the only artist to simultaneously occupy all 10 Billboard Hot 100 positions, repeating the feat with “The Tortured Poets Department.”

On Spotify, Swift has repeatedly set single-day streaming records. “The Life of a Showgirl” became the most-streamed album in a single day, surpassing her previous marks, while “The Fate of Ophelia” became the most-streamed song in a single day. The releases also set records on Apple Music and Amazon Music. Swift has held Spotify’s single-day record for most-streamed artist and previously set the female artist record with “Red (Taylor’s Version).” Her Eras Tour grossed a record $2 billion, and her reported net worth reached $1.6 billion, making her the world’s richest female musician.

The article explains that an exponential moving average (EMA) weights recent prices more heavily than a simple moving average, making it more responsive to current market conditions while still lagging actual prices. It is calculated as EMA = K(C − P) + P, where C is the current price, P is the previous EMA, and K = 2/(N + 1); an SMA initializes the first period.

Backtests using SPY found that short-term mean-reversion strategies work best with low-period EMAs: buying when price crosses below and selling when it crosses above. A 5-day EMA produced a 7.41% CAGR with a 30.54% maximum drawdown. Long-term trend-following strategies work best with high-period EMAs: buying when price crosses above and selling when it crosses below. A 200-day EMA returned 7.84%, with roughly half the drawdown of buy-and-hold. Strategies with fixed holding periods were not crossover systems; the best involved buying below a 50-day EMA and selling 200 days later, producing 10.17% per trade. Results excluded reinvested dividends.

EMAs can identify trends, support and resistance, and guide crossover or directional trading, and may be combined with indicators such as the MACD and RSI. However, EMAs lag turning points, and shorter periods can generate false signals, so settings should be backtested and EMAs preferably used with other strategy parameters.

A systematic literature review examined papers published from 2000 to 2017 in selected leading Information Systems journals, using “Digital business strategy,” “Digital transformation,” and “Business digitalization” as search terms. The search produced 292 articles, narrowed to 54 through title, abstract, and keyword assessment and to 28 after full-text review. The final studies were coded using open, axial, comparative, and selective coding to identify dimensions and themes.

Publication activity increased from 2009 and rose considerably in 2016. Research concentrated on automotive, banking, telecommunications, healthcare, oil and gas, and manufacturing, primarily in the United States and Western Europe, with fewer studies in Asia, the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa.

The review identified 12 dimensions of digital transformation, six of digital business strategy, and ten of organizational capability. Shared dimensions included digital-platform ecosystem collaboration across all three concepts; technology use and structural changes across digital transformation and strategy; and digital leadership, agile and scalable operations, digitally enabled customer service, and digital artefacts across transformation and organizational capabilities. Dynamic capabilities were shared by strategy and organizational capabilities.

The resulting framework presents digital transformation as digital business strategy in action, with strategy serving as a blueprint and organizational capabilities enabling implementation. It emphasizes continuously developing and reconfiguring capabilities, competitive digital strategies, and market alignment. The findings are intended to help executives identify suitable capabilities and to provide IS researchers with a framework for understanding relationships among the three concepts.

April the giraffe’s YouTube livestream ranked second, behind Riot Games’ League of Legends, with over 232 million views. Her calf’s birth drew over 1.2 million simultaneous viewers, and the channel reached 200 million views in 54 days.

The Foreign Relations series editors use State Department central, decentralized, Executive Secretariat, and overseas post files, along with restricted records from the Reagan Presidential Library and other agencies. State Department files from 1981–1989 are slated for National Archives transfer and eventual public access after declassification and processing. Although all printed material has been declassified, some source documents remain under review, and scanning limitations sometimes prevent confirmation of attachments, resulting in “Not found attached” notices.

Documents are arranged chronologically by time in Washington, with memoranda of conversations dated by the conversation’s time. Editors preserve original spelling, capitalization, punctuation, abbreviations, underlining, marginalia, brackets, and ellipses; silently correct obvious typographical errors; and use bracketed insertions for corrections, additions, unrelated omissions, and material still classified. Omissions are identified by length and nature where possible, while fully withheld documents receive headings, source notes, and page counts.

The paper addresses multi-period resource allocation under stochastic, potentially correlated demands, with applications including supply chains, pricing, healthcare, and energy dispatch. A static formulation allocates a fixed resource limit across all periods to maximize expected revenue. It is a convex program dependent only on each period’s marginal demand distribution and can be solved efficiently by bisection on a dual variable using demand quantile functions.

Because the static open-loop policy ignores temporal correlations and information revealed as demands occur, the paper proposes a sequential shrinking-horizon policy resembling model predictive control. At each period, it allocates only current resources, re-optimizes over the remaining horizon, and updates the joint demand distribution by conditioning on observed demand. The method is a heuristic and does not guarantee global optimality. For independent demands, it reduces to the static solution.

Simulations use jointly log-normal demands and compare the static and sequential policies with a noncausal oracle allocation and a causal roll-forward baseline. With independent demands, static and sequential revenues are identical. With correlated demands, the sequential policy consistently achieves higher revenue than the static policy, approaches oracle performance, and generally has the lowest revenue variance. The roll-forward baseline performs poorly. Future work will integrate the sequential algorithm with demand-model learning and examine the importance of accurate demand-distribution modeling.

The passage specifies SD Memory Card behavior for writes, erasing, protection, function switching, initialization, CRC handling, timeouts, and command formatting.

- **Block writes:** Data blocks include CRC protection, and the card checks each block before programming. Writes are rejected for block-length or address errors. SDHC and SDXC block writes use 512-byte blocks regardless of `WRITE_BL_LEN`. Partial blocks may be permitted; otherwise, invalid lengths produce `BLOCK_LEN_ERROR`. Misaligned writes are aborted before programming with `ADDRESS_ERROR`. A CRC failure is signaled on DAT, discards the data, and stops further writing. Writes to protected areas fail with `WP_VIOLATION`. CSD programming is also CRC-protected and must match any ROM-backed portion.

- **Busy and multi-block operation:** The card indicates busy status by holding DAT0 low. The host can poll with CMD13, deselect the card with CMD7 without interrupting programming, and interleave operations among multiple cards. ACMD23 can pre-erase blocks to accelerate multiple-block writes; its count defaults to one after the operation, and ACMD22 reports the number of successfully written blocks.

- **Erase, discard, and FULE:** Erasing uses CMD32, CMD33, and CMD38. Sequence errors set `ERASE_SEQ_ERROR` or `ERASE_RESET`. Protected sectors remain intact and `WP_ERASE_SKIP` is set. DISCARD uses the same range commands with CMD38 argument `00000001h`; discarded contents become “don’t care,” the operation has a 250 ms timeout, and it is supported only by SDHC/SDXC cards over SD mode. Full User Area Logical Erase uses argument `00000002h`, logically erases the complete user area, and has a one-second timeout. Unsupported commands fall back to ERASE. Post-erase data may be either zero or one as defined by `DATA_STAT_AFTER_ERASE`.

- **Write protection and passwords:** Three methods are identified: a mechanical write-protect switch, optional internal card protection, and password-based locking. Passwords and their lengths are stored in nonvolatile PWD and PWD_LEN registers. CMD42 carries CRC-protected data specifying erase, lock, unlock, set-password, and clear-password operations. Incorrect passwords set `LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED`. A configured password causes the card to lock after power-up. Locked cards accept specified basic, initialization, status, and lock-class commands but reject other and security commands.

- **Card Ownership Protection:** COP adds FEP and FEP_LEN registers. When FEP is set, CMD42[1Fh] is required after reset to unlock COP functions and enter CMD42 version 2.0 mode. COP functions include managing FEP, resetting FEP, and controlling force-erase behavior. Setting FEP disables ordinary Force Erase and PWD reset operations. Force Erase erases the user area and PWD data, unlocks the card, and does not erase the secure area; FEP Force Erase requires the matching FEP and leaves FEP unchanged.

- **Application and generic commands:** CMD55 causes the following command to be interpreted as an ACMD. The APP_CMD status bit indicates whether the command was interpreted accordingly; legal undefined ACMDs act as regular commands, while illegal commands produce an error and leave the next command as normal. Several ACMD numbers are reserved for proprietary use.

- **CMD6 function switching:** CMD6 selects functions across six groups, principally access mode, command system, driver strength, and power limit. Mode 0 checks supported and selected functions and reports maximum power consumption; Mode 1 changes functions. Invalid selections cause all requested changes to be ignored. The command returns a predefined 512-bit status block and supports busy indications for functions. The default power limit is 0.72 W, while the maximum allowed for removable cards is 1.80 W. In UHS-II mode, function group 4 is mandatory, while groups 1 and 3 are unused. Selected functions reset to defaults after CMD0, CMD6 defaults, or a power cycle. High-Speed mode uses a 50 MHz clock for 25 MB/s operation and permits only one differently timed card on the bus.

- **Initialization and addressing:** CMD8 is issued while the card is idle, before ACMD41, to check the host voltage; an accepted voltage produces an R7 response echoing the voltage and check pattern. CCS distinguishes byte-addressed SDSC cards from block-addressed SDHC and SDXC cards. SDHC/SDXC use fixed 512-byte memory-access blocks and do not support partial or misaligned access; CMD42 remains governed by CMD16.

- **Bus, CRC, and errors:** The host may stop or reduce the bus clock to control data flow, subject to required clock cycles and timing. CRC7 protects commands, most responses, CID, and CSD; CRC16 protects transferred data blocks. Failed command CRCs and illegal commands leave card state unchanged, produce no response, and set the corresponding error bit.

- **Timeouts and commands:** Standard-capacity read and write timeouts use the lower of 100 times the typical access or program time or 100 ms and 250 ms, respectively. High-capacity and extended-capacity cards use a minimum 100 ms read timeout; write busy normally reaches 250 ms, with specified SDXC exceptions up to 500 ms. UHS-II busy after a data burst may reach one second. Every command has a fixed 48-bit format containing start, transmission-direction, command-index, argument, CRC7, and end bits. Command support is advertised through CCC fields, with mandatory and optional classes specified for SD, SDHC, and SDXC cards.

Benally and Anthony-Stevens examine how anti-CRT legislation affects Native content instruction in teacher education at predominantly white public institutions in Arizona, Idaho, and Utah. Drawing on Tribal Critical Race Theory and the concept of “colonial unknowing,” they argue that bans compound existing exclusions of Native peoples, histories, sovereignty, and culturally sustaining pedagogy.

The article reviews laws restricting race-related teaching. Arizona’s 2021 restrictions were ruled unconstitutional, and a proposed constitutional amendment failed to reach the ballot. Utah’s 2021 resolution recommended curriculum excluding claims of racial superiority and recommended guidance on discussing racism. Idaho’s 2021 HB 377 limits discussion of race and gender and bans specified CRT tenets; a state task force found no consistent evidence of classroom indoctrination.

Teacher education already lacks adequate Native knowledge, professional development, and institutional support. Although several states require instruction about Native histories and sovereignty, few provide funding or competency requirements. Predominantly white teaching workforces, fear of discussing race, and curricular neglect continue to marginalize Native perspectives.

Using stories, interviews, and observations from a decade of research and teaching, the authors identify three effects of CRT bans: continued silencing of Native perspectives and content, perpetuation of Native invisibility in public education, and refusal to learn culturally sustaining pedagogies. Their examples include districts suspending culturally responsive training, ignored Arizona Native-history mandates, students dismissing sovereignty and Native erasure, and teacher candidates resisting critical examination of race. The authors conclude that teacher education is a foundational space for confronting colonial and racial hierarchies, teaching Native history, recognizing Native nationhood and sovereignty, and advancing critical, socially just democracy.

Research based on surveys of more than 150 firms and interviews with digital leaders and laggards found that technological maturity correlates with stronger three-year revenue and enterprise-value growth. Cultural change, however, is often harder than adopting technology.

Digital leaders distinguish themselves through four cultural practices:

- They embrace continuous learning, sensible risk-taking, experimentation, and long-term employee development, treating data as essential feedback for adaptation.
- They promote transparent data sharing and organization-wide context for collaboration and decisions, while applying appropriate governance and privacy controls.
- They empower teams to examine data, track performance against meaningful metrics, and pursue realistic goals with autonomy and creativity.
- They connect team objectives to company strategy through transparent goals and a combination of top-down and bottom-up alignment, while avoiding excessive analysis that could undermine intuition.

Digital laggards tend to prioritize short-term work, discourage risk, offer narrow training, restrict data access, silo information, favor individual judgment over evidence, and set poorly grounded goals. This reinforces process adherence, power dynamics, innovation constraints, and misalignment between stated values and actual behavior.

A pharmaceutical company created a controlled environment for experimentation that reduced compliance-check time to one-quarter of the previous process, boosted team morale and autonomy, and led to adoption elsewhere. A transforming retailer introduced real-time sales reporting, pushing data three times daily to improve inventory, marketing, supply-chain, and other decisions.

Even digital leaders face challenges balancing experimentation with failure, analysis with intuition, and long-term learning with short-term demands. Cultivating learning requires sustained effort, and regulated industries can support it through bounded, responsible experimentation. Successful data cultures align beliefs, values, and daily behavior; 88% of digital leaders had standardized APIs supporting data flow between departments, compared with 27% of laggards.

Organizations commonly fall into four patterns: data novices recognize the need but lack enabling culture or systems; insight-ready firms support experimentation but lack advanced analytical capabilities; tech-enabled firms have technology but limited experimentation; and data-reliant firms may over-rely on data and discourage critical thinking. Each can build on its strengths through targeted actions toward a strong data culture and successful digital transformation.

The study estimated county-month mask-wearing behavior across all U.S. states and the District of Columbia from September 2020 through May 2021 using 8,338,877 valid responses from the COVID-19 Trends and Impact Survey. Responses of “all” or “most of the time” were classified as masking and aggregated by county and month. Bayesian binomial regression addressed small county sample sizes, while survey raking and resampling adjusted for age, sex, and education differences. Potential response bias was estimated by comparing self-reported vaccination rates with county-level ground-truth data and then used to correct masking estimates, assuming similar bias in both behaviors.

Bias-corrected masking proportions ranged from 0.11 to 0.96 and showed substantial spatial clustering and variation within states. Masking was consistently higher in urban than rural counties; median estimates exceeded 0.8 in urban counties and were below 0.6 in the most rural counties. Masking peaked in January 2021 and was lowest in May 2021. The decline coincided with rising vaccination, fewer infections, reduced reported concern, mask-mandate expirations, and updated CDC guidance, but the study did not establish causality.

Community-reported masking closely approximated bias-corrected self-reported estimates, with differences between −6% and 5%. The study identified limitations including unmeasured demographic and response biases, recall and dishonest reporting, exclusion of people under 18, possible differences between Facebook and non-Facebook users, and small sample sizes. It recommends locally targeted behavioral data collection and policies, and inclusion of spatiotemporal behavioral variation in infectious-disease models.

Walking robots pose a fundamental control challenge, involving periodic motions, limit cycles, impacts, and hybrid dynamics. Unlike robotic arms, they must carry their actuators, but Tedrake identifies control—not actuator technology or power density—as the primary obstacle. The Van der Pol oscillator illustrates stable limit-cycle behavior: trajectories from different initial conditions converge to the same periodic orbit without synchronizing in time. Because trajectories approach a manifold rather than a single trajectory, ordinary Lyapunov convergence arguments do not directly apply. Poincaré sections and Poincaré maps convert continuous-time limit-cycle stability into discrete-time fixed-point stability; local stability requires the map’s derivative at the fixed point to have magnitude below one.

Historical work includes Muybridge’s photographic studies of animal gaits, McMahon’s ballistic-walker model, which treats the stance leg as a rod vaulted over during a largely passive swing phase, and McGeer’s passive dynamic walkers, which walk down ramps without motors or controllers. Passive walking inspired later controlled machines, but nonlinear, discontinuous dynamics make effective control difficult.

The rimless-wheel model represents walking as a point mass with massless, evenly spaced legs. It assumes a pinned stance foot, instantaneous support transfer, and inelastic impulsive ground collisions without bouncing. Between impacts, pendulum dynamics conserve energy; impacts dissipate a fraction of velocity according to  
\(\dot{\theta}_{after}=\cos(2\alpha)\dot{\theta}_{before}\).  
On a slope, the walker approaches a stable rolling speed where gravitational potential-energy gain balances collision losses. Its Poincaré map has stable rolling and standing fixed points, with basins of attraction separated by exceptional initial conditions near a homoclinic orbit. Ground impact is the dominant energy loss, exceeding joint friction; push-off immediately before impact can reduce collision velocity and substantially improve efficiency.

Adding a swinging leg with mass and a hip joint produces the compass-gait model, which can walk passively down a small slope but requires suitable initial conditions. Adding articulated, point-foot legs with knees yields more natural-looking limit cycles, though additional collision and stance-leg constraints apply. Future work will address optimization of hybrid limit-cycle dynamics and the state of the art in walking control.

The article presents a simple gold trend-following strategy based on a 12-month simple moving average. Since 1971, when the dollar and gold became formally independent, gold has moved in large jumps separated by long inactive periods. The strategy holds gold when its price is above the moving average and holds cash when below it. Excluding slippage and commissions, a backtest starting with $100,000 grew to $10 million by May 2021, versus $4 million with buy-and-hold, across 26 trades. The best results came from averages around 12 months, or 200–250 trading days, primarily because the strategy avoided major drawdowns. Practical implementations include the GLD ETF or gold futures, although only spot prices were tested. Past performance is emphasized, with no guarantee of future results. The article also notes that gold produces no cash flow or significant services, requires storage costs, and has historically hedged inflation, though stocks may be a better hedge.

The passage presents electrical specifications and detailed descriptions for the MSPM0G3519, MSPM0G3518, MSPM0G1519, and MSPM0G1518 MCUs, including ADC, VREF, comparator, DAC, SPI, UART, timer, power-management, memory, security, and communication details. Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, including KPC- and MBL-producing strains, pose major clinical challenges because of limited treatment options and horizontal spread of resistance genes. This study evaluated the disc potentiation test (DPT) for detecting KPC and MBL in clinical gram-negative isolates.

From January to June 2020, 147 imipenem-nonsusceptible isolates were collected from outpatient, inpatient, and intensive care units at Evercare Hospital in Dhaka. KPC was detected using imipenem disks augmented with phenylboronic acid, with a zone-diameter increase greater than 5 mm considered positive. MBL was detected using 0.5 M EDTA, with a zone increase greater than 7 mm considered positive.

All 147 isolates were resistant to imipenem, and 126 had imipenem MICs of at least 16 µg/ml. The highest number of resistant isolates occurred among patients over 60, and isolates from male patients accounted for 78.2%, compared with 21.8% from female patients. The ICU had the greatest prevalence of resistant isolates. Overall, 39 isolates (26.53%) were KPC-positive, 66 (44.89%) were MBL-positive, 36 (24.49%) produced both enzymes, three produced KPC alone, 30 produced MBL alone, and 78 produced neither. KPC positivity occurred in 23 ICU, 14 inpatient, and two outpatient isolates; MBL positivity occurred in 33, 28, and five, respectively. Co-production was most common in the ICU. Acinetobacter baumannii was the predominant producer of both enzymes and the leading KPC- and MBL-producing organism. Tracheal aspirates contained the largest number of isolates producing both enzymes.

The findings indicate substantial carbapenemase prevalence, particularly in ICU patients, and support enhanced antimicrobial stewardship, surveillance, and infection-control measures to limit the spread of multidrug-resistant organisms.

Florida’s Second District Court of Appeal reversed the financial portions of a divorce judgment and remanded for an alimony award consistent with Sharon Kaylor’s needs and Kenneth Kaylor’s ability to pay. His 20% interest in an insurance agency was not readily marketable for cash, while the payments plus Sharon’s income exceeded her stated needs by $175 monthly. The judgment’s other provisions were affirmed.

The passage documents stackless native assembler AGESA procedures for x86-64 and their host-environment dependencies. AMD_ENABLE_STACK allocates pre-memory stack space among processor cores, maps it into global address space, configures MTRRs, and must run on all cores. It preserves SS in protected mode, otherwise configures SS:ESP for 16- or 32-bit execution, and creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF structure. It can report success, stack reentry with stack reset, or an unknown processor-family fatal error.

A complementary procedure removes the pre-memory stack after memory becomes available. It must be invoked by the BSP, disables CAR mode without changing MTRRs, and flushes all cache lines without write-back. AARCH64 systems with a PSP do not use these stack and very-early macros because the PSP initializes DRAM.

AmdCreateStruct allocates and default-initializes specified AGESA structures using an internal pre-memory heap, a post-memory allocator, or host-preallocated storage. It requires an established stack, must be paired with AmdReleaseStruct, and may fail if storage is insufficient or the processor family is unrecognized.

Other stack-requiring services return a 31-by-32-bit DIMM data-eye bitmap, determine the APIC address of a specified socket and core, and report the current core’s available pre-memory execution-cache size. The first two require operational coherent HyperTransport links; the cache-size and APIC services apply only to x86-64 APUs.

The paper assesses the state and future of digitalization in Vietnamese higher education and recommends measures to support institutional transformation. The centralized higher education system comprises 237 universities—172 public and 67 private—with programs overseen by the Ministry of Education and Training (MOET) and other governing agencies. Government policy has driven digitalization, although progress before COVID-19 was slow and uneven. Most institutions lacked adequate infrastructure, ICT capacity, funding, digital skills, and standardized systems, while fragmented governance and regulations also impeded transformation. Although most universities had adopted learning management systems, distance learning remained uncommon, and digitized materials and shared data warehouses were limited.

The National Digital Transformation Program through 2025, with a vision to 2030, identifies education as a priority and sets higher education targets including distance-learning platforms, broader use of digital technologies, digitized materials, shared data warehouses, online examinations, MOOCs, information-technology training, and personalized learning. A 2022–2025 project further promotes innovative online teaching, technology-based management, a national education database, and paperless student services.

COVID-19 substantially accelerated online teaching and institutional digitalization. Regulatory changes permitted up to 30% online delivery in regular bachelor’s programs, 20% in joint master’s and doctoral programs, and 50% online assessment. Learning management systems, blended learning, digital administrative services, national databases, digital repositories, MOOCs, and unified management systems expanded, although capability gaps, funding constraints, copyright concerns, quality control, and fragmented data remain.

Recommendations call for clearer MOET guidance, national policy dissemination, increased funding for infrastructure and cybersecurity, partnerships with private and international organizations, research on good practices, and digital-literacy training for institutional leaders. Universities should train lecturers in intellectual property, cybersecurity, privacy, online pedagogy, digital tools, personalized learning, and mentorship, while expanding student training and paperless services for enrollment, coursework, tuition, theses, and scholarship applications.

This study examines the scope, importance, and role of curriculum literacy in education and identifies barriers to its development. Curriculum literacy is presented as the ability to understand curriculum structure and purpose, evaluate content, teaching methods, materials, and outcomes, assess applicability, adapt programs to students’ needs, and integrate technology effectively. Although teachers’ curriculum literacy levels are often reported as insufficient, the literature review attributes this to inadequate training, time constraints, bureaucratic obstacles, and frequent curriculum changes.

Using thematic content analysis, the study reviewed 29 eligible Scopus journal articles retrieved through the keyword “curriculum literacy.” Titles, keywords, abstracts, and conclusions were classified by year, subject, and country. Six of the 35 initially retrieved studies were excluded as insufficiently related to the field.

The findings indicate that research interest has increased substantially over time, particularly in 2020–2025, when digital learning tools, artificial intelligence, dyslexia, diagnosis, and empowerment became prominent themes. Earlier periods emphasized social studies education, activity theory, and cultural contexts. Research is concentrated in social sciences, with limited representation in psychology, arts and humanities, and several interdisciplinary fields. Australia and the United States have the most studies, followed by Türkiye, South Africa, and the United Kingdom, demonstrating uneven global coverage.

The reviewed studies associate curriculum literacy with stronger pedagogical practices, effective use and evaluation of instructional materials, curriculum adaptation, student development, and more inclusive and equitable education. Digital technology use has a positive but weak relationship with curriculum literacy, indicating that teachers need additional digital skills, resources, and training. Research also emphasizes aligning learning opportunities with student needs and contexts, integrating cultural and social factors, supporting low-income students, and developing critical reflection and 21st-century skills.

Recommendations include providing pre-service and in-service teachers with training on digital platforms, teaching materials, and contemporary methods; expanding curriculum literacy beyond social sciences; adopting interdisciplinary approaches; increasing access to digital resources; revising policies and practices; and supporting more active student participation. The study concludes that curriculum literacy is central to effective educational processes and digital transformation, requiring sustained institutional and governmental support.

Nasdaq 100 E-mini futures are electronic derivative contracts based on the Nasdaq 100, an index of the 100 largest nonfinancial companies listed on Nasdaq and dominated by technology stocks. The E-mini is one-fifth the size of the full Nasdaq futures contract and is traded on CME Globex. It debuted on June 21, 1999, and expires quarterly in March, June, September, and December.

One contract equals the index value multiplied by $20. At an index value of 11,615.75 on December 6, 2022, its value was $232,315. The trading symbol is NQ. The tick value is $5 for outright Globex trading and $1 for BTIC, TACO, and calendar spreads; minimum price fluctuations are 0.25 and 0.05 index points, respectively. Contracts trade from 6:00 p.m. ET Sunday to 5:00 p.m. ET Friday, with a daily break from 5:00 to 6:00 p.m. They are cash-settled using the index’s special opening quotation on the third Friday of the contract month, when trading ends at 9:30 a.m. ET.

Trading strategies may use fundamental and technical analysis, defined entry and exit points, position sizing, risk management, and market psychology for hedging or speculation. A described paywalled volatility strategy, F101 for NQ, has three buy variables, one sell variable, and years of out-of-sample data. Its backtest used daily bars, trades at the close, and continuous back-adjusted CME data from Norgate Data from contract inception to the stated present, without stop-loss or other risk controls. The passage reports that the contract historically tends to perform better in spring and fall than in winter and summer.

To trade the contracts, investors must open and fund an account with a futures broker that provides CME access; positions are leveraged and cleared through the broker. CFDs offer similar speculative exposure without contract expiry or rollover, although some brokers provide index-tracking CFDs rather than futures-based products.

Prices are influenced by Federal Reserve decisions, component-stock prices, economic news, and the US Dollar Index. Major risks arise from leveraged price movements. TradingView, Barcharts, Yahoo Finance, and CME provide charting options. The reported all-time high is 16,676.50 from November 2021, while the all-time low is 797.50 from October 3, 2002.

A bear trap is a false bearish reversal in an uptrend that prompts short sellers to sell, often triggering stop-loss orders, before prices reverse upward and resume the prior trend. NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture combines dedicated RT and Tensor Cores with advances in memory, display, rendering, AI, and connectivity. Lossless compression and increased raw bandwidth raise TU102-based RTX 2080 Ti’s effective bandwidth by approximately 50% over Pascal-based GTX 1080 Ti. Turing’s display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, DSC 1.2, HDR, tone mapping, and two 8K displays at 60 Hz. Its NVENC encoder supports 8K H.265 at 30 fps and reduces HEVC and H.264 bitrates, while NVDEC adds high-bit-depth HEVC, VP9, and HDR support.

VirtualLink uses a single USB-C connector to provide VR headset power, display, and data, reducing cabling requirements and enabling VR on smaller devices. For SLI, TU102 and TU104 replace MIO and PCIe transfers with second-generation NVLink. TU102 has two x8 links and TU104 one, providing 25 GB/s per direction per link; only two-way SLI is supported.

RT Cores in each Streaming Multiprocessor accelerate bounding-volume hierarchy traversal and ray-triangle intersection tests, freeing other GPU resources for shading and computation. Combined with BVH acceleration, denoising, and rasterization in hybrid rendering, they enable real-time ray-traced reflections, refractions, shadows, ambient occlusion, and indirect lighting on a single GPU. Turing reportedly reaches more than 10 Giga Rays per second and is about ten times faster than software-based ray tracing on Pascal. Compatible technologies include NVIDIA RTX, OptiX, Microsoft DirectX Ray Tracing, and the forthcoming Vulkan ray-tracing API.

NVIDIA NGX applies deep neural networks through Tensor Cores. Deep Learning Super-Sampling renders at lower internal resolution and reconstructs target-resolution images comparable to temporal anti-aliasing with roughly half the shading work, contributing to RTX 2080 Ti delivering twice the performance of GTX 1080 Ti in the cited demo. DLSS is trained using 64-times-supersampled reference images, while DLSS 2X combines target-resolution inputs with a larger network. Other NGX services include AI Inpainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez for realistic content replacement, interpolated slow-motion frames, and 2x, 4x, or 8x upscaling.

Turing also introduces Task and Mesh Shaders, which use cooperative processing to reduce CPU draw-call bottlenecks, support dynamic level-of-detail selection, and efficiently render hundreds of thousands of objects. Variable Rate Shading controls shading independently for each 16×16-pixel region, enabling content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering while optionally increasing shading under multisample anti-aliasing. Texture Space Shading separates visibility and appearance sampling, stores shading results as reusable texels, and can reuse results across stereo views or frames. Multi-View Rendering supports up to four views per hardware pass and 32 at the API level, enabling efficient rendering of stereo, shadow, and repeated-character views. Turing also adds bindless constant-buffer and unordered-access views, Tier 2 resource heaps, and mixed resource types within a single heap.

The full TU104 contains six GPCs, 48 SMs, 256-bit memory, 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores. TU106 has 36 SMs, 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores but no NVLink or SLI support. The TU104-based Tesla T4 is configured with 40 SMs, 2,560 CUDA Cores, 320 Tensor Cores, a 256-bit interface, and 320 GB/s memory bandwidth. NVIDIA also introduces RTX-OPS, a workload-weighted metric that discounts peak Tensor, CUDA, RT, and INT32 throughput according to their representative utilization during a frame.

The passage provides PCB-layout guidance for the UC1825B-SP controller across push-pull, forward, half-bridge, and full-bridge converters. Low-EMI ferrite closed-core inductors are recommended; open cores require low EMI and placement away from low-power circuitry, while stick cores generally produce the most noise. Feedback traces should be direct, somewhat thick, and separated from the inductor and noisy power traces, preferably on the opposite PCB side with a ground plane between them.

Input filter, feed-forward, and compensation capacitors should be placed close to the IC, with surface-mount components recommended. Power traces should be short, direct, and thick, with a minimum of 15 mils per ampere. The inductor, output capacitors, and output diode should be close together, and switching-current loops should be arranged to flow in the same direction to reduce radiated EMI.

Ground planes are required and are recommended on both PCB sides. Multilayer boards can separate power and signal planes, using approximately one via per 200 mA for significant interplane current. Because each output driver supports 2-A peak current, high-di/dt power ground paths require careful layout. Power ground should connect to the PGND pin, MOSFET sources, input power return, and bulk input capacitor. VCC and VREF require high-frequency ceramic bypassing, analog circuitry should connect to signal ground, and the output requires a high-current Schottky clamp to VCC and PGND.

Additional sections cover documentation updates, TI E2E support, ESD handling precautions, mechanical and orderable information, trademarks, and TI resource and liability disclaimers.
