Rural special education teacher shortages are linked to geographic and social isolation, limited training and resources, lower compensation, heavy workloads, and inadequate administrative and collegial support. Annual attrition in rural districts may range from 30% to 50%, with reported five-year turnover as high as 100%.

This study examined factors attracting and retaining special education teachers in rural remote districts. A 32-question survey, adapted from Berry (2012), was completed by 93 teachers from three special education cooperatives in the rural Midwest. Data were analyzed descriptively, through correlations and t-tests, and through inductive thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

Respondents identified four themes. For retention, 70% emphasized provision of support, 53% financial incentives, 44% job-related factors, and 2% rural initiatives. Recommended support included administrative respect and involvement, collaboration with general educators, and community connections. Financial measures included higher salaries, loan forgiveness, lower insurance costs, housing, and sign-on bonuses. Job-related recommendations included reducing paperwork and caseloads, providing resources and rural-specific professional development, and improving work-life balance. Grow Your Own programs were the principal rural initiative mentioned.

For attraction, 96% cited financial incentives, 31% provision of support, 15% job-related factors, and 9% rural initiatives. Salary increases were the most common financial response, followed by improved health insurance, tuition assistance, housing, and sign-on bonuses. Recommendations also included respectful administrative support, general educator collaboration, community outreach, lower caseloads, professional development, Grow Your Own programs, and career fairs hosted by rural educators.

Teachers reporting greater support were more likely to plan to remain in their positions, while teachers planning to leave reported lower support and satisfaction. Satisfaction was also positively associated with remaining in the profession. Among 22 respondents planning to leave special education, job-related factors were the most frequently cited reason, followed by insufficient support and limited rural initiatives.

The study’s limitations include reliance on self-reported data, a small and geographically limited sample, and predominantly descriptive analyses. The authors conclude that recruiting and retaining rural special educators likely requires coordinated policies combining financial incentives, administrative and collegial support, manageable workloads, relevant professional development, and locally focused recruitment initiatives. They also caution that the observed associations do not establish causality.

Malaria remains a major public health problem in Africa, where emerging artemisinin partial resistance threatens the efficacy of artemisinin-based combination therapies. Pfk13-associated resistance has expanded across East and Horn Africa, while the WHO candidate mutation P441L has recently been detected across several African countries, including Zambia.

This study used amplicon deep sequencing to assess drug-resistance markers in samples collected from 2018 to 2023 in a low-transmission area of southern Zambia. Of 570 samples assayed, 540 were successfully sequenced at one or more loci. P441L occurred in 30 of 501 successfully assessed samples (6%), rising from 0% in 2018 to 7.2% in 2023, with a peak of 9.3% in 2022. It first appeared in 2019 and was found at all four health centers. Pfk13 A578S was detected in three individuals (0.6%) in 2023 but is not associated with artemisinin resistance. MDR1 Y184F, associated with chloroquine and amodiaquine resistance, had a stable prevalence of 41%; MDR1 N86 was present in all samples, and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine resistance markers were common.

The six-year and 2023 P441L prevalences exceeded the WHO’s 5% threshold for concern, suggesting possible selective pressure in southern Zambia. However, the mutation’s relationship to artemisinin resistance remains uncertain. Limitations included missing data in low-parasitemia samples, incomplete coverage of the Pfk13 propeller domain, and variable sample sizes. The authors recommended therapeutic-efficacy and ex-vivo studies, whole-genome sequencing of P441L-positive parasites, and routine molecular surveillance for emerging resistance mutations.

Thomas H. Fisher sued Homer P. Hargrave and Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Beane for an accounting, alleging that the firms had succeeded to or merged with Fuller, Rodney & Co., which had handled his commodity transactions and received $6,500 from him. The court granted Hargrave’s motion for summary judgment. Affidavits and the parties’ agreement showed that only selected accounts were transferred with customer consent, that no merger or consolidation occurred, and that defendants did not assume liabilities for untransferred accounts, including Fisher’s. Fisher’s opposing affidavit relied on information and belief and speculative allegations unsupported by admissible evidence. He also had not pursued available discovery procedures, and the record contained no court order denying discovery. The court held that the equitable accounting suit was eligible for summary judgment and that defendants’ assumption of one office lease and admission of two Fuller partners did not create liability for the dissolved firm. The decree granting summary judgment to Hargrave was affirmed.

Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2016 describes its strategy as a productivity and platform company serving a mobile-first, cloud-first market. Founded in 1975, Microsoft operates in more than 190 countries and develops, licenses, and supports software, cloud services, devices, games, advertising, consulting, and training. Its three strategic priorities are reinventing productivity and business processes, building an intelligent cloud platform, and creating more personal computing.

Microsoft reports through three operating segments. Productivity and Business Processes includes Office Commercial, Office Consumer, Office Consumer Services, and Dynamics products. Intelligent Cloud includes server products, Azure, Premier Support Services, and Microsoft Consulting Services. More Personal Computing includes Windows, Surface and other devices, gaming and Xbox Live, and search advertising. Windows 10, launched in July 2015, is central to Microsoft’s cross-device strategy and includes features such as Cortana, Windows Hello, Windows Ink, and Microsoft Edge. Microsoft also operates Xbox, Surface, Lumia phones, Azure, Office 365, Dynamics, OneDrive, Skype, Minecraft, Bing, and related services.

The company operates regional support centers, datacenters, and product-localization activities worldwide. Phones are manufactured predominantly in Vietnam, while most non-phone devices are produced by third-party manufacturers. Microsoft announced plans in May 2016 to streamline its smartphone business and sell its entry-level feature-phone business and associated Vietnam manufacturing facility.

Research and development is conducted through engineering groups focused on applications and services, cloud and enterprise technologies, and Windows and devices. Microsoft Research also collaborates with universities worldwide. R&D expense was $12.0 billion in each of fiscal 2016 and 2015 and $11.4 billion in 2016, representing 14%, 13%, and 13% of revenue, respectively. Microsoft reported more than 61,000 issued U.S. and international patents and more than 35,000 pending applications.

Products and services are distributed through OEMs, distributors, resellers, online channels, Microsoft stores, and carrier networks. Organizational licensing includes Enterprise Agreements, the Microsoft Products and Services Agreement, Select Plus, and Open programs, while online-only and partner programs address cloud services. Customers include consumers, businesses, enterprises, public-sector organizations, service providers, developers, and OEMs; no individual customer represented more than 10% of revenue in fiscal 2016, 2015, or 2014.

Microsoft employed approximately 114,000 people at June 30, 2016, including 63,000 in the United States and 51,000 internationally. Fiscal 2016 restructuring eliminated about 7,400 positions, primarily in phone hardware. Further restructuring approved during fiscal 2016 was expected to reduce approximately 2,850 roles, mainly in smartphones and global sales, by the end of fiscal 2017.

Principal risks include intense competition, execution of cloud strategies, uncertain returns on product and infrastructure investments, acquisition integration, goodwill and intangible-asset impairment, intellectual-property protection and claims, cybersecurity and data-privacy exposures, service outages, regulatory and antitrust scrutiny, tax liabilities, hardware quality and supply constraints, difficulty retaining talent, litigation, and international operating and currency risks. The filing also notes that its June 2016 LinkedIn acquisition was valued at approximately $26.2 billion.

A cross-sectional study led by Daisuke Matsushita at Osaka Metropolitan University used an online, stratified random survey to examine how commute time and home size affect insomnia and daytime sleepiness among Tokyo metropolitan residents. Researchers calculated commutes using transportation modes and participants’ home and workplace postal codes, assessed sleep with the Athens Insomnia Scale and Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and adjusted for demographic and socioeconomic factors. Longer commutes predicted both insomnia and daytime sleepiness, while smaller homes predicted insomnia, revealing a trade-off between commuting time and floor area. In 95-square-meter homes—the urban-oriented standard for four-person households—commutes exceeding 52 minutes reached the insomnia cutoff. Researchers suggested that housing planning and supply considering this trade-off could improve sleep health and reduce sleep-related economic losses.

A proper one-on-one defensive stance requires a balanced position with one foot forward (lead) and one back (trail), knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet, and arms slightly extended. This enables quick reactions, slows or redirects attackers, prevents being beaten, and prepares for a tackle. Lead-foot selection depends on field position: left foot on the right side, right foot on the left, and either foot centrally, generally forcing attackers toward the sideline. Coaches should teach stance changes for right, center, and left positions through progressively faster movement drills that add a ball and emphasize maintaining goal side using field markings. Defenders may not extend their arms to impede opponents.

The Iso Play is a downhill running scheme in which a fullback leads and isolates a linebacker while offensive linemen use base blocks and double teams to overpower defenders and help the tailback gain yardage vertically. Its main strengths are getting the ball downhill quickly, consistent yardage with a powerful tailback and offensive line, and simplicity that makes it easy to teach and execute. Its primary weakness is dependence on personnel: successful teams need large linemen capable of winning one-on-one blocks and a rugged fullback who can engage linebackers effectively.

Assignments vary by defensive front. Against a 3-4, linemen use leverage and double teams to create second-level gaps; against an even 4-3, they use combination blocks and verticality. The fullback squares up the appropriate linebacker, the tailback follows the blocking leverage, and receivers climb to safeties.

Variations include Shotgun Iso, which gives spread offenses a downhill run without a defender read and is often paired with an RPO, and Weakside Iso, which can create more favorable double-team angles.

The passage cites a GBPJPY futures strategy with favorable statistics and an equity curve, but withholds its rules.

This literature review compares eight leadership models used in educational organizations: administrative/managerial, instructional, transformational, distributed, transactional, ethical, contingent and participative leadership. Administrative leadership provides clear structure and defined responsibilities but can be rigid, inhibit innovation and discourage staff engagement. Instructional leadership emphasizes mission and goals, educational management, a positive learning climate and a supportive work environment, but may reinforce hierarchy, require specialized expertise and overlook student wellbeing. Transformational leadership promotes shared vision, motivation, innovation, staff development and participation, but can produce authoritarian relationships without suitable principal selection, training, autonomy and reduced bureaucracy.

Distributed leadership shares leadership across the school community, strengthening collaboration, trust, engagement and learning outcomes, although implementation may require considerable time and cause communication problems or role conflicts. Transactional leadership uses authority, rewards and negotiated exchanges to influence performance and maintain order, but risks lower morale, exploitation, overconfidence and limited innovation. Ethical leadership emphasizes honesty, fairness, accountability, justice, respect and democratic relations, while potentially creating conflicts when personal and organizational ethics differ or when other school needs are neglected. Contingent leadership requires principals to assess changing circumstances and adapt their approach rather than apply predetermined solutions. Participative leadership incorporates stakeholders into decision-making, improving trust, morale, creativity, collaboration and ownership, but may slow decisions, generate conflict and create information-sharing risks.

The review concludes that no single model can address the changing demands of schools. It recommends a synthetic approach combining managerial structure, transformational inspiration, distributed and participative collaboration, ethical integrity, contingent adaptability and transactional operational practices.

The passage describes methods and apparatus for improving binaural or 3D sound localization in calls, games, virtual or augmented reality, advertising, and device alerts. To address unreliable and computationally intensive near-field head-related transfer functions (HRTFs), sound from a visible or known source may be convolved with far-field HRTFs positioned behind the source or along the listener’s line of sight. The listener then perceives the sound as originating from the source despite the different convolution location. Volume may be adjusted to reflect the source’s apparent distance, and multiple sources may be rendered separately using different HRTF coordinates.

Other embodiments track the listener’s head, gaze, face, and orientation to update sound localization as devices or images move. Portable devices may also switch between externally localized binaural sound and mono or stereo sound when sensors detect device rotation, movement, blocked cameras or sensors, changes in lighting, facial orientation, distance from the device, headphone connection, or low-battery status. These detections can also trigger muting, volume changes, pausing, call control, or adjustment of virtual-auditory-space participation.

This excerpt from the SD Memory Card Physical Layer Simplified Specification Version 6.00 defines "shall/will" as mandatory, "should" as recommended, and "may" as optional. It covers card characteristics, bus operation, and command behavior.

**Card characteristics:** Capacities are SDSC (up to 2 GB), SDHC (over 2 GB to 32 GB), and SDXC (over 32 GB to 2 TB); hosts able to access larger cards must also access smaller ones. Operating voltage is 2.7–3.6 V, with UHS-II adding VDD2 at 1.70–1.95 V. Read/write cards (Flash, OTP, MTP) are sold blank, while ROM cards contain fixed data. Speed Classes 0, 2, 4, 6, and 10 define minimum performance. Form factors are standard-size SD, miniSD, and microSD (standard card: 24 × 32 × 2.1 mm or 1.4 mm). Features include a switch function, memory field error correction, safe card removal during reads, content protection, password protection (CMD42), and mechanical plus built-in write protection.

**Bus and protocol:** Command, response, and data tokens use start/stop bits and CRC (7-bit for commands/responses, 16-bit CCITT for block data); MSB is transmitted first and wide-bus transfers use four data lines with per-line CRC. Single and multiple block transfers are defined, with multiple block preferred for faster writes and busy signaled on DAT0. Cards are addressed by a session address (RCA) assigned during initialization. Registers include CID, RCA, DSR, CSD, SCR, SSR, and Card Status. ROM cards treat CMD24, 25, 27, 28, 29, 30, 32, 33, and 38 as illegal, may optionally support CMD42 and security commands, and have no write-protect switch.

**UHS-I:** Provides up to 104 MB/s on a 4-bit bus with modes DS, HS, SDR104, and DDR50 using 1.8 V signaling; it does not apply to SDSC but applies to SDHC/SDXC, with DDR50 mandatory for microSD. CMD0 selects SD or SPI mode; 1.8 V signaling is available only in SD mode and is not reverted by CMD0 (power cycle resets to 3.3 V). ACMD41 with S18R requests a voltage switch, CMD11 performs it, and CMD19 tuning (40 executions within 150 ms) is mandatory for SDR-VD hosts and optional for SDR-FD hosts. CMD6 function groups select bus speed mode, driver strength, and current limit.

**UHS-II:** SD bus modes are DS, HS, optional SDR104, and optional DDR50; UHS-II interface modes are FD156 (156 MB/s), optional HD312 (312 MB/s), FD312, and FD624 (624 MB/s); HD312 cannot be used in ring topology. Supported hosts provide both legacy SD and UHS-II interfaces, with removable slots connected to both. Initialization steps are PHY, device, enumeration, configuration, and SD-TRAN; CMD0 restarts SD-TRAN initialization, and the card must disable the UHS-II interface before ACMD41 completes. FD624 was newly introduced in Version 6.00 (UHS-III): UHS-II cards support Range A and B, UHS-III cards Range A to D. Other features include Application Performance Class (500 write/1500 read IOPS, or 2000/4000 with command queue and cache; 10 MB/s sustained write), cache (data loss possible if not flushed), self maintenance, command queue modes, and a low voltage interface.

**Initialization and data transfer:** The host is master, sending broadcast and addressed commands in card identification and data transfer modes. CMD0 is software reset; CMD8 verifies operating voltage and is mandatory before the first ACMD41 for SDHC/SDXC; CMD55 must precede ACMD41, which carries the voltage window, HCS, XPC, and S18R; initialization must complete within one second; CMD2 retrieves CID and CMD3 assigns RCA. In data transfer mode, CMD9 reads CSD, CMD4 (SET_DSR) switches the clock from fOD to fPP, and CMD7 selects one card. Transfers can be aborted with CMD12; write buffering permits pipelined writes with busy on DAT0, while no buffering exists for CSD writes, write protection, or erase; parameter-set and read commands are disallowed during programming; CMD0 or CMD15 terminates pending programming. Block reads use CMD17/CMD18 with a 512-byte maximum block and CMD16 up to 512 bytes; misaligned or partial blocks set ADDRESS_ERROR. Writes use CMD24/CMD25 with per-block CRC checks, set WP_VIOLATION on protected areas, and can be polled with CMD13; interleaving across cards is possible.

**Erase:** The CMD32/CMD33/CMD38 sequence is required; out-of-sequence commands set ERASE_SEQ_ERROR or ERASE_RESET, and protected sectors are skipped with WP_ERASE_SKIP. DISCARD (argument 00000001h) and FULE (00000002h) apply only to SDHC/SDXC and not via SPI, with busy timeouts of 250 ms and 1 second respectively; FULE logically erases the entire user area. ACMD23 pre-erase speeds multiple block writes, and ACMD22 returns the number of well-written blocks.

**Write protection and security:** Three methods exist — mechanical switch, internal write protection, and password protection. CMD42 uses 128-bit PWD/PWD_LEN registers, with optional FEP/FEP_LEN registers for Card Ownership Protection (COP). COP defines COP Unlock (CMD42[1Fh]), Force Erase, FEP Force Erase, and Reset PWD inhibit; COP cards begin in CMD42 Ver.1.0 compatible mode and enter Ver.2.0 mode after COP Unlock. Setting FEP disables Force Erase and CLR_PWD, and errors set LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED.

Sputtered RuO₂ thin films were investigated to determine whether exchange bias in incoherent TiO₂/RuO₂/Fe/Ru heterostructures reflects intrinsic antiferromagnetic or altermagnetic order in RuO₂. SQUID magnetometry, polarized neutron diffraction and reflectometry, atom-probe tomography, HRTEM/FFT, and EELS showed no detectable compensated RuO₂ sublattice moments, with an upper limit of 0.01 μB per Ru atom. Forbidden diffraction peaks were attributed to multiple scattering from TiO₂.

Exchange bias appeared below about 50 K and depended on field-cooling history. Neutron reflectometry identified chemically intermixed, magnetically active interfacial layers containing uncompensated, in-plane canted moments whose orientations varied with magnetic history and pinned the Fe layer. Chemical and structural analyses found reduced Ru, Fe oxidation extending into RuO₂, and an iron-oxide reaction layer with detectable magnetite (Fe₃O₄). RuO₂/Ni heterostructures showed no exchange bias, while Fe/Ru bilayers without RuO₂ exhibited weaker bias, supporting an interfacial Fe-oxidation mechanism rather than intrinsic RuO₂ magnetism. Thus, exchange bias and related magnetotransport in RuO₂/Fe heterostructures alone do not establish antiferromagnetism or altermagnetism in RuO₂, although the results do not exclude altermagnetism under other conditions.

The lecture extends projection and Fourier-series ideas from finite dimensions to infinite-dimensional inner-product spaces. For an orthonormal sequence, successive projections produce partial sums converging to the vector’s projection onto the closed span. The residual is orthogonal to every vector in the expansion. Truncated and sinc-weighted sinusoids span \(L^2\), so an arbitrary \(L^2\) function’s Fourier-series residual vanishes in the \(L^2\) sense. The inner products remain finite for arbitrary \(L^2\) expansion functions by Schwarz’s inequality.

Prolate spheroidal functions provide an orthonormal expansion optimized for simultaneous time and frequency concentration. The zero-order function maximizes the fraction of energy retained within specified time and frequency intervals; for large intervals, roughly \(2wt\) functions concentrate nearly all their energy in the band, while later functions contain little band energy.

The lecture then turns to communication systems organized in layers: a source is converted to binary data, a digital encoder converts bits to symbols, and modulation maps symbols to signals and waveforms for transmission. This layering avoids constructing a separate device for every source-channel pairing. Grouping \(b\) bits per symbol requires an alphabet of size \(2^b\), so alphabet size grows exponentially as transmission rates increase, corresponding to the logarithm appearing in Shannon’s capacity formula.

Symbols are distinguished from numerical signal constellations, and modulation is defined as converting symbol sequences into waveforms. A basic example maps binary digits to \(+1\) and \(-1\), then uses sinc pulses. Although sinc filtering introduces impractical delay and is noncausal, communication systems commonly separate delay and attenuation through timing recovery and link-budget analysis. Attenuation can be handled separately because amplification scales signal and noise together, leaving signal-to-noise ratio as the relevant quantity. Decibels provide a convenient logarithmic measure for combined link losses.

Pulse-amplitude modulation generalizes the binary example by using an arbitrary pulse response and a one-dimensional real signal constellation. Standard PAM constellations use equally spaced points centered at zero; for \(m=2^b\) equiprobable signals with spacing \(d\), their mean-square energy is \(d^2(m^2-1)/12\). Increasing the number of bits represented by each signal therefore raises energy requirements rapidly. Under additive, signal-independent noise, all constellation points are affected equally, making their separation the primary concern.

For PAM transmission and reception, the transmit filter \(p(t)\) and receive filter \(q(t)\) act together through their composite convolution \(g(t)\). A linear receiver samples the received waveform without intersymbol interference exactly when \(g\) is an ideal Nyquist waveform: \(g(0)=1\) and \(g(kT)=0\) for every nonzero integer \(k\). A sinc pulse satisfies this condition but decays slowly and causes excessive delay. Maintaining the strict bandwidth limit \(1/(2T)\) forces the sinc solution; improving delay requires some excess bandwidth. Nyquist’s band-edge-symmetry criterion characterizes the allowed filters. Raised-cosine filters provide a practical compromise, with a controllable excess-bandwidth rolloff commonly chosen near 15%, yielding faster time-domain decay than the sinc waveform.

The paper develops a probabilistic computational model of conversational implicature comprehension based on relevance theory and implements it in ProbLog. It distinguishes explicatures—developed logical forms that resolve references and yield truth conditions—from implicatures, which are contextual premises and conclusions not obtained through further logical-form development. In the coffee example, “Coffee is an energizing drink” and “Mary does not want coffee at 6 pm” are implicatures, while the temporally and referentially resolved statement about not drinking energizing drinks is the explicature.

Drawing on Grice and Sperber and Wilson, the paper treats communication as ostension and comprehension as intention attribution. Manifestness depends on both epistemic strength and accessibility, while relevance concerns the cognitive effects produced relative to processing effort. Overtly intentional communication conveys a presumption of optimal relevance. The proposed comprehension heuristic accesses the most accessible interpretive hypothesis, checks whether it produces the expected cognitive effects, and accepts it if it satisfies relevance expectations; otherwise, it considers less accessible alternatives or abandons the search. This process yields a continuum between strongly and weakly communicated implicatures.

The model treats the relevance heuristic as cognitively given while modeling the conversational exchange probabilistically. Candidate interpretive hypotheses are manually constructed and ordered by accessibility. It represents parallel bottom-up and top-down adjustment among explicatures, contextual assumptions, and implicatures. Encyclopedic knowledge is encoded as probabilistic graphs, rules connect words to concepts, and a Bayesian network links the utterance, conceptual adjustment, explicature, contextual premise, and implicature. Relevance expectations are evaluated through ProbLog queries about expected cognitive effects.

Utterance utility is represented indirectly by the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the audience’s prior and posterior probability distributions over relevant propositions. Five interpretive hypotheses illustrate the evaluation: one fails relevance expectations, another adds unnecessary knowledge and lowers aggregate divergence, and another has the same divergence as the preferred hypothesis but a larger Herbrand base and thus greater processing cost. An additional relevant knowledge graph can produce a higher divergence and a more relevant interpretation. The resulting optimization procedure eliminates hypotheses that fail relevance expectations, uses the smaller Herbrand base to resolve equal-divergence cases, and selects the remaining hypothesis with the highest divergence.

The model focuses on audience comprehension, requires experimenters to construct candidate hypotheses, and leaves the speaker’s perspective, higher-level explicature recognition, modal meanings, and metarepresentational uses for future research.

Strange Brigade, a 1–4 player cooperative shooter, launches August 28 on PS4, Xbox One, and PC. Rebellion’s pre-orders include the Secret Service Weapons Pack with a pistol, submachine gun, and rifle. A Deluxe Edition adds a season pass featuring campaign missions, characters, weapons, and items. Set in the 1930s British Empire, the game has players explore ancient locations, battle mythological enemies, and overcome traps and puzzles.

BioSafe Systems appointed Carleton Birk as Operations Manager at its East Hartford, Connecticut headquarters, and Tenaya Becker, Ester Mastronardi, Patrick Clark, and Kyle Pickles as Technical Sales Representatives in Southern California, Canada, Eastern Pennsylvania, and Central California, respectively. The hires bring experience in operations, horticulture, agricultural sales, agronomy, and technical support.

Georgia Tech researchers developed a simulated ransomware attack that took control of a water-treatment plant, shut valves, altered chlorine levels, and displayed false readings. The demonstration highlighted weaknesses in industrial control systems, although no real ransomware attacks on their process-control components have been reported. Researchers recommended stronger passwords, restricted connections, and intrusion monitoring.

The coach said his team’s convincing win improved momentum and confidence but did not change its position, as the series remains 2–0 against its opponent. He praised the power play’s improved puck movement, the penalty kill’s shot-blocking and sacrifice, and goalie Tim Thomas’s adjustment, which helped keep Tampa Bay outside. He emphasized that the team must improve puck management, forechecking, neutral-zone decisions, turnover avoidance, and physical play while maintaining emotional composure. He rejected unsportsmanlike conduct after the win and urged players to live by his standards.

The coach expressed concern for hospitalized teammate Horty, who was injured by a blindside hit that he believes should be reviewed by the league. He said roster and line adjustments may be needed. Despite the loss of a player and the opponent’s aggressive forechecking and counterattacks, he believes the fourth line can match the opposition and that the team has enough time to recover. He expects a tough Game 3 at home, wants a strong start and fan support, and said the team will remain balanced as it attempts to turn the series around.

Mary Meeker’s report said global internet growth slowed to 7%, with 3.6 billion users. E-commerce rose to 13% of retail sales, and Amazon Echo reached 30 million homes. Netflix led subscriptions with 117 million subscribers, ahead of Amazon Prime and Spotify. Uber averaged $21 hourly; unemployment was 3.9%, with seven million job openings.

This July 2001 compilation of news clippings (compiled by Ann Schmidt for Jeff Dasovich) covers energy-sector developments in California, India, Brazil, and Argentina:

**California power crisis and Gov. Gray Davis.** A Cato Institute article by Jerry Taylor and Peter VanDoren ("The Suits Tell the Tale") argues that lawsuits show Davis's price-gouging claims against Houston firms are undercut: publicly owned utilities averaged $344/MW in the first quarter versus under $250/MW for private companies, with Enron, Reliant and Dynegy charging less than the L.A. Department of Water & Power ($292/MW), Sacramento Municipal Utility District ($330/MW), and the market average. State agents allegedly named prices with no negotiation, and high natural gas costs drove most asking prices. Separately, a Dow Jones Energy Service report describes the California Senate Select Committee's market-manipulation investigation, which subpoenaed trading documents from Duke, Mirant, Dynegy, Williams, AES, NRG, Enron and Reliant; Enron and Reliant have not complied and were cited for contempt, Enron sued California in federal court, and Morgan Stanley was criticized over document disposal. The committee's use of closed-door witness depositions is unprecedented; Enron calls the probe a witch hunt and objects to the exclusion of LADWP and Calpine.

**Company earnings.** Reliant Energy reported second-quarter net income up 22% to $273.7 million ($11.97 billion revenue, more than double a year earlier), citing wholesale-energy earnings of $205 million, but it is owed $318 million from California wholesale buyers, its gas-distribution loss widened to $49 million, and European results fell; it reiterated 10%–12% 2001 earnings growth. Peoples Energy's fiscal third-quarter profit rose 6.6% to $11.6 million ($318.5 million revenue), helped by more than tripled equity-investment income from the Enovate joint venture with Enron and by South Texas oil-and-gas acquisitions, offset by warm weather hurting gas distribution.

**Enron's Dabhol project in India.** Enron wants the Indian government to buy out its 65% stake in Dabhol Power, seeking other remedies if terms are unacceptable. A seven-month dispute with the Maharashtra State Electricity Board over $64 million in unpaid bills led the board to stop buying power in May and Dabhol to halt production and give notice to end the contract. Four Indian states offered to buy power at roughly Rs 1.65–3.00 per unit versus Rs 7.0 under the Maharashtra contract; Dabhol rejected these as "unrealistic and unattainable," and a Godbole committee meeting made little progress. Analysts see the dispute, India's largest foreign direct investment, as a test of the country's ability to attract investment; U.S. official Christa Rocca said the climate problem could be summed up in one word, "Enron." Enron shares fell 74 cents to $46.10.

**Energy investment.** An Associated Press report notes that power deregulation and the California crisis have drawn venture capital into "energy technology" — software, microturbines, flywheels, Web-based trading — though funding tightened (77 companies raised $1.2 billion last year versus 17 raising $132 million this year). Enron invested $90 million in 12 strategic partners; Capstone Turbine's shares fell from as high as $100 to under $20 without a profit.

**Brazil.** Energy czar Pedro Parente said GDP would grow 2.7% in 2001 and 3.6% in 2002, supported by mandatory demand cuts (20% residential, 20–25% industrial, 20% commercial), penalties and rebates, and a "transfer of rights" trading scheme; 93% of Brazilian power is hydro, and Southeast Brazil demand fell about 27% from May to July. Brazil plans 6,523 MW of thermal and 7,783 MW of new hydro through 2003, spending about 30 billion reais. The real has lost over a fifth of its value this year.

**Markets and Argentina.** On CNNfn's "Talking Stocks," Argus Research's John Eade called the market volatile but possibly at "tentative wavering steps of a baby bull market," rated Tellabs fine long term, and called Enron a long-term buy despite a weak chart, citing strength in energy generation and trading. In Buenos Aires, Governor Carlos Ruckauf ordered $500 million of "patacones" printed to pay part of workers' wages at one peso each with 7% interest upon redemption in a year, beginning circulation August 3; utilities and supermarkets have been hesitant to accept them, economists fear erosion of the peso's dollar peg, and Argentina must curb spending to avoid defaulting on $153 billion in debt.

The Sansa c200 manual covers connecting the player to a computer via USB and transferring, converting, deleting, and synchronizing files. It identifies MTP and MSC modes, explains media-folder placement, and lists supported audio and photo formats. Sansa Media Converter can import and convert supported media.

Instructions are provided for powering the device, navigating menus, playing music, voice recordings, and FM radio, using repeat, shuffle, equalizer, and GoList settings, viewing photos, running slideshows, saving and scanning radio presets, recording broadcasts and voice recordings, and adjusting display, power, and connection settings. Files can be safely removed using the appropriate operating-system icon.

The FAQ addresses copying files, unsupported formats, podcasts, missing ID3 information, firmware updates, and playback rights. It also provides technical-support contact information. The manual includes a one-year limited warranty, Microsoft WM-DRM notices, a SanDisk software license agreement, and instructions for proper electronic-device disposal.

During a southern Korean rebellion, the government requested Chinese aid, and 2,000 troops were sent to Asan, but Korean forces captured the rebel leaders and retook Chon-ju before the Chinese actively fought. Japan then landed marines and soldiers at Chemulpo and Seoul, citing protection of Japanese subjects and the legation. After 3,000 more Japanese troops arrived, they encamped with batteries near the foreign settlement, prompting a joint diplomatic protest.

Chinese and Japanese troops refused to withdraw first, while the Korean king urged China to leave and China conditioned its departure on Japanese withdrawal. Korean and Chinese residents feared widespread violence, and further troop movements risked bloodshed. Admiral Skerrett arrived aboard the Baltimore and promised to remain amid the tensions. The U.S. minister was instructed to preserve peaceful conditions and reported that simultaneous withdrawal was China’s preference, Japan was resistant, and Korea’s integrity was threatened.

This medRxiv preprint by Craig MacFadyen, Ajay Duraiswamy and David Harris-Birtill (University of St Andrews) presents a deep neural network classifier for medical image modality at hyper-scale. The authors combined 102 open-access datasets, chiefly from The Cancer Imaging Archive, plus Stanford ML Group and Kaggle, to classify images by modality (CT, MRI, PET and X-ray; ultrasound was excluded for lack of data). After capping large datasets to correct class imbalance, the corpus held 6,433,838 images, split at the dataset level into train (4,104,184), validate (1,393,307) and test (936,347) sets to prevent data leakage and ensure even modality and location coverage. Three-dimensional scans were treated as 2D slices, resized to 224×224 and min-max normalised.

ResNet-18, ResNet-50 and VGG16 (single grayscale input channel) were trained for 10 epochs with batch size 128 using stochastic gradient descent (learning rate 0.1 divided by 10 on plateau, momentum 0.9, L2 weight decay 0.005) on a Xeon CPU with two GTX 1080Ti GPUs; code is on GitHub under an MIT licence, and ethics approval was granted (UTREC CS15171). Test-set results were ResNet-18 96.00% accuracy / 86.17% balanced accuracy, ResNet-50 95.60% / 85.65%, and VGG16 94.58% / 81.08%. Small train-validation gaps indicated little overfitting. Performance was very high for CT, MR and PET but lower for X-rays, notably 28% on MURA and 62% on the Osteoarthritis Initiative, attributed to training data being dominated by chest X-rays. The authors conclude such classifiers suit image repositories and national healthcare institutions, with future work extending to 3D scan modalities.

The DAX (Deutscher Aktienindex) is Germany’s main equity index and one of the world’s most popular trading vehicles. The DAX 40, formerly the DAX 30, contains the 40 largest or most liquid blue-chip stocks listed on Deutsche Börse Xetra. Its high liquidity, distinct trading hours, and movements that differ from US equities offer diversification, and mean-reversion, breakout, gap, and momentum strategies can perform well on it.

DAX can be traded through futures, CFDs, or ETFs. Futures are the most popular and liquid option. Three contracts are available: the original contract has a €25 multiplier, the Mini €5, and the Micro €1, with a minimum price fluctuation of 0.5 points. They are traded electronically on Eurex from 07:50 to 22:00 CET, expire quarterly, and settle in cash. Futures require margin and expose traders to leverage, margin calls, and possible liquidation. CFDs are also derivatives, while ETFs are mainly intended for investment; the US-listed EWG tracks a broader German market and trades during US hours.

Two overnight DAX futures strategies enter at 17:30 CET and exit at 09:00 the following day. The November 2021 strategy’s unleveraged backtest produced 209 trades from 2000 onward, a 65% win rate, 2 profit factor, 5.1% maximum drawdown, and 0.22% average gain per trade. A November 2022 strategy recorded 303 trades with an average gain of 0.23%. Both use rules and settings that differ from S&P 500 futures and have lower-than-expected correlation with them.

The passage develops “educational pacifism,” the view that educational practices are unjust when they harm students and treat them merely as means to educational or social goals. Mass formal schooling is presented as causing significant, often normalized harm, though not necessarily in every case or at all times. Personal harms include bullying, violence, humiliation, and exclusion. More pervasive systemic harms are divided into structural, objective, and symbolic forms: coercive hierarchies and restrictive practices, preparation for subordinate roles in an unequal capitalist economy, and normalized subordination reinforced through curricula, testing, ranking, surveillance, and disciplinary methods. These practices can undermine motivation, confidence, engagement, privacy, critical and creative thinking, autonomy, and well-being.

Using a Kantian framework, the passage argues that students are generally innocent targets of harm whether or not they are regarded as persons. Harmful coercion goes beyond legitimate guidance because it damages important interests and treats students as means rather than ends. Because peaceful educational alternatives exist, mass formal schooling cannot be considered a last resort.

Montessori’s philosophy is presented as broadly aligned with educational pacifism, despite differing terminology. Montessori regarded education as central to positive, lasting peace and emphasized freedom, harmonious activity, dignity, and agency. She criticized mass schooling for domination, obedience, competition, arbitrary discipline, rewards and punishments, and preparation for industrial and subordinate life. Contemporary Montessori practice should likewise reject coercive and paternalistic practices while retaining helpful guidance and structure. The passage also warns that testing, rigid scheduling, hierarchy, segregation, and weak implementation can compromise Montessori’s nonharmful and peace-oriented aims, urging Montessorians to protect student agency and provide a just alternative to mass formal schooling.

The Yankees and Blue Jays, tied for the best American League record, meet in a best-of-five ALDS as the No. 4 and No. 1 seeds, respectively. Toronto won their 13-game season series 8–5. The 2025 series begins Oct. 4, with Games 1, 2 and 5 in Toronto and Games 3 and 4 in the Bronx. Game 1 airs on Fox, Game 2 on FS1, and Games 3–5 have TBD broadcasts.

MIT 6.832 lecturer Russ Tedrake introduces underactuated robotics, assuming comfort with differential equations, linear algebra, and MATLAB, but not prior robotics coursework. He argues that robots should exploit their natural dynamics rather than override them with conservative, high-gain feedback. ASIMO’s rigid, energy-intensive gait and conventional aircraft’s restricted flight regimes contrast with passive dynamic walkers and birds that use gravity, unsteadiness, pressure drag, and other natural dynamics for efficient, agile motion. Examples involving albatrosses, falcons, bats, trout, and robotic birds further illustrate these principles.

Tedrake defines underactuated systems using second-order manipulator dynamics of the form \(\ddot q=F_1+F_2u\). A system is fully actuated when \(F_2\) has full rank, allowing controls to generate arbitrary accelerations and enabling feedback linearization; it is underactuated when \(F_2\) has insufficient rank, so inputs cannot accelerate every direction. This status can depend on the system’s state. Factory manipulators are commonly treated as fully actuated, while walking, jumping, flying, and some manipulation problems are underactuated. He notes that practical feedback linearization is also constrained by torque limits.

The lecture derives the kinematics, kinetic and potential energy, and Lagrangian equations for a two-link arm, then presents the standard manipulator form \(H\ddot q+C\dot q+G=Bu\), including the symmetric positive-definite inertial matrix \(H\). Removing the shoulder motor creates an underactuated acrobot that must swing up by managing and pumping energy, illustrating a more difficult control problem. The two-link arm also resembles a compass-gait walking robot, where the connection to the ground cannot directly exert torque. Similarly, an airborne humanoid cannot change its center-of-mass trajectory through internal joint motion.

The course will progress from pendulums, cart-pole systems, and acrobots to walking robots, impacts, limit cycles, higher-dimensional systems, uncertainty, stochasticity, and unknown models. Its computational approach will cover analytical and numerical optimal control, dynamic programming, policy search, reinforcement learning, machine learning, approximate methods, and motion planning techniques such as randomized planners.

Nick Mathewson, a Tor paper author and principal developer, explains Tor’s purpose, design, operation, vulnerabilities, and future development. Tor is described as a volunteer-run anonymity network with roughly 6,000 relays, hundreds of thousands to millions of users, and substantial traffic volume. Its users include citizens seeking privacy, researchers avoiding location-based bias, companies protecting sensitive information, law enforcement conducting covert investigations, and people avoiding harassment or unwanted public records. Tor is also used for criminal activity, which Mathewson acknowledges but considers an unavoidable consequence of broadly usable security technology.

The lecture distinguishes anonymity from unobservability and unlinkability. Anonymity means an observer cannot identify a particular person as the source of an action, whether categorically, probabilistically, or across multiple actions. Unobservability hides whether an action occurred at all, while unlinkability prevents an observer from associating a person with a particular online profile. Mathewson argues that anonymity requires a large user population because its security depends on users blending into a crowd.

Tor is presented as a circuit-based onion-routing system designed for usable, low-latency web browsing. Clients establish encrypted, multi-hop circuits, negotiate symmetric session keys, and layer messages so each relay removes only one layer of encryption. Integrity checking is necessary to prevent tampering from revealing circuit membership. Tor relays TCP stream contents rather than raw IP packets, avoiding differences among operating-system TCP implementations and allowing end-to-end application encryption. Its practical anonymity guarantees are generally probabilistic rather than absolute. Node discovery uses multiple trusted authorities that vote on and sign a consensus directory, allowing clients to reject unauthorized or misbehaving relays.

The lecture reviews abuse concerns, including file sharing, criminal activity, seizures of operator computers, and IP-based blocking by websites. Exit policies restrict the ports relays will serve, while proposed alternatives include anonymous accounts and revocable blacklisting credentials. Tor cannot protect operators from poor operational security or misuse of their identities.

Hidden services allow a responder to publish a public key without revealing its location. Clients locate introduction points through a distributed directory, establish an introduction cell, and connect through rendezvous circuits. Existing designs face enumeration and censorship risks, while a proposed key-blinding approach would derive temporary signing keys from a long-term key to make service enumeration harder.

Major attacks include malicious or insecure applications, traffic tagging by collaborating relays, denial-of-service attacks, and cryptographic implementation errors. Defenses include end-to-end encryption, circuit-failure detection, relay capacity requirements, and more secure cryptographic primitives. For censorship resistance, Tor uses bridges and pluggable transport programs that transform traffic so it resembles other protocols and can be updated as blocking methods change.

Future work includes revamping hidden services and cryptography, improving path selection, padding and traffic-analysis defenses, congestion control, scaling beyond tens of thousands of relays, and potentially replacing centralized directory authorities. Mathewson also points researchers toward related systems such as I2P, Gnunet, Mixmaster, Mixminion, DC-nets, and academic anonymity research.

After months of DOGE-driven cuts to the U.S. Education Department, researchers express cautious optimism that federal education research may be rebuilt. The department plans to reinstate 20 terminated research contracts, is seeking public input on modernizing the Institute of Education Sciences, and appointed Amber Northern for a six-month advisory assignment. The National Center for Education Statistics is updating surveys and hiring for NAEP work, while 10 regional education labs are expected to restart.

Concerns remain. Severe staff shortages—NCES reportedly fell from about 100 employees to three—could undermine data quality, while reduced NAEP staffing, reporting and infrastructure raise questions about the assessment’s future. A new mandate to collect extensive admissions data also adds pressure. Researchers cited uncertainty in federal funding, staffing and data access despite the administration’s commitment to maintaining a national education research entity.

Cement and realty stocks rose 2%–5% on the BSE after Modi announced housing incentives, despite the Sensex falling 0.39% to 26,523. Table data shows declines from Nov. 8 to Dec. 26, followed by gains on Dec. 30.

The speaker credits an early power-play goal and Donovan’s second goal with building momentum and confidence, praising Khabibulin, Saprykin, and the team’s unsung-hero traditions. He describes Donovan as increasingly vocal but primarily a leader on the ice, and considers Jarome a natural leader despite not wearing the captain’s “C.” Facing St. Louis, he stresses limiting time and space, finishing checks, and using his body against skilled forwards. He praises goalie Kipper’s consistency and resilience after allowing six goals, and notes wins over Colorado after the All-Star break as evidence the team could defeat elite opponents. Tactically, he recommends moving the puck through the middle or high off the glass and having defensemen skate out more to create odd-man rushes. Overall, he credits coach Darryl with accountability, motivation, and playoff preparation, while emphasizing collective success, strong young players, quiet veteran leadership, and effective acquisitions.

Penalty-kick saving is among a goalkeeper’s most difficult tasks. Studies cited indicate that roughly 80% of penalties are scored, about 5% miss the goal, and the overall chance of a save is generally below 15%. Law 14 of the IFAB Laws of the Game governs the restart, requiring the ball to be stationary on the 12-yard penalty mark, the goalkeeper to face the kicker while keeping at least one foot on, behind, or in line with the goal-line, and other players to remain behind the mark, outside the penalty area, and at least 10 yards away. Goalkeepers may not unfairly distract or delay the kicker. Violations can result in a goal, a retaken kick, a warning for a first offense, and a caution for later offenses.

Coaches should select and specially train a capable goalkeeper through regular practice and dedicated one-on-one sessions. They should openly support the goalkeeper, reject teammate blame for missed saves, provide encouragement, and avoid giving instructions during a penalty. Training should combine psychological, mental, physical, and technical preparation. Psychological qualities include determination to stop the kick, fearlessness and concentration, and the ability to reset immediately after the attempt. Mental techniques include visualization, positive self-talk, consistent pre-kick routines, controlled breathing, and staying present. Physical preparation requires fitness, agility, proper clothing, gloves and landing pads, and specialized reaction, footwork, jumping, and diving work.

The recommended approach is generally to “read and react” rather than guess. Goalkeepers should study teammates and opponents through observation, video, notes, and live games, looking for reliable cues such as ball placement, approach angle, run-up, plant-foot direction, hip orientation, body lean, chin direction, dominant leg, and kneecap position. Research should be used to identify a small number of dependable cues rather than attempt to track every possible signal. At the highest levels, coaches and goalkeepers may also decide whether guessing is preferable to reacting.

During the kick, the goalkeeper should establish a calm routine, remain focused on the ball, and adopt a balanced ready position with knees bent and weight on the balls of the feet. Legal distraction methods may be used, but they must not obscure cues or breach the Law. The goalkeeper should generally stay on the line until the ball is struck, resist diving at a fake, read the kicker’s cues, and then react quickly. Low dives should move outward and close to the ground while cutting down the angle. Both hands should be used to secure the ball when possible; otherwise, it should be pushed away, ideally outside the post to produce a corner rather than a rebound.

After the kick, the ball is live, and the goalkeeper must be prepared for an immediate rebound. A save should lead to rapid distribution or a fast break, not celebration. Teammates must avoid mobbing the goalkeeper, defenders must cover rebounds, and an outlet should be available. If a goal is scored, the goalkeeper should retrieve the ball without emotion; if the kick misses or is deflected away, the defense must promptly reset for the resulting restart. Advanced goalkeepers should also maintain current records of opponents’ penalty tendencies, while recognizing that kickers may deliberately alter patterns when they know they are being studied.

Metagenomic binning clusters fragmented DNA reads by their likely genome of origin, supporting functional annotation, phylogenetic profiling, and strain-level analysis. Conventional k-mer and large language model approaches produce deterministic embeddings that map each fragment to one point, making shared or ambiguously represented sequences difficult to separate, especially when different genomes have similar k-mer profiles. The paper proposes UNCERTAINGEN, a scalable framework that maps each DNA sequence to a probability distribution in embedding space, capturing uncertainty from inter-species DNA sharing and ambiguous representations. It uses contrastive learning so non-Euclidean distances emerge naturally, yielding closed-form expected pairwise likelihoods for efficient optimization. Theoretical results address embedding distinguishability, covariance, and model capacity, while reported experiments on real metagenomic datasets show improvements over deterministic k-mer and LLM-based embeddings. The approach builds on lightweight k-mer-based contrastive methods and is presented as the first probabilistic sequence-embedding framework for metagenomic binning.

Jeff Davis Parish opened schools Friday after summer preparations emphasizing streamlined operations, campus readiness, teacher commitment, bus-driver training and curriculum planning tailored to students’ needs. Its on-time graduation rate rose three points to 92.5%, ranking fourth-best in the state.

A 2023 scoping review examined barriers and facilitators to belonging in graduate health professions education and implications for occupational therapy education. Belonging was treated separately from inclusion: belonging is an individual’s feeling of acceptance, fit, and connection, whereas inclusion concerns organizational behaviors and culture. The review found that belonging is associated with academic engagement, mental health, self-concept, and reduced emotional distress, with potentially greater effects on students from historically minoritized identities.

Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidance, researchers searched multiple databases and journals. Of 202 identified records, 70 remained after title-and-abstract screening and duplicate removal; 61 were excluded after full-text review, leaving nine articles covering occupational therapy, physical therapy, and medical education. Qualitative analysis identified three themes affecting belonging: environment, relationships, and personal factors.

Environmental influences included physical-space accessibility, décor, imagery, and signage, as well as institutional values, policies, practices, and broader culture. Relationships included faculty-to-student mentoring and peer-to-student connections. Supportive, identity-congruent faculty relationships and peer groups facilitated belonging, while bias, microaggressions, and exclusion were barriers, especially for historically minoritized students. Personal factors included students’ perceptions of their belonging, academic ability, and how their identities were received. Prior identity-related experiences, stereotypes, shame, fear, and anxiety could undermine confidence and reinforce self-fulfilling expectations of not belonging.

The authors recommended that occupational therapy programs evaluate and make educational spaces representative and accessible, review inclusive teaching practices, revise policies that may disaffirm students, strengthen mentoring and peer relationships, train students and faculty to address bias and microaggressions, support affinity groups and research opportunities, and connect students with relevant community resources. They called for longitudinal research specifically in occupational therapy education and an overarching educational theory of belonging. Limitations included the possibility of missed articles, researcher bias, no evaluation of evidence quality, and the subjectivity of belonging.

The Supreme Court denied review in several cases, including Alex Jones’s appeal of a Connecticut defamation and emotional-distress judgment for families of children killed at Sandy Hook Elementary School. It also declined to hear a Colorado parents’ challenge to school district policies concerning discussions of students’ gender identity and constitutional rights. Justice Samuel Alito, joined by Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, said he remained concerned about whether school districts may assist students’ gender transitions without parental knowledge or consent.

The court also declined review of a Section 230 challenge by a plaintiff who alleged that Grindr exposed him to adult sexual predators when he was 15, as well as a death sentence challenged over juror misconduct. This study evaluated a world-model reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous mechanical thrombectomy (MT) navigation. Five MT navigation tasks were defined and tested in a clinically based SOFA/stEVE simulation using guide catheters and guidewires across 10 patient-specific vascular anatomies. Single-task SAC agents provided replay data for subsequent multi-task training.

TD-MPC2, a model-based reinforcement-learning agent with an LSTM observation embedder, achieved a mean success rate of 65% across tasks and anatomies, compared with 37% for SAC (p < 0.001), and improved the mean path ratio from 47% to 73%. Particularly large gains occurred in A2R, A3L, and A3R, while improvements in A1 and A2L were not significant. TD-MPC2 required more procedure time than SAC, with mean times of 15.2 and 8.2 seconds, respectively. Single-task SAC performed strongly in some tasks, reaching 100% success in A1 and A2R, but generalized less effectively across multiple tasks and anatomies.

The results support world-model-based reinforcement learning for multi-task MT navigation while showing that performance remains suboptimal, particularly on left-sided tasks. Proposed future work includes improving generalization, optimizing the balance between navigation efficiency and exploration, incorporating vessel deformation and contact forces, developing differentiable physics simulators, expanding patient datasets, and transitioning toward in vitro testing.

The bankruptcy court granted summary judgment for Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. and Dynamic Management Company, LLC against SCS General Contractors, Inc. SCS sought equitable liens and damages for construction work at three Mississippi restaurants. It also alleged that Dynamic was Barnhill’s Buffet, Inc.’s alter ego and that lessors were unjustly enriched by its improvements.

The court held that SCS’s claimed equitable lien on Barnhill’s leasehold interests terminated when Barnhill filed for bankruptcy because the debtor in possession was treated as a bona fide purchaser without notice. The leasehold sale proceeds therefore passed to Wells free of SCS’s lien. SCS also could not enforce lease repair or anti-lien provisions because it was neither a party to the leases nor a third-party beneficiary.

As to the lessors’ fee interests, Mississippi law required written owner consent for a lien arising from a tenant’s improvements. Because the landlords provided no such consent, the court found that neither an equitable nor statutory lien attached. Wells was awarded the escrowed funds, while SCS retained its claim as an unsecured creditor in Barnhill’s bankruptcy case.

The court also granted Dynamic’s motion. SCS failed to present credible evidence satisfying Mississippi’s requirements for piercing a corporate veil, including frustration of expectations, disregard of corporate formalities, and fraud or equivalent misfeasance. Dynamic’s affidavit stated that it had no employees, separate finances, ownership, control, or contractual relationship with SCS and did not authorize the work. The invoices and payments showed that Barnhill, not Dynamic, requested and paid for the work. SCS’s contrary affidavit relied on speculative or unauthenticated documents and did not create a genuine dispute.

The court denied SCS’s requested continuance for further discovery and granted the unopposed motion to dismiss Spirit Finance Corporation’s cross-claims. Mississippi law governed the dispute.

Westerners' aversion to insects stems from their unusual movement, constant presence, and concerns about digesting exoskeletons. Yet the UN estimates that two billion people regularly eat insects; at least 1,900 species are edible and nutritious and more ecologically sustainable than other animal proteins. Research on 34 primates found most retain genes for an enzyme that breaks down chitin, while cooking improves digestibility. In 2017, the Seattle Mariners sold more roasted grasshoppers in three games than their restaurant typically sells annually.

The article urges the U.S. Department of Education, as it revisits the Institute of Education Sciences (IES), to protect and strengthen federal education research and development. Drawing on recommendations from a coalition of education organizations, it outlines three priorities: identify urgent state and local research needs through collaborative learning agendas; accelerate high-priority work with faster research tracks, streamlined approvals, and real-time data; and help states and districts implement evidence through improved communication and support. Specific proposals include modernizing federal reporting, restarting Regional Education Laboratories and Comprehensive Centers, using technology and professional networks to reach teachers, requiring practitioner-facing resources for relevant IES-funded studies, and recognizing effective use of research. The goal is a responsive, efficient, effective, and accountable system that turns evidence into scalable improvements for students, educators, and families.

The article outlines eight strategies for overcoming distraction and sustaining focus:

1. Act urgently to turn ideas and dreams into reality, avoiding future regret.
2. Work one or two days weekly in a distraction-free location, using preparation rituals, exercise, and 45-minute focus blocks.
3. Pursue only “heck-yes” opportunities that suit the present; use a trusted advisory board when tempted to overcommit.
4. Eliminate unnecessary diversions and complete one top-priority task at a time.
5. Focus on work that inspires genuine interest and dedication.
6. Create a personalized routine that harnesses stress, protects the first morning hour, works in 90-minute blocks with 25-minute breaks, includes recovery rituals, and prioritizes sleep.
7. Avoid multitasking; schedule each activity separately on a calendar to preserve structure and freedom.
8. Build an organizational culture of “fierce focus” by defining each person’s purpose, setting measurable goals, and rejecting projects that do not contribute to the organization’s core purpose.

The passage sets out a diplomatic offensive. Bulgaria, a weak point in the German line, should be pressed by public recognition of its just national claims and of Serbia's independence and access to the sea; Italy should receive assurances supporting frontier rectification, evacuation of her territory, and her economic needs. For Austria-Hungary, agitation among subject nationalities should be kept alive while repeatedly assuring that no dismemberment of the Empire is intended; its debts to Germany should be referenced but not openly cancelled, and its wish to discuss disarmament accepted while explaining the danger of disarmament faced by an autocratic Germany. Against Germany, failure to democratize should mean exclusion from postwar intercourse, while democratization earns a partnership among all nations in postwar problems, without intent to dictate Germany's form of government. Toward Russia, success lies in stating war aims, promoting a league of nations, and showing the diplomatic offensive is under way. French morale may warrant interest in Alsace-Lorraine. The western Allies should press for economic unity of control, American utterances leading Liberals in Great Britain and France, and a liberal offensive stimulating American pride. Suggested peace terms: Belgium and Northern France evacuated and restored by Germany, Belgium retaining full sovereignty; Luxemburg left to negotiation; Alsace-Lorraine restored, since "the wrong done in 1871 must be undone."

Strength training builds muscle, strength and endurance, but correct technique, appropriate loads, gradual increases in intensity, and proper warm-ups and cool-downs help prevent injury. Warm-ups increase heart rate and blood flow, while dynamic, full-range movements prepare the body for exercise; static exercises are more beneficial after a workout. Recovery also requires rest, hydration, a good diet, and time between sessions.

Common strength-training injuries include rotator cuff tears and tendinopathy, often linked to repetitive overhead movements; hamstring strains caused by sudden powerful movements; herniated discs linked to extreme or repetitive poor movement; and tendonitis caused by minor stress, repetitive motion, or sudden impact. Tennis elbow and golfer’s elbow can result from repetitive wrist and arm movements and may affect non-athletes.

Prevention includes good shoulder-blade posture, regular stretching, warm-ups, and adjusting exercises that cause discomfort. Stop exercising and seek medical advice if pain persists. Treatment may involve rest, gentle exercise, pain medication, physiotherapy, injections, or surgery, depending on severity. A doctor or qualified fitness professional can help diagnose injuries and develop a safe, achievable strength-training programme.

The lecture introduces graph limits as analytic objects representing limits of sequences of graphs, analogous to real numbers completing the rationals. For example, among graphs with edge density \(p\), the minimum possible 4-cycle density is \(p^4\), approached by a sequence of quasirandom graphs rather than attained by one specific graph. A graphon provides a single object representing such limiting behavior.

A graphon is a symmetric measurable function \(W:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\). A finite graph can be represented by a pixelated graphon derived from its adjacency matrix, although vertex relabeling and rearrangement make the informal “blurry picture” interpretation potentially misleading.

For a fixed graph \(H\), the homomorphism density of \(H\) in \(G\) is the fraction of vertex maps \(V(H)\to V(G)\) that preserve edges. This encodes quantities such as triangle counts and proper colorings and becomes asymptotically equivalent to subgraph density for large \(G\). For graphons, the corresponding density is defined by an integral whose factors correspond to the edges of \(H\), preserving agreement with the finite-graph definition.

A sequence converges when its homomorphism densities converge for every fixed graph \(H\). The lecture also introduces the cut norm, cut distance, and measure-preserving transformations, which allow graphons to be optimally rearranged and compared. Edit distance is rejected as an unsuitable measure because two random graphs remain far apart under it despite converging to the same limit.

Three principal results are stated: convergence in homomorphism densities is equivalent to being Cauchy in cut distance; every convergent sequence of graphs or graphons has a graphon limit; and the space of graphons modulo zero cut distance is compact. The compactness result is closely related to Szemerédi’s regularity lemma, which will be used to prove it, while quasirandom graphs correspond to constant graphons.

The passage documents AGESA UEFI integration across SEC, PEI, DXE, and runtime phases, including build organization, platform-specific options, PEIM and DXE responsibilities, initialization routines, host services, and required call-outs. AGESA core files are arranged into libraries and build targets for 16-, 32-, and 64-bit development using MASM, Microsoft Macro Assembler, and Microsoft C/C++ compilers.

Platforms can use distributed binary modules or integrate AGESA source directly. Binary builds route core call-outs through a common host-implemented portal and router. Integration requires platform option files, environment variables identifying the AGESA source and options directories, and UEFI build control files. PEI modules perform early processor initialization, post-reset memory initialization, and reset coordination. The DXE CPU driver performs late initialization, publishes generated tables through a protocol, and the GPU VGA driver controls iGPU resource decoding when installed.

Before many interfaces are called, the host must establish a stack. Supplied x86-64 assembly routines create and later remove the pre-memory Cache-as-RAM stack, initialize processor cores, configure execution caching, create the SEC-to-PEI handoff frame, and transfer execution to the specified return address. AArch64 systems using the PSP do not use these stack and very-early macros because the PSP initializes DRAM.

Published initialization procedures progress from minimal reset processing and execution-cache setup through full processor and power-management configuration, memory initialization, artifact handling, display configuration, and late generation of ACPI, DMI, WHEA, CRAT, CDIT, and related tables. Suspend routines save critical and volatile processor state, while resume routines restore memory, silicon registers, processor state, and PCI control structures before OS handoff.

Helper interfaces allocate and release AGESA structures, obtain DIMM data-eye results, APIC and PCI addresses, the current socket/core identity, memory-device locations for a system address, merge MMIO ranges, and read event-log entries. Required host call-outs allocate and release permanent buffers and initiate cold or warm resets. Many procedures depend on correct preservation of MTRRs, APIC state, cache controls, and memory across initialization and suspend transitions.

The CCAT Collaboration is constructing the six-meter Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST) at 5,600 m in Chile’s Atacama Desert, with observations planned for 2026. FYST will host Mod-Cam, a cryogenic testbed receiver, and Prime-Cam, its primary science instrument, for broadband and spectroscopic observations targeting questions including structure formation during the Epoch of Reionization and cosmological constraints from the Sunyaev–Zel’dovich effect. Mod-Cam contains a 280 GHz camera with more than 10,000 kinetic inductance detectors, while Prime-Cam can accommodate seven modules and approximately 100,000 detectors.

The paper characterizes the flexible stripline circuits used to carry detector signals between cryogenic stages and warm readout electronics. Mod-Cam uses six 46 cm striplines. Prime-Cam’s first harness is planned to use 18 striplines, with reduced copper thickness and increased length between the 4 K and 40 K stages to limit thermal loading. Measurements found a copper residual resistance ratio of approximately 120, consistent with high-purity OFHC copper. Direct thermal-conductivity measurements agreed with theoretical values for comparable copper purity. Thermal-loading estimates indicated that, despite containing three times more striplines, a Prime-Cam harness would have lower estimated loading at 4 K than the Mod-Cam harness.

Warm S21 tests found that the striplines themselves produced inter-channel crosstalk at least 50 dB below transmission. Elevated crosstalk was instead traced to the SMP-to-SMA transition PCBs, with stronger pickup between channels sharing a PCB and between more closely spaced traces. The PCBs were redesigned with an impedance-matched via and buried stripline signal traces between ground planes. Simulations predicted crosstalk no greater than −60 dB for one transition and −57 dB across a full PCB, an improvement of about 20 dB over the original design. The results support stripline as a scalable readout method for large KID arrays and guide Prime-Cam circuit fabrication.

The Inverted Hammer is a single-candle bullish reversal pattern formed near the bottom of a downward price swing or during a pullback in an uptrend. It has a small body at the candle’s lower end, little or no lower shadow, and a long upper shadow at least twice the body’s length. The long upper wick suggests buyers attempted to raise prices but faced selling pressure, potentially signaling growing bullish momentum. Body color is less important than location.

The pattern is most useful near support and when confirmed by trendlines, moving averages, momentum indicators, volume, or oversold conditions. Traders may use it for swing entries at support or for mean-reversion strategies. It should not be used as a standalone signal because results depend on market context, and it is subjective, can produce false signals, and may not suit every timeframe. Unlike the bearish Shooting Star, which appears after a rise and indicates possible rejection, the Inverted Hammer is generally stronger after a decline.

A UC Davis study of 50,921 California firearm deaths from 2000 to 2015 found gun homicide rates declined from 4.19 per 100,000 in 2000 to 3.13 in 2014, with a slight rise in 2015. Researchers attributed the decrease largely to reduced gang violence, especially in Los Angeles County.
